topics.title: Why the casing is split horizontally
topics.body:
In a horizontal split case pump the volute casing is divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, so it consists of an upper and a lower half bolted together along a long, flat joint. It is called axially split because the joint plane contains the shaft axis.

The split suits the between-bearings, double-suction layout. The rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and bearings) runs right through the casing with a bearing at each end, so it cannot be withdrawn axially like the rotor of an overhung end-suction pump. Splitting the casing along the shaft axis lets the complete rotor be lowered into, or lifted out of, the lower half as one assembly.

The split also helps manufacture. The two side suction chambers and the volute are complex shapes, and two halves are easier to cast, core and inspect than one closed casting. Bores that cross the joint are finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together.

The price is a long gasketed joint that must be flat, carefully bolted and able to seal against discharge pressure, plus heavy joint bolting. This is one reason the axially split concept becomes less attractive at very high pressures and temperatures.
keyPoints: The joint plane contains the shaft axis, so the rotor can be lifted out vertically as one unit.
It suits between-bearings rotors, which cannot be withdrawn axially.
Two halves make the complex double-suction passages easier to cast and inspect.
The trade-off is a long joint that must be machined, gasketed and bolted carefully.

topics.title: Why the split casing helps maintenance
topics.body:
In this arrangement both the suction and discharge nozzles are cast on the lower casing half. The lower half therefore stays connected to the piping and bolted to the baseplate, and the motor stays where it is, while the upper half is unbolted and lifted off. This is a feature of this side-suction, side-discharge arrangement rather than of every design; some pumps carry a nozzle on the upper half.

With the upper half removed, the impeller, both wear-ring pairs, the sleeves, seals and bearings can be seen in place. Clearances can be measured directly, the volute, tongue and suction chambers can be checked for erosion, cavitation and deposits, and damage at the two eyes can be compared. For deeper work the seal glands are released, the coupling spacer removed and the bearing housing bolts taken out, after which the complete rotor can be lifted out for bench work or exchanged for a spare rotor.

A typical outline is: isolate and lock out, drain and depressurise, remove the spacer and auxiliary piping, remove the joint nuts in sequence, break the joint with jacking screws, then lift the upper half level on its lugs. Because the pump body and motor are not moved, alignment is largely preserved, but it must still be checked after reassembly.
keyPoints: With both nozzles on the lower half, the main piping stays connected during internal inspection in this arrangement.
Internals are visible in place, so clearances and damage can be assessed directly.
The complete rotor can be lifted out as a unit or exchanged for a spare rotor.
Pump body and motor stay in place, though alignment must still be checked afterwards.
topics.caution: The upper casing lifting lugs are for the upper half only. Every lift needs rated gear, a lifting plan and site permits; follow the OEM manual for the specific dismantling sequence.

topics.title: How the casing joint is sealed
topics.body:
The horizontal joint must seal along its whole length, but it does not see one single pressure. Beside the volute and discharge passage it sees close to discharge pressure; beside the suction chambers it sees suction pressure. A joint that is not tight can therefore leak in two ways: externally to atmosphere, which is visible, and internally from the volute region across the joint face into the suction region, which is invisible but wastes energy and can erode channels in the faces over time.

A common method is a thin sheet gasket cut to the joint profile and compressed between the two machined faces by the joint studs. Some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a thin film of liquid sealing compound, and some use O-rings in machined grooves. The method is chosen by the OEM together with the internal fits, because joint thickness affects how parts held in the split bores, such as casing wear rings and seal housings, are clamped and how round those bores are.

Good sealing depends on clean, flat, undamaged faces; a new gasket of the specified material and thickness; accurate trimming at the bores so nothing protrudes into passages; correct location on the dowels; and even bolt preload applied in the specified sequence.
keyPoints: The joint sees near-discharge pressure beside the volute and suction pressure beside the suction chambers.
Internal leakage across the joint is invisible but wastes energy and erodes the faces.
Sheet gaskets, metal-to-metal joints with sealant and O-ring grooves are all used, depending on design.
Gasket thickness is part of the design because it affects internal fits.
topics.caution: Use only the OEM-specified gasket material and thickness. Never reuse a compressed gasket, and do not add jointing compound unless the OEM permits it.

topics.title: Why dowel pins are used
topics.body:
The joint studs pass through clearance holes in the upper flange. The clearance is needed for assembly, but it means the bolts alone cannot return the upper half to exactly the same place. A small sideways or endwise shift would leave the split bores oval or stepped. Those bores hold the casing wear rings and the seal or packing housings, so a shift can cause uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing, misaligned seal glands and steps in the volute and suction passages.

Dowel pins solve this. They are close-fitting pins in holes made through both flanges while the halves were machined together, so they put the upper half back in its original machined position. They also resist any tendency of the joint to slide under load, and as the upper half is lowered they guide it squarely so it does not swing into the impeller or damage the gasket.

The correct order is therefore to locate on the dowels first and then clamp with the bolts. Dowels may be parallel or tapered, and many have a threaded end or tapped hole for extraction. Whether they are withdrawn before lifting or stay as guides depends on the design. Bearing housings are commonly dowelled to their brackets for the same reason.
keyPoints: Bolts clamp; dowels locate.
Accurate location keeps the split bores round and concentric with the rotor.
Dowels guide the upper half during lowering and protect the gasket and internals.
Fit the dowels before tightening any joint nut.
topics.caution: Do not hammer the casing onto or off its dowels; use the extractor and lifting method given in the OEM procedure.

topics.title: Why casing bolts require proper tightening
topics.body:
Internal pressure acting on the projected area inside the joint produces a large force trying to separate the casing halves. The joint stays sealed only if the total bolt preload exceeds this force with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere. Preload is what matters, not torque as such: applied torque is converted into stud stretch, and a large part of it is used up overcoming friction in the threads and under the nut. Thread condition and the specified lubricant therefore change the preload obtained for a given torque.

Even loading matters as much as total load. If nuts are tightened one at a time to the full value, or in a random order, the upper half can be pulled down unevenly. Some regions of the gasket are then under-compressed and prone to leakage while others are over-compressed, and the split bores can distort so that wear rings rub and seals run out of square.

OEM procedures therefore give a tightening sequence applied in several passes at increasing values. Many sequences start near the middle of the joint, around the impeller, and work outwards towards the ends, alternating from side to side, but the OEM sequence always takes precedence. Afterwards the rotor should still turn freely by hand; new stiffness indicates distortion or a rub that must be investigated.
keyPoints: Bolt preload must exceed the pressure separating force with margin.
Friction absorbs much of the applied torque, so thread condition and lubrication affect preload.
Uneven tightening distorts the casing and gasket, causing leaks and internal rubs.
Follow the OEM sequence in several passes, then check that the rotor turns freely.
topics.caution: No tightening values are given in this module. Use the OEM values, sequence and lubricant with calibrated tools.

topics.title: How the volute collects the liquid and builds pressure
topics.body:
The impeller discharges liquid all round its periphery, from both halves at once. The liquid leaves with high velocity, mostly in the tangential direction, so a large share of the energy added by the impeller is still kinetic energy at the impeller outlet. The volute has two jobs: to collect this flow and lead it to a single discharge nozzle, and to convert part of that kinetic energy into static pressure.

The volute is a spiral passage that starts at the tongue (cutwater) close to the impeller and grows in cross-section around the circumference, because every further part of the impeller periphery adds more flow. At design flow the area growth roughly matches the accumulated flow, so velocity and pressure around the impeller stay nearly uniform. The spiral ends at the throat, after which the discharge passage diverges. Slowing the liquid in this diverging section raises its static pressure, in line with the Bernoulli relation between velocity and pressure, less friction and mixing losses.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow. Below design flow the liquid decelerates along the volute and pressure rises from tongue to throat; above it, the liquid accelerates and pressure falls. Either way, pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and a net radial force acts on the rotor.
keyPoints: The impeller adds the energy; the volute collects the flow and recovers part of the kinetic energy as pressure.
Volute area grows from the tongue to the throat to match the accumulating flow.
The diverging passage after the throat acts as a diffuser.
Away from design flow, uneven pressure around the impeller produces a net radial force.
topics.caution: The volute adds no energy. It converts part of the kinetic energy leaving the impeller into pressure, with some losses.

topics.title: Why casing geometry affects hydraulic performance
topics.body:
The impeller adds the energy, but the casing largely decides how much of it reaches the discharge flange and how smoothly the pump runs.

Tongue clearance. The gap between impeller outer diameter and cutwater is a compromise. Too small, and each passing vane produces strong pressure pulses at vane passing frequency, causing noise, vibration and possible vane tip damage. Too large, and more liquid recirculates past the tongue, reducing efficiency.

Throat area. The volute throat area, relative to the impeller, largely sets the flow at which the pump reaches its best efficiency point and influences the shape of the head curve. Impeller and volute are designed as a matched pair.

Surface finish and casting quality. Rough surfaces, casting fins, core shift and steps at the joint between the halves add friction and turbulence losses, which are relatively more important in smaller pumps. Deposits and corrosion in service have a similar effect.

Suction chamber shape. The two side chambers must deliver liquid to both eyes with a uniform velocity profile and controlled swirl. Poor shape or obstruction raises NPSH required, can start cavitation at one eye first and upsets the axial force balance.

Side rooms. The gaps between the shrouds and the casing walls affect disc friction loss and the pressures acting on the shrouds.
keyPoints: Tongue clearance trades pressure pulsations against recirculation losses.
Throat area largely sets where the best efficiency point occurs.
Surface finish, casting accuracy and steps at the joint affect friction losses.
Suction chamber shape governs inflow uniformity, NPSH required and thrust balance.
topics.caution: Modifying casing geometry, for example by grinding the tongue, changes performance and rotor loads; it should only be done to an OEM-approved design.

topics.title: Why high-pressure designs may use different casing configurations
topics.body:
Two separate problems grow as pumps become larger or operate at higher pressure: radial load on the rotor, and containment of pressure at the casing joint.

Radial load. In a single volute the net radial force on the impeller is smallest near the best efficiency point and grows as operation moves away from it; it also grows with head and impeller size. A double volute adds a splitter rib that forms a second passage with its tongue roughly opposite the first. The two halves of the impeller periphery then see approximately opposed pressure distributions, so much of the radial force cancels, reducing shaft deflection, bearing load and wear-ring and seal distress. The cost is a more complex casting with narrower passages. Diffuser casings with stationary guide vanes are another way of distributing radial forces, used particularly in multistage pumps.

Pressure containment. An axially split joint is long and non-circular, and its bolting must resist a separating force that rises with pressure and joint area. At high pressure, and especially at high temperature or with hazardous or flammable liquids, such a joint is harder to keep tight under pressure and thermal distortion. For these duties radially split designs, including double-casing barrel pumps whose main closures are circular, are commonly preferred, and purchaser specifications or applicable standards may require them.
keyPoints: Single-volute radial force grows as operation moves away from BEP.
A double volute reduces net radial load by opposing two pressure distributions.
Long axially split joints become harder to seal at high pressure and temperature.
Radially split and barrel casings are commonly used for more severe duties.
topics.caution: A double volute reduces, but does not eliminate, radial load. Limits for selecting a casing type come from the OEM and the applicable specification, not from this module.

topics.title: What double suction means
topics.body:
A double-suction (double-entry) impeller has two inlets, called eyes, one on each side, instead of the single eye of an end-suction impeller. It can be pictured as two single-suction impellers placed back to back and cast as one piece: a central hub and web separate two sets of vanes, each enclosed by its own outer shroud, and both halves discharge from a common outer periphery into one volute.

In this pump, liquid enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half and is divided into two side suction chambers. One feeds the drive-end eye and the other the non-drive-end eye, so the two streams approach the impeller axially from opposite directions. Inside the impeller each stream turns outwards through its own vane passages, and the two streams merge at the impeller outlet and leave through the single discharge nozzle.

The pump is still single-stage: the liquid passes through one impeller once. Double suction describes the number of inlets, not the number of stages. Because the shaft passes right through the impeller and needs support on both sides, double-suction impellers pair naturally with between-bearings rotors and axially split casings, although they are also used elsewhere, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.
keyPoints: Two eyes, one on each side, feed two mirror-image vane sets.
Both halves discharge into one volute and one discharge nozzle.
Still a single-stage pump: one pass through one impeller.
Naturally suited to between-bearings rotors and split casings.

topics.title: Why liquid enters from both sides
topics.body:
Feeding the impeller from both sides divides the total flow between two eyes. Several tendencies follow, although the size of each benefit depends on the individual design.

Suction performance. For a given total flow and speed, each eye handles only part of the flow, so inlet velocities can be lower for a given eye size. Lower inlet velocity tends to reduce NPSH required, which helps where available suction head is limited, or allows a higher speed for the same NPSH margin. For this reason suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.

Flow capacity. For a given impeller diameter and speed, a double-suction impeller can usually pass more flow than a comparable single-suction impeller because it has roughly twice the inlet area. This makes the type common for large flows at moderate head, for example in water supply, cooling water, irrigation and fire service.

Axial thrust. With the inlets facing in opposite directions, the axial hydraulic forces on the two halves largely oppose each other in a symmetrical arrangement, so thrust bearing duty is much lower than for a single-suction impeller of similar size, though not zero.

The trade-offs are a more complex casting, two shaft seals, a rotor supported at both ends, and sensitivity to uneven inflow from the suction piping.
keyPoints: Lower eye velocity tends to reduce NPSH required for a given flow and speed.
Higher flow capacity for a given impeller size and speed, as a tendency.
Axial forces largely oppose each other, reducing but not removing thrust.
Costs: complex casting, two seals and sensitivity to uneven inflow.
topics.caution: These are tendencies, not guarantees. Actual NPSH required and flow capacity come from the OEM performance curves, and conventions for calculating specific speed (total flow or flow per eye) should always be stated when comparing values.

topics.title: How liquid moves through the impeller passages
topics.body:
Each half of the impeller works in the same way. Liquid leaves its side suction chamber and enters the eye moving mainly axially, sometimes with a little pre-swirl set by the chamber shape. In the eye it turns from axial towards radial, guided by the shroud on the outside and the hub and central web on the inside, and meets the vane leading edges.

Velocity triangles describe the flow. Relative to the rotating vanes the liquid has a relative velocity w; the vanes move at peripheral speed u = omega r; the absolute velocity c seen by a stationary observer is the vector sum of w and u. Near design flow the relative flow meets the vanes with small incidence. Away from design flow incidence increases, raising losses and possibly triggering cavitation or recirculation at the eye.

As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller and its angular momentum increases. The Euler equation gives the ideal head: H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g, where cu is the tangential component of absolute velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). Static pressure rises through the passages because of the centrifugal effect and because the relative velocity is slowed in the widening, backward-curved passages. At the outlet the liquid has higher pressure and high absolute velocity, and the two streams merge into the volute.
keyPoints: Flow enters each eye axially and turns radially through the vane passages.
Velocity triangles relate relative velocity, vane speed and absolute velocity.
Euler equation: ideal head H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g.
Pressure and absolute velocity both rise; the volute then recovers part of the velocity as pressure.
topics.caution: The Euler head is an ideal value. Real head is lower because the flow does not follow the vanes perfectly (slip) and because of hydraulic losses.

topics.title: How double suction influences hydraulic loading
topics.body:
The impeller experiences three broad kinds of hydraulic load: axial, radial and fluctuating.

Axial forces come mainly from pressure on the outer faces of the shrouds. Liquid in each side room rotates at a fraction of impeller speed, so its pressure falls from the periphery towards the wear ring. In a single-suction impeller the eye side is at suction pressure inside the wear ring while the back shroud sees higher pressure over a larger area, giving a net thrust towards the suction. In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds face side rooms with similar pressure distributions acting in opposite directions, and the incoming flows also enter from opposite directions, so these forces ideally cancel.

Radial forces come from the pressure distribution around the impeller periphery. Double suction does not reduce them in itself: they depend on head, impeller diameter, total outlet width and operating point relative to BEP, and they are addressed by volute design, for example a double volute.

Fluctuating forces arise as each vane passes the tongue, giving pulses at vane passing frequency, and from recirculation at part load. Staggering the DE and NDE vane sets, as many designs do, spreads these pulses in time and reduces their amplitude.

The torque reaction on the impeller passes to the shaft through the key.
keyPoints: Axial forces on the two shrouds act in opposite directions and largely balance in a symmetrical impeller.
Radial force depends on head, size, outlet width and operating point, not on the number of eyes.
Vane passing at the tongue produces pulsating forces; staggered vanes reduce them.
Torque reaction passes to the shaft through the key.

topics.title: Why symmetrical flow distribution matters
topics.body:
The advantages of a double-suction impeller depend on its two halves working under similar conditions. In practice each eye receives a share of the flow set by suction chamber geometry, casting accuracy, wear-ring condition, operating point and, very often, the upstream piping. The shares are never exactly equal, but large differences cause problems.

If one eye receives more flow, or a distorted, swirling velocity profile, its local inlet velocity and incidence increase. Its NPSH required rises, so cavitation can begin on that side while the other is still clear, and damage then appears mainly on one side of the impeller and casing. The pressure distributions on the two shrouds also differ, so residual axial thrust increases, and the uneven loading can add noise, vibration and fluctuating forces.

A classic cause is an elbow, branch or partly open valve close to the suction flange. An elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft throws more liquid towards one side of the pipe, and therefore towards one eye. Intake and piping guidance commonly recommends that an elbow close to the suction of a double-suction pump lies in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, so any velocity skew is shared by both eyes, and that adequate straight pipe is provided upstream; follow the OEM and recognised guidance for details. Vortices, entrained air and blocked strainers can cause similar asymmetry.
keyPoints: Each eye's share of the flow depends on geometry, piping and operating point; it is never exactly half.
Uneven inflow raises NPSH required on one side and can start cavitation there first.
Asymmetry increases residual axial thrust and vibration.
An elbow near the suction should normally lie in a plane perpendicular to the shaft, per the OEM and intake guidance.
topics.caution: Do not assume each eye receives exactly half the flow. Clearly asymmetric damage at the two eyes is a strong hint to review the suction piping.

topics.title: How axial thrust is balanced in an ideal symmetrical arrangement
topics.body:
Consider an ideal double-suction impeller: the two halves are exact mirror images, the wear rings at both eyes have the same diameter and clearance, the impeller is centred in the volute so both side rooms have the same geometry, and both eyes receive identical, uniform inflow.

Under these conditions the DE and NDE side rooms have the same pressure distribution, falling from the periphery towards the wear ring in the same way. Acting on equal shroud areas in opposite directions, the two pressure forces cancel. Inside the wear rings both eyes are at suction pressure, so those areas cancel too. The two incoming streams change direction from axial to radial and produce equal and opposite momentum reaction forces. Finally, the shaft passes out through both seal chambers; when both are at similar pressure, the pressure forces on the shaft cross-section at the two ends also balance.

In this ideal case the net hydraulic axial force is approximately zero, which is why a double-suction pump needs far less thrust capacity than a single-suction pump of similar size. The rotor still needs a locating bearing: in this pump the NDE locating bearing (paired angular-contact, back to back, in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries any residual thrust in either direction, while the DE bearing floats to allow thermal expansion.
keyPoints: Ideal conditions: mirror-image geometry, equal clearances, centred impeller and equal inflow.
Shroud pressure forces, momentum forces and shaft-end pressure forces then oppose and balance.
The ideal net force is approximately zero, greatly reducing thrust bearing duty.
A locating bearing is still required to fix the rotor and carry residual thrust.
topics.caution: Double suction substantially balances hydraulic axial thrust only in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. It does not eliminate axial thrust in a real pump.

topics.title: Why residual axial thrust still exists
topics.body:
Real pumps depart from the ideal symmetrical arrangement in several ways. Each departure leaves a net axial force, the residual thrust, which can act towards either end and can change with operating conditions.

Asymmetric inflow: elbows, valves or strainers near the suction, or vortices in the intake, give the two eyes different flow and velocity profiles. Wear-ring clearances: new rings have tolerances, and in service the rings at the two eyes rarely wear at the same rate; a larger clearance on one side increases leakage through that side room and changes its swirl and pressure. Casting variations: shroud profiles, vane positions and side-room widths are never perfectly identical. Rotor axial position: if the impeller is not centred on the volute, the side rooms differ; centring is set during assembly by the OEM procedure. Off-design operation: at low flow, recirculation at the eyes and outlet need not be symmetrical, and the force can fluctuate. Unequal seal chamber pressures act on the shaft cross-section. Transients such as starting, stopping and one-sided cavitation add temporary thrust.

In this design the residual thrust is carried by the NDE locating bearing. Because its direction can reverse, the baseline uses paired angular-contact bearings mounted back to back, which carry axial load in both directions; the deep-groove ball bearing variant also carries moderate axial load in both directions.
keyPoints: Uneven inflow, unequal wear-ring clearances and casting variations upset the balance.
An impeller not centred on the volute gives unequal side rooms.
Off-design operation and transients can make thrust fluctuate or reverse.
The NDE locating bearing carries residual thrust in both directions.
topics.caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A rise in NDE bearing temperature or a change in axial vibration after wear-ring renewal, rotor reassembly or piping changes can indicate increased residual thrust and should be investigated.

topics.title: Why wear rings and clearances affect performance
topics.body:
Each eye has a pair of wear rings, one on the impeller and one in the casing, separated by a small radial running clearance. Outside the gap is the side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure; inside is the eye, at suction pressure, so liquid leaks back continuously. As a simple approximation the leakage behaves like flow through an annular orifice, QL = Cd A sqrt(2 dp / rho), where A is the clearance area and dp the pressure difference, so leakage rises roughly in proportion to the clearance.

Efficiency. The leakage has received energy from the impeller but is not delivered, so the impeller must pass more flow than the pump delivers. As rings wear, delivered flow at a given head falls, head at a given flow falls, and power per unit of delivered flow rises.

Suction behaviour. The leakage jet re-enters the eye and disturbs the inlet flow; heavy leakage can raise NPSH required and promote eye recirculation.

Pressure distribution and thrust. Leakage through each side room modifies its swirl and pressure, so unequal DE and NDE clearances unbalance the shroud forces and increase residual thrust.

Rotordynamics. The liquid film in a tight annular gap acts like a weak bearing, adding stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). Worn rings lose this support, which tends to lower the wet critical speed and increase vibration.
keyPoints: Leakage through the clearance is recirculated, not delivered, so efficiency falls as rings wear.
Leakage rises roughly in proportion to clearance.
Leakage jets disturb the eye flow and can affect suction performance.
Unequal clearances unbalance thrust; worn rings reduce rotor stiffness and damping.
topics.caution: A clearance that is too tight risks rubbing, galling and seizure. Use the OEM clearances and renewal limits, and measure both eyes.

topics.title: Why impeller balance is important
topics.body:
No impeller is perfectly uniform. Variations in shroud and vane thickness, machining offsets and the keyway mean that the mass centre does not lie exactly on the rotation axis. This residual unbalance U (mass multiplied by its radius) produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, which rises with the square of speed: doubling the speed quadruples the force for the same unbalance.

The force rotates with the shaft and is reacted by both bearings, so it appears as vibration at running speed (1x). It adds cyclic load to the bearings and shaft, makes seal faces and packing work with more movement, and can make the wear rings rub, which opens clearances and reduces efficiency. Near a critical speed the response is amplified.

A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (static plus couple unbalance). Two-plane dynamic balancing is therefore commonly used, with correction by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds within OEM limits. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11; the grade, and whether the impeller alone or the complete rotor is balanced, come from the OEM or purchaser specification. The key convention used during balancing must match the assembled rotor.

Balance can change in service through erosion, corrosion, deposits, repairs and trimming. Mechanical balancing cannot correct hydraulic unbalance from vane-to-vane differences.
keyPoints: Unbalance force F = U omega^2 rises with the square of speed.
It shows as 1x vibration and loads bearings, seals and wear rings.
Wide double-suction impellers are commonly two-plane (dynamically) balanced.
Rebalance after repairs, trims or coatings, and keep the key convention consistent.

topics.title: How the shaft transmits torque
topics.body:
Power flows from the motor shaft through the motor coupling hub, the flexible elements and spacer, and the pump coupling hub into the pump shaft at its drive-end extension. The shaft then carries the torque past the DE bearing and DE seal to the impeller seat, where the impeller key transfers it into the hub. The NDE section beyond the impeller carries only small torques from bearing and seal friction.

Torque, power and speed are related by P = T omega, with omega = 2 pi N / 60 for N in rev/min. In practical units, T (N m) = 9549 x P (kW) / N (rev/min). For example, a pump absorbing 200 kW at 1480 rev/min transmits about 9549 x 200 / 1480, roughly 1290 N m, through its DE shaft section. This is an illustrative calculation only.

At each keyed joint the torque is passed as a tangential force at the shaft surface, approximately F = 2T / d, carried by contact pressure on the key sides and by shear across the key section. Keyed joints are therefore checked for key shear, key-side bearing pressure and keyway stress. Starting transients, for example direct-on-line starting, can produce torques above the steady running value, so the OEM sizes the shaft and keys with margin for such conditions.
keyPoints: Torque path: motor, coupling, DE shaft extension, shaft, impeller key, impeller.
T = P / omega; in practical units T (N m) = 9549 P (kW) / N (rev/min).
The DE section between coupling and impeller carries full torque; the NDE end carries very little.
Keys carry torque by side pressure and shear; transient torques can exceed running torque.
topics.caution: The worked figure is illustrative. Shaft and key sizing for a real pump is done by the OEM, including starting and transient torques.

topics.title: Shaft bending
topics.body:
Between its two bearings the shaft behaves like a beam. The main transverse loads are the weight of impeller and shaft, the radial hydraulic force from the volute, the rotating force from residual unbalance, and forces from the coupling, which increase with misalignment. Because the impeller sits roughly at mid-span in this design, a simple model is a simply supported beam with a central point load F over span L. The maximum bending moment is then M = F L / 4 at the load, and the bending stress at the surface of a solid round section of diameter d is sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3).

The key feature of a pump shaft is that it rotates while most of these loads, such as gravity and the volute radial force, stay fixed in direction. A point on the surface passes from tension to compression and back every revolution, so the bending stress is fully reversed. Over millions of cycles this is a fatigue problem: stresses must stay below the material's fatigue strength, with allowance for stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders, threads and press fits, and for surface condition and corrosion.

In a single volute the radial hydraulic load grows as operation moves away from BEP, so prolonged running at very low or very high flow raises bending stress and fatigue risk.
keyPoints: Loads: weight, volute radial force, unbalance and coupling forces.
Simple model: M = F L / 4 for a central load; sigma = 32 M / (pi d^3) for a solid round shaft.
Rotation under a stationary load makes bending stress fully reversed, so fatigue governs.
Stress raisers and off-BEP operation increase fatigue risk.
topics.caution: The beam formulas assume a uniform solid shaft, rigid simple supports and a single central load. Real shafts are stepped and run in flexible bearings; design checks are the OEM responsibility.

topics.title: Torsional stress in the shaft
topics.body:
When a solid round shaft of diameter d carries a torque T, the shear stress varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the surface: tau = T r / J, where J = pi d^4 / 32 is the polar second moment of area. At the surface (r = d / 2) this gives tau = 16 T / (pi d^3). For a hollow shaft of outer diameter D and bore di, tau = 16 T D / (pi (D^4 - di^4)). These formulas assume a straight, homogeneous, linear-elastic shaft of uniform circular section in pure torsion, away from changes of section.

The angle of twist over a length L is theta = T L / (G J), where G is the shear modulus. Twist is rarely limiting in a short pump shaft, but the torsional natural frequencies of the complete pump, coupling and motor train may need checking, for example with variable-speed drives.

In a pump shaft torsion never acts alone: the DE section between coupling and impeller carries full torque together with bending. For a solid shaft the maximum shear stress theory gives tau_max = (16 / (pi d^3)) sqrt(M^2 + T^2), and the distortion-energy (von Mises) approach gives sigma_e = sqrt(sigma^2 + 3 tau^2). Keyways, shoulders and threads raise local stresses above these nominal values, so stress concentration factors and fatigue criteria are applied in real design.
keyPoints: Solid shaft: tau = 16 T / (pi d^3) at the surface.
Hollow shaft: tau = 16 T D / (pi (D^4 - di^4)).
Twist: theta = T L / (G J); drive-train torsional frequencies may need checking.
Combined with bending: tau_max = (16 / (pi d^3)) sqrt(M^2 + T^2).
topics.caution: Nominal formulas ignore stress concentration and fatigue. They are for understanding, not for sizing a shaft.

topics.title: Critical speed
topics.body:
A rotor on its bearings has natural frequencies of lateral (bending) vibration. When running speed coincides with one of them, even a small unbalance force excites a large response; that speed is a critical speed.

A simple estimate treats the rotor as a single mass m on a massless shaft of lateral stiffness k: omega_c = sqrt(k / m). Since the static deflection under the rotor's own weight is delta = m g / k, this can also be written omega_c = sqrt(g / delta), or approximately N_c = 946 / sqrt(delta) rev/min with delta in millimetres. A stiffer or lighter rotor therefore has a higher critical speed. Real rotors are analysed with methods that include distributed mass, stepped diameters and bearing and support flexibility.

Pump rotors behave differently dry and wet. Running in liquid adds mass, while the close clearances at the wear rings add stiffness and damping (the Lomakin effect). As the rings wear this support decreases and the wet critical speed tends to fall, possibly towards running speed.

Many single-stage between-bearings pumps are designed with the first critical speed sufficiently above the operating speed range (a stiff-shaft design), but this is design-specific, and separation margins are set by the OEM and applicable specification. With variable-speed drives the whole speed range must be considered, including resonances of bearing housings, baseplate and foundation.
keyPoints: A critical speed is a running speed that coincides with a lateral natural frequency.
Simple estimate: omega_c = sqrt(k / m) = sqrt(g / delta); N_c is about 946 / sqrt(delta in mm) rev/min.
Wet critical speed depends on liquid added mass and wear-ring (Lomakin) stiffness.
Wear-ring wear tends to lower the wet critical speed.
Variable-speed operation widens the range that must be checked.
topics.caution: The single-mass formula is a rough first estimate that ignores bearing flexibility, gyroscopic effects and fluid forces. Rotordynamic assessment of a real pump is the OEM responsibility.

topics.title: Shaft deflection
topics.body:
Under radial load the shaft bends, and the deflection at the impeller, wear rings and seal faces often matters more for reliability than the stress. For a simply supported uniform shaft with a central point load F over span L, the mid-span deflection is delta = F L^3 / (48 E I), with I = pi d^4 / 64 for a solid round section and E the elastic modulus. The slope at each support is theta = F L^2 / (16 E I).

These relations show the sensitivity: deflection rises with the cube of span and falls with the fourth power of diameter, so designs are often compared using a shaft flexibility index proportional to L^3 / d^4.

The main deflecting loads are the radial hydraulic force, which in a single volute grows as operation moves away from BEP, impeller and shaft weight, coupling forces and unbalance. Excessive deflection can close the wear-ring clearance on one side and cause rubbing, tilt the mechanical seal faces and increase leakage or face wear, wear packing and sleeves unevenly, and misalign the bearings, raising their temperature. Typical evidence is one-sided rub marks on wear rings and sleeves.

Remedies are mainly operational and design-related: running close to BEP, a double volute for wide operating ranges, a stiffer shaft, and correct coupling alignment.
keyPoints: Simple model: delta = F L^3 / (48 E I), with I = pi d^4 / 64.
Deflection is proportional to L^3 / d^4.
Main loads: radial hydraulic force (larger away from BEP), weight, coupling forces and unbalance.
Excess deflection causes wear-ring rubs, seal face tilt and bearing misalignment.
topics.caution: Allowable deflection at the seals and wear rings is set by the OEM and seal supplier. Simple beam formulas ignore stepped diameters, bearing flexibility and fluid-film stiffness.

topics.title: Shaft alignment
topics.body:
Two kinds of alignment matter in this pump.

Internal alignment: the rotor must run concentric with the casing bores. This is set by the bearing housings seated on the lower casing brackets, usually located by dowels or spigots, and by correct assembly of the casing halves on their dowels. Errors show as uneven wear-ring clearance, one-sided rubbing and seal problems.

Pump-to-motor alignment: the pump and motor shaft axes should be collinear when running. Misalignment is described as offset (parallel displacement) and angularity (an angle between the axes), each in both the vertical and horizontal planes. A flexible coupling tolerates some misalignment but reacts with forces and moments on both shafts, adding bearing load, shaft bending stress, vibration and coupling wear.

Alignment is measured with dial indicators (rim-and-face or reverse-indicator methods) or laser systems. Good practice is to correct soft foot first, confirm the piping does not strain the nozzles, allow for thermal growth using the cold offsets given by the OEM, and recheck after grouting, after piping connection and, where the site procedure requires, after a run at operating temperature. The spacer coupling lets seals and bearings be serviced without moving the motor, which helps preserve alignment.
keyPoints: Internal alignment centres the rotor in the casing bores.
External alignment is described by offset and angularity in both vertical and horizontal planes.
Correct soft foot and pipe strain first, and allow for thermal growth.
Misalignment loads bearings, bends the shaft and wears the coupling.
topics.caution: Alignment tolerances and cold offsets must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard; none are given here.

topics.title: Purpose of the shaft sleeves
topics.body:
The shaft sleeves on each side of the impeller do several jobs at once.

Wear protection. With gland packing, the packing rubs continuously on the rotating surface beneath it and gradually wears a groove. With a mechanical seal, the secondary sealing elements can fret the surface they sit on. Putting a renewable sleeve under these parts means the shaft itself is not worn; replacing a sleeve is far quicker and cheaper than repairing or replacing a shaft.

Corrosion protection. In many designs the sleeves, the impeller hub and the O-rings or gaskets at their joints keep pumped liquid off the shaft, so the shaft can be made from a strong, economical material while the wetted sleeves use a corrosion-resistant one.

Running surface. The sleeve provides the finish, hardness and runout that the packing or seal needs. Under packing the surface may be hard-coated in some designs.

Impeller location. Each sleeve is clamped between the impeller hub and a sleeve nut, so the two sleeves position and hold the impeller axially on the shaft.

In the mechanical seal variant the sleeves also carry the seal rotating parts, or a cartridge seal's own sleeve fitted over them. Sleeve end faces must be square, and their O-rings renewed whenever they are disturbed.
keyPoints: A renewable wearing surface under packing or seal elements.
Keeps pumped liquid off the shaft in many designs.
Provides the finish, hardness and runout the seal or packing needs.
With the sleeve nuts, locates the impeller axially.

topics.title: Protecting the shaft from corrosion
topics.body:
A pump shaft is highly stressed and subject to fatigue, and corrosion greatly reduces fatigue strength: pits act as stress raisers, and corrosion fatigue can crack a shaft at stresses a clean shaft would tolerate. Protecting the shaft is therefore a reliability issue, not a cosmetic one.

Isolation. In many split case designs the wetted length of the shaft is covered by the sleeves and impeller hub, with O-rings or gaskets at each joint, so the pumped liquid never reaches the shaft. Damaged or omitted O-rings let liquid creep under the sleeves, where crevice corrosion can develop out of sight.

Material selection. Where the shaft may be wetted, its material must suit the liquid; stainless or duplex grades are used in corrosive services. Shaft, sleeve and impeller materials should be compatible, because dissimilar metals in contact in a conductive liquid such as seawater can promote galvanic corrosion of the less noble metal.

Keeping water out of bearings. Deflectors (flingers) and bearing housing seals stop leakage running along the shaft into the bearing housings, protecting journals and bearings.

Idle periods. Stand-by pumps and spare rotors should be protected according to OEM and site preservation procedures, since standing liquid and condensation can pit journals and other surfaces.
keyPoints: Corrosion pits reduce fatigue strength and can start cracks.
Sleeves, hub and O-rings isolate the shaft from the liquid in many designs.
Select compatible materials to limit corrosion and galvanic attack.
Deflectors and housing seals keep water away from journals and bearings.

topics.title: Why shaft stiffness matters
topics.body:
Stiffness is the shaft's resistance to bending under load. For the simple central-load model the lateral stiffness at the impeller is k = 48 E I / L^3, with I = pi d^4 / 64, so k is proportional to E d^4 / L^3. Doubling the diameter increases stiffness sixteen-fold; doubling the bearing span reduces it to one eighth.

An important practical point is that the steels used for shafts, whether carbon, alloy or stainless, have broadly similar elastic moduli. Choosing a stronger steel raises the allowable stress but does little for stiffness, which comes mainly from geometry: diameter and span.

Stiffness controls several things at once. It limits deflection at the wear rings, keeping clearances uniform and avoiding rubs. It limits movement and tilt at the mechanical seal faces and uneven wear of packing and sleeves. It limits the slope at the bearings, keeping them aligned. And it raises the lateral critical speeds, since omega_c is proportional to sqrt(k / m), helping to keep them away from the running speed range.

The designer balances stiffness against other needs: a larger shaft needs larger seals and bearings, and in a double-suction impeller a larger shaft and hub take up eye area, which raises inlet velocity. Supporting the impeller near mid-span between two bearings is an efficient way to obtain stiffness with a moderate diameter.
keyPoints: Lateral stiffness is proportional to E d^4 / L^3.
Shaft steels have similar elastic moduli, so stiffness depends mainly on diameter and span.
Stiffness limits deflection at wear rings and seals and raises critical speeds.
Larger diameters cost seal and bearing size and reduce eye area.
topics.caution: These proportionalities come from simple beam theory and are for comparison only; they ignore stepped sections and bearing flexibility.

topics.title: Radial loads on the bearings
topics.body:
Radial loads act at right angles to the shaft axis. In a between-bearings split case pump the main sources are the weight of the rotor (shaft, impeller, sleeves and part of the coupling), the hydraulic radial force on the impeller, and forces transmitted through the coupling, mainly from misalignment. Dynamic loads are added by residual unbalance, hydraulic pulsations and rotor-dynamic effects.

The hydraulic radial force exists because the pressure around the impeller periphery is not perfectly uniform. In a single-volute casing it is typically smallest near the best efficiency point (BEP) and grows as the flow moves away from BEP, towards both shut-off and run-out. A double-volute casing, with its splitter rib, substantially reduces this force by setting two opposed volute passages against each other, but does not remove it. The direction of the force also changes with flow rate, so the bearings see a load that varies in both size and direction.

Both bearings share the radial load; how much each carries depends on where the impeller sits along the span and on any overhung load at the coupling end (see 'Bearing reactions'). The drive-end floating bearing carries radial load only; the non-drive-end locating bearing carries its radial share plus the residual axial thrust.

Sustained operation far from BEP increases radial load, shaft deflection, the risk of wear-ring and seal contact, and bearing temperature.
keyPoints: Radial load comes from rotor weight, the impeller's hydraulic radial force, coupling forces and dynamic effects.
Hydraulic radial force is typically lowest near BEP and rises towards shut-off and run-out.
A double volute reduces radial force substantially but does not eliminate it.
Both bearings share radial load; only the locating bearing also carries thrust.
topics.caution: A double volute or robust bearings do not make every operating point acceptable. Operate within the allowable operating region stated by the OEM.

topics.title: Axial loads on the rotor
topics.body:
Axial (thrust) loads act along the shaft axis. A double-suction impeller is nominally symmetrical, so the hydraulic thrusts from its two sides largely cancel, but never exactly.

Residual hydraulic thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances in the impeller and casing halves, an impeller not exactly centred in the volute, unequal wear-ring clearances (especially as the rings wear unevenly), unequal flow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping layout, recirculation or cavitation starting at one eye at part load, and transient conditions such as start-up, shutdown and pressure surges. Mechanical sources add to it: axial force through the coupling (for example a gear coupling that locks under torque, or a disc coupling installed at the wrong axial spacing), and thermally induced load if the floating bearing is unable to move.

This residual thrust can act in either direction and can change direction with operating conditions or as the pump wears. It therefore has to be carried by a bearing that takes thrust both ways and holds the rotor in a defined axial position: the locating bearing at the non-drive end. The drive-end bearing is deliberately left free axially so that it carries radial load only.

Rotor weight does not create axial load on a horizontal shaft, although it does on a vertical one; load paths always depend on machine orientation.
keyPoints: Double suction largely cancels hydraulic thrust, but residual thrust always remains.
Residual thrust comes from manufacturing asymmetry, wear, suction flow distortion, part-load effects and transients.
Couplings and restrained thermal growth can add mechanical axial load.
Thrust may act in either direction, so the locating bearing must carry both.
topics.caution: Double suction does not eliminate axial thrust. A locating (thrust) bearing is always required.

topics.title: Bearing reactions: a simple beam model
topics.body:
For a first estimate, treat the rotor as a simply supported beam: the drive-end bearing is one support, the non-drive-end bearing the other, and L is the span between bearing centres. Let a radial load F act at the impeller, at distance a from the drive-end bearing and distance b from the non-drive-end bearing, so that a + b = L.

Taking moments about the non-drive-end bearing: R_DE × L = F × b, so R_DE = F × b / L. Taking moments about the drive-end bearing: R_NDE = F × a / L. As a check, R_DE + R_NDE = F. The bearing nearer the load carries the larger share; with the impeller at mid-span each carries half.

The rotor weight W acts vertically downwards, while the hydraulic radial force acts in a direction set by the operating point. In practice each load is resolved into vertical and horizontal components, the reactions are found for each component, and the components are combined vectorially to give the resultant reaction at each bearing.

An overhung load outside the span, such as a coupling weight W_c at distance c outboard of the drive-end bearing, increases R_DE by W_c × (L + c) / L and reduces R_NDE by W_c × c / L.

This model ignores shaft flexibility, bearing stiffness, dynamic loads and misalignment forces; OEMs use more detailed rotor analysis. It is, however, the starting point for most bearing-load calculations in machine design.
keyPoints: R_DE = F × b / L and R_NDE = F × a / L, where a + b = L.
The bearing nearer the load carries the larger share.
Resolve weight and hydraulic force into components and combine the reactions vectorially.
An overhung coupling load increases R_DE and slightly reduces R_NDE.
topics.caution: This is a teaching model for understanding load sharing, not a substitute for the OEM's bearing selection and rotor analysis.

topics.title: Locating and floating bearing arrangement
topics.body:
The two bearings in this pump do different jobs, and they are not interchangeable.

The non-drive-end bearing is the locating (fixed) bearing. Both of its rings are clamped: the inner rings against a shaft shoulder by the locknut, the outer rings between a housing shoulder and the blind end cover. It holds the rotor in a defined axial position and carries residual thrust in both directions as well as its share of radial load. In the baseline it is a back-to-back pair of angular-contact ball bearings; a single deep-groove ball bearing is the variant for lighter thrust duty.

The drive-end bearing is the floating (non-locating) bearing. Its inner ring is clamped to the shaft, but its outer ring can slide axially in the housing bore, so it carries radial load only.

Why only one locating bearing? The shaft and casing run at different temperatures and may be made of different materials, so they change length by different amounts. If both bearings were fixed axially, that difference would be forced into the bearings as an axial load, possibly a large one, causing heat, high contact stress and early failure. One locating bearing fixes the rotor; the floating bearing absorbs the change in length.

The locating bearing also fixes the impeller's axial position in the volute and wear rings, which matters for hydraulic symmetry and therefore for the level of residual thrust. Some manufacturers put the locating bearing at the drive end, or use other bearing types.
keyPoints: One locating bearing (NDE in the baseline) fixes the rotor axially and carries thrust both ways.
One floating bearing (DE) carries radial load and lets the shaft expand.
Two locating bearings would turn differential thermal expansion into bearing load.
The locating bearing also sets the impeller's axial position in the casing.
topics.caution: A floating bearing that has seized in its bore, or has been clamped by a wrong cover or gasket, silently turns the arrangement into two locating bearings. Check axial freedom after assembly as the OEM specifies.

topics.title: How double suction affects thrust-bearing duty
topics.body:
In a single-suction closed impeller, the pressure behind the back shroud acts over a larger area than the pressure on the front shroud, where the eye is at low suction pressure. The result is a substantial net axial thrust towards the suction side. Single-suction pumps therefore need balancing features (balance holes, back wear rings or pump-out vanes) and a thrust bearing sized for what remains.

A double-suction impeller is, in effect, two single-suction impellers back to back on one hub. Liquid enters through two opposed eyes and the pressure distributions on the two shrouds are mirror images, so their thrusts largely cancel. The thrust bearing in a double-suction pump therefore typically carries a residual load that is small in comparison, which allows a compact locating bearing and contributes to this pump type's reputation for long, reliable runs at large flows.

Largely cancelling is not the same as cancelling. Residual thrust comes from asymmetry: casting and machining tolerances, axial mispositioning of the impeller, uneven wear-ring clearances, unequal flow to the two eyes from poor suction piping, part-load recirculation or cavitation at one eye, and transients. Its size and direction can change with flow rate and over the pump's life as clearances wear.

Thrust-bearing duty is therefore never zero, and the OEM assesses it over the full operating range. When the conditions that keep the impeller balanced deteriorate, the signs are rising non-drive-end bearing temperature, higher axial vibration and shorter bearing life.
keyPoints: Single suction: large net thrust towards the suction, needing balancing features.
Double suction: opposing thrusts largely cancel, so thrust duty is typically much smaller.
Residual thrust remains and can change size and direction.
Rising NDE bearing temperature or axial vibration can indicate increased thrust.
topics.caution: Never assume that double suction eliminates axial thrust. Residual thrust always exists, which is why the pump has a locating bearing.

topics.title: Bearing lubrication
topics.body:
Rolling bearings depend on a very thin lubricant film between the rolling elements and the raceways. Under the high contact pressures this film is elastohydrodynamic: the lubricant's viscosity rises sharply under pressure and the surfaces deform elastically, so a film can separate them even though the contact area is tiny. The lubricant also reduces friction at the cage, protects the surfaces from corrosion and, in the case of oil, carries heat away.

Film thickness depends on the lubricant's viscosity at operating temperature, on speed and on load. Too thin a film, from the wrong grade, overheated or degraded oil, or water contamination, allows metal-to-metal contact, surface distress and early fatigue. Too much lubricant also does harm: excess oil or grease is churned by the rolling elements and generates heat.

Contamination matters as much as quantity. Hard particles dent the raceways, and water, a real risk next to a leaking seal or packing, weakens the film, promotes corrosion and shortens fatigue life. Housing seals, shaft deflectors and clean handling of lubricants are part of the lubrication system.

In this pump each bearing housing has its own lubricant. The baseline is an oil bath with constant-level oilers, sight glasses and drain plugs; the variant is grease with grease nipples and relief plugs. Lubricant type, grade, quantity, level and change or regreasing intervals must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site lubrication schedule.
keyPoints: An elastohydrodynamic film separates rolling elements and raceways.
Viscosity at operating temperature, speed and load set the film thickness.
Both too little and too much lubricant cause problems.
Water and particle contamination are major causes of bearing damage.

topics.title: Oil versus grease lubrication
topics.body:
Both methods are widely used on split case pumps, and the choice is made by the OEM for the bearing size, speed, load, temperature and maintenance regime.

Oil bath lubrication (the baseline): the lower part of the bearing runs in an oil sump held at a set level by a constant-level oiler and checked through a sight glass. Oil removes heat well, suits higher speeds and loads, and makes condition easy to check: level, colour and water can be seen, samples can be taken, and contaminants are removed when the oil is drained. In return it needs correct level setting, effective housing seals to keep oil in and water out, and regular attention to oilers and oil changes. Leaks and incorrect levels are common problems.

Grease lubrication (the variant): grease is a base oil held in a thickener, which stays in the bearing and helps seal it against contaminants. The arrangement is simpler, with no level to control and less risk of leakage. However, grease removes little heat, and its success depends on getting the type, quantity and regreasing interval right. Over-greasing causes churning and high temperature, under-greasing starves the bearing, and mixing incompatible greases can destroy lubrication. The relief plug must be used as the OEM instructs so that old grease can escape.

Some larger pumps use oil rings, flinger discs, oil mist or circulating oil systems instead.
keyPoints: Oil: better heat removal, easy condition checks, but needs level control and good sealing.
Grease: simpler and self-sealing, but limited heat removal and sensitive to quantity and compatibility.
Over-greasing is as harmful as under-greasing.
The method, lubricant and intervals are specified by the OEM.
topics.caution: Never mix lubricants or change grease type without confirming compatibility with the OEM or lubricant supplier.

topics.title: Bearing temperature
topics.body:
Temperature is one of the simplest and most useful indicators of bearing condition. After start-up it rises and then settles at a level set by load, speed, lubricant, ambient conditions and how easily heat flows away to the casing and baseplate. The settled value, recorded at commissioning at a known operating point, becomes the baseline for that bearing.

Trend monitoring compares readings with that baseline, with the other bearing, with ambient temperature and with the operating point at the time. A gradual rise can indicate lubricant degradation, contamination or developing damage. A sudden rise can point to loss of lubricant, over-greasing, a floating bearing that has locked, increased thrust, misalignment or a rubbing housing seal. A short-lived rise after regreasing is normal while excess grease is purged.

Temperature may be measured by permanently installed resistance temperature detectors or thermocouples, where fitted, or with contact or infrared thermometers on the housing surface. Readings taken by different methods or at different points are not directly comparable; a housing surface is cooler than the bearing outer ring. For trending, use the same method at the same marked point every time.

Alarm and trip settings and acceptable temperatures must come from the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site procedure.
keyPoints: Establish a baseline at commissioning and trend against it.
Compare DE with NDE, and always note ambient and operating point.
Sudden changes matter more than a single absolute value.
Use a consistent method and measurement point.
topics.caution: Do not judge temperature by touching the housing; it can be hot enough to burn, and the coupling and shaft are close by. Use instruments and keep clear of rotating parts.

topics.title: Bearing vibration
topics.body:
Vibration is measured at the bearing housings because that is where the rotor's forces pass into the stationary structure. Readings are normally taken in three directions (horizontal, vertical and axial) at both bearings, with permanently mounted sensors or portable instruments at marked points so that results can be trended.

Overall vibration, often expressed as velocity, indicates the general condition of the machine and is compared with the OEM's limits, the applicable vibration standard or site criteria. Spectrum analysis then helps find the cause. A dominant component at running speed (1x) commonly suggests unbalance. 1x and 2x components with high axial readings often suggest misalignment. Vane-pass frequency (number of impeller vanes multiplied by running speed) relates to the interaction between impeller and volute tongue. Broad-band, random vibration may indicate cavitation or recirculation. Non-synchronous frequencies linked to bearing geometry indicate rolling-bearing defects.

Early bearing defects produce small, high-frequency impacts that are often hidden in overall readings, so techniques such as acceleration enveloping (demodulation), shock pulse or other high-frequency methods are used. The defect frequencies for outer race, inner race, rolling elements and cage are calculated from the bearing geometry and speed.

At the non-drive-end locating bearing, axial vibration deserves particular attention because it reflects thrust conditions. As with temperature, trends matter more than single readings.
keyPoints: Measure horizontal, vertical and axial at both bearings at marked points.
1x often means unbalance; 1x/2x with high axial often means misalignment.
Enveloping and high-frequency methods detect early bearing defects.
Axial vibration at the locating bearing reflects thrust conditions.
topics.caution: Use acceptance limits from the OEM, the applicable standard or the site procedure; do not import limits from unrelated machines.

topics.title: Bearing life: the rating life concept
topics.body:
The basic rating life of a rolling bearing, L10, is the life that 90 percent of a sufficiently large group of apparently identical bearings, running under identical conditions, can be expected to reach or exceed before the first evidence of material fatigue appears. It is a statistical concept, defined in ISO 281; it does not predict when any individual bearing will fail.

In its basic form L10 = (C / P)^p, in millions of revolutions, where C is the basic dynamic load rating given by the bearing manufacturer, P is the equivalent dynamic load combining the radial and axial loads, and the exponent p is 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. Because of the exponent, life is very sensitive to load: doubling the load on a ball bearing reduces its basic rating life to one eighth.

Modified rating life methods add factors for the required reliability, the lubrication condition (through the viscosity ratio), contamination and the fatigue load limit. These show how strongly clean, adequate lubrication extends life and how contamination shortens it.

In practice most pump bearings are removed for reasons other than classic fatigue: inadequate or contaminated lubrication, water ingress, misalignment, incorrect mounting, excessive thrust and vibration. The required rating life for a particular pump is set by the purchaser's specification, the applicable pump standard and the OEM's design; use values only from those sources.
keyPoints: L10 is a statistical fatigue life reached by 90 percent of a bearing population.
Basic form: L10 = (C / P)^p, with p = 3 for ball and 10/3 for roller bearings.
Life is very sensitive to load, lubrication and contamination.
Most real bearing failures are not classical fatigue.
topics.caution: Rating life is not a guaranteed service life. Do not quote life figures for this pump that are not in the OEM's documentation.

topics.title: Common bearing failures
topics.body:
Most rolling-bearing failures in pumps start with a cause outside the bearing itself.

Lubrication problems: too little lubricant, the wrong grade, degraded oil, over-greasing that causes churning and heat, or incompatible greases mixed together. Signs include rising temperature, noise and discoloured or glazed surfaces.

Contamination: water from seal or packing leakage, or from washdown and condensation, and solid particles. Water causes corrosion and weakens the film; particles dent the raceways and start early spalling. Milky oil and dented, rusty or etched raceways are typical findings.

Misalignment and excessive load: shaft-to-motor misalignment, pipe strain, soft foot, or thrust above design from off-design operation or wear. These produce abnormal wear paths, overheating and early fatigue; at the locating bearing, excess thrust shows as high axial vibration and heat.

Mounting errors: hammering, force passed through the rolling elements, wrong fits, angular-contact pairs mounted in the wrong orientation or mixed between sets, a floating bearing that cannot move, or a loose locknut.

Standstill damage: false brinelling, which marks raceways at ball spacing when a stationary standby pump is exposed to vibration from nearby machines.

Electrical erosion: current passing through the bearing, more common in motor bearings with variable-speed drives, produces pitting and fluting.

ISO 15243 classifies the damage modes. Examining the failed bearing, its lubricant and its mounting surfaces is the key to fixing the root cause rather than just replacing the bearing.
keyPoints: Lubrication and contamination problems are the leading causes.
Misalignment, pipe strain and excess thrust overload bearings.
Incorrect mounting and wrong pair orientation cause early failure.
Standby pumps can suffer false brinelling; investigate root cause, not just the bearing.
topics.caution: Replacing a failed bearing without finding why it failed usually leads to a repeat failure.

topics.title: How the shaft is sealed
topics.body:
Wherever a rotating shaft passes through a stationary casing there must be a running clearance, and that clearance is a leakage path for the pumped liquid. Shaft sealing controls this path. On this pump the shaft runs inside replaceable sleeves where it passes through the casing, so wear and corrosion affect the sleeves rather than the shaft.

Two arrangements are used, one or the other at both ends. Compression packing fills the stuffing box with rings squeezed by a gland follower; it throttles leakage but must leak slightly to lubricate and cool itself. A mechanical seal uses two flat faces, one rotating and one stationary, held together by springs and liquid pressure; the leakage is very small and often leaves as vapour. Mechanical seals may be single or dual, component or cartridge, and in some cases split for easy replacement.

The stuffing box or seal chamber at each end is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. Supporting systems include the seal flush or packing seal water, venting of the chamber, and, outside the seal, shaft deflectors (flingers) that throw any leakage clear of the bearing housings.

Shaft sealing is different from bearing housing sealing. The shaft seal keeps the pumped liquid in the casing; the bearing housing seals (lip seals or isolators) keep lubricant in the bearing housings and contaminants out. Both matter, because shaft seal leakage that reaches the bearing housing contaminates the lubricant.
keyPoints: Each shaft exit through the casing needs a seal.
Packing controls leakage by throttling and must leak slightly; mechanical seals use lapped faces with minimal leakage.
The stuffing boxes or seal chambers are split with the casing.
Shaft seals and bearing housing seals do different jobs.

topics.title: Why two sealing locations are required
topics.body:
In a between-bearings pump the shaft passes right through the casing: the impeller is in the middle, a bearing is outside the casing at each end, and the shaft leaves the casing at both the drive end and the non-drive end. Each exit has a running clearance between the rotating sleeve and the stationary casing, so each needs its own seal: two mechanical seals, or two packed stuffing boxes. The same arrangement is used at both ends, and a mechanical seal and packing are never combined in one stuffing box.

In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box or seal chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so both see approximately suction pressure rather than discharge pressure. This has two consequences.

First, the pressure duty on the seals is usually moderate, which helps seal life.

Second, when the pump works with a suction lift, or the suction pressure is near or below atmospheric, the stuffing boxes may be under vacuum and can draw air in along the shaft. Air ingress reduces performance, can cause loss of prime, and starves packing or seal faces of liquid. Seal water supplied to the packing lantern ring, or a seal and flush arrangement selected for these conditions, prevents it.

The actual stuffing-box pressure depends on the particular design, the wear-ring clearances and the flush arrangement, so confirm it from the OEM data.
keyPoints: The between-bearings shaft leaves the casing at both ends, so two seals are needed.
Both ends use the same type: two mechanical seals or two packed boxes.
In a typical double-suction design both boxes see approximately suction pressure.
Under suction lift, seal water or a suitable seal arrangement prevents air ingress.
topics.caution: Do not assume the stuffing boxes are always above atmospheric pressure. Check suction conditions and the OEM data before deciding seal water or flush arrangements.

topics.title: Mechanical seal versus gland packing
topics.body:
Both arrangements are legitimate and widely used on split case pumps; each has trade-offs.

Leakage: packing must leak continuously to stay cool and lubricated. A mechanical seal's leakage is very small and often not visible. Where the pumped liquid is hazardous, valuable or environmentally harmful, a mechanical seal, often a dual seal, is normally required.

Power and wear: packing rubs on the sleeve and absorbs more power, and over time it grooves the sleeve. A mechanical seal absorbs less power and the sleeve wears little, although pusher seals can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.

Maintenance: packing needs periodic gland adjustment and repacking, but in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. A mechanical seal needs little routine attention, but replacing it usually means removing the coupling spacer and the bearing housing, or lifting the rotor, unless a split or cartridge design simplifies the job.

Tolerance: packing tolerates shaft movement, brief dry periods and poor conditions better, and fails gradually by leaking more. Mechanical seals are sensitive to dry running, vibration, misalignment and poor flush, and can fail suddenly.

Cost and skills: packing is cheaper to buy; mechanical seals often cost less over their life once leakage, water use, power and sleeve wear are counted, but they need careful installation.

The choice depends on the liquid, environmental and safety requirements, site practice and life-cycle cost.
keyPoints: Packing: simple, tolerant, repairable in place, but leaks continuously and wears the sleeve.
Mechanical seal: very low leakage and power loss, but sensitive to operating conditions and installation.
Hazardous or valuable liquids normally require mechanical seals.
Both are legitimate; the choice depends on service and life-cycle cost.

topics.title: Seal face contact and the fluid film
topics.body:
The primary seal of a mechanical seal is the interface between two flat, smooth faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary. The faces are lapped to extreme flatness, checked optically in light bands with an optical flat, because any waviness opens a leakage path or causes local contact.

Between the faces a very thin film of the sealed liquid lubricates and partly separates them. In many liquid applications the faces run in a mixed regime, partly supported by the film and partly in light contact. The film is what keeps friction, heat and wear acceptable; without it the faces run dry.

The faces are pushed together by the closing force, which is the spring force plus the liquid pressure acting on the closing area behind the flexible face. The film pressure between the faces pushes them apart. The net load divided by the face area is the face pressure, which governs film thickness, heat generation, leakage and wear. The balance ratio compares the hydraulic closing area with the face area. In an unbalanced seal, face pressure rises steeply with sealed pressure; a balanced seal uses a stepped sleeve or seal geometry to reduce the closing area so that face pressure rises more slowly, suiting higher pressures. Actual balance ratios and face pressures are design values of the seal manufacturer.

Anything that disturbs the faces, such as distortion from uneven gland tightening, thermal gradients, vibration, shaft runout or dry running, upsets the film and shortens seal life.
keyPoints: Faces are lapped extremely flat and run on a very thin liquid film.
Closing force = spring force + hydraulic force; film pressure opposes it.
Face pressure controls heat, leakage and wear.
Balanced seals limit face pressure at higher sealed pressures.
topics.caution: Dry running destroys the fluid film and can damage seal faces very quickly. Never run a mechanically sealed pump without liquid, even to check rotation.

topics.title: Leakage control
topics.body:
Packing and mechanical seals control leakage in fundamentally different ways.

Packing works by throttling, and it needs a controlled leakage: the liquid passing along the sleeve lubricates the packing and carries away frictional heat. The gland follower is adjusted to give the leakage rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends. Tightening to stop the leak completely makes the packing overheat, harden and burn, scores the sleeve, raises power absorption and eventually leads to more leakage, not less. New packing is started with generous leakage and taken up gradually as it beds in. Adjust the nuts evenly in small steps and allow time between adjustments.

A mechanical seal has very small leakage across its faces, much of which evaporates and is not visible. A steady visible drip generally indicates a problem, although some seals show slight leakage while bedding in; the seal manufacturer states what is acceptable. Rising leakage over time shows face wear, damage or a secondary seal problem.

In both cases, leakage must be collected and drained safely, for example to a gland drain or the baseplate drain rim, especially where the liquid is hot, hazardous or slippery, and it must be kept away from the bearing housings, where shaft deflectors and housing seals provide protection. Under suction lift, a sealing point can leak air in rather than liquid out; reduced performance or noise may be the only sign.
keyPoints: Packing must leak; overtightening causes overheating and sleeve damage.
Mechanical seal leakage is very small; visible steady leakage usually indicates a problem.
Collect and drain leakage, and keep it away from bearing housings.
Under suction lift a sealing point can draw air in.
topics.caution: Gland adjustment on a running pump puts hands close to the rotating shaft and coupling. Do it only where the site procedure permits, with all guards fitted and loose clothing and tools kept clear.

topics.title: Cooling and flushing
topics.body:
Seal faces and packing generate heat by friction, and that heat must be removed continuously. Flush (for mechanical seals) and seal water (for packing) do this, and serve several other purposes: they keep the sealing surfaces wetted, keep the liquid around the seal from flashing to vapour, sweep solids away, and help prevent air or vapour from collecting in the top of a horizontal chamber.

In clean-water service a common arrangement takes liquid from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or volute, through small-bore tubing with an orifice into each seal chamber. In many water-service pumps the flush is taken by a small external line, and some designs use internal passages. Where the pumped liquid contains solids or is otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid is injected from an external source, and accessories such as strainers, cyclone separators or coolers may be added. Dual seals use a separate buffer or barrier fluid system.
