The numbered seal piping plans defined in API 682 are widely used, even outside the oil and gas industry, as a shorthand for these arrangements; for example, one plan describes recirculation from the pump discharge to the seal chamber, and another describes injection of clean fluid from an external source. The plan for a given pump is stated on its seal datasheet.

For packing, seal water to the lantern ring must be at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure; it cools and lubricates the packing and, under suction lift, stops air ingress.
keyPoints: Flush removes heat, keeps faces wet, prevents flashing and sweeps away solids.
Clean service often uses recirculation from the pump; dirty service uses external clean injection.
Seal piping plan numbers (API 682) are a common shorthand; the seal datasheet states the plan.
Packing seal water must be above stuffing box pressure.
topics.caution: Do not isolate, re-route or resize flush lines without consulting the seal manufacturer. A blocked or closed flush is a common cause of seal failure.

topics.title: Common causes of seal failure
topics.body:
Most mechanical seal failures are caused by the conditions around the seal rather than by the seal itself.

Dry running: starting without priming, an air-bound casing or seal chamber that was not vented, loss of suction, or running against a closed suction valve. Face damage can occur very quickly.

Flush problems: blocked orifices or strainers, closed valves, a failed external supply or the wrong piping plan, leading to overheating and vaporisation at the faces.

Solids and deposits: abrasive particles wearing the faces, or crystals and deposits that clog springs and hang up pusher secondary seals.

Mechanical causes: misalignment between pump and motor, pipe strain, excessive shaft runout or end play, worn bearings, and vibration from unbalance or cavitation.

Operation: running far from the best efficiency point, which increases shaft deflection and vibration; cavitation; and pressure or temperature outside the seal's design.

Installation errors: wrong setting length, dirty or damaged faces, wrong or damaged O-rings, incompatible fitting lubricants, uneven gland tightening, cartridge setting clips left in place, and a step or protruding gasket at the split-case chamber face.

Chemical and thermal attack: elastomers incompatible with the liquid or temperature, and thermal shock to brittle faces.

For packing, the equivalent problems are overtightening, loss of seal water, poor installation, worn sleeves and abrasive liquids. Examining the failed parts, especially the wear pattern on the faces, usually reveals which of these was the cause.
keyPoints: Dry running and flush failures are leading causes.
Misalignment, vibration, pipe strain and off-BEP operation shorten seal life.
Installation errors include wrong setting, contamination and leaving cartridge clips in place.
Read the failed faces to identify the root cause.

topics.title: Torque transmission
topics.body:
The coupling transmits the motor's torque to the pump. Torque, power and speed are related by T = P / ω, where ω = 2πN / 60 is the angular speed in rad/s for a speed N in rpm. For a given power, a slower pump transmits more torque, which is why large, slow split case pumps need relatively large couplings and shafts.

The torque path runs from the motor rotor through the motor shaft, the motor key and hub, the first flexible element, the spacer, the second flexible element, the pump hub and key, and into the pump shaft, which carries it to the impeller. Keys transmit torque through shear and bearing pressure on their sides; in some designs hubs are mounted by an interference fit that carries torque by friction, with or without a key.

The coupling must carry the steady operating torque and also transient torques. A direct-on-line start, for example, can produce a starting torque well above the running torque for a short time, and torsional excitation may arise from the driver or the driven system. Coupling manufacturers allow for this through selection factors that depend on the driver, the driven machine and the duty.

Coupling size, type, bore fits and fastener tightening values come from the coupling manufacturer and the OEM. A coupling that has been under-selected, or assembled with the wrong bolts, can fail suddenly, which is one reason the guard must always be in place.
keyPoints: T = P / ω, with ω = 2πN / 60.
Torque path: motor shaft, key, hub, flexible elements and spacer, hub, key, pump shaft.
Couplings must also handle starting and transient torques.
Selection, fits and bolt torques come from the coupling manufacturer.

topics.title: What a flexible coupling does
topics.body:
A flexible coupling transmits torque while accommodating small amounts of angular, parallel and axial misalignment between two shafts. Some types also damp torsional vibration and shock. It cannot make poor alignment harmless: misalignment still produces reaction forces and moments on the bearings, wears or fatigues the flexible element, and causes vibration and heat. The coupling's misalignment capacity is for small changes in service, such as thermal growth and settling, not for installation errors.

A spacer coupling has two flexible planes separated by a spacer. This lets it take parallel offset as a small angle at each plane, and removing the spacer gives access to the drive-end seal and bearing housing, or allows the rotor to be lifted out, without moving the motor.

Common element types differ in important ways. Elastomeric couplings (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) are tolerant and damp vibration, but the elements age and wear, and some are not fail-safe if the element fails. Disc couplings use flexing stainless steel laminations; they need no lubrication and have low maintenance, but have limited misalignment capacity and definite axial stiffness, so their axial setting matters. Gear couplings carry high torque for their size, but need lubrication and can lock up and transmit axial force if the teeth wear or the lubricant fails. Grid couplings use a spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, offer some damping and need lubrication.

Allowable misalignment and service requirements are given in the coupling manufacturer's data.
keyPoints: Flexible couplings accommodate small misalignment; they do not make poor alignment acceptable.
Spacer couplings have two flexible planes and allow maintenance without moving the motor.
Elastomeric, disc, gear and grid types differ in damping, lubrication, stiffness and failure behaviour.
Allowable misalignment comes from the coupling manufacturer.

topics.title: Angular misalignment
topics.body:
Angular misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines meet at an angle instead of lying on one straight line. It is usually described separately in the vertical and horizontal planes, and is commonly expressed as the difference in gap measured across the coupling face divided by the diameter at which it was measured, or as a slope.

As the shafts rotate, angular misalignment makes the flexible element bend back and forth once per revolution. In a spacer coupling the angle is taken at the two flexible planes. The effects include cyclic stress and wear in the element, extra reaction moments at the coupling-end bearings, heat in elastomeric elements, and vibration, typically with significant axial components at once and twice running speed.

Angularity in the vertical plane is corrected by changing the shims under the front and rear feet of the movable machine (normally the motor) by different amounts. Horizontal angularity is corrected by moving the front and rear of the movable machine sideways by different amounts, using the jacking screws. Because angular and parallel corrections interact, alignment calculations or alignment tools work out the moves needed at each foot.

Acceptable angular misalignment depends on speed and coupling type and must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.
keyPoints: Shaft centrelines meet at an angle.
Causes cyclic flexing of the element and axial vibration.
Vertical angularity is corrected with differential shims; horizontal with sideways moves.
Tolerances come from the OEM, coupling manufacturer or site standard.

topics.title: Parallel (offset) misalignment
topics.body:
Parallel, or offset, misalignment exists when the two shaft centrelines are parallel but displaced from each other. Like angularity, it is described in the vertical and horizontal planes and is measured at a stated position, usually at the coupling or at the flexible planes.

In a spacer coupling, offset is taken up as an angle at each flexible plane. For small angles that angle is approximately the offset divided by the distance between the flexible planes, so for the same offset a longer spacer gives a smaller angle at each element. Real installations normally have a combination of offset and angularity in both planes.

Offset causes radial forces on the coupling-end bearings and cyclic loading of the element, and typically shows as radial vibration at once and twice running speed. It also adds to seal and bearing problems through shaft deflection.

Vertical offset is corrected by adding or removing equal shim thickness under all feet of the movable machine. Horizontal offset is corrected by moving the whole movable machine sideways with the jacking screws.

Pump and motor shafts often grow by different amounts as they reach operating temperature, so the cold alignment target may deliberately include an offset that disappears when the machines are hot. Any such allowance must come from the OEM, and acceptable offset from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site alignment standard.
keyPoints: Shaft centrelines are parallel but displaced.
In a spacer coupling, angle at each flexible plane is roughly offset divided by the distance between planes.
Vertical offset is corrected with equal shims; horizontal offset by moving the motor sideways.
Cold alignment targets may include an OEM-specified thermal growth allowance.

topics.title: Axial misalignment, end float and axial spacing
topics.body:
Axial misalignment means the shafts are not at the correct axial spacing. The coupling manufacturer specifies a distance between shaft ends, or a gap between hubs, that suits the spacer and flexible elements, often with an allowable range.

The pump rotor's axial position is fixed by its locating bearing, and the motor rotor's by the motor's own bearings. Each rotor still has some end float, and both shafts grow as they warm up, so the actual spacing changes between cold and hot conditions.

The effect of a wrong spacing depends on the coupling type. Disc couplings have definite axial stiffness, so incorrect spacing pre-stresses the discs, shortens their fatigue life and pushes an axial force into the pump's locating bearing and the motor bearings. Gear couplings allow axial sliding, but under torque the teeth can lock, transmitting axial force. Elastomeric couplings tolerate some axial variation, but compressing or stretching the element shortens its life.

Motors with sleeve bearings have a magnetic centre: the rotor tends to run at a particular axial position within its end float. For such motors the coupling must be set with the motor at its magnetic centre, and limited-end-float couplings are often used to keep the motor rotor within its float. The typical rolling-bearing TEFC motor shown in the model is located axially by its own bearings.

Set the spacing to the coupling manufacturer's and OEM's values, and check it when the spacer is refitted.
keyPoints: Shaft-end spacing is specified by the coupling manufacturer.
End float and thermal growth change the spacing in service.
Wrong spacing pre-stresses disc couplings and can load the thrust bearing.
Sleeve-bearing motors must be coupled at their magnetic centre.

topics.title: Alignment procedures
topics.body:
Shaft alignment brings the motor shaft into line with the pump shaft within the tolerance specified by the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard. The pump is usually the stationary machine, since it is connected to the piping, and the motor is moved.

Preparation comes first: isolate and lock out the driver, clean feet and pads, check that the baseplate is grouted and the pipework connected without strain, and check hub runout. Then check soft foot: with indicators or an alignment system on the shafts, slacken each hold-down bolt in turn and correct any foot that moves, whether by parallel gap, angular gap or a springy shim pack. Measuring alignment with soft foot present gives unreliable results.

The main measuring methods are:

Rim and face: one dial indicator reads the hub rim (offset), another the hub face (angularity); face readings are affected by axial float.

Reverse indicator: rim readings are taken on both hubs from brackets on the opposite shaft. It is less affected by axial float and suits spacer couplings and longer spans. Indicator bracket sag must be measured and allowed for.

Laser alignment: laser emitters and detectors on both shafts calculate offset, angularity and the corrections at each foot directly.

Correct vertical misalignment with shims and horizontal misalignment with the jacking screws, then re-measure. Apply any thermal growth allowance that the OEM specifies. Record the final readings, then re-check after the piping is finally connected and, where specified, after a hot run.
keyPoints: Check soft foot and pipe strain before aligning.
Rim and face, reverse indicator and laser methods are all in common use.
Allow for indicator bracket sag and the OEM's thermal growth offsets.
Record results and re-check after piping connection and, where specified, hot running.
topics.caution: Alignment work is done with the driver isolated and locked out. Numerical alignment tolerances must come from the OEM, the coupling manufacturer or the site standard, not from this module.

topics.title: Coupling guard safety
topics.body:
Rotating couplings and shaft ends are among the most dangerous parts of a pump set. They can catch clothing, hair, gloves, rags or tools in a fraction of a second, causing entanglement, amputation or death. At operating speed a coupling can look blurred or almost stationary, which misleads people about the danger.

The coupling guard is a fixed guard: it is fastened so that it can only be removed with a tool, it covers the coupling and all exposed shaft between the bearing housing and the motor, and any openings are sized and placed so that fingers and hands cannot reach rotating parts. Machinery safety regulations and standards require such guarding; safety-distance standards such as ISO 13857 relate opening sizes to reach distances. In potentially explosive atmospheres, guard materials and clearances may also need to meet hazardous-area requirements so that contact cannot cause sparks.

Rules that apply on every site:

Never run the pump with the guard removed, open or damaged.

Remove the guard only after the driver has been electrically isolated and locked out under the permit system, and zero energy has been verified. Consider also that liquid flowing back through the pump can turn the rotor.

Refit and secure the guard before the isolation is removed and before any test run.

For an uncoupled motor rotation check, remove or secure the motor key and keep clear of the shaft end.

Check the guard on rounds for security, damage and rubbing marks.
keyPoints: Rotating couplings cause severe entanglement injuries.
The guard is fixed, tool-removable only, and covers all exposed rotating parts.
Remove it only under isolation and lockout; refit before any run.
Secure or remove the motor key for uncoupled rotation checks.
topics.caution: The 3D viewer can hide or make the guard transparent for learning purposes. A real pump must never be operated without its guard fitted and secure.

topics.title: Importance of foundation stiffness
topics.body:
The foundation's job is to hold the pump and motor so steadily that alignment does not change and vibration is not amplified. It must carry the static weight of the machines, baseplate and liquid; react the torque between pump and motor; resist the dynamic forces from residual unbalance and hydraulic pulsation; and take any loads that the piping applies.

Stiffness and mass work together. A stiff, massive foundation deflects little under load, so the shafts stay aligned, and it raises the natural frequencies of the installed system. Ideally those natural frequencies are well separated from running speed and its main multiples, because operating near a resonance can turn a small force into large vibration. A flexible or lightweight foundation, or one standing on soft or settling ground, lets the baseplate move and the alignment drift.

The baseplate alone is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to the foundation so that both act as one body. Many installations isolate the foundation block from the surrounding floor slab with a joint, so that vibration is not passed to the building and other machines do not shake the pump.

Rules of thumb relating foundation mass to machine mass are often quoted, but foundation design should follow the OEM's loading data, the applicable guidance and the work of a civil or structural engineer.
keyPoints: The foundation keeps alignment stable and prevents vibration amplification.
Stiffness and mass reduce deflection and help keep natural frequencies away from running speed.
The baseplate becomes stiff only when it is properly grouted to the foundation.
Foundation design is a site-specific engineering task.

topics.title: Grouting
topics.body:
Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation. When it is placed correctly it makes full contact with both surfaces, spreads the load, bonds the baseplate to the foundation so they behave as one stiff structure, adds damping and protects the underside of the baseplate.

The usual sequence is: prepare the foundation surface by removing the weak top layer to sound concrete and cleaning it; set the baseplate on its levelling screws or packers and level it as the OEM specifies; build formwork; prepare anchor bolt sleeves and protect the levelling screw threads; then place the grout through the grout holes, working from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, until the space is completely filled. The grout is then cured as its manufacturer specifies.

Epoxy grouts generally offer higher strength, better bond and better resistance to oil and chemicals, and cure quickly, but they are sensitive to temperature during placement and cure and are more expensive. Non-shrink cementitious grouts are cheaper and simpler to use but need careful curing, and they are attacked by oil over time.

After curing, the baseplate is tapped to find hollow-sounding voids, which are filled by injection as the grout manufacturer recommends. Only then are the anchor bolts tightened and, in many procedures, the levelling screws backed off so the grout carries the load. Alignment is then checked again.

Factory pre-grouted baseplates reduce the risk of voids under the deck but still need field grouting.
keyPoints: Grout gives full, void-free load transfer and bonds baseplate to foundation.
Surface preparation, venting and curing are critical.
Epoxy and cementitious grouts each have advantages and limitations.
Check for voids, then tighten anchor bolts and re-check alignment.
topics.caution: Grout materials, thicknesses, temperatures and curing times must come from the grout manufacturer, the OEM and the project specification.

topics.title: Alignment and the baseplate
topics.body:
Good shaft alignment depends on a good baseplate installation; the baseplate is the reference to which both machines are bolted.

Before grouting, the baseplate is levelled and its machined pads checked for flatness and co-planarity, against values from the OEM, using levelling screws or packers. If the pads are twisted or uneven, the machines will distort when they are bolted down, producing soft foot that no amount of alignment can correct. After grouting and anchor bolt tightening the pads are checked again, because grouting and bolting can shift the baseplate.

The pump is normally fixed first as the stationary machine, because the piping will be attached to it; its feet should sit on the pads with little or no shimming. The motor is the movable machine. Its pads are often slightly low so that it sits on a shim pack, allowing adjustment both up and down, and the jacking screws on the baseplate allow controlled sideways moves.

A typical sequence is: rough alignment before piping is connected; connection of piping without strain; checks for soft foot and pipe strain; precise alignment; and recording of the results. Some sites dowel the machines after final alignment. Alignment is re-checked after commissioning runs and whenever the baseplate, piping or foundation has been disturbed.
keyPoints: Level the baseplate and check pad flatness before and after grouting.
Pump stationary, motor movable on shims and jacking screws.
Connect piping without strain before final alignment.
Re-check alignment after commissioning and any disturbance.

topics.title: Pipe strain
topics.body:
Pipe strain is the force and moment that the connected piping applies to the pump nozzles. It arises when flanges are pulled together that did not line up, when pipes and valves are not properly supported, when thermal expansion is not accommodated, and when expansion joints are left unrestrained.

In a split case pump, nozzle loads act on the lower casing half. Excessive loads can distort the casing, upsetting internal clearances and the split joint; shift the pump on its pads; and move the shaft out of alignment with the motor. The results are bearing overloading, seal failures, coupling wear, vibration and casing joint leaks. An unrestrained expansion joint is especially damaging, because the pressure inside it pushes on the pump with a force equal to the pressure times the joint's effective area.

Good practice is to support the pipes independently near the pump, so that the pump does not carry their weight; to make flanges meet squarely and concentrically, with the right gap, before any bolt is tightened; to restrain expansion joints with tie rods or anchors; and to make the final connection at the pump after the pipework is fixed. A practical check is to mount dial indicators on the coupling, or use the alignment system, and watch for movement while the flange bolts are tightened or loosened; significant movement shows strain that must be corrected in the piping, not by forcing the pump.

Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM.
keyPoints: Pipe strain comes from misfit, poor support, thermal growth and unrestrained expansion joints.
It distorts the casing, disturbs alignment and damages bearings, seals and couplings.
Support piping independently and make flanges meet without forcing.
Check for movement at the coupling while flange bolts are tightened.
topics.caution: Never use the pump as an anchor for the piping, and never pull misaligned flanges together with the bolts.

topics.title: Foundation vibration
topics.body:
Vibration measured on a pump is not always caused by the pump. Weaknesses in the baseplate, grout, anchor bolts or foundation can allow normal forces to produce excessive vibration, or can amplify it through resonance.

Typical causes include voids under the baseplate, cracked or delaminated grout, loose anchor or hold-down bolts, soft foot, a foundation that is too light or flexible, a natural frequency close to running speed or one of its multiples, foundation settlement, and vibration from nearby machines transmitted through a shared floor.

Symptoms include vibration that stays high after balancing and alignment are corrected, vibration that changes greatly with small changes in speed (a sign of resonance), and readings that are higher in one direction, often horizontal, than would be expected.

Investigation compares vibration measured on the machine feet, the baseplate, the grout and the foundation at the same time. A sudden step in amplitude or phase across a joint shows looseness at that joint. An impact (bump) test with the machine stopped identifies natural frequencies. Tap-testing the baseplate locates voids. Checking bolt tightness and soft foot is quick and often revealing.

Corrective action targets the cause: re-grouting or injecting voids, tightening or replacing anchors, correcting soft foot, or stiffening or detuning the structure under engineering guidance. In building services, spring-isolated inertia bases with flexible pipe connectors are sometimes used to limit transmission, but they must be designed for the purpose.
keyPoints: Weak baseplates, grout, anchors or foundations can cause or amplify vibration.
Resonance shows as vibration very sensitive to speed.
Compare readings and phase across feet, baseplate, grout and foundation.
Bump tests find natural frequencies; tap tests find voids.

topics.title: Baseplate deflection
topics.body:
A baseplate must stay flat and stable so that the pump and motor shafts stay aligned. Any deflection or twist between the pump and motor pads appears directly as misalignment.

Deflection can occur at several stages. During lifting and transport, an ungrouted fabricated baseplate is relatively flexible; lifting it at the wrong points, or with equipment mounted when the OEM does not allow it, can bend or twist it. During installation, levelling on too few supports, uneven levelling screws or tightening anchor bolts over voids can distort it. In service, loads from unsupported or strained piping, the reaction torque between pump and motor, and thermal effects (for example a hot pump on one side) can deflect it.

Designers provide stiffness with deep sections, cross members and torsional bracing between the pump and motor pads; pumping standards for some industries specify stiffness requirements or tests. The most important stiffening step on site is correct, void-free grouting, which turns the baseplate and foundation into one body.

On site, check pad flatness and co-planarity after levelling and again after grouting; check that alignment does not change when anchor bolts are tightened, when piping is connected or after the pump has reached operating temperature; and investigate any alignment that repeatedly drifts, since it often points to deflection, a weak foundation or pipe strain.
keyPoints: Deflection between pads appears directly as shaft misalignment.
Lifting, levelling, bolting over voids, pipe loads and heat can all deflect a baseplate.
Correct grouting provides most of the installed stiffness.
Alignment that keeps drifting often points to deflection or pipe strain.
topics.caution: Lift the baseplate only at its designated points and in the condition (empty or with equipment mounted) that the OEM permits.

componentRecords.function: The upper casing half is the top part of the pressure-containing volute casing. It closes the impeller chamber, the upper parts of the volute and suction chambers and the upper halves of both seal chambers, and it can be lifted off in one piece to give access to the complete rotor.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
In operation it is a stationary pressure boundary. Internal pressure acting over its projected area tries to lift it off the lower half; this separating force is resisted by the preloaded joint studs and nuts, while the gasket (or sealing compound, depending on design) seals the joint.

Its internal surfaces form part of the hydraulic passages, so their shape and surface condition influence the velocity and pressure distribution around the impeller in the same way as the lower half.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a single casting with a machined flat split flange, clearance holes for the joint studs, dowel holes, the upper halves of the casing wear-ring bores and seal chamber bores, lifting lugs and vent connections. Bores that are split across the joint are usually finish-machined with both halves bolted and dowelled together, so they are round and concentric only when the halves are correctly reassembled. In this baseline arrangement no suction or discharge piping is attached to the upper half.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Because both nozzles are on the lower half in this arrangement, the upper half can be removed for internal inspection without disconnecting the main piping or disturbing the motor. Its stiffness and the accuracy of its joint face govern how well the joint seals and how round the split bores remain, and therefore how well the wear rings and shaft seals perform. A crack or casting defect in it is a pressure-boundary defect.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the half removed, inspect the joint face for nicks, erosion channels across the sealing land (wire drawing), corrosion and gasket residue, and clean it without scoring. Inspect internal passages for erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage, deposits and coating breakdown, and check the split bores for damage. Lift only with the designated lugs and rated lifting gear, keeping the half level and guided off the dowels so it cannot swing into the impeller or seals. Repairs to a pressure-retaining casting must follow the OEM and site repair procedures.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs place a nozzle on the upper half (for example top discharge), which changes the maintenance advantage described here; always check the specific pump. In the 3D model the wall thickness, ribs and external profile of the upper half are illustrative, not taken from OEM drawings.

componentRecords.function: The upper split flange is the machined flange around the upper casing half that mates with the lower half on the horizontal split plane. It carries the stud and dowel holes, and its machined face forms one side of the sealed casing joint.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: When the joint nuts are tightened the flange is clamped against the gasket and the lower flange. The clamping load must exceed the separating force from internal pressure with enough margin to keep the gasket compressed everywhere, including next to the volute, where the pressure is highest.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the upper half and machined flat. The flange is made thick and wide enough to keep the bolt pitch close and to spread bolt load evenly over the gasket. Bolt holes are clearance holes; accurate location comes from the dowels, not the bolts. Many designs include tapped jacking-screw holes for breaking the joint without levering between the faces.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The flatness and condition of this face directly decide whether the joint seals. Because the joint runs between regions at discharge pressure (around the volute) and regions at suction pressure (around the suction chambers), a poor face can leak internally, bypassing liquid from discharge to suction, as well as externally to atmosphere.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for nicks, radial scratches across the sealing land, erosion paths, corrosion and distortion. Remove old gasket material with non-damaging scrapers and solvent. If leakage or distortion is suspected, check flatness by the method in the OEM or site procedure. Do not file or grind the face: any machining changes the joint thickness and internal fits and must follow the OEM procedure. Never lever the joint apart with chisels or screwdrivers; use the jacking screws.
componentRecords.notes: Flange width, bolt pitch and jacking-screw positions vary between manufacturers. The model shows an illustrative flange with a simplified pattern of 16 joint nuts.

componentRecords.function: These are the upper halves of the two stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the upper casing half at the DE and NDE shaft exits. With the lower halves they form the bores that house the mechanical seals in the baseline configuration, or the gland packing in the packing variant.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Each housing is filled with pumped liquid. In a double-suction pump both seal chambers sit on the suction side of the impeller, so their pressure is related to suction pressure (it also depends on any throat bushing, flush or balance connection). The housing provides the stationary bore and the face to which the seal gland plate or packing gland follower is bolted.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the casing half and machined together with the lower half, so the split bore is concentric with the shaft axis when the casing is assembled. The outer face carries tapped holes for gland studs, and flush or seal-water connections lead into the housing where fitted. Some designs include a throat bushing at the inner end.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Because the housing is split with the casing, its roundness, concentricity and face squareness depend on correct dowelling, gasket thickness and joint bolt tightening. Distortion or misalignment of this bore is a direct cause of seal face misalignment, packing wear and leakage. Integral split housings allow the upper half to be lifted after the seal glands are released, with the seals staying on the shaft sleeves.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the upper half removed, inspect the bore, gland face and the split line at the housing for corrosion, erosion, scoring and gasket intrusion, and confirm flush passages are clear. After the casing is closed, check bore concentricity and face squareness relative to the shaft where the OEM or seal supplier requires it, using their method and limits.
componentRecords.notes: Housing geometry differs between packed and mechanical-seal designs, and some pumps use separate bolted seal chambers or covers instead of integral split housings. The model uses one housing shape for both sealing variants; only the seal or packing inside it changes. Never fit a mechanical seal and packing in the same housing.

componentRecords.function: The lifting lugs on the upper casing half are the designated attachment points for slings or shackles when the upper half is lifted off and refitted.
componentRecords.construction: Typically cast integral lugs, or bosses with tapped holes for eyebolts, positioned so that the upper half hangs approximately level when lifted on correctly rigged slings.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: They are intended for the weight of the upper casing half only. Using them to lift the complete pump, or the pump on its baseplate, can overload them and is a serious, common safety error; the complete pump is lifted only by the method shown in the OEM manual. A level lift lets the half rise squarely off the dowels without binding or swinging into the impeller and seals.
componentRecords.maintenance: Before every lift, inspect the lugs for cracks, corrosion and damage, and inspect eyebolt threads where used. Use rated lifting gear with correct sling angles under a lifting plan prepared to site procedure. Lift slowly at first to confirm the joint has fully released, and never stand or place hands under a suspended casing half.
componentRecords.notes: Lug type, number and position vary between designs. The model shows two illustrative lugs; their size is not a rating.

componentRecords.function: Vent connections at the high points of the upper casing allow trapped air or gas to escape when the pump is filled (primed) and before start-up.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Air collects at the highest points of the casing, typically the top of the volute and the upper parts of the suction chambers. Opening the vents while the pump is filled from the suction side lets the air out until a steady stream of liquid without bubbles appears, so the pump starts full of liquid.
componentRecords.construction: Usually tapped connections fitted with plugs, small valves or cocks, sometimes piped to a drain or safe location. Size and position are design-specific.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Starting with trapped air can cause loss of prime, little or no discharge, and dry running of the mechanical seals or packing and of the wear rings. For hot, toxic or flammable liquids the vents must be piped to a safe place and operated only under the site procedure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that vent plugs or valves are free, not blocked by deposits or paint, and leak-tight when closed. Vent the pump before every start-up after it has been drained or opened. Replace damaged plugs and thread sealants with items suitable for the liquid.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs vent the seal chambers separately, and in some installations venting is done through high-point vents on the piping. Vent positions in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: In the double-volute variant, this is the upper part of the splitter rib that divides the volute into two passages with their tongues roughly opposite each other. Each passage collects flow from approximately half of the impeller circumference.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a single volute operating away from the best efficiency point (BEP), the pressure around the impeller is not uniform, so a net radial force acts on the impeller. With two symmetrically arranged passages, the pressure distributions of the two halves are approximately opposed and a large part of this force cancels. Cancellation is not complete, because the two passages differ in their path to the single discharge nozzle.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the upper casing half and matched at the split plane to the lower part of the rib. The rib forms a second cutwater; its leading-edge shape, its gap to the impeller and the match of the two rib halves across the joint all matter hydraulically.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Lower radial load means less shaft deflection and bending stress, lower bearing loads and better protection of wear rings and mechanical seals, which is valuable for larger pumps and for duties that run over a wide flow range. The penalties are a more complex casting, slightly more wetted surface and narrower passages that are harder to inspect and clean.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the rib leading edge for erosion, cavitation damage, cracks and build-up of debris or fibrous material, and check that the upper and lower rib halves meet at the joint without a large step. Damage to or loss of the rib changes radial loading and can increase vibration.
componentRecords.notes: Present only when the double-volute variant is selected. Double volutes are common in larger split case pumps but are not universal. The rib shape and wrap angle in the model are simplified and illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The lower casing half is the main body of the pump. It contains the lower parts of the volute, suction chambers, impeller chamber and seal chambers, carries the suction and discharge nozzles, supports both bearing housings and is bolted to the baseplate through its feet.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Liquid enters through the suction nozzle, is divided into two side suction chambers leading to the two impeller eyes, and leaves through the volute and the discharge nozzle; most of these passages are formed in this half. Mechanically it is the stationary pressure boundary and the structural backbone of the pump: it reacts the weight of the pump and rotor, nozzle loads from the piping, and the radial and axial forces passed to it by the bearing housings.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a single casting with integral suction and discharge nozzles, feet, bearing brackets and the lower halves of the seal housings and wear-ring bores. Its machined split face is the reference plane for the joint, and bores split across the joint are generally finish-machined with the upper half bolted on. Drain and pressure-tapping connections are usually located on this half.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: With both nozzles on the lower half, it stays connected to the piping and fixed to the baseplate during internal maintenance, so pump-to-motor alignment is largely undisturbed when the upper half and rotor are removed. Excessive piping loads on its nozzles can distort it, disturbing bore alignment, bearing housing alignment and coupling alignment. The casting quality of its internal passages strongly affects hydraulic performance and suction behaviour.
componentRecords.maintenance: During internal inspection examine the volute, tongue, suction chambers and split face for erosion, corrosion, cavitation pitting and deposits, and confirm drains and tappings are clear. Check feet and hold-down bolts for cracks and looseness. Check for pipe strain, for example by monitoring coupling alignment with dial indicators or a laser system while nozzle flange bolts are released, as described in the site procedure. Pressure-boundary repairs must follow OEM and site procedures.
componentRecords.notes: Nozzle positions, foot arrangements and bracket designs vary between manufacturers. In the model the suction chambers and volute are simplified shapes with illustrative proportions; they are not OEM hydraulic profiles.

componentRecords.function: The lower split flange is the machined flange of the lower casing half on which the gasket is laid and the upper half is seated. It carries the tapped holes for the joint studs and the dowel holes.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It forms the reference side of the joint. Stud preload clamps the upper flange and gasket against it; internal pressure acts to separate the two faces, and the joint stays sealed only while enough gasket compression remains along its full length.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the lower half and machined flat in the same set-up as the main bores. In many designs the joint studs are screwed into tapped holes in this flange and remain in place when the upper half is lifted. The internal edges follow the outline of the volute, suction chambers, wear-ring bores and seal housings.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: As the fixed reference face, its flatness and condition set the quality of every reassembly. Thread damage in its tapped holes reduces the preload the studs can carry. Erosion channels across it from past internal leakage between the volute and the suction chambers reduce efficiency and get worse with time.
componentRecords.maintenance: Clean old gasket material without scoring, inspect for nicks, erosion and corrosion, and protect the exposed face while the upper half is off (for example with a clean cover) so tools and parts are not dropped on it. Inspect tapped stud holes and dowel holes. Any machining repair must follow the OEM procedure because it changes joint thickness and internal fits.
componentRecords.notes: Whether studs are fixed in the lower flange or through-bolts are used depends on the design. The model's flange is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The suction nozzle is the flanged inlet cast on the lower casing half. It receives liquid from the suction pipe and delivers it to the internal suction passages, where the flow divides towards the two impeller eyes.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Liquid arrives here at the lowest pressure in the system on the pump side. The nozzle and the passages just downstream accelerate the flow gently towards the splitter. Whatever velocity profile and swirl the upstream piping produces is carried into the casing, so the piping arrangement affects how evenly the flow divides between the two eyes.
componentRecords.construction: Horizontal and on the opposite side of the casing from the discharge nozzle (side suction, side discharge), cast integral with the lower half. It is usually larger than the discharge nozzle to keep inlet velocity low. The flange is drilled to the specified flange standard and rating, and a pressure tapping is normally provided close to it.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is the reference point for suction pressure and NPSH available, and the place where suction pipe loads enter the casing. Fittings close to it, especially an elbow lying in a plane parallel to the shaft, can send more liquid to one eye than the other, which raises the local NPSH required on that side and causes uneven loading, noise and vibration. Leaks at the suction flange gasket are a common route for air ingress when suction pressure is below atmospheric.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the flange joint for air or liquid leaks, inspect the nozzle bore for erosion, corrosion and debris during internal inspection, and confirm that pipe supports carry the suction pipe so the nozzle is not acting as an anchor. Where a suction strainer is fitted, monitor its pressure drop and keep it clean.
componentRecords.notes: Upstream straight lengths, reducer type and elbow orientation should follow the OEM and recognised intake and piping guidance; a common practice on horizontal suction lines is an eccentric reducer installed flat side up to avoid an air pocket. Some designs use top suction. Nozzle proportions in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The discharge nozzle is the flanged outlet on the lower casing half that leads liquid from the volute throat to the discharge pipe.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Downstream of the volute throat the passage normally diverges like a diffuser, slowing the liquid and converting part of its remaining kinetic energy into static pressure before the flange. The whole nozzle is at discharge pressure.
componentRecords.construction: Horizontal, cast integral with the lower half on the side opposite the suction nozzle. It is usually smaller than the suction nozzle. The flange is made to the specified standard and pressure rating, with a pressure tapping normally provided near it.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Pressure measured here, corrected for gauge elevation and velocity head, is used with suction pressure to determine the head the pump is producing. Discharge pipe weight, thermal expansion and reaction forces must be carried by supports and anchors, not by the nozzle; excessive nozzle loads can distort the casing and disturb internal and coupling alignment. Isolation and non-return valves are installed in the discharge pipework, not on the nozzle itself.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the flange joint and bolting for leaks, check pipe supports and expansion arrangements, and inspect the internal diffusing section for erosion, corrosion and deposits during internal inspection.
componentRecords.notes: Allowable nozzle loads are given by the OEM, and by the applicable pump standard where the pump is built to one. Some designs use top or angled discharge. The diffuser shape of the model nozzle is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: These are the lower halves of the DE and NDE stuffing box / seal chamber housings, cast integral with the lower casing half. With the upper halves they complete the bores for the mechanical seals (baseline) or gland packing (variant).
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Together with the upper halves they contain liquid at a pressure related to suction pressure and provide the stationary bore and gland face for the sealing arrangement. Because they stay with the lower half, they also support the seal or packing while the upper half is removed.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the lower half and machined with the upper half in place. In many designs a drain or leakage-collection arrangement is provided below the gland area to lead away packing leakage or any seal leakage. Flush, seal-water or quench connections may enter through either half depending on design.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Their alignment with the upper halves depends on the dowels, gasket and joint bolting, so a poorly assembled casing can produce an oval or stepped seal bore. Blocked leakage drains let liquid accumulate and reach the deflectors and bearing housings.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the bore and gland face for corrosion, erosion and scoring; clear leakage drains and flush passages; check gland stud threads. Check the split line at the housing for a step or gasket intrusion after reassembly.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs use separate bolted seal chamber covers. The model uses one illustrative housing shape for both sealing variants.

componentRecords.function: The bearing brackets are cast extensions of the lower casing half at each end that support the DE and NDE bearing housings and hold them, and therefore the shaft, concentric with the casing bores.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: They transfer rotor weight and radial loads from both bearings, and residual axial thrust from the NDE locating bearing, into the casing and from there to the baseplate. Because the bearing housings bolt onto them, they define where the shaft axis sits relative to the wear-ring and seal bores.
componentRecords.construction: Integral with the lower half, with machined seating faces and holes for the bearing housing hold-down bolts. Many designs use dowels, spigots or locating faces so the bearing housings return to the same position after removal; some include adjusting or jacking screws for setting rotor height and centring.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Bracket stiffness and machining accuracy affect rotor centring in the casing, the uniformity of wear-ring clearances, seal alignment and vibration behaviour. Because the bearing housings remain on the lower half brackets, the upper casing half can be removed without disturbing the bearings.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect seating faces for damage, corrosion and fretting marks (which can indicate looseness), and check dowels and hold-down bolts. Make sure faces are clean before refitting the bearing housings, then check rotor centring and free rotation by the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Some pumps use separate bolted brackets or pedestals rather than integral brackets. The bracket shape in the model is simplified.

componentRecords.function: The casing feet are the mounting pads by which the pump casing is bolted to the pump mounting pads on the baseplate.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: They carry the pump weight, nozzle loads and dynamic forces into the baseplate and foundation. When the pump runs hot, the casing grows thermally from its supports, so the height of the feet relative to the shaft centreline influences how much the shaft rises.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the lower half (in this model) and machined on their underside, with holes for hold-down bolts and, in many installations, provision for dowelling to the baseplate after final alignment. Some designs place the supports near the shaft centreline height (centreline mounting) to limit vertical shaft movement from thermal expansion.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Uneven support (soft foot) distorts the casing when the hold-down bolts are tightened, changing alignment and internal clearances. Loose or cracked feet can lead to vibration and misalignment.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check hold-down bolt tightness per the site procedure, check for soft foot during alignment, inspect feet for cracks and corrosion, and use clean, flat shims of the correct size, kept to as few as practical. Recheck coupling alignment whenever the feet are disturbed.
componentRecords.notes: The model shows foot-mounted lower-half feet with illustrative geometry. Centreline-supported arrangements are more common in hot services.

componentRecords.function: Drain connections at the low points of the lower casing allow the pump to be fully drained before maintenance, to protect an idle pump from freezing, or to flush out deposits.
componentRecords.construction: Tapped connections with plugs, or piped connections with valves, located at the low points of the volute and suction chambers. Their number and size vary with design.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Complete draining is needed before the casing joint is broken so that liquid does not spill and hazardous liquids can be handled safely. Liquid trapped in a stand-by pump can freeze and crack the casing or promote corrosion and settling of solids.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check drain plugs and valves for leaks and blockage. Before opening the pump: isolate it electrically and hydraulically, relieve pressure, drain through the drains to a safe collection point and confirm the casing is empty and depressurised, following the site lockout and permit procedures.
componentRecords.notes: Positions shown in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: Pressure tapping connections close to the suction and discharge flanges allow gauges or transmitters to measure the pressures used to determine pump head and NPSH available.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Pump total head is the difference in total head between the discharge and suction measuring points: H = (p2 - p1) / (rho g) + (z2 - z1) + (v2^2 - v1^2) / (2g), where p is static gauge pressure, z the elevation of each gauge reference point, v the mean velocity in the pipe at that point, rho the liquid density and g gravitational acceleration. Taking readings close to the flanges keeps pipe friction out of the result.
componentRecords.construction: Small tapped connections in the nozzles, usually fitted with plugs, isolation valves or gauge assemblies, with pulsation dampers (snubbers) where needed.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Without reliable suction and discharge readings, operators cannot confirm where the pump is running on its curve, detect wear-ring wear (falling head at a known flow), or diagnose low suction pressure and cavitation risk.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep tappings and gauge lines clear of deposits and vented of air, use calibrated instruments, and record each gauge's elevation relative to a common datum. Take readings with isolation valves fully open and the pump at steady conditions.
componentRecords.notes: Formal performance tests follow recognised test standards with specified measurement sections and instrumentation; site tappings are for operational monitoring. Tapping positions in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: In the double-volute variant, this is the lower part of the splitter rib. It continues the dividing wall between the two volute passages and guides one of the passages around to join the other before the common discharge nozzle.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: With the upper part of the rib, it creates a second volute passage whose tongue is roughly opposite the main tongue. The two passages develop approximately opposing pressure distributions around the impeller, so much of the net radial force, which in a single volute grows as operation moves away from BEP, cancels. Some residual radial force remains.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the lower casing half and matched at the split plane to the upper rib. Its surfaces form walls of two passages, so casting accuracy on both faces matters.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: By reducing radial load, the rib helps limit shaft deflection at the wear rings and seals and reduces bearing loads. Because the lower rib is a long, thin wall inside the casing, it must be robust enough for pressure differences across it and for any solids carried by the liquid.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for erosion, cavitation at the leading edge, cracks at the rib roots and blockage of the narrower passages by debris. Check the joint match with the upper rib.
componentRecords.notes: Present only in the double-volute variant. The rib wrap and passage shapes in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The volute tongue (cutwater) is the point where the volute wall comes closest to the impeller and separates the start of the volute spiral from the discharge throat. This marker identifies its location on the lower casing half.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: At design flow the tongue divides the stream cleanly: liquid leaving the impeller either passes into the throat towards discharge or continues around the spiral. Away from design flow the liquid meets the tongue at an angle, causing incidence losses, local high velocity, pressure fluctuations and, at low flow, recirculation around the tongue. Each vane passing the tongue produces a pressure pulse at vane passing frequency, equal to the number of vanes multiplied by the rotational speed.
componentRecords.construction: Cast as part of the volute in the lower casing half in this model. Its leading-edge radius, angle and radial gap from the impeller outer diameter are hydraulic design choices.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The tongue gap is a compromise: a very small gap increases pressure pulsations, noise and vibration and can damage vane tips; a large gap tends to increase recirculation and reduce efficiency. Trimming the impeller diameter increases this gap. Erosion or cavitation damage at the tongue changes performance and pulsation levels.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the tongue for erosion, cavitation pitting, cracking and build-up of debris or fibrous material on its edge. Record the impeller-to-tongue gap where the OEM requires it, and take the tongue gap into account before any impeller trim.
componentRecords.notes: A double-volute casing has two tongues. The tongue's angular position relative to the split plane varies between designs. This entry is annotation geometry; the tongue shape in the model is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The casing joint gasket seals the horizontal split joint between the upper and lower casing halves, preventing leakage to atmosphere and internal leakage between high-pressure and low-pressure regions along the joint.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Bolt preload compresses the gasket so that it fills the small irregularities of the two flange faces. Internal pressure then acts to separate the faces; the joint stays sealed as long as enough residual compression remains on the gasket everywhere along its length.
componentRecords.construction: Commonly a thin sheet gasket cut to the profile of the joint face, with holes for studs and dowels and cut-outs around the internal passages. It must be trimmed accurately at the wear-ring and seal-housing bores. Some designs instead use a metal-to-metal joint with a liquid sealing compound, or O-ring seals in grooves.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Gasket material and thickness are part of the pump design: thickness affects how components held in the split bores (such as casing wear rings and seal housings) are clamped, and the roundness of those bores. A wrong, reused or poorly trimmed gasket can leak, protrude into the hydraulic passages or seal bores, or distort internal fits.
componentRecords.maintenance: Replace the gasket every time the joint is opened, using the OEM-specified material and thickness. Clean and inspect both faces, lay the gasket without wrinkles or overlaps, and trim it at the bores only as the OEM instructs. Use jointing compounds or adhesives only if the OEM permits them. Check for external leaks after start-up.
componentRecords.notes: Material choice depends on the liquid, temperature and pressure and is made by the OEM. The model shows a uniform thin sheet with simplified cut-outs.

componentRecords.function: Casing joint bolting is the group of studs, nuts, washers and dowel pins that clamp and locate the upper casing half on the lower half.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The studs and nuts provide the preload that compresses the gasket and holds the joint closed against internal pressure; the dowel pins provide accurate location. These are separate jobs: bolts clamp, dowels locate.
componentRecords.construction: In many designs studs are screwed into the lower flange and pass through clearance holes in the upper flange, with nuts and washers on top; dowels are fitted near opposite ends of the joint.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The bolting is part of the pressure-retaining system. Wrong material, damaged threads, uneven preload or missing fasteners can cause joint leakage, casing distortion and internal rubs, and in the worst case loss of containment.
componentRecords.maintenance: Follow the OEM removal and tightening sequences and values using calibrated tools; inspect fasteners and replace damaged ones with parts of the correct specification. Locate the upper half on the dowels before tightening any nut.
componentRecords.notes: Fastener number, size and grade are OEM-specific. This is a logical group; its meshes are those of the studs, nuts and dowels.

componentRecords.function: The casing joint studs pass from the lower flange through the upper split flange and carry the clamping force that holds the casing joint together.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Tightening the nuts stretches each stud elastically so it acts like a stiff spring clamping the flanges. The stud tension (preload) must stay high enough to keep the gasket compressed when internal pressure adds its separating force, while remaining within the stud's allowable stress.
componentRecords.construction: Threaded studs screwed into tapped holes in the lower half, or through-bolts in some designs. Diameter, thread engagement and material grade are set by the OEM; material is chosen for strength and, where needed, for corrosion resistance and temperature.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: For a given tightening torque the preload achieved depends strongly on thread and nut-face friction, so thread condition and lubrication matter as much as the torque value. An overloaded or corroded stud can yield or crack; an under-tightened one lets the joint open and leak.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect threads for damage, corrosion and galling, and look for necking or bending; replace doubtful studs with ones of the correct specification. Clean tapped holes. Lubricate threads only with the lubricant named in the procedure, because it changes the preload obtained. Avoid removing studs from the lower half unless necessary.
componentRecords.notes: Some pumps use bolts instead of studs. Thread form and length in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The nuts and washers on the joint studs are tightened to apply clamping preload to the casing joint, and are removed in a defined order when the upper half is to be lifted.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Turning a nut against its washer stretches the stud. A hard, flat washer face gives a consistent friction surface so that tightening torque converts to preload more predictably.
componentRecords.construction: Hexagon nuts with washers in many designs, with material matched to the studs. In the model there are 16 nuts, numbered for the removal and tightening sequence used in the maintenance simulator.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Uneven nut tightening distorts the upper half and gasket, leaving leakage paths and out-of-round bores. Tightening in several passes, in the OEM sequence, brings the joint together evenly.
componentRecords.maintenance: Remove nuts in the sequence given by the OEM or site procedure. On reassembly, inspect nut and washer faces and threads, lubricate as specified, and tighten in several passes to the OEM value with a calibrated tool, recording or marking each completed pass. Confirm that the rotor still turns freely by hand afterwards.
componentRecords.notes: The nut numbering in the simulator is an illustrative teaching sequence, not a specific manufacturer's sequence.

componentRecords.function: The dowel pins locate the upper casing half accurately on the lower half so that the split bores and internal passages line up the same way every time the casing is reassembled.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: A dowel is a closely fitting pin in matching holes made through both flanges when the halves were machined together. It prevents sideways and endwise movement of the upper half and restores its original position. The joint studs, which pass through clearance holes, cannot do this.
componentRecords.construction: Typically two dowels near opposite ends of the joint, either parallel or taper pins. Taper dowels, and many parallel ones, have a threaded end or tapped hole so they can be withdrawn with an extractor.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Correct location keeps the casing wear-ring bores and seal housings round and concentric with the rotor, keeps the two halves of the volute and suction chambers aligned without steps, and stops the joint shifting under load. Missing or damaged dowels can lead to wear-ring rubs, seal failures and joint leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Withdraw dowels before lifting the upper half when the design requires it, using the proper extractor rather than hammering. Inspect pins and holes for burrs, wear and corrosion. On reassembly fit the dowels before tightening any joint nut, so the half is located first and then clamped. Replace damaged dowels with correct parts.
componentRecords.notes: Whether dowels are withdrawn before lifting or stay in the lower half as guides depends on the design. The model shows two illustrative dowels.

componentRecords.function: The casing wear rings are the stationary, renewable rings fitted in the casing at each impeller eye. With the impeller wear rings they form the close running clearances that limit leakage from the high-pressure region around the impeller back to the suction eyes.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The narrow annular gap between the rotating impeller ring and the stationary casing ring is a flow restriction. Liquid in the side rooms, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure, tries to return to the eyes at suction pressure; leakage through the gap grows roughly with the gap area and with the square root of the pressure difference across it. This leakage has received energy from the impeller but is not delivered, so it is a direct loss. The liquid film in the gap also acts like a weak bearing, adding stiffness and damping to the rotor (often called the Lomakin effect).
componentRecords.construction: Two rings, one per eye (DE and NDE), seated in bores or grooves that are split across the casing joint, and held against rotation by an anti-rotation feature such as a pin, tongue or lug engaging the casing. In many designs they can be lifted out with the rotor and slid off the impeller rings, or removed once the rotor is out.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Wear-ring clearance is a major factor in volumetric efficiency, and its growth through wear is one of the most common reasons for falling pump performance. Clearances at the two eyes also influence the side-room pressures and so the residual axial thrust. The rings protect the casing from wear: renewing a ring is far cheaper than repairing a casing bore.
componentRecords.maintenance: During inspection measure the running clearance at each eye by the method and against the limits in the OEM manual, and compare DE with NDE. Look for rubbing on one side (which suggests deflection, misalignment or bearing problems), scoring, corrosion, galling and loose fits. Renew rings when clearance exceeds the OEM limit, and confirm new rings seat correctly in their bores with anti-rotation features engaged.
componentRecords.notes: Some pumps run without separate rings, with the impeller running directly in a casing bore, or use stepped, L-shaped or grooved rings. Ring pairs are selected together for resistance to galling and wear; non-metallic composite rings are used in some services only where the OEM approves them. Ring profiles and clearances in the model are illustrative and exaggerated for visibility.

componentRecords.function: The drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the DE impeller eye. It forms the DE running clearance with the DE impeller wear ring.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It restricts leakage from the DE side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure, back into the DE eye at suction pressure. Its clearance also influences the pressure distribution on the outer face of the DE shroud and so the axial force acting on that side of the impeller.
componentRecords.construction: Seated in the DE wear-ring bore, which is split across the casing joint, and prevented from turning by an anti-rotation feature. Its bore is the stationary half of the DE running clearance.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its clearance should stay similar to that of the NDE ring. Unequal clearances at the two eyes change the side-room pressures differently and are one source of residual axial thrust, which the NDE locating bearing must carry.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure and record the DE clearance alongside the NDE value and investigate any significant difference between them. Check for one-sided rub marks, cracking, corrosion and loss of fit or anti-rotation. Renew per OEM limits, normally as a matched set with the DE impeller ring.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry in the model is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The non-drive-end casing wear ring is the stationary ring surrounding the NDE impeller eye. It forms the NDE running clearance with the NDE impeller wear ring.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It restricts leakage from the NDE side room back into the NDE eye. Leakage returning to the eye mixes with the incoming flow, so a worn ring both wastes energy and disturbs the inflow at the vane inlets on that side, which can affect suction performance.
componentRecords.construction: Seated in the NDE wear-ring bore, split across the casing joint, with an anti-rotation feature. It mirrors the DE ring.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Together with the DE ring it sets the balance of leakage and side-room pressures on the two sides of the impeller. A significant difference between NDE and DE clearances is one source of residual axial thrust and of uneven hydraulic behaviour.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure the NDE clearance and compare it with the DE clearance and with previous records. Look for rubbing, scoring, corrosion and loose fit. Renew per OEM limits, normally together with the NDE impeller ring.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry in the model is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The hydraulic passages group shows the liquid-filled spaces inside the casing as translucent volumes: the suction passages and side chambers, the impeller chamber, and the volute with its discharge throat.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The flow path is: suction nozzle, splitter and two side suction chambers, two impeller eyes, impeller passages, volute, throat and discharge nozzle. Looking at the liquid rather than the metal makes it easier to see how passage area and direction change along the path.
componentRecords.construction: These volumes are not physical parts. In the model they are simplified approximations of the internal cavities, generated for teaching, and they do not reproduce OEM hydraulic profiles.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The shape of these passages largely determines hydraulic losses, NPSH required, flow uniformity at the two eyes, and the radial and axial forces on the rotor.
componentRecords.maintenance: Passages are inspected indirectly, by examining the casing internal surfaces for erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage and deposits, and by checking for debris, whenever the upper half is removed.
componentRecords.notes: Shown when fluid display or flow mode is enabled. Proportions are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The suction passages carry liquid from the suction nozzle into the casing and divide it into two side suction chambers, one leading to each impeller eye. This translucent volume shows the splitter region and both chambers.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
Liquid enters the lower half horizontally, flows beneath the shaft region and is split into two streams that turn and travel axially in opposite directions to the DE and NDE eyes. In many designs the chambers are shaped (for example semi-spiral) to accelerate the flow slightly and give each eye a reasonably uniform inflow with controlled swirl.

The two streams are intended to be similar, but in practice they are not exactly equal: the share reaching each eye depends on casing geometry, casting accuracy, upstream piping and operating point.
componentRecords.construction: Formed by cored passages mainly in the lower casing half and closed by the upper half. A dividing rib or splitter directs the flow into the two chambers, which surround the shaft between the seal housings and the impeller eyes.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Suction passage shape governs flow uniformity at the eyes and the pressure loss before the impeller, both of which affect NPSH required, cavitation inception, noise and the balance of axial forces. Distorted or swirling inflow, whether from casting defects, deposits or poor upstream piping, can make one eye work harder than the other.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the casing open, inspect suction chamber surfaces for deposits, debris, erosion and casting flash, and remove obstructions. Compare cavitation or erosion damage at the DE and NDE eyes; a clear difference may indicate uneven inflow and should prompt a review of the suction piping.
componentRecords.notes: Actual suction chamber geometry is manufacturer-specific. The fluid volume in the model is an educational approximation with simplified chamber shapes.

componentRecords.function: The impeller chamber is the liquid-filled space in which the impeller rotates, including the side rooms between the outer faces of the impeller shrouds and the casing walls.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Liquid in each side room is dragged into rotation by the shroud and turns at a fraction of impeller speed. This rotating liquid creates a pressure that falls from the impeller outer diameter towards the wear rings, acting on the outer face of each shroud. In a double-suction impeller these shroud forces act in opposite directions on the two sides, which is the basis of axial thrust balance. Leakage through the wear-ring clearances flows inwards through the side rooms and modifies their swirl and pressure.
componentRecords.construction: Bounded by the casing walls of both halves, the wear rings and the impeller. Side-room widths and wall shapes are design-specific.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Side-room geometry and leakage flow influence disc friction loss (power absorbed by shroud friction), the axial force on each side and the pressure field around the impeller. An impeller set off-centre in the chamber gives unequal side rooms and can add residual axial thrust.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect casing walls facing the shrouds for erosion, deposits and rub marks. Rubbing between shroud and casing points to errors in rotor axial position, bearing problems or excessive deflection; check impeller centring by the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Simplified volume in the model; side-room gaps are exaggerated for visibility.

componentRecords.function: The volute passage is the spiral channel around the impeller that collects liquid leaving the full impeller periphery, from both halves of the impeller, and leads it through the throat to the single discharge nozzle.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
Starting at the tongue, the volute cross-section increases progressively around the circumference because each further part of the impeller adds more flow. At design flow this keeps velocity and pressure around the impeller roughly uniform. Liquid leaves the impeller with high, largely tangential velocity; the volute and the diverging passage after the throat convert part of this kinetic energy into static pressure.

Away from design flow the area progression no longer matches the flow, the pressure around the impeller becomes non-uniform, and a net radial force acts on the rotor.
componentRecords.construction: Mostly formed in the lower casing half and closed by the upper half. The throat is the minimum section where the spiral ends and the discharge passage begins. In the double-volute variant a splitter rib divides the volute into two passages.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Throat area and area distribution largely determine the flow at which the pump reaches best efficiency and strongly influence the shape of the head curve near BEP and the radial load on the rotor. Surface roughness and casting accuracy affect friction losses, which matter more in smaller pumps.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect volute surfaces, throat and tongue for erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage, deposits and blockage. Heavy deposits reduce passage area and roughen surfaces, which can reduce head and efficiency.
componentRecords.notes: The volute shape and area progression in the model are illustrative; real profiles are designed by the OEM for each hydraulic size.

componentRecords.function: The double-suction impeller is the rotating component that adds energy to the liquid. It receives liquid through two eyes, one on each side, and discharges it from its full outer periphery into the single volute.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
The rotating vanes increase the angular momentum of the liquid, raising both its pressure and its velocity. The ideal (Euler) head is H = (u2 cu2 - u1 cu1) / g, where u is the vane peripheral speed and cu the tangential component of the absolute liquid velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). Real head is lower because of hydraulic losses and because the liquid does not follow the vanes perfectly.

Because the two inlets face in opposite axial directions, the axial hydraulic forces on the two halves largely oppose each other in an ideal symmetrical arrangement. They do not cancel completely in practice; a residual thrust remains and is carried by the NDE locating bearing.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a single closed casting comprising a central hub and web, two outer shrouds, two sets of vanes and two eyes, with a wear ring or wear surface at each eye. It is keyed to the shaft and located axially by the shaft sleeves and sleeve nuts on both sides. Many designs stagger the DE and NDE vane sets by part of a vane pitch to reduce pressure pulsations at the tongue.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Impeller diameter, width, vane design and speed set the head and flow the pump delivers. The impeller's symmetry, balance and wear-ring clearances directly affect efficiency, axial and radial loads, vibration and the life of bearings and seals. Trimming the impeller diameter is a common way of matching a pump to its duty, within OEM limits.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for cavitation damage near the vane inlet edges, erosion, corrosion, cracks, blockage and wear-ring condition. The position of cavitation damage on the vanes (low-pressure or pressure side) gives clues as to whether the pump ran at low or high flow relative to BEP. Compare damage on the DE and NDE sides; clearly asymmetric damage may indicate uneven inflow. Check bore, keyway and hub faces, and rebalance after any repair or trim, following OEM limits and procedures.
componentRecords.notes: In the model, vane count, vane shape and shroud profiles are illustrative. Real impellers have three-dimensional vanes designed for a specific hydraulic duty. Double-suction impellers are also used outside split case pumps, for example as the first stage of some multistage pumps.
