componentRecords.function: The hub is the central part of the impeller that fits on the shaft, and the central web is the disc that separates the two halves of the impeller. Together they carry torque from the shaft to the vanes and separate the two incoming streams.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Torque passes from the shaft through the key into the hub, then through the web to the vanes and shrouds. The web acts as a common back plate for both halves, turning each incoming axial stream outwards into the vane passages.
componentRecords.construction: Cast with the rest of the impeller. The hub is bored and keyed, and its end faces are machined square to the bore because the shaft sleeves bear against them to locate the impeller axially. In many designs O-rings or gaskets between the hub faces and the sleeves keep pumped liquid off the shaft.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The bore fit, keyway and end-face squareness determine how accurately the impeller runs concentric and true on the shaft, which affects balance, wear-ring clearance uniformity and runout. Damaged hub faces can allow liquid under the sleeves and onto the shaft.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the bore and keyway for fretting, corrosion and damage, the hub faces for burrs and loss of squareness, and the web for cracks. Check impeller runout on the shaft where the OEM requires it. Remove an impeller with a tight fit only by the OEM method; avoid uncontrolled heating or hammering.
componentRecords.notes: Hub length and web thickness are illustrative in the model.

componentRecords.function: The NDE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the non-drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the NDE eye, where the NDE impeller wear ring is fitted.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It contains the liquid between the vanes so it cannot short-circuit across the vane edges. Its outer face is exposed to the rotating liquid in the NDE side room; the pressure on this face, opposing the pressure on the DE shroud, is one half of the axial force balance.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the vanes and hub. At the eye it carries the impeller wear ring or a machined wear surface. Its outer face is also where balance corrections are commonly made, within OEM limits.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its profile and the side-room gap affect disc friction loss and the axial force on the NDE side. Wear or damage at the eye affects wear-ring clearance and leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for erosion, corrosion, cracks (especially near the eye and at the vane roots), rub marks on the outer face and damage to the wear-ring seat.
componentRecords.notes: In a double-suction impeller both outer shrouds are inlet (eye) shrouds. The labels 'front' (NDE) and 'rear' (DE) used in this module only identify the sides; they do not mean the front and back shrouds of a single-suction impeller. Shape is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The DE outer shroud closes the vane passages on the drive-end side of the impeller and forms the outer wall of the DE eye, where the DE impeller wear ring is fitted.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It mirrors the NDE shroud. The pressure of the rotating liquid in the DE side room acts on its outer face in the opposite direction to the corresponding force on the NDE shroud, so the two largely balance when the arrangement is symmetrical.
componentRecords.construction: Cast integral with the vanes and hub, carrying the DE impeller wear ring or wear surface at the eye. Its outer face is a common location for balance corrections, within OEM limits.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Any difference between DE and NDE shroud geometry, side-room gaps or wear-ring clearances upsets the axial force balance. Damage at the eye increases DE leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect as for the NDE shroud and compare the two sides; differences in erosion, rubbing or cavitation damage are diagnostic.
componentRecords.notes: 'Rear' is a side label only (see the NDE shroud note). Shape is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The NDE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the NDE eye. They transfer energy from the rotating impeller to the liquid entering from the non-drive-end side.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Liquid entering the eye meets the vane leading edges; near design flow the relative flow approaches roughly in line with the vane inlet angle (low incidence). As the liquid moves outwards, the vanes force it to rotate with the impeller, increasing its angular momentum, so its pressure and absolute velocity rise. Backward-curved vanes, usual in centrifugal pumps, tend to give a head that falls steadily as flow increases.
componentRecords.construction: Cast between the NDE shroud and the central web. Vane number, inlet and outlet angles, thickness and wrap are hydraulic design choices. In many designs the NDE vanes are angularly offset (staggered) from the DE vanes.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The vane inlet region largely determines NPSH required and cavitation behaviour on this side; the outlet region influences head and pressure pulsations. Damage or blockage on one side makes the two halves unequal, affecting hydraulic balance and vibration.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect inlet edges for cavitation pitting and erosion, outlet tips for erosion and cracking, and passages for blockage; compare with the DE vanes. Repairs such as weld build-up or coatings need OEM-approved procedures followed by rebalancing.
componentRecords.notes: Vane count and shape in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The DE-side vanes are the blades in the half of the impeller fed by the DE eye. They transfer energy to the liquid entering from the drive-end side.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: They work in the same way as the NDE vanes. Both vane sets discharge into the same volute, so the two streams merge at the impeller outlet. Staggering the two sets, where used, means vane tips pass the tongue at different instants, reducing the amplitude of pressure pulses at vane passing frequency.
componentRecords.construction: Cast between the DE shroud and the central web, normally a mirror image of the NDE vane set, possibly rotated by part of a pitch.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Equality of the two vane sets in casting accuracy, condition and inflow is what allows the two halves to share the work and the axial forces evenly. Uneven wear or blockage between DE and NDE vanes upsets that balance.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect as for the NDE vanes and record DE and NDE findings side by side.
componentRecords.notes: Vane count and shape in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The NDE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the non-drive-end side, between the hub and the shroud lip, through which liquid from the NDE suction chamber enters the impeller. This marker identifies it in the model.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The lowest pressure in the pump occurs around the eye and the vane leading edges. If local pressure falls to the vapour pressure of the liquid, vapour bubbles form and then collapse as pressure rises inside the passages: this is cavitation. Eye area and inlet velocity are therefore central to NPSH required. Suction specific speed is conventionally calculated using the flow per eye.
componentRecords.construction: Defined by the shroud inner lip (with its wear ring), the hub surface and the vane leading edges.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Dividing the flow between two eyes reduces the flow each eye must handle. For a given total flow and speed this tends to allow lower eye velocities and lower NPSH required than a comparable single-suction impeller, although the real benefit depends on the design. In practice each eye receives a share set by the inflow conditions, not exactly half.
componentRecords.maintenance: During inspection examine the eye and vane inlet edges for cavitation damage, rags, fibres and debris, and compare with the DE eye.
componentRecords.notes: Annotation geometry; eye proportions in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The DE eye is the annular inlet of the impeller on the drive-end side, through which liquid from the DE suction chamber enters the impeller. This marker identifies it in the model.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It works in the same way as the NDE eye, with flow approaching from the opposite axial direction. The DE suction chamber surrounds the shaft on the coupling side, so its flow path differs slightly from the NDE chamber in many designs.
componentRecords.construction: Defined by the DE shroud lip and wear ring, the hub surface and the DE vane leading edges.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the DE eye receives more or less flow than the NDE eye, or a distorted velocity profile, its local NPSH required and its share of axial force change; cavitation may start on one side before the other.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect as for the NDE eye and record differences between the two sides.
componentRecords.notes: Annotation geometry; proportions are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The impeller bore is the machined central hole through the hub that fits on the shaft impeller seat and centres the impeller on the shaft axis.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The fit between bore and seat keeps the impeller concentric while it rotates. In this keyed design torque is transmitted mainly through the key; the fit provides centring and resists fretting.
componentRecords.construction: Precision machined and normally held concentric with the wear-ring diameters and square to the hub faces. The fit class (clearance, transition or light interference) is OEM-specific.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: An oversize or worn bore lets the impeller sit off-centre, causing unbalance, wear-ring rubs and fretting; an excessively tight fit makes removal difficult and can damage parts.
componentRecords.maintenance: Clean and inspect for fretting, corrosion, scoring and ovality; measure the bore and the shaft seat and compare with the OEM fit specification. Use anti-seize or assembly compounds only if the OEM permits them.
componentRecords.notes: A feature of the impeller; the marker highlights its location.

componentRecords.function: The impeller keyway is the axial slot in the impeller bore that receives the impeller key, which locks the impeller to the shaft in rotation.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The key sits partly in the shaft keyway and partly in the impeller keyway. Torque passes from the shaft keyway wall into the key and from the key into the side wall of the impeller keyway.
componentRecords.construction: Machined (typically broached or slotted) along the bore. Width tolerance and angular position relative to the vanes are controlled.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The keyway side walls carry the full impeller torque as contact pressure. A worn or deformed keyway, or a loose key, allows angular movement that damages key, keyway and shaft, and affects balance.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for deformed side walls, cracks at the corners, burrs and corrosion, and check the key fit. Remove burrs without creating sharp notches.
componentRecords.notes: Keyway corners are stress raisers in the hub. The marker shows location only; size is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The impeller key is a rectangular key that transmits torque from the shaft to the impeller.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In operation the key is loaded in shear across its section at the shaft-to-hub interface and in compression on its sides. For a key of width w and engaged length L on a shaft of diameter d carrying torque T, the average shear stress is approximately tau = 2T / (d w L), assuming the force acts at the shaft surface and is evenly spread along the key. Real stress is not uniform, so design uses margins and the OEM's sizing.
componentRecords.construction: Usually a parallel key fitted in the shaft keyway and engaging the impeller keyway; length, section and material are set by the OEM.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A correctly fitted key prevents relative rotation and fretting. A key that is too high can lift the impeller off-centre; one that is too loose allows movement. Key length and fit also matter for rotor balance.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for deformation, shear marks, fretting and corrosion; replace with a key of the correct material and size. Check that it does not bottom in the impeller keyway and does not prevent the sleeves seating against the hub.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs use more than one key, or other drive methods. The model's key is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The impeller wear rings are renewable rotating rings fitted on the impeller at each eye. They run inside the casing wear rings with a small radial clearance.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: They are the rotating half of each running clearance. The leakage path runs from the side room, at a pressure approaching discharge pressure, through the gap between impeller ring and casing ring and back into the eye.
componentRecords.construction: Shrunk or pressed onto machined diameters at the eyes and secured against movement by set screws, pins, tack welds or interference, depending on design. Material pairs are chosen with a hardness difference or a galling-resistant combination so the rings survive occasional contact.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: They provide renewable wearing surfaces so the impeller itself is protected, and together with the casing rings they control internal leakage, volumetric efficiency and part of the rotor's fluid-film stiffness.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check rings for rubbing, cracking, looseness and runout. Measure the ring outer diameters and casing ring bores to determine clearance per the OEM method and limits. When renewing, follow the OEM fitting method, including any final machining after fitting, and rebalance if required.
componentRecords.notes: Some impellers have no separate rings; their wear surfaces are restored or the impeller renewed per OEM practice. Geometry in the model is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The DE impeller wear ring is the rotating ring at the DE eye that runs inside the DE casing wear ring.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It forms the rotating half of the DE running clearance, limiting leakage from the DE side room back to the DE eye.
componentRecords.construction: Fitted on the DE eye diameter of the impeller and secured by the OEM method.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its wear, together with that of the DE casing ring, sets the DE clearance. If DE and NDE clearances become unequal, side-room pressures differ and residual axial thrust changes.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure and record its outer diameter and runout, inspect for rubbing and looseness, and renew together with the DE casing ring when the OEM limit is reached.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The NDE impeller wear ring is the rotating ring at the NDE eye that runs inside the NDE casing wear ring.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It forms the rotating half of the NDE running clearance, limiting leakage from the NDE side room back to the NDE eye.
componentRecords.construction: Fitted on the NDE eye diameter of the impeller and secured by the OEM method.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its condition sets the NDE clearance and must be compared with the DE side, because unequal clearances are a source of residual axial thrust.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure and record outer diameter and runout, inspect for rubbing and looseness, and renew together with the NDE casing ring when the OEM limit is reached.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The impeller locating and locking arrangement fixes the impeller's axial position on the shaft. In this design the impeller hub is clamped between the DE and NDE shaft sleeves, which are held by sleeve nuts threaded onto the shaft on each side.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Tightening the sleeve nuts pushes the sleeves against the hub faces from both sides, clamping the impeller. The axial position of the nuts on their threads sets where the impeller sits on the shaft; the NDE locating bearing then fixes the whole rotor axially in the casing, so together they determine whether the impeller is centred on the volute.
componentRecords.construction: Sleeves slide over the shaft and abut the hub; sleeve nuts retain them and are secured by locking screws or similar devices. In many designs the nut threads are handed so that the drag of rotation tends to tighten rather than loosen them. O-rings or gaskets at the sleeve-to-hub joints keep liquid off the shaft in many designs.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Correct impeller centring is important for hydraulic symmetry: an impeller set off-centre changes the side-room geometry and flow on the two sides and can add residual axial thrust. Loose locking can let the impeller move, rub the casing and damage the wear rings.
componentRecords.maintenance: During rotor assembly set the impeller axial position by the OEM procedure (typically by measurement from shaft or casing references), tighten and lock the nuts, and confirm free rotation after the casing is closed. Check thread hand before trying to loosen a nut, and inspect threads and locking devices.
componentRecords.notes: This feature entry borrows the sleeve and sleeve nut meshes. Other designs use split rings, impeller nuts, shoulders or locking collars to locate the impeller.

componentRecords.function: The impeller balance arrangement refers to how the impeller's mass distribution is corrected so it rotates without significant unbalance. Corrections are commonly made by removing material from the outer faces of the shrouds.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Any offset between the mass centre and the rotation axis produces a rotating force F = U omega^2, where U is the residual unbalance (mass multiplied by its radius) and omega the angular speed. This force turns with the shaft and appears as once-per-revolution (1x) vibration. A double-suction impeller is relatively wide, so unbalance can exist in two planes (couple unbalance) and two-plane dynamic balancing is commonly used.
componentRecords.construction: Material is removed by machining or grinding on the shroud outer faces at the positions found on the balancing machine, within the depth and location limits set by the OEM, without thinning shrouds excessively or cutting into vanes.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Unbalance raises bearing loads, vibration and seal face movement and increases the risk of wear-ring rubs. Balance quality grades are defined in ISO 21940-11 (which replaced ISO 1940-1); the grade and method required come from the OEM or purchaser specification.
componentRecords.maintenance: Rebalance after any repair, trim, coating or wear-ring renewal, as the OEM requires. Record the key convention used during balancing (for example the half-key convention) so the assembled rotor matches it. Erosion, corrosion or deposits can change balance in service, so trend vibration at running-speed frequency.
componentRecords.notes: Mechanical balancing does not correct hydraulic unbalance caused by vane-to-vane casting differences. This feature entry highlights the shroud meshes; balance correction marks are not modelled.

componentRecords.function: The pump shaft carries the impeller between the two bearings and transmits torque from the motor, via the coupling, to the impeller. It also carries the sleeves, seals, deflectors, bearings and the pump coupling hub.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
Torque enters at the coupling end (DE) and leaves through the impeller key, so the section between coupling and impeller carries essentially full torque, while the NDE end carries only small torques such as bearing and seal friction. The shaft is also loaded in bending by impeller weight, radial hydraulic force and coupling forces, and is supported by the DE floating bearing and the NDE locating bearing, which also carries residual axial thrust.

Because the shaft rotates under largely stationary loads, every point on its surface goes through a complete reversal of bending stress each revolution, so fatigue strength is a key design criterion.
componentRecords.construction: A stepped, machined round bar with an impeller seat and keyway, threads for sleeve nuts and bearing locknuts, bearing journals, shoulders and a keyed coupling end. Critical diameters are ground or finish turned to close tolerances and concentricity. In many designs the shaft is isolated from the pumped liquid by sleeves, the impeller hub and O-rings, often described as a dry shaft.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Shaft stiffness governs deflection at the wear rings and seals and the critical speeds; strength governs fatigue margin at stress raisers such as keyways, shoulders and threads; straightness and concentricity affect runout and balance.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the rotor out, check runout at the journals, seal areas, impeller seat and coupling end using V-blocks or centres, per the OEM method and limits. Inspect for cracks (particularly at keyway ends, shoulders and threads), corrosion, fretting under fits and thread damage, using crack detection where the site procedure requires. A bent shaft is normally replaced; straightening only with OEM approval. Support the rotor at suitable points during handling and storage so it is not bent or damaged.
componentRecords.notes: Diameters, steps and lengths in the model are illustrative. Material selection depends on strength, corrosion exposure (wet or dry shaft) and OEM practice.

componentRecords.function: The shaft keyways are axial slots machined in the shaft that receive the impeller key and the coupling key, locking these parts to the shaft in rotation.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Torque is transferred by contact pressure between the key sides and the keyway walls. The coupling keyway carries the full driving torque into the shaft; the impeller keyway carries it out to the impeller.
componentRecords.construction: Milled into the shaft at the impeller seat and at the coupling end. Keyway ends are either rounded (end-milled, profile type) or run out gradually (sled-runner type) depending on design; the end form and root radii influence stress concentration.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Keyways are among the most highly stressed locations on the shaft, combining torsional stress with reversing bending stress and a geometric stress raiser. Fatigue cracks in shafts commonly start at keyway ends or root corners, so keyway geometry and finish matter for shaft life.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect keyway walls for deformation (rolled edges), fretting, corrosion and cracks, especially at the ends and root corners, using a crack-detection method suited to the material (for example dye penetrant or magnetic particle) where the site procedure requires. Remove burrs without leaving sharp notches and check the key fit.
componentRecords.notes: The marker indicates keyway locations; sizes are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The impeller seat is the machined shaft diameter on which the impeller hub bore fits; its locating diameter centres the impeller on the shaft axis.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The seat-to-bore fit keeps the impeller concentric while running. The axial position is not set by the seat but by the sleeves and sleeve nuts clamping the hub from both sides.
componentRecords.construction: Usually one of the largest shaft diameters, ground or finish turned concentric with the bearing journals and carrying the impeller keyway. The sleeves and the threads for the sleeve nuts lie outboard of it on each side.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Concentricity of the seat with the journals controls impeller runout and therefore wear-ring rub risk and rotor balance. Fretting or corrosion of the seat loosens the fit.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure diameter and runout relative to the journals by the OEM procedure, inspect for fretting, corrosion and damage from impeller removal, and clean and protect before reassembly.
componentRecords.notes: Feature of the shaft; geometry illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The bearing journals are the precision shaft diameters on which the inner rings of the DE and NDE rolling bearings are mounted.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The inner rings rotate with the shaft relative to a largely stationary load direction, so they are commonly given an interference fit to stop them creeping on the shaft; the fit is chosen to the bearing manufacturer's and OEM's recommendations. The two journals do different jobs: at the NDE the locating bearing is clamped axially between a shaft shoulder and the locknut and carries residual axial thrust; at the DE the floating bearing allows axial movement, commonly by letting its outer ring slide in the housing, so the shaft can expand thermally without loading the bearings axially.
componentRecords.construction: Ground diameters with controlled roundness, cylindricity and surface finish, concentric with the impeller seat, with adjacent shoulders and threaded sections for locknuts.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Journal size, form and finish influence bearing internal clearance after mounting, ring seating and bearing life. A damaged or undersize journal lets the inner ring creep, generating wear, heat and eventually bearing failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: When bearings are removed, inspect journals for creep marks, fretting, scoring and corrosion and measure them against OEM limits. Mount bearings by the recommended method (for example an induction heater or a press tool acting on the correct ring); never hammer on bearing rings or use an open flame. Protect journals during handling.
componentRecords.notes: Depending on design, the floating function may be provided at the outer ring or inside the bearing (for example with some cylindrical roller bearings). Marker only; geometry illustrative.

componentRecords.function: Shaft shoulders are the steps between diameters that give positive axial location to the bearings and, depending on design, to other parts such as spacers or the coupling hub.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: At the NDE the locating bearing inner ring is clamped against a shoulder by the locknut, so residual axial thrust passes from the shaft through the shoulder into the bearing. Every change of diameter also concentrates stress under bending and torsion.
componentRecords.construction: Machined square to the axis with a fillet radius at the root. At bearing seats the fillet must be smaller than the bearing ring's corner chamfer so the ring seats fully, as given in bearing manufacturer data; elsewhere larger radii reduce stress concentration.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Shoulder squareness affects bearing alignment and running accuracy. Sharp or damaged fillets are fatigue crack initiation sites.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for loss of squareness, burrs, fretting and fillet cracks. On assembly confirm that bearings and spacers seat fully against their shoulders.
componentRecords.notes: Marker only; the number and position of shoulders in the model are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The coupling mounting section is the drive-end shaft extension on which the pump coupling hub is fitted. All the driving torque enters the pump shaft here.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Motor torque passes through the coupling into the pump hub and then into the shaft through the coupling key and fit. This section carries torsion plus bending from coupling weight and from the reaction forces a flexible coupling produces when it accommodates misalignment.
componentRecords.construction: A parallel or tapered extension with a keyway, often with a tapped hole or thread in the end for the hub retainer. The fit type depends on the coupling and the OEM.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is often a reduced diameter carrying full torque, so it is a critical section for torsional and combined stress. Its runout is checked as part of shaft alignment because it affects the readings and the coupling's running.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for fretting, keyway damage and cracks, and check runout. Fit and remove coupling hubs by the OEM method (controlled heating or pullers), not by hammering, which can damage bearings. Confirm the hub retainer is secure.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The shaft sleeves are renewable tubes fitted over the shaft on each side of the impeller. They protect the shaft where it passes through the seal chambers, provide the running surface for packing or seal components and, with the sleeve nuts, locate the impeller axially.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Each sleeve is clamped between the impeller hub and a sleeve nut. O-rings or gaskets at its ends, where fitted, keep pumped liquid from reaching the shaft beneath it. In the packing variant the packing rubs on the sleeve rather than the shaft; in the mechanical seal variant the seal's rotating parts are mounted on the sleeve, or on the seal's own cartridge sleeve fitted over it.
componentRecords.construction: Two sleeves (DE and NDE), usually a close sliding fit on the shaft and driven by a key, a pin or by clamping, with end faces machined square to the bore. In packed pumps the running surface under the packing may be hard-coated in some designs.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Renewing a worn sleeve is far simpler and cheaper than repairing a shaft. Sleeve runout, roundness and surface finish affect seal and packing life.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for grooving under packing, fretting under seal elastomers, corrosion and damaged end faces; check runout once assembled. Renew O-rings at the sleeve ends whenever sleeves are disturbed.
componentRecords.notes: Sleeve arrangements vary widely between manufacturers and seal types. This is a logical group of the DE and NDE sleeves.

componentRecords.function: The DE shaft sleeve covers the shaft from the DE face of the impeller hub out through the DE seal chamber, protecting the shaft and carrying the DE seal or packing running surface.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It is clamped against the impeller hub by the DE sleeve nut, so it also forms half of the impeller's axial location. It rotates with the shaft inside the stationary DE seal chamber.
componentRecords.construction: A machined tube with square end faces, a sealing arrangement at the hub joint where fitted, and a drive key or pin. It is renewable.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its condition directly affects DE seal or packing life, and its end faces affect impeller axial position and runout.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the running surface, end faces and bore; renew when grooved, corroded or out of OEM limits. Check runout after assembly.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The NDE shaft sleeve covers the shaft from the NDE face of the impeller hub out through the NDE seal chamber, protecting the shaft and carrying the NDE seal or packing running surface.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: It is clamped against the impeller hub by the NDE sleeve nut and forms the other half of the impeller's axial location.
componentRecords.construction: A machined, renewable tube mirroring the DE sleeve, with square end faces and a sealing arrangement at the hub joint where fitted.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Its condition affects NDE seal or packing life. Sleeve face condition on both sides together keeps the impeller true and correctly positioned.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect as for the DE sleeve and compare wear patterns between the two ends.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: Shaft locking components are the threaded and retaining parts that hold rotor components in position: the DE and NDE sleeve nuts that clamp the sleeves and impeller, and the shaft-end retainer that holds the coupling hub.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: They convert threaded or bolted clamping into axial location. They do not carry torque in normal operation; that is the job of the keys.
componentRecords.construction: Sleeve nuts on shaft threads, secured by locking screws or similar devices, and an end plate with a screw, or a nut, at the coupling end.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If any of them loosens, components can move axially, causing rubs, seal damage, coupling problems or changed impeller position.
componentRecords.maintenance: Confirm all locking devices are fitted and secure on reassembly; inspect threads and renew damaged locking parts.
componentRecords.notes: Logical group. Locking methods vary between manufacturers.

componentRecords.function: The DE sleeve nut screws onto the shaft outboard of the DE sleeve and clamps the sleeve against the impeller hub.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Tightened against the NDE nut acting from the other side, it clamps the impeller between the two sleeves. Its position on the thread contributes to the impeller's axial position on the shaft.
componentRecords.construction: A threaded nut, often with slots or holes for a spanner and a locking screw. In many designs its thread hand is chosen so that the drag of normal rotation tends to tighten it, which may make it a left-hand thread.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A loose nut lets the sleeve and impeller move; overtightening can damage threads or distort the sleeve.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the thread hand before attempting removal. Inspect threads and locking features, and tighten and lock by the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The NDE sleeve nut screws onto the shaft outboard of the NDE sleeve and clamps the sleeve against the impeller hub from the NDE side.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: With the DE nut, it holds the impeller clamped between the sleeves at the set axial position.
componentRecords.construction: Similar to the DE nut; where thread handing is used, it typically has the opposite hand to the DE nut so that each tends to tighten with rotation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A loose or incorrectly set nut changes impeller position, which can upset hydraulic symmetry and increase residual axial thrust.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check thread hand before removal; inspect threads and locking features; set and lock per the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The shaft-end locking arrangement holds the pump coupling hub axially on the drive-end shaft extension.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: A retaining plate and screw, or a nut, at the shaft end prevents the hub sliding along the shaft. Torque is carried by the key and fit, not by the retainer.
componentRecords.construction: Typically an end plate or washer secured by a screw into a tapped hole in the shaft end, or a nut on a threaded end, with a locking feature.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A loose hub can move axially, change the coupling gap and load the bearings or the coupling elements.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check security and locking whenever the coupling is disturbed, and confirm the coupling gap (distance between shaft ends) per the coupling and OEM data.
componentRecords.notes: Arrangement varies with coupling type. Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The water deflectors (flingers) are rings on the shaft between each seal or stuffing box and the adjacent bearing housing. They throw leakage liquid outwards so it does not run along the shaft into the bearing housings.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Any liquid creeping along the rotating shaft reaches the deflector and is flung off radially by centrifugal action, away from the bearing housing seals. This is especially important with gland packing, which is designed to leak slightly for lubrication and cooling.
componentRecords.construction: Commonly an elastomer ring gripping the shaft or a metal ring secured by a set screw, positioned close to the bearing housing face with a small gap so it does not rub.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Water entering a bearing housing contaminates the lubricant and is a frequent contributor to bearing corrosion and premature failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that deflectors are present, intact and correctly positioned and not rubbing; replace hardened or split elastomer deflectors. Investigate the leakage source if liquid is reaching the deflectors regularly.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs use labyrinth or bearing isolator seals on the housings in addition to or instead of deflectors. Geometry is illustrative.

componentRecords.function: Supports and encloses the drive-end (inboard, coupling-side) bearing, holds it concentric with the casing bore, contains its lubricant and keeps contaminants out.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Radial load from the shaft passes through the bearing outer ring into the housing bore, then through the housing and its hold-down bolts into the bearing bracket cast on the lower casing half. In the baseline arrangement the bore lets the outer ring of the floating bearing slide axially as the shaft grows with temperature, so this housing carries radial load only.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a cast housing with a precision bore, an oil sump below the bearing (oil variant) or a grease cavity (grease variant), connections for the oiler, sight glass and drain or for the grease nipple and relief plug, and covers on both sides. It is located on the bracket by a spigot or dowels so that it returns to the same concentric position when refitted. In many split case designs the bearing housings come out with the rotor as part of the complete rotating element.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The condition and alignment of the housing bore decide the bearing fit, its running temperature and the position of the shaft relative to the casing, wear rings and seal. A distorted, worn or misaligned housing can pinch the bearing, stop the floating bearing from moving, or let the outer ring creep (turn slowly) in the bore.
componentRecords.maintenance: Trend housing temperature and vibration. At overhaul, check the bore for wear, fretting, ovality and creep marks and compare with the OEM limits; check that the housing seats squarely on the bracket and that spigots and dowels are undamaged. Keep vents and breathers clear and the outside clean so that heat can escape.
componentRecords.notes: Proportions in the 3D model are illustrative. Constructions (one-piece, split, cartridge-type) and features such as cooling fins, water jackets or oil coolers vary between manufacturers and duties.

componentRecords.function: Carries the radial load at the coupling end of the rotor (its share of the impeller's hydraulic radial force, the rotor weight and any loads from the coupling) while letting the shaft expand axially. In the baseline arrangement it is not intended to carry axial load.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
A deep-groove ball bearing: balls roll between inner- and outer-ring raceways, spaced by a cage, separated from the raceways by a very thin elastohydrodynamic lubricant film. The inner ring rotates with the shaft and is clamped against a shaft shoulder by the locknut and lockwasher. The outer ring is stationary and has a fit in the housing bore that allows it to slide, with axial clearance left at the covers. When the shaft lengthens relative to the casing as it warms, the whole bearing moves with the shaft and the outer ring slides in the bore. This is the 'floating' bearing; the axial position of the rotor is set by the locating bearing at the non-drive end.

The inner ring sees a rotating load (the load direction moves round it as it turns), which is why it needs an interference fit on the shaft; the outer ring sees a stationary load, which allows the looser fit needed for floating.
componentRecords.construction: A standard single-row deep-groove ball bearing, open, shielded or sealed to suit the lubrication method. Internal radial clearance class, cage type and the shaft and housing fits are selected by the OEM and the bearing manufacturer.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Correct floating is essential. If the outer ring cannot slide, because of a wrong fit, corrosion or fretting in the bore, a cover that clamps it, or the wrong gasket thickness, the shaft's thermal growth is resisted and both bearings see an induced axial load. The result is overheating and early failure of both bearings. Deep-groove ball bearings can carry some axial load, but in this arrangement their duty is radial.
componentRecords.maintenance: Trend temperature, vibration (including bearing defect frequencies or enveloping) and lubricant condition. At overhaul, replace bearings as the OEM recommends rather than re-using them. Mount by controlled heating, for example with an induction heater, or with proper mounting tools that load only the ring being fitted; never hammer, and never pass mounting force through the rolling elements. Check journal and bore against the OEM limits, and after assembly confirm that the outer ring is free to move axially.
componentRecords.notes: 'Floating' refers to axial freedom, not radial looseness. Other designs use a cylindrical roller bearing as the floating bearing (axial movement then takes place inside the bearing), spherical roller bearings, or hydrodynamic sleeve bearings on large machines. Silicon nitride appears only in hybrid bearings for special duties; cages may be pressed steel, brass or polyamide. The model shows a simplified bearing without internal clearance detail.

componentRecords.function: Closes the casing side of the drive-end bearing housing, retains the lubricant and carries the inboard bearing housing seal (lip seal or bearing isolator).
componentRecords.construction: A bolted ring cover, spigoted into the housing, with a gasket or O-ring and a bore through which the shaft passes, machined to hold the housing seal. In the floating arrangement this cover does not clamp the bearing's outer ring; an axial gap is left so that the bearing can move.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: This cover faces the seal or stuffing box, where leakage and spray are most likely. Its seal, together with the shaft deflector (flinger), is the first line of defence against water getting into the lubricant, which is one of the main causes of rolling-bearing failure in pumps.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the spigot, gasket face and seal bore. Renew the gasket or O-ring and any lip seal at reassembly, and confirm that the shaft runs centrally in the bore with no rubbing. Keep the isolator's drain or expulsion port clear and in the orientation the manufacturer specifies.
componentRecords.notes: In some designs the cover is integral with the housing, or the isolator is pressed directly into the housing. Bolting is simplified in the model.

componentRecords.function: Closes the coupling side of the drive-end bearing housing. The shaft passes through an opening in this cover to the coupling hub, and the cover carries the outboard bearing housing seal.
componentRecords.construction: A bolted cover with a shaft opening and seal bore, a spigot and a gasket or O-ring. As with the inboard cover, in the floating arrangement it leaves axial clearance to the bearing's outer ring.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: This cover helps define the floating bearing's axial freedom. A wrong gasket thickness, a damaged spigot or an incorrect cover can clamp the outer ring and turn the floating bearing into a second locating bearing, which then carries thermally induced axial load. It also sits next to the coupling, so the guard must cover the exposed shaft between this cover and the coupling.
componentRecords.maintenance: After fitting, confirm that the floating bearing still has the axial freedom the OEM specifies, checked by the method in the manual. Inspect the seal bore and gasket face, renew the seal and gasket, and fit lip seals the right way round with a protective sleeve over the keyway.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end only: the non-drive-end cover is blind. Shown simplified in the model.

componentRecords.function: Clamps the drive-end bearing's inner ring axially against the shaft shoulder so that it moves with the shaft and cannot creep along the journal.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Tightening the threaded nut presses the inner ring against the shoulder, giving an axial clamp. A tab of the lockwasher, engaged in a slot in the shaft, is bent into a slot in the nut to stop it turning.
componentRecords.construction: A slotted round locknut on a fine thread at the end of the bearing journal, tightened with a hook or C-spanner, or with a socket designed for the slots.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A loose nut lets the inner ring move, causing fretting, wear of the journal and loss of the bearing's axial location on the shaft. A nut that is not square to the shaft can tilt the inner ring. Over-tightening can damage threads or the ring face. At the floating end the clamp is not intended to carry thrust, but it must still be secure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the threads and slots, and replace a damaged nut. Tighten by the method the OEM or bearing manufacturer specifies and lock with a new lockwasher. Check that the nut face bears squarely on the ring or spacer.
componentRecords.notes: Thread hand and locking method are chosen by the OEM. Some designs use a locknut with an integral locking screw, or clamp the bearing through a spacer. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Locks the bearing locknut so that it cannot slacken in service.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: An internal tang on the washer engages a slot or keyway in the threaded part of the shaft, so the washer cannot turn on the shaft. After the locknut has been tightened, one of the washer's external tabs is bent into a slot in the nut, locking nut and shaft together.
componentRecords.construction: A thin pressed-steel tab washer matched to the locknut size, fitted between the bearing inner ring (or a spacer) and the locknut.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is small and cheap, but if it fails or is left out the nut can work loose and the inner ring can move on the shaft. That leads to fretting, loss of clamping, noise and eventually bearing failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Fit a new lockwasher at each reassembly, because re-bent tabs can crack. Check that the internal tang is straight and sits in the shaft slot without being forced. Tighten the nut by the method the OEM or bearing manufacturer specifies; if no nut slot lines up with a tab, follow their guidance, which is generally to tighten slightly further to the next slot rather than slacken the nut. Bend the tab fully into the slot without damaging the nut.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end: locks the nut that clamps the floating bearing's inner ring against the shaft shoulder. Some designs use locknuts with an integral locking screw or insert instead of a tab washer. Shown simplified in the model.

componentRecords.function: Keep the lubricant in and keep water, dust and process liquid out where the shaft passes through the drive-end housing covers, at both the inboard (casing side) and outboard (coupling side) openings.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: A lip seal has a flexible elastomer lip, often spring-energised, that runs in light contact on the shaft and seals on a very thin film; it wears and generates some heat. A labyrinth seal or bearing isolator is non-contacting: a rotor turning with the shaft and a stator fixed in the cover form a winding path with drain ports that return lubricant to the housing and expel contaminants. Some isolators add a dynamic O-ring or a vapour-blocking feature.
componentRecords.construction: Pressed or fitted into the cover bores. Isolator rotors are usually driven by an O-ring on the shaft, and the stator has an expulsion port that must face the position the manufacturer specifies, normally downwards.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Water contamination of the lubricant is a leading cause of rolling-bearing failure in pumps, and the inboard seal sits directly beside the shaft seal or packing. Lip seals can groove the shaft over time; isolators avoid contact wear but depend on correct installation.
componentRecords.maintenance: Watch for oil weeping and for water in the oil. Renew lip seals at each reassembly, protecting the lip over keyways and threads with a fitting sleeve, and check the shaft for grooving. Fit isolators exactly as the manufacturer instructs and keep the expulsion port clear.
componentRecords.notes: Two seals at the drive end (inboard and outboard), shown in the model as two simplified rings. Seal types vary; some housings rely on a plain labyrinth machined into the cover. Bronze isolators are covered by the tin-bronze family as an approximation.

componentRecords.function: Seal the bolted joints between the bearing housing and its covers, so that lubricant stays in and water, dust and process liquid stay out.
componentRecords.construction: Depending on the design: thin flat gaskets of compressed fibre or paper-type jointing, O-rings in machined grooves, or an approved liquid sealant on metal-to-metal joints. Flat gaskets are cut to the cover spigot and bolt pattern.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Cover gaskets also affect axial geometry. A gasket of the wrong thickness under a cover can clamp a bearing that is meant to float, or fail to clamp one that is meant to be located, so substituting a different or home-made gasket can change how the bearing arrangement works. Leaking joints let oil out and moisture in, and both shorten bearing life.
componentRecords.maintenance: Fit new gaskets or O-rings at every reassembly, using only the type and thickness specified by the OEM. Clean joint faces without scoring them, remove burrs, and tighten cover bolts evenly. Apply liquid sealant sparingly so that none is squeezed into the bearing cavity. Look for oil weeping at the joints on routine rounds.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end: the gaskets under the inboard and outboard covers must not take up the axial clearance that lets the floating bearing's outer ring slide in the housing bore. The 3D model shows the gaskets as thin rings; real gasket shapes follow each cover.

componentRecords.function: Fasten the drive-end bearing housing to its bracket on the lower casing half and hold it in its concentric position.
componentRecords.construction: Bolts or studs with nuts and washers. Location is provided by a spigot or dowels rather than by the bolts; in some designs, shims or adjusting screws set the housing position so that the rotor is centred in the casing bore.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Loose hold-down bolts let the housing move, causing vibration and misalignment of the rotor relative to the casing. Uneven tightening can distort the housing and pinch the bearing. At the floating end the bolts mainly carry radial load.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check tightness during routine inspections and tighten to the OEM's values. Inspect dowels and holes. Mark the housing position and any shims before removing the rotor, and after reassembly check rotor centring as the OEM describes.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Provides the entry point for adding fresh grease to the bearing housing in the grease-lubricated variant. The relief plug opens an exit so that displaced old grease and any excess can escape instead of pressurising and over-filling the housing.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: A grease gun forces grease past a spring-loaded ball check in the nipple, which stops grease and dirt from coming back out. The fresh grease is directed into the bearing and pushes old grease through the bearing towards the relief opening, renewing the lubricant in the working area.
componentRecords.construction: A threaded hydraulic-type grease nipple on the housing, usually feeding a passage that delivers grease close to the bearing, and a threaded relief or drain plug on the other side of the bearing, often at the bottom of the grease cavity.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Grease quantity is critical. Too much grease is churned by the rolling elements, which raises temperature and can force grease past the housing seals; too little starves the bearing. Greases with incompatible thickeners or base oils can soften or harden when mixed and lose their lubricating ability, so the grease type must not be changed without checking compatibility.
componentRecords.maintenance: Wipe the nipple clean before connecting the gun. Use only the grease specified by the OEM, at the interval and quantity given by the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site lubrication schedule. Where the procedure requires it, remove the relief plug while regreasing, let the excess purge, then refit it. Record each regreasing. A short-lived temperature rise after regreasing is normal; a persistent rise is not.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Whether regreasing may be done with the pump running depends on the design, the guarding around the coupling and the site safety rules; never reach near the coupling or shaft to do it. Some sites fit automatic single-point lubricators. The model shows the nipple and plug as simple fittings.

componentRecords.function: Shows the oil level in the bearing housing sump against a reference mark, and allows the oil's condition (colour, cloudiness, foaming) to be seen without opening the housing.
componentRecords.construction: Usually a round bull's-eye window screwed into the side of the housing at the required level, with a level mark or centre line; some designs use a tubular level gauge. The window is glass or a transparent polymer sealed into a metal or polymer body.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: In an oil-bath housing the level must be right: too low and the bearing may be starved, too high and the oil is churned, heats up and may leak past the housing seals. Milky or cloudy oil is a strong sign of water contamination, frequently from seal or packing leakage, and calls for an oil change and a search for the source.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the level and appearance on every operator round. The OEM states whether the level is read at standstill or while running, as the two can differ. Keep the window clean and replace it if it is crazed, discoloured or weeping. The sight glass and the constant-level oiler should agree; if they do not, find out why before adding oil.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. The window material (glass or transparent polymer) is not a family in the material library; the listed materials cover the body and its seal. The model shows a simplified window on the side of the housing.

componentRecords.function: Allows the bearing housing sump to be drained completely for oil changes, and provides a point from which an oil sample can be taken where the site uses oil analysis.
componentRecords.construction: A threaded plug with a sealing washer at the lowest point of the sump. Some designs use a magnetic plug that collects fine ferrous wear debris; some sites fit a small valve or a sampling point instead of a plain plug.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Water and wear debris settle at the bottom of the sump, so draining from the lowest point removes them with the old oil. Debris on a magnetic plug, or metal particles and water in a sample, are early warnings of bearing distress.
componentRecords.maintenance: Change the oil at the interval set by the OEM or the site schedule, or earlier if it is contaminated. Drain into a clean container and look at the oil and any debris before disposal. Fit a new sealing washer, tighten the plug, refill with the specified oil to the correct level and check for leaks after start-up. Dispose of used oil in line with environmental requirements.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Fitted in the oil-lubricated variant. Shown in the model as a simple plug at the bottom of the housing.

componentRecords.function: A constant-level oiler automatically tops up the bearing housing sump to hold a set oil level, and carries a visible reserve of oil.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The oiler works on the 'bird-feeder' principle. Its transparent reservoir is inverted and sealed at the top. When the sump level falls below the oiler's lower opening, air bubbles up into the reservoir and oil flows out until the opening is covered again. The level held is therefore set by the oiler's height adjustment relative to the housing, not by how full the reservoir is.
componentRecords.construction: A transparent reservoir bulb on a metal or polymer body with a level-setting device, connected to the housing below the oil level through an elbow or pipe nipple.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The oiler makes up small losses, but it cannot lower a level that is too high, does not show oil condition, and cannot keep up with a housing that leaks faster than it can supply. Rapid consumption points to leaking housing seals or gaskets. Pressure differences between the inside of the housing and the atmosphere, and in some designs the direction of shaft rotation relative to the oiler's position, can upset the level, so the oiler must be fitted and set as the OEM specifies.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the reservoir on each round and refill with the specified oil before it empties. Confirm at commissioning, and after any work on the housing, that the oiler setting gives the required sump level as shown on the sight glass. Track consumption; a change in rate is a useful early sign of a seal or gasket problem. Keep the bulb clean so the level can be seen.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Fitted only in the oil-lubricated variant. Larger or higher-duty pumps may use oil rings, oil mist or circulating oil systems instead. The model shows a generic oiler.

componentRecords.function: Supports and encloses the non-drive-end (outboard) locating bearing, passes both radial load and the rotor's residual axial thrust into the casing, and fixes the rotor's axial position relative to the casing.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The locating bearing's outer rings are clamped between a shoulder in the housing and the blind end cover. Thrust in one direction passes from the shaft through the inner rings and balls to the outer rings, then into the housing shoulder; thrust in the other direction passes into the end cover and its bolts. Either way it reaches the housing and, through the hold-down bolts and location features, the bracket on the lower casing half. Because the rotor is fixed axially here, the housing position also sets the impeller's axial position in the volute.
componentRecords.construction: A cast housing similar to the drive-end housing, but with a machined thrust shoulder, a blind outboard end and a seal only on the inboard side. It carries the same lubrication fittings as the drive end for the selected lubrication variant.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: This housing, its fixings and the bracket must carry axial load as well as radial load. Its position governs impeller centring, which matters for hydraulic symmetry, wear-ring clearance and the level of residual thrust. Temperature and axial vibration measured here are key indicators of thrust conditions.
componentRecords.maintenance: Trend temperature and vibration in all three directions, paying attention to the axial reading. At overhaul, check the bore, the shoulder face and its squareness for wear, fretting and creep marks. After reassembly, check rotor end float and impeller axial position as the OEM specifies.
componentRecords.notes: The model follows the baseline with the locating bearing at the non-drive end; some manufacturers locate at the drive end. Some designs set the rotor's axial position with shims or spacers in the housing. Proportions are illustrative.

componentRecords.function: The locating (thrust) bearing in the baseline arrangement: carries residual axial thrust in both directions plus its share of radial load at the non-drive end, and holds the rotor in a fixed axial position.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple:
In an angular-contact ball bearing the raceways are offset so that the line of contact between ball and raceways is inclined to the radial plane at the contact angle. Each bearing can therefore carry combined radial and axial load, but axial load in one direction only. Mounting two bearings back-to-back (wide outer-ring faces together, sometimes called the O arrangement) lets the pair take thrust in both directions, one bearing per direction. In this arrangement the load lines diverge towards the shaft axis, giving a wide effective spread and good stiffness against tilting.

The bearings are supplied as matched or universally matchable sets made to give a defined internal clearance or preload once the rings are clamped. The inner rings are clamped together against a shaft shoulder by the locknut, and the outer rings are clamped between the housing shoulder and the blind end cover.
componentRecords.construction: Two single-row angular-contact ball bearings mounted back-to-back. Contact angle, preload or clearance class, cage design and fits are chosen by the OEM and the bearing manufacturer. Some manufacturers mark matched sets, for example with a V-shaped mark across the outer rings, to show the correct orientation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Because a double-suction impeller is never perfectly balanced axially, this bearing is essential. Mounting errors are serious: a pair fitted in tandem or face-to-face instead of back-to-back, bearings from different sets mixed, or rings not properly clamped change the preload, reduce the thrust capacity in one direction or allow the rotor to move. If residual thrust rises, for example because of uneven wear-ring wear, poor suction flow or off-design operation, this bearing runs hotter and its life shortens.
componentRecords.maintenance: Replace the pair as a matched set; never replace one bearing of a pair. Check the arrangement and markings before mounting, heat for mounting as the bearing manufacturer instructs, and clamp both rings by the OEM's method. After assembly verify rotor end float or axial position. In service, trend temperature, axial vibration and lubricant condition.
componentRecords.notes: Variant: a single deep-groove ball bearing for lighter thrust duty. Heavier-duty designs may use other thrust arrangements, such as paired tapered roller bearings or hydrodynamic thrust bearings on large machines. Silicon nitride appears only in hybrid bearings; cages may be brass, pressed steel or polyamide. The model shows the pair in simplified form.

componentRecords.function: Variant locating bearing for lighter thrust duty: carries radial load plus moderate axial load in both directions at the non-drive end and fixes the rotor axially.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The deep raceway grooves of a deep-groove ball bearing let it carry axial load in either direction: under axial load the balls shift slightly in the grooves and a contact angle develops. Its axial capacity is lower than that of a back-to-back angular-contact pair. As a locating bearing both rings are clamped: the inner ring by the locknut against the shaft shoulder, the outer ring between the housing shoulder and the end cover.
componentRecords.construction: A single-row deep-groove ball bearing with clearance class, cage and fits chosen by the OEM. The end cover or a spacer is arranged to clamp the outer ring.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is suitable where the OEM has assessed the residual thrust as small over the operating range. Substituting it for an angular-contact pair, or the reverse, changes thrust capacity, stiffness and rotor end float, and must not be done without OEM approval. The bearing's axial internal play allows a small rotor end float.
componentRecords.maintenance: As for the baseline bearing: correct mounting method, clamping of both rings and an end-float check after assembly as the OEM specifies. Trend temperature and axial vibration; a rising trend can indicate thrust above what the bearing was selected for.
componentRecords.notes: The model uses the same housing for both variants; real designs may use a different housing, cover or spacer. Some pumps use a double-row angular-contact bearing instead.

componentRecords.function: Closes the casing side of the non-drive-end bearing housing, retains the lubricant and carries the inboard bearing housing seal.
componentRecords.construction: A bolted ring cover with a spigot, a gasket or O-ring and a shaft bore holding the seal. In the baseline the outer rings of the locating bearing are clamped between a shoulder in the housing and the blind end cover, so this cover only closes and seals the housing; in other designs the inboard cover provides one of the clamping faces.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It faces the non-drive-end seal or stuffing box, so, together with the shaft deflector, it is the main barrier against water entering the lubricant. Where a design uses it as a clamping face, it also carries thrust.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the spigot, gasket face and seal bore, renew the gasket and seal at reassembly, and confirm that the shaft runs centrally without rubbing. Keep the isolator's expulsion port clear and correctly oriented.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified in the model.

componentRecords.function: Closes the outboard end of the non-drive-end housing (the cover is blind; the shaft does not pass through it) and clamps the locating bearing's outer rings against the housing shoulder, so that outward axial thrust passes into the cover and its bolts.
componentRecords.construction: A blind bolted cover with a spigot and a clamping face, sealed with a gasket or O-ring. The clamp is often set by a gasket, shim or machined dimension. Where fitted, it may carry a temperature sensor port or a mounting point for a vibration sensor.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The outer rings must be held firmly so they cannot shuffle axially, otherwise the rotor loses its location and the bearings can be damaged; at the same time the cover must not distort the rings. Because the cover carries thrust in one direction, its bolts are load-carrying.
componentRecords.maintenance: When refitting, establish the outer-ring clamp by the OEM's method, for example by measuring cover recess against bearing projection and selecting the gasket or shim accordingly. Renew the gasket, tighten bolts evenly and check the clamping face for fretting.
componentRecords.notes: Blind cover: no outboard housing seal is needed at this end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Clamps the locating bearing's inner rings against the shaft shoulder, so that they rotate as one with the shaft and transmit thrust in both directions between shaft and bearing.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Thrust towards the shoulder passes from the inner rings into the shoulder; thrust in the opposite direction passes through the locknut and its thread. Unlike the drive-end nut, this nut is therefore part of the thrust load path.
componentRecords.construction: A slotted round locknut on a fine thread, locked by a tab washer, tightened with a hook spanner or slotted socket.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the nut slackens, the rotor can move axially by the amount of the looseness, upsetting impeller centring and the seal setting and damaging the bearing. With a paired angular-contact set, firm and square clamping of the inner rings is part of achieving the preload or clearance the set was made for.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect threads and slots, replace a damaged nut, tighten by the OEM or bearing manufacturer's method, and lock with a new lockwasher. Check that the nut face bears squarely on the ring.
componentRecords.notes: Some designs use a locknut with an integral locking screw. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Locks the bearing locknut so that it cannot slacken in service.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: An internal tang on the washer engages a slot or keyway in the threaded part of the shaft, so the washer cannot turn on the shaft. After the locknut has been tightened, one of the washer's external tabs is bent into a slot in the nut, locking nut and shaft together.
componentRecords.construction: A thin pressed-steel tab washer matched to the locknut size, fitted between the bearing inner ring (or a spacer) and the locknut.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is small and cheap, but if it fails or is left out the nut can work loose and the inner ring can move on the shaft. That leads to fretting, loss of clamping, noise and eventually bearing failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Fit a new lockwasher at each reassembly, because re-bent tabs can crack. Check that the internal tang is straight and sits in the shaft slot without being forced. Tighten the nut by the method the OEM or bearing manufacturer specifies; if no nut slot lines up with a tab, follow their guidance, which is generally to tighten slightly further to the next slot rather than slacken the nut. Bend the tab fully into the slot without damaging the nut.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: locks the nut that clamps the locating bearing's inner rings, a nut that is part of the thrust load path, so correct locking is especially important. Some designs use a locknut with an integral locking screw instead. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Keeps the lubricant in and water, dust and process liquid out where the shaft enters the non-drive-end bearing housing from the casing side.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Either a contacting lip seal, whose elastomer lip runs on a thin film on the shaft, or a non-contacting labyrinth seal or bearing isolator, whose rotor and stator form a winding path with drain ports that return lubricant and expel contaminants.
componentRecords.construction: Fitted in the inboard cover bore. Isolators usually have an O-ring-driven rotor and a stator with an expulsion port that must be oriented as the manufacturer specifies, normally at the bottom.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is the main barrier between the non-drive-end shaft seal or packing, with its possible leakage or spray, and the locating bearing's lubricant. Water in the lubricant is a leading cause of rolling-bearing failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Watch for oil weeping and water in the oil. Renew lip seals at reassembly using a fitting sleeve, check the shaft for grooving, and fit isolators exactly as the manufacturer instructs.
componentRecords.notes: Only one housing seal at this end, because the end cover is blind. Bronze isolators are covered by the tin-bronze family as an approximation. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Seal the bolted joints between the bearing housing and its covers, so that lubricant stays in and water, dust and process liquid stay out.
componentRecords.construction: Depending on the design: thin flat gaskets of compressed fibre or paper-type jointing, O-rings in machined grooves, or an approved liquid sealant on metal-to-metal joints. Flat gaskets are cut to the cover spigot and bolt pattern.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Cover gaskets also affect axial geometry. A gasket of the wrong thickness under a cover can clamp a bearing that is meant to float, or fail to clamp one that is meant to be located, so substituting a different or home-made gasket can change how the bearing arrangement works. Leaking joints let oil out and moisture in, and both shorten bearing life.
componentRecords.maintenance: Fit new gaskets or O-rings at every reassembly, using only the type and thickness specified by the OEM. Clean joint faces without scoring them, remove burrs, and tighten cover bolts evenly. Apply liquid sealant sparingly so that none is squeezed into the bearing cavity. Look for oil weeping at the joints on routine rounds.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: the gasket or shim under the blind end cover may set the clamp on the locating bearing's outer rings, so its thickness directly affects whether the rotor is held axially. Use only the type and thickness the OEM specifies. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Fasten the non-drive-end bearing housing to its bracket on the lower casing half and hold it in position against both radial load and the axial thrust carried by the locating bearing.
componentRecords.construction: Bolts or studs with nuts and washers, with a spigot or dowels for location. In some designs, shims, adjusting screws or spacers set the housing and rotor position.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: At the locating end the housing fixings carry the residual thrust into the casing. Loose bolts allow axial and radial movement, altering impeller centring and causing vibration and bearing damage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check tightness during routine inspections and tighten to the OEM's values. Inspect dowels and holes. Mark the housing position and any shims before removing the rotor, and check rotor centring and end float after reassembly as the OEM describes.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Provides the entry point for adding fresh grease to the bearing housing in the grease-lubricated variant. The relief plug opens an exit so that displaced old grease and any excess can escape instead of pressurising and over-filling the housing.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: A grease gun forces grease past a spring-loaded ball check in the nipple, which stops grease and dirt from coming back out. The fresh grease is directed into the bearing and pushes old grease through the bearing towards the relief opening, renewing the lubricant in the working area.
componentRecords.construction: A threaded hydraulic-type grease nipple on the housing, usually feeding a passage that delivers grease close to the bearing, and a threaded relief or drain plug on the other side of the bearing, often at the bottom of the grease cavity.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Grease quantity is critical. Too much grease is churned by the rolling elements, which raises temperature and can force grease past the housing seals; too little starves the bearing. Greases with incompatible thickeners or base oils can soften or harden when mixed and lose their lubricating ability, so the grease type must not be changed without checking compatibility.
componentRecords.maintenance: Wipe the nipple clean before connecting the gun. Use only the grease specified by the OEM, at the interval and quantity given by the OEM, the bearing manufacturer or the site lubrication schedule. Where the procedure requires it, remove the relief plug while regreasing, let the excess purge, then refit it. Record each regreasing. A short-lived temperature rise after regreasing is normal; a persistent rise is not.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: lubricates the locating bearing, which also carries thrust, so correct grease quantity matters as much here as at the drive end. Regreasing a running pump is allowed only where the design and site safety rules permit it. Shown as simple fittings in the model.

componentRecords.function: Shows the oil level in the bearing housing sump against a reference mark, and allows the oil's condition (colour, cloudiness, foaming) to be seen without opening the housing.
componentRecords.construction: Usually a round bull's-eye window screwed into the side of the housing at the required level, with a level mark or centre line; some designs use a tubular level gauge. The window is glass or a transparent polymer sealed into a metal or polymer body.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: In an oil-bath housing the level must be right: too low and the bearing may be starved, too high and the oil is churned, heats up and may leak past the housing seals. Milky or cloudy oil is a strong sign of water contamination, frequently from seal or packing leakage, and calls for an oil change and a search for the source.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the level and appearance on every operator round. The OEM states whether the level is read at standstill or while running, as the two can differ. Keep the window clean and replace it if it is crazed, discoloured or weeping. The sight glass and the constant-level oiler should agree; if they do not, find out why before adding oil.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. The window material (glass or transparent polymer) is not a family in the material library; the listed materials cover the body and its seal. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Allows the bearing housing sump to be drained completely for oil changes, and provides a point from which an oil sample can be taken where the site uses oil analysis.
componentRecords.construction: A threaded plug with a sealing washer at the lowest point of the sump. Some designs use a magnetic plug that collects fine ferrous wear debris; some sites fit a small valve or a sampling point instead of a plain plug.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Water and wear debris settle at the bottom of the sump, so draining from the lowest point removes them with the old oil. Debris on a magnetic plug, or metal particles and water in a sample, are early warnings of bearing distress.
componentRecords.maintenance: Change the oil at the interval set by the OEM or the site schedule, or earlier if it is contaminated. Drain into a clean container and look at the oil and any debris before disposal. Fit a new sealing washer, tighten the plug, refill with the specified oil to the correct level and check for leaks after start-up. Dispose of used oil in line with environmental requirements.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Fitted in the oil-lubricated variant. Debris from the locating bearing can indicate thrust-related distress, so inspect the drained oil carefully. Shown as a simple plug.

componentRecords.function: A constant-level oiler automatically tops up the bearing housing sump to hold a set oil level, and carries a visible reserve of oil.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The oiler works on the 'bird-feeder' principle. Its transparent reservoir is inverted and sealed at the top. When the sump level falls below the oiler's lower opening, air bubbles up into the reservoir and oil flows out until the opening is covered again. The level held is therefore set by the oiler's height adjustment relative to the housing, not by how full the reservoir is.
componentRecords.construction: A transparent reservoir bulb on a metal or polymer body with a level-setting device, connected to the housing below the oil level through an elbow or pipe nipple.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The oiler makes up small losses, but it cannot lower a level that is too high, does not show oil condition, and cannot keep up with a housing that leaks faster than it can supply.
