Rapid consumption points to leaking housing seals or gaskets. Pressure differences between the inside of the housing and the atmosphere, and in some designs the direction of shaft rotation relative to the oiler's position, can upset the level, so the oiler must be fitted and set as the OEM specifies.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check the reservoir on each round and refill with the specified oil before it empties. Confirm at commissioning, and after any work on the housing, that the oiler setting gives the required sump level as shown on the sight glass. Track consumption; a change in rate is a useful early sign of a seal or gasket problem. Keep the bulb clean so the level can be seen.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Fitted only in the oil-lubricated variant. Each housing has its own oiler, set for its own sump level. The model shows a generic oiler.

componentRecords.function: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Two very flat faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary in the gland plate, are pressed together by spring force and by the liquid pressure in the seal chamber. A thin fluid film between the faces lubricates and cools them while restricting leakage. Elastomer secondary seals seal each face to its mounting, and the springs keep the faces closed as they wear and as the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
componentRecords.construction: Baseline: a single, spring-loaded component seal. The rotating unit (rotating face, springs, shaft-side secondary seal and retainer or drive collar) is mounted on the shaft sleeve. The stationary face (seat) is held in a gland plate bolted to the face of the seal chamber, which is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. A flush connection supplies liquid to the chamber. Many pumps instead use cartridge seals, which arrive pre-assembled on their own sleeve and gland with the setting fixed by the seal manufacturer.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Shaft seals are one of the most frequent reasons for unplanned pump maintenance. Most seal failures are caused by operating and installation conditions, such as dry running, loss of flush, operation far from the best efficiency point, vibration, misalignment and incorrect fitting, rather than by a defect in the seal itself.
componentRecords.maintenance: Watch for visible leakage, unusual noise, heat at the gland and the condition of the flush line. Never run the pump dry, not even briefly to check rotation. When replacing, follow the seal manufacturer's instructions on cleanliness, setting dimension, elastomer lubricants and gland tightening. In a between-bearings pump, seal replacement normally involves either removing the bearing housing at that end (and, at the drive end, the coupling spacer and pump hub) or lifting out the complete rotor after removing the upper casing; follow the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end: the coupling spacer must be removed for access. Variants include single or dual seals (unpressurised buffer or pressurised barrier), pusher or bellows designs, component or cartridge seals, and split seals that can be fitted without dismantling the pump. The model is simplified: anti-rotation pins, set screws and internal clearances are not shown. Fitted only in the mechanical-seal configuration; never combined with packing in the same stuffing box.

componentRecords.function: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In the baseline seal the rotating face is the flexibly mounted ring. The springs push it against the stationary seat, and it floats on its secondary seal so that it can follow face wear, small axial shaft movement and slight misalignment. Its lapped surface runs on a very thin film of the sealed liquid, across which a tiny leakage passes radially.
componentRecords.construction: A ring of carbon-graphite, or of a hard face material such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide, lapped flat and polished on its sealing face. It is driven by lugs, pins or notches in the retainer and sealed to the sleeve by the secondary seal. A common pairing is a carbon face against a hard face; hard-against-hard pairs are often used where abrasive particles are present.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The face material pair decides wear rate, tolerance of brief dry running, resistance to abrasives and chemical compatibility. Face materials are hard but brittle: they chip if knocked, can crack from thermal shock and lose flatness if distorted, and any of these causes leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Handle faces only by their edges and never touch the lapped surface with bare fingers; keep them in their packaging until fitting and clean them only as the seal manufacturer specifies. At removal, read the wear track: an uneven or over-wide track suggests misalignment or runout, heat checking or blistering suggests overheating or dry running, and chipped edges suggest vibration or flashing between the faces. Faces are normally replaced or refurbished as a matched pair.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Some seal designs carry the springs on the stationary side instead (stationary flexible element), in which case the rotating face is the rigidly mounted ring. The model shows a plain ring.

componentRecords.function: The non-rotating mating ring (seat) mounted in the gland plate; it provides the counter-face against which the rotating face runs.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The seat is held against rotation, usually by an anti-rotation pin or slot, and sealed into the gland bore by an O-ring that also cushions it. Because it is fixed, its sealing face must be held square to the shaft axis so that the rotating face can run on it with a uniform film.
componentRecords.construction: A lapped ring, commonly silicon carbide or tungsten carbide in a carbon-against-hard pairing, or carbon where the rotating face is the hard ring. It sits in a machined recess in the gland plate.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Squareness matters. Uneven tightening of the gland nuts, a gland face that is not flat, or an anti-rotation pin that bottoms in the seat can tilt or distort it and cause leakage. A sudden temperature change, for example cold liquid reaching a hot seat, can crack brittle seat materials.
componentRecords.maintenance: Protect the lapped face as for the rotating face. Before fitting, check that the anti-rotation pin engages without bottoming and that the O-ring is the specified compound and size. Tighten the gland nuts evenly in a diagonal sequence as the seal manufacturer instructs. Inspect for chips, cracks and the wear-track pattern at every removal.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown as a plain ring in the gland plate; anti-rotation details are not modelled.

componentRecords.function: Provide the mechanical closing force that keeps the seal faces in contact when there is little or no liquid pressure, and keep them closed as the faces wear and the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: When the seal is set to its working length the springs are compressed by a defined amount, giving a known spring load. In operation, the pressure in the seal chamber adds hydraulic closing force, so the total face load is spring load plus hydraulic load; the hydraulic share depends on the seal's balance.
componentRecords.construction: Either a single large coil spring or several small springs spaced around the retainer. In metal bellows seals the welded bellows acts as both spring and secondary seal. In the baseline the springs rotate with the shaft as part of the rotating unit.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the seal is set at the wrong length the springs are over- or under-compressed: too much load causes heat and rapid face wear, too little lets the faces open and leak. Springs in contact with the pumped liquid can clog with solids or corrode. Multiple small springs are generally more sensitive to clogging, while a single large spring tolerates dirt better but may be sensitive to the direction of rotation.
componentRecords.maintenance: Set the seal to the working length or setting dimension given by the seal manufacturer, measured from the datum it specifies. At overhaul, check springs for clogging, corrosion, loss of free length and cracks, and renew them with the seal repair kit.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Other corrosion-resistant alloys are used for aggressive liquids. The model represents the springs schematically.

componentRecords.function: Seals between the rotating seal parts and the shaft sleeve, so that liquid cannot bypass the faces along the sleeve, while still allowing the rotating face to move axially and tilt slightly.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a pusher seal the secondary seal (an O-ring or wedge) slides a short distance along the sleeve as the face wears and the shaft moves. In an elastomer bellows seal the bellows flexes instead of sliding. Either way it must stay flexible for the face to follow.
componentRecords.construction: An elastomer O-ring, a PTFE wedge or an elastomer bellows, fitted in the rotating unit on the sleeve.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The elastomer must be compatible with the pumped liquid, the flush and the operating temperature; the wrong compound swells, hardens or cracks. Deposits or crystals on the sleeve can stop a pusher secondary seal from sliding ('hang-up'), so the faces open. Small repeated movements can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.
componentRecords.maintenance: Replace at every seal rebuild and confirm the compound against the seal datasheet. Use only fitting lubricants compatible with the elastomer; for example, EPDM is generally not compatible with mineral-oil-based lubricants. Protect it from sharp edges, keyways and threads during fitting, and inspect the sleeve under it for fretting or corrosion.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown as a simple ring in the model.

componentRecords.function: Static seals for the stationary parts: the seat O-ring seals and cushions the stationary face in the gland plate, and the gland O-ring or gasket seals the gland plate to the seal chamber face.
componentRecords.construction: Elastomer O-rings in machined grooves, or a flat gasket between gland plate and chamber face, depending on the design.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Although static, these seals are exposed to the pumped liquid and to temperature, so the compound must suit the service. In a split case pump the chamber face is formed by both casing halves, so a step at the split or a protruding casing gasket can stop the gland seal from seating properly.
componentRecords.maintenance: Renew at every seal installation using the specified size and compound. Lubricate only with a compatible lubricant, check grooves and faces for damage, and make sure the seal chamber face is clean and flush across the casing split before fitting the gland.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
componentRecords.construction: A machined plate with a register or spigot that centres it on the seal chamber, a recess for the seat and its O-ring, tapped ports, and bolt holes for the studs and nuts on the seal chamber face. Cartridge seals have their own gland, supplied with setting clips or plates fitted for installation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The gland is the reference that keeps the seat square and centred, and uneven tightening distorts the seat. The register, not the bolts, should provide concentricity. With cartridge seals the setting devices must be removed or disengaged after the gland is bolted up and the sleeve is locked, and before the shaft is turned; leaving them in place is a classic cause of immediate failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the faces and register for damage and corrosion, clean the ports, and tighten the nuts evenly as the seal manufacturer instructs. Make sure the auxiliary piping is connected to the correct ports and that unused ports are plugged as the seal drawing shows.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. In split case pumps the face the gland bolts to spans the casing split, so the casing gasket must be trimmed flush and the halves must align without a step. Shown simplified in the model.

componentRecords.function: Holds the rotating seal parts together and fixes the rotating unit to the shaft sleeve, driving the rotating face and setting its axial position.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Set screws or a separate drive collar grip the sleeve, and lugs or pins in the retainer drive the rotating face. The axial position at which the retainer is locked decides how much the springs are compressed.
componentRecords.construction: A machined ring carrying the springs, with drive lugs and tapped holes for hardened set screws, or a split drive collar clamped to the sleeve.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the retainer slips on the sleeve, the spring setting changes and the seal leaks or overheats. Worn drive lugs show that the faces have been transmitting high friction torque, for example during dry running or with poor face lubrication.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure and record the setting position before dismantling. On reassembly, set to the seal manufacturer's dimension from the specified datum, tighten the set screws as instructed, and check drive lugs and set-screw seats for wear.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Supplies a controlled flow of liquid to the seal chamber close to the seal faces, to carry away the heat generated at the faces, keep them wetted, stop the liquid around them from flashing to vapour, and help keep solids and trapped air or vapour away from the seal.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In clean-water service the flush is commonly taken from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or the volute, through small-bore tubing and a flow-limiting orifice into the seal chamber. Where the pumped liquid is dirty or otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid can be injected from an external source instead. The arrangement is defined by the seal piping plan.
componentRecords.construction: A tapped connection in the gland plate or seal chamber, with tubing, an orifice or other flow control, an isolating valve and, in some arrangements, a strainer, cyclone separator or cooler.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A blocked orifice, a closed valve or a failed external supply removes the seal's cooling and lubrication, and is a common cause of seal overheating and failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that the flush is flowing (for example, a flow indicator shows flow or the line temperature is as expected), that valves are open, and that orifices, strainers or separators are not blocked. Vent the seal chamber before start-up as the OEM instructs. Do not change orifice sizes or the piping plan without consulting the seal manufacturer.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. The model shows only the connection. The actual piping plan is stated on the seal and pump datasheets.

componentRecords.function: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing, keeping the pumped liquid in with only a very small leakage, much of which normally leaves the seal faces as vapour.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Two very flat faces, one rotating with the shaft and one stationary in the gland plate, are pressed together by spring force and by the liquid pressure in the seal chamber. A thin fluid film between the faces lubricates and cools them while restricting leakage. Elastomer secondary seals seal each face to its mounting, and the springs keep the faces closed as they wear and as the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
componentRecords.construction: Baseline: a single, spring-loaded component seal. The rotating unit (rotating face, springs, shaft-side secondary seal and retainer or drive collar) is mounted on the shaft sleeve. The stationary face (seat) is held in a gland plate bolted to the face of the seal chamber, which is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves. A flush connection supplies liquid to the chamber. Many pumps instead use cartridge seals, which arrive pre-assembled on their own sleeve and gland with the setting fixed by the seal manufacturer.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Shaft seals are one of the most frequent reasons for unplanned pump maintenance. Most seal failures are caused by operating and installation conditions, such as dry running, loss of flush, operation far from the best efficiency point, vibration, misalignment and incorrect fitting, rather than by a defect in the seal itself.
componentRecords.maintenance: Watch for visible leakage, unusual noise, heat at the gland and the condition of the flush line. Never run the pump dry, not even briefly to check rotation. When replacing, follow the seal manufacturer's instructions on cleanliness, setting dimension, elastomer lubricants and gland tightening. In a between-bearings pump, seal replacement normally involves either removing the bearing housing at that end (and, at the drive end, the coupling spacer and pump hub) or lifting out the complete rotor after removing the upper casing; follow the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: identical in function to the drive-end seal. Because the two seals face in opposite directions along the shaft, each sees the opposite sense of rotation relative to its own orientation; rotation-sensitive seals (for example some single-spring designs) are therefore handed and may not be interchangeable between ends, so check the OEM part numbers. The coupling does not obstruct access at this end, but replacement still normally involves removing the bearing housing or lifting the rotor. Variants and modelling simplifications are as for the drive-end seal. Never combined with packing in the same stuffing box.

componentRecords.function: The primary seal ring that turns with the shaft and runs against the stationary face; together the two faces form the main sealing interface.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In the baseline seal the rotating face is the flexibly mounted ring. The springs push it against the stationary seat, and it floats on its secondary seal so that it can follow face wear, small axial shaft movement and slight misalignment. Its lapped surface runs on a very thin film of the sealed liquid, across which a tiny leakage passes radially.
componentRecords.construction: A ring of carbon-graphite, or of a hard face material such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide, lapped flat and polished on its sealing face. It is driven by lugs, pins or notches in the retainer and sealed to the sleeve by the secondary seal. A common pairing is a carbon face against a hard face; hard-against-hard pairs are often used where abrasive particles are present.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The face material pair decides wear rate, tolerance of brief dry running, resistance to abrasives and chemical compatibility. Face materials are hard but brittle: they chip if knocked, can crack from thermal shock and lose flatness if distorted, and any of these causes leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Handle faces only by their edges and never touch the lapped surface with bare fingers; keep them in their packaging until fitting and clean them only as the seal manufacturer specifies. At removal, read the wear track: an uneven or over-wide track suggests misalignment or runout, heat checking or blistering suggests overheating or dry running, and chipped edges suggest vibration or flashing between the faces. Faces are normally replaced or refurbished as a matched pair.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: same function and material options as the drive-end rotating face. Some seal designs carry the springs on the stationary side, making the rotating face the rigid ring. The model shows a plain ring.

componentRecords.function: The non-rotating mating ring (seat) mounted in the gland plate; it provides the counter-face against which the rotating face runs.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The seat is held against rotation, usually by an anti-rotation pin or slot, and sealed into the gland bore by an O-ring that also cushions it. Because it is fixed, its sealing face must be held square to the shaft axis so that the rotating face can run on it with a uniform film.
componentRecords.construction: A lapped ring, commonly silicon carbide or tungsten carbide in a carbon-against-hard pairing, or carbon where the rotating face is the hard ring. It sits in a machined recess in the gland plate.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Squareness matters. Uneven tightening of the gland nuts, a gland face that is not flat, or an anti-rotation pin that bottoms in the seat can tilt or distort it and cause leakage. A sudden temperature change, for example cold liquid reaching a hot seat, can crack brittle seat materials.
componentRecords.maintenance: Protect the lapped face as for the rotating face. Before fitting, check that the anti-rotation pin engages without bottoming and that the O-ring is the specified compound and size. Tighten the gland nuts evenly in a diagonal sequence as the seal manufacturer instructs. Inspect for chips, cracks and the wear-track pattern at every removal.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end: same function as the drive-end seat. Shown as a plain ring; anti-rotation details are not modelled.

componentRecords.function: Provide the mechanical closing force that keeps the seal faces in contact when there is little or no liquid pressure, and keep them closed as the faces wear and the shaft moves slightly along its axis.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: When the seal is set to its working length the springs are compressed by a defined amount, giving a known spring load. In operation, the pressure in the seal chamber adds hydraulic closing force, so the total face load is spring load plus hydraulic load; the hydraulic share depends on the seal's balance.
componentRecords.construction: Either a single large coil spring or several small springs spaced around the retainer. In metal bellows seals the welded bellows acts as both spring and secondary seal. In the baseline the springs rotate with the shaft as part of the rotating unit.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the seal is set at the wrong length the springs are over- or under-compressed: too much load causes heat and rapid face wear, too little lets the faces open and leak. Springs in contact with the pumped liquid can clog with solids or corrode. Multiple small springs are generally more sensitive to clogging, while a single large spring tolerates dirt better but may be sensitive to the direction of rotation.
componentRecords.maintenance: Set the seal to the working length or setting dimension given by the seal manufacturer, measured from the datum it specifies. At overhaul, check springs for clogging, corrosion, loss of free length and cracks, and renew them with the seal repair kit.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. A single coil spring wound for one direction of rotation will be handed opposite to the drive-end spring, because the seal faces the other way along the shaft. Other corrosion-resistant alloys are used for aggressive liquids. Shown schematically.

componentRecords.function: Seals between the rotating seal parts and the shaft sleeve, so that liquid cannot bypass the faces along the sleeve, while still allowing the rotating face to move axially and tilt slightly.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a pusher seal the secondary seal (an O-ring or wedge) slides a short distance along the sleeve as the face wears and the shaft moves. In an elastomer bellows seal the bellows flexes instead of sliding. Either way it must stay flexible for the face to follow.
componentRecords.construction: An elastomer O-ring, a PTFE wedge or an elastomer bellows, fitted in the rotating unit on the sleeve.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The elastomer must be compatible with the pumped liquid, the flush and the operating temperature; the wrong compound swells, hardens or cracks. Deposits or crystals on the sleeve can stop a pusher secondary seal from sliding ('hang-up'), so the faces open. Small repeated movements can fret the sleeve under the secondary seal.
componentRecords.maintenance: Replace at every seal rebuild and confirm the compound against the seal datasheet. Use only fitting lubricants compatible with the elastomer; for example, EPDM is generally not compatible with mineral-oil-based lubricants. Protect it from sharp edges, keyways and threads during fitting, and inspect the sleeve under it for fretting or corrosion.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Shown as a simple ring in the model.

componentRecords.function: Static seals for the stationary parts: the seat O-ring seals and cushions the stationary face in the gland plate, and the gland O-ring or gasket seals the gland plate to the seal chamber face.
componentRecords.construction: Elastomer O-rings in machined grooves, or a flat gasket between gland plate and chamber face, depending on the design.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Although static, these seals are exposed to the pumped liquid and to temperature, so the compound must suit the service. In a split case pump the chamber face is formed by both casing halves, so a step at the split or a protruding casing gasket can stop the gland seal from seating properly.
componentRecords.maintenance: Renew at every seal installation using the specified size and compound. Lubricate only with a compatible lubricant, check grooves and faces for damage, and make sure the seal chamber face is clean and flush across the casing split before fitting the gland.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Holds the stationary seat square and concentric to the shaft, closes the seal chamber, and carries the connection ports (flush and, where fitted, vent, quench or drain).
componentRecords.construction: A machined plate with a register or spigot that centres it on the seal chamber, a recess for the seat and its O-ring, tapped ports, and bolt holes for the studs and nuts on the seal chamber face. Cartridge seals have their own gland, supplied with setting clips or plates fitted for installation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The gland is the reference that keeps the seat square and centred, and uneven tightening distorts the seat. The register, not the bolts, should provide concentricity. With cartridge seals the setting devices must be removed or disengaged after the gland is bolted up and the sleeve is locked, and before the shaft is turned; leaving them in place is a classic cause of immediate failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the faces and register for damage and corrosion, clean the ports, and tighten the nuts evenly as the seal manufacturer instructs. Make sure the auxiliary piping is connected to the correct ports and that unused ports are plugged as the seal drawing shows.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. As at the drive end, the face the gland bolts to spans the casing split, so the casing gasket must be trimmed flush and the halves must align without a step. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Holds the rotating seal parts together and fixes the rotating unit to the shaft sleeve, driving the rotating face and setting its axial position.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Set screws or a separate drive collar grip the sleeve, and lugs or pins in the retainer drive the rotating face. The axial position at which the retainer is locked decides how much the springs are compressed.
componentRecords.construction: A machined ring carrying the springs, with drive lugs and tapped holes for hardened set screws, or a split drive collar clamped to the sleeve.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If the retainer slips on the sleeve, the spring setting changes and the seal leaks or overheats. Worn drive lugs show that the faces have been transmitting high friction torque, for example during dry running or with poor face lubrication.
componentRecords.maintenance: Measure and record the setting position before dismantling. On reassembly, set to the seal manufacturer's dimension from the specified datum, tighten the set screws as instructed, and check drive lugs and set-screw seats for wear.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Supplies a controlled flow of liquid to the seal chamber close to the seal faces, to carry away the heat generated at the faces, keep them wetted, stop the liquid around them from flashing to vapour, and help keep solids and trapped air or vapour away from the seal.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In clean-water service the flush is commonly taken from a higher-pressure point on the pump, such as the discharge or the volute, through small-bore tubing and a flow-limiting orifice into the seal chamber. Where the pumped liquid is dirty or otherwise unsuitable, clean liquid can be injected from an external source instead. The arrangement is defined by the seal piping plan.
componentRecords.construction: A tapped connection in the gland plate or seal chamber, with tubing, an orifice or other flow control, an isolating valve and, in some arrangements, a strainer, cyclone separator or cooler.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A blocked orifice, a closed valve or a failed external supply removes the seal's cooling and lubrication, and is a common cause of seal overheating and failure.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that the flush is flowing (for example, a flow indicator shows flow or the line temperature is as expected), that valves are open, and that orifices, strainers or separators are not blocked. Vent the seal chamber before start-up as the OEM instructs. Do not change orifice sizes or the piping plan without consulting the seal manufacturer.
componentRecords.notes: Non-drive end. Where both seals are flushed from one source, each line normally has its own orifice or flow control so that both chambers receive flow. The model shows only the connection; the actual piping plan is stated on the seal and pump datasheets.

componentRecords.function: The annular cavity around the shaft sleeve at each casing exit that houses the mechanical seal and holds liquid around it. Each chamber is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a typical double-suction design each chamber sits behind one impeller eye and is connected to the adjacent suction region, so it runs at approximately suction pressure. The flush keeps liquid moving through the chamber to remove heat and solids. Because the chamber is horizontal, air or vapour can collect at the top of it unless it is vented.
componentRecords.construction: The chamber bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so the gland plate face spans the horizontal split. Designs range from a conventional stuffing box adapted for a seal to an enlarged-bore chamber that gives more radial space and better circulation. Some designs have a throat bushing at the inner end.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Chamber size, venting and circulation strongly influence seal life. Because the chamber is split, the casing gasket must be trimmed flush at the chamber bore and face and the halves must align without a step; otherwise the gland gasket or seat O-ring may not seal and the seat may be distorted.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect the bore and face for erosion, corrosion and a step across the split. Check that the casing gasket is trimmed as the OEM instructs and that flush and vent passages are clear. Vent the chambers before every start-up following the OEM procedure.
componentRecords.notes: In the model this feature borrows the meshes of the casing seal housings: it is the same casting, viewed in its sealing role. Actual chamber pressure depends on the design, wear-ring clearances and flush arrangement; confirm it from the OEM data.

componentRecords.function: Seals the point where the shaft sleeve leaves the casing using compression packing: a set of packing rings squeezed by a gland follower, with a small, controlled leakage that lubricates and cools the packing.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Tightening the gland follower compresses the packing set axially, and the packing turns part of this into radial pressure against the sleeve and the stuffing box bore, throttling flow along the shaft. The compression is not uniform; the rings nearest the gland carry the most. A steady leakage across the packing is essential because it carries away frictional heat. Seal water fed through the lantern ring keeps the box full of clean liquid and, when the box is below atmospheric pressure, stops air being drawn in.
componentRecords.construction: Several packing rings in the stuffing box, with a lantern ring positioned under the flush (seal water) connection, retained by a gland follower on two or more studs. The stuffing box is cast integral with, and split with, the casing halves.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Packing is simple, tolerant of shaft movement and inexpensive, and in many split case designs it can be renewed without dismantling the pump. In return it leaks continuously, needs periodic adjustment, absorbs more power than a mechanical seal and wears the shaft sleeve. It is unsuitable where leakage of the pumped liquid is not acceptable.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep leakage at the rate the OEM or packing manufacturer recommends, adjusting the gland nuts evenly in small steps and allowing time to settle between adjustments. Repack when the follower has run out of adjustment or leakage can no longer be controlled. Inspect the sleeve for grooving whenever the box is repacked.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Fitted only in the packing configuration; never combined with a mechanical seal in the same stuffing box. Adjusting a gland close to the coupling on a running pump is a rotating-equipment hazard, so follow the site procedure. The model shows simplified rings without braid detail.

componentRecords.function: The sealing elements of the stuffing box: deformable rings compressed against the sleeve and bore to restrict leakage along the shaft.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Under gland load the rings deform and bear lightly on the rotating sleeve. Friction at this contact generates heat, which the controlled leakage removes. In service the rings consolidate and lose some of their impregnated lubricant, so the gland has to be re-tightened from time to time to hold the leakage rate.
componentRecords.construction: Typically square-section braided rings made from yarns such as PTFE, graphite-filled PTFE, carbon or aramid fibres with lubricating impregnants, or die-formed rings of flexible graphite. Braided packing is cut into individual rings with butt or skive joints, and the joints of successive rings are staggered around the shaft.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Correct size, number of rings and installation are essential. Oversize rings hammered into the box, a continuous spiral instead of separate rings, or excessive gland tightening cause overheating, burned packing, a grooved sleeve and high power absorption. Too little compression gives excessive leakage.
componentRecords.maintenance: Remove all old rings with proper packing extractors without scratching the sleeve, then clean the box and inspect the sleeve. Cut new rings on a mandrel of the sleeve diameter, or use pre-formed rings, of the specified size and type. Seat each ring individually, stagger the joints as the packing manufacturer recommends, and locate the lantern ring under the flush port. Start with the gland nuts just finger-tight and generous leakage, then tighten gradually over the run-in period to the recommended leakage.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. The number of rings either side of the lantern ring varies between designs. The model shows plain rings.

componentRecords.function: A spacer ring within the packing set that creates an annular space under the flush connection, so that seal water is distributed all the way round the shaft.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Seal water supplied at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure enters the lantern ring and flows both inwards towards the pump, preventing air ingress and keeping abrasive particles out of the packing, and outwards through the outer rings, where it becomes the lubricating and cooling leakage.
componentRecords.construction: A ring with internal and external grooves connected by radial holes, made solid or split for fitting. Many have tapped holes so that they can be extracted.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The lantern ring only works if it sits under the flush port. Because packing consolidates as the gland is tightened, it is positioned so that it ends up under the port in service. A misplaced lantern ring blocks the seal water, so the packing runs dry and air can enter.
componentRecords.maintenance: Note its depth in the box before removal. Clean the holes and grooves, check for wear or distortion, and refit it in the position the OEM specifies. Confirm seal water flow after start-up.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Some services do not need seal water and omit the lantern ring, as the OEM specifies. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Compresses the packing set axially when its nuts are tightened, and holds the packing in the stuffing box.
componentRecords.construction: A flanged ring whose spigot enters the stuffing box bore, with holes or slots for the gland studs. It is often split so that it can be removed from the shaft without dismantling the pump.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The follower must enter the box squarely. If the nuts are tightened unevenly it tilts, compresses the packing unevenly and may rub on the sleeve, generating heat and damaging both parts. Its remaining travel shows how much adjustment is left before repacking is needed.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that the follower is square (equal projection on both sides), that its bore clears the sleeve all round, and that the spigot is not worn or corroded. Adjust the nuts evenly in small increments.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: The studs and nuts that draw the gland follower into the stuffing box to compress the packing.
componentRecords.construction: Two or more studs screwed into the stuffing box face, which is formed by both casing halves, with nuts and washers. Some designs use swing bolts so that the gland can be swung clear.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: They allow fine, even adjustment of packing compression. Seized or corroded threads make adjustment uneven and can lead to one side being over-tightened.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep threads clean and protected with a compatible anti-seize compound. Adjust nuts by equal small amounts and replace corroded or damaged studs and nuts. Adjust a gland on a running pump only where the site procedure permits it, with all guards in place, keeping hands, clothing and tools clear of the rotating shaft.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Supplies seal water to the lantern ring.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: For clean liquids the water may be taken from the pump discharge through a small tube. Where the pumped liquid contains solids, where the stuffing box may be under vacuum, or where the pump's own pressure is not a reliable source, clean water is supplied from an external source. In either case its pressure must be above the stuffing box pressure.
componentRecords.construction: A tapped port in the stuffing box over the lantern ring, connected by tubing with an isolating valve and, in some installations, a flow indicator or pressure regulator.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Loss of seal water lets the packing overheat and, if the stuffing box is below atmospheric pressure, allows air into the pump, which reduces performance and can cause loss of prime.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check flow and pressure on each round, keep the line clear, and confirm that an external supply is on before the pump is started. Isolate it at shutdown only where the site procedure says so.
componentRecords.notes: Drive end. The model shows only the connection.

componentRecords.function: The annular cavity at each casing exit that contains the packing set, lantern ring and the inner end of the gland follower. Each box is cast integral with, and split with, the upper and lower casing halves.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a typical double-suction design each stuffing box is connected to the adjacent suction region and runs at approximately suction pressure. Under suction lift that pressure may be below atmospheric, which is why seal water is fed to the lantern ring to keep air from being drawn in along the shaft.
componentRecords.construction: A bore sized for the packing cross-section and number of rings, ending at an inner shoulder or a throat bushing, with a seal water port over the lantern ring position and stud holes in the face. Bore and face are machined with the casing halves bolted together, so both span the horizontal split.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The bore must be round, smooth and concentric with the shaft for the packing to seal evenly. Because the box is split, the casing gasket must be trimmed flush at the bore and the halves must meet without a step, or leakage will bypass the packing along the joint.
componentRecords.maintenance: When repacking, inspect the bore for wear, scoring and corrosion, check for a step at the split, and make sure the seal water port is clear. Measure bore wear against the OEM limits at overhaul.
componentRecords.notes: In the model this feature borrows the meshes of the casing seal housings; it is the same casting as the seal chamber, shown in its packing role. Some pumps can be converted between packing and mechanical seal, but a chamber designed for seals may differ from a packing box, so conversions should follow the OEM's instructions.

componentRecords.function: Connects the pump shaft to the flexible coupling and transmits the driving torque from the coupling into the pump shaft.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Torque passes from the flexible elements into the hub flange, then through the key and the hub bore fit into the shaft. The hub is held axially on the shaft by the shaft end retainer or a set screw.
componentRecords.construction: A bored and keyed steel or iron hub with a flange or other features for attaching the flexible elements. The bore fit (interference or close clearance) is specified by the OEM or coupling manufacturer. Some designs use a tapered or keyless hydraulically fitted bore.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A loose bore fit allows fretting and key wear and can lead to hub failure. The hub's axial position sets the distance between shaft ends, which must suit the spacer length and any axial setting the coupling requires. Hub runout adds to apparent misalignment and unbalance.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check face and rim runout after mounting. For interference fits, mount by controlled heating as the coupling manufacturer instructs and remove with a proper puller; never hammer a hub on or off, since impacts pass straight into the bearings. Check key fit and the hub retainer.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified; the model does not distinguish coupling types.

componentRecords.function: Connects the motor shaft to the flexible coupling and transmits the motor's torque into the coupling.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Torque passes from the motor shaft through the key and bore fit into the hub, then through the hub flange into the flexible elements.
componentRecords.construction: A bored and keyed hub, usually the same type as the pump hub, with the bore fit specified by the coupling or motor manufacturer and a set screw or retainer to hold it axially.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The motor rotor's own axial position is set by its bearings, so the hub position on the motor shaft and the pump hub position together set the distance between shaft ends. Hammering this hub on can damage the motor bearings.
componentRecords.maintenance: As for the pump hub: controlled mounting, runout check, key fit and retention. Use the balancing key convention agreed between the motor and coupling suppliers.
componentRecords.notes: Motors with sleeve bearings have a magnetic centre and limited end float; for those, the coupling setting follows the motor manufacturer's instructions. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: The flexible members that transmit torque between the hubs and the spacer while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement between the shafts.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Each flexible plane allows a small angle between the parts on either side of it. With a spacer coupling there are two flexible planes, one at each end of the spacer, so a parallel offset between the shafts is taken up as a small angle at each plane, and angular misalignment is shared between them. Depending on type, flexibility comes from deforming an elastomer, flexing thin metal discs, sliding of crowned gear teeth, or flexing of a spring-steel grid.
componentRecords.construction: Elastomeric types (tyre, jaw and spider, pin and bush) use rubber or polyurethane elements and give some damping. Disc couplings use laminated packs of thin stainless steel discs bolted alternately to hub and spacer flanges, need no lubrication, and have limited misalignment capacity and a definite axial stiffness. Gear couplings use crowned external teeth in internal sleeve teeth, carry high torque for their size, and need lubrication. Grid couplings use a tapered spring-steel grid in grooved hubs, need lubrication and give some damping.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The coupling's misalignment capacity is there for small changes in service, not to excuse poor alignment; misalignment still loads the bearings, wears or fatigues the element and causes vibration. Elastomers age with heat, ozone, oils and chemicals; disc packs crack from excessive misalignment or wrong axial spacing; gear and grid types wear rapidly and can lock up without lubrication, transmitting axial force to the bearings. Some elastomeric designs are fail-safe and keep driving if the element fails; others are not.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the unit isolated, inspect the elements: elastomers for cracking, swelling, hardening and rubber dust inside the guard (often a sign of misalignment); disc packs for cracks, buckled laminations and fretting at bolt holes; gear and grid types for lubricant condition, leakage and tooth or grid wear. Tighten element bolts as the coupling manufacturer specifies and re-check alignment after any element change.
componentRecords.notes: The model shows a generic flexible element; real elements vary by type and manufacturer, and allowable misalignment, axial gap and lubricant are given in the coupling manufacturer's data.

componentRecords.function: Spans the gap between the pump and motor hubs. Removing it leaves a clear space between the shaft ends, so that the drive-end bearing housing and seal can be worked on, or the rotor lifted out, without moving the motor and losing its alignment.
componentRecords.construction: A tube or flanged spool bolted to the flexible elements at each end. Its length matches the specified distance between shaft ends.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Spacer length sets the geometry of the two flexible planes; for a given parallel offset, a longer spacer means a smaller angle at each plane. The spacer and its bolts form part of the balanced rotating assembly, so their orientation and fasteners matter.
componentRecords.maintenance: Match-mark the spacer to the hubs before removal and refit it in the same orientation. Use only the bolts, grade and type supplied by the coupling manufacturer, tightened to their values. Check the distance between shaft ends before refitting.
componentRecords.notes: Shown as a simple spool in the model, and removed in the maintenance animations.

componentRecords.function: Transmit torque between each shaft and its coupling hub through shear in the key and bearing pressure on the key sides.
componentRecords.construction: Parallel keys in keyways cut in the shaft and hub, sized to the shaft diameter and fitted as the OEM specifies.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Worn or loose keys allow movement that frets the keyway, and can lead to cracking or loss of drive. A key that projects beyond the hub adds unbalance and is a catch point. During balancing a key convention (for example half-key) is used, and the same convention must apply to both shaft and hub. During an uncoupled motor run a loose key can be thrown out, so it must be removed or secured.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for side wear, shear marks and fretting; inspect keyways for spreading or cracks. Deburr keyways, use new keys of the correct size and fit, and check that the key length suits the hub.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified as two keys.

componentRecords.function: A fixed guard that encloses the coupling and the exposed shaft ends between the pump and motor, preventing contact with rotating parts and helping to contain debris if the coupling fails.
componentRecords.construction: Usually two or more sheet-metal or mesh sections fastened to the baseplate or bearing housing so that they can only be removed with a tool. It must cover the full rotating length and keep a clearance to rotating parts. Any openings must be small enough, and far enough from the rotating parts, to prevent a hand or finger reaching them.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Rotating couplings and shafts can catch clothing, hair, gloves or tools in a fraction of a second, causing severe injury or death; at running speed a coupling can look stationary or blurred. Machinery safety regulations require a guard to be in place whenever the machine can run. Where the atmosphere is potentially explosive, guard material and design may also have to meet hazardous-area requirements.
componentRecords.maintenance: Remove the guard only when the driver is electrically isolated and locked out under the site permit system, with zero energy verified. Refit and secure it before the isolation is removed and before any test run. On routine rounds check that it is secure, undamaged and complete, and look for rubbing marks that show contact with rotating parts.
componentRecords.notes: The 3D viewer may show the guard transparent or hidden for learning purposes. That is a teaching aid only: a real pump must never be run with the guard removed or open.

componentRecords.function: Houses and supports the stator, carries the end shields that hold the motor bearings, provides the feet and terminal box mounting, and dissipates the motor's losses as heat through its fins.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: In a totally enclosed fan-cooled (TEFC) motor the inside is sealed from the outside air. Heat from the windings and core passes into the frame, and the external fan blows air along the fins to carry it away.
componentRecords.construction: A cast iron, aluminium or fabricated steel frame with external axial cooling fins, machined spigots for the end shields, cast or bolted feet, lifting eyes and an earth terminal.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Cooling depends on clean fins and unobstructed airflow; dirt build-up raises winding temperature and shortens insulation life. The frame's stiffness and the way its feet sit on the baseplate affect vibration and alignment.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep fins clean and the area around the motor free of obstructions. Trend frame temperature and vibration. Use the motor's lifting eyes for the motor alone, never to lift the pump set or baseplate.
componentRecords.notes: An illustrative TEFC induction motor. Ratings, frame size, enclosure and protection class come from the motor nameplate and datasheet, not from this model.

componentRecords.function: The stationary electromagnetic part of the motor. When its three-phase winding is connected to an alternating supply, it produces a magnetic field that rotates at synchronous speed.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The three phase currents, displaced in time and in space around the stator, combine to give a rotating field. Its speed, the synchronous speed, is n_s = 120 f / p rpm, where f is the supply frequency in Hz and p is the number of poles. The field induces currents in the rotor cage, and their interaction with the field produces torque.
componentRecords.construction: A core of thin, insulated electrical steel laminations (to limit eddy-current loss) with slots holding insulated copper windings, varnish-impregnated as a unit. Where fitted, winding temperature detectors and anti-condensation heaters are built in.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Winding insulation life depends strongly on operating temperature. Overload, supply voltage imbalance, loss of a phase, frequent starting, poor cooling and the fast voltage pulses from some variable-speed drives all stress the insulation.
componentRecords.maintenance: Electrical testing, such as insulation resistance measurement, must be done by competent, authorised electrical personnel following the site electrical safety procedure. Monitor current and winding temperature where instrumented, and keep the motor dry during standstill.
componentRecords.notes: Shown as a simplified internal part. Any work inside the motor or terminal box is electrical work and requires isolation and authorisation.

componentRecords.function: The rotating electromagnetic part of the induction motor; currents induced in its cage conductors interact with the stator field to produce torque.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: The rotor turns slightly slower than the stator field. This difference, the slip, is what allows the field to induce current in the cage bars; the slip increases with load.
componentRecords.construction: A laminated electrical steel core shrunk or keyed onto the motor shaft, with conductor bars in its slots joined by end rings to form a squirrel cage; the cage is commonly die-cast aluminium or fabricated copper. The rotor is dynamically balanced.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Broken or cracked rotor bars cause vibration and current fluctuations; an uneven air gap between rotor and stator causes unbalanced magnetic pull and vibration.
componentRecords.maintenance: Assessed mainly by condition monitoring: vibration analysis (electrically related components are often linked to twice line frequency) and motor current analysis. Rebalance after repair or rewinding.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Carries the rotor, is supported by the motor bearings in the end shields, and transmits the motor's torque to the coupling through its keyed drive end.
componentRecords.construction: A machined steel shaft with bearing journals, a keyed shaft extension at the drive end (facing the pump) and, at the other end, a seat for the cooling fan. In many rolling-bearing motors one motor bearing locates the rotor axially and the other floats.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Runout and keyway condition at the shaft extension affect coupling fit and alignment readings. The motor rotor's axial position and end float influence the coupling's axial setting.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check runout and the keyway when fitting the coupling hub. Protect the shaft extension from corrosion during storage, and rotate stored motors periodically as the motor manufacturer recommends to protect the bearings.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Close the ends of the motor frame, house the motor bearings, and centre the rotor in the stator bore so that the air gap is uniform.
componentRecords.construction: Cast end shields spigoted into the frame, with machined bearing seats, bearing caps and, on larger motors, grease nipples and grease relief outlets.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Accurate spigots keep the air gap even. Motor bearings have their own lubrication requirements, often stated on the motor nameplate or in the motor manual, separate from the pump's. With variable-speed drives, shaft currents can cause electrical erosion in motor bearings; insulated bearings or shaft grounding are used where the motor manufacturer specifies.
componentRecords.maintenance: Lubricate motor bearings as the motor manufacturer instructs (type, quantity and interval). Trend motor bearing temperature and vibration in the same way as the pump bearings.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified; motor bearing types and arrangement vary.

componentRecords.function: Encloses the connections between the supply cable and the winding leads, and usually auxiliary terminals for temperature detectors or heaters.
componentRecords.construction: A cast or fabricated box with a gasketed lid, cable gland entries, terminal block and earth terminal. On many motors it can be turned to suit the cable entry direction.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Sound terminations, correct earthing and a well-sealed lid are essential for electrical safety and to keep moisture out. The phase sequence at the terminals sets the direction of rotation, which must match the pump's rotation arrow. Running a pump in reverse reduces performance and, in some designs, can loosen threaded rotor parts that are arranged to tighten in the normal direction.
componentRecords.maintenance: Work in the terminal box only by authorised electrical personnel with the supply isolated, locked off and proved dead. Check terminations, glands and the lid seal. At commissioning, check rotation with the coupling spacer removed (motor uncoupled) and the motor key removed or secured.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: An external fan, driven by the motor shaft, that blows cooling air along the finned frame.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Because the fan is on the motor shaft, its airflow falls as speed falls. On a variable-speed drive, prolonged running at low speed can therefore reduce cooling, and the motor manufacturer may require derating or a separately driven fan.
componentRecords.construction: A polymer or aluminium fan fixed to the shaft extension at the non-drive end of the motor, inside the fan cover. Blades are commonly designed to work in either direction of rotation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A damaged, unbalanced or clogged fan reduces cooling and causes vibration. Fan blades are a rotating hazard, guarded by the fan cover.
componentRecords.maintenance: With the motor isolated, check the fan for cracks, missing blades, looseness and debris. Keep the air inlet clear.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Guards the external fan and directs its air along the cooling fins.
componentRecords.construction: A pressed steel or moulded cowl with a perforated inlet grille, bolted to the frame or end shield.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is a machine guard as well as an air duct; the motor must never run with it removed or damaged. The air inlet needs a clear space in front of it, as specified by the motor manufacturer, or cooling suffers.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that it is secure, undented (a dent can let the fan rub) and that the grille is not blocked by dirt, lint or stored material.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Mount the motor on its pads on the baseplate, and provide the surfaces for the shims and hold-down bolts used in alignment.
componentRecords.construction: Feet cast integral with the frame or bolted to it, with holes or slots that allow horizontal movement during alignment.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: If one foot does not sit flat on its pad and shims (soft foot), tightening the hold-down bolt distorts the frame, which changes alignment, can alter the air gap and increases vibration. Bolts that bind in their holes ('bolt bound') limit the horizontal adjustment available.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check and correct soft foot before alignment. Use clean, flat shim packs with as few shims as practical, covering the foot contact area. Check hold-down bolt tightness, and re-check alignment after any disturbance of the feet.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: The common support for pump and motor. It holds them in alignment, carries their weight and operating loads into the foundation through the grout and anchor bolts, and in many designs collects leakage in a drain rim.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a fabricated structure of steel sections with a deck or top plates, machined mounting pads for pump and motor, grout and vent holes, levelling-screw bosses, lifting lugs and a drain connection. Some baseplates are delivered pre-filled with grout in the factory.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The baseplate on its own is relatively flexible; it gains most of its stiffness when it is properly grouted to a sound foundation, becoming one structure with it. Flatness and co-planarity of the pads, and the stiffness of the grouted assembly, determine how well alignment holds and how much vibration is transmitted.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for corrosion, cracked welds, loose bolts and separation from the grout (detected by tapping). Keep the drain clear. Lift the baseplate only by its designated lifting points and in the condition (empty or with equipment mounted) that the OEM permits.
componentRecords.notes: Cast iron and polymer-concrete baseplates are also used, mainly on smaller units. The model shows an illustrative fabricated baseplate.

componentRecords.function: Machined surfaces on the baseplate on which the pump casing feet sit; they set the pump's height and provide the level reference for installation.
componentRecords.construction: Raised pads machined, usually after welding, so that they are flat and co-planar, with tapped holes for the pump hold-down bolts. In some installations the pump feet are doweled to the pads after final alignment.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: In many installations the pump is the stationary machine during alignment because it is connected to the piping, so its pads need little or no shimming. If a pump foot does not sit flat, tightening it can distort the casing, which in a split case pump can affect the split joint and internal clearances.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check pad level, flatness and co-planarity against the OEM requirements before grouting. Protect machined surfaces from corrosion and damage, and check the pump feet for soft foot.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Pedestals and machined pads that bring the motor shaft to the pump shaft height and provide space for shims and horizontal adjustment during alignment.
componentRecords.construction: Fabricated pedestals with machined pads, tapped holes for the motor hold-down bolts and, typically, lugs for horizontal positioning (jacking) screws. Pads are often made slightly low so that the motor sits on a shim pack, allowing adjustment both up and down.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The motor is normally the machine moved during alignment. Pad flatness, the shim allowance and working jacking screws make precise alignment practical; worn or corroded pads make it difficult to hold.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep pads clean and free of corrosion. Check that jacking screws turn freely and are set after alignment as the site practice specifies, and that hold-down bolts are tight.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Jacking screws used to raise, level and support the baseplate at the correct height on the foundation before grouting.
componentRecords.construction: Threaded screws through bosses on the baseplate, bearing on small steel plates placed on the foundation so that they do not sink into the concrete.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: They make it possible to level the baseplate accurately and keep it flat while the grout is placed. After the grout has cured, many procedures require them to be backed off so that the grout carries the load evenly, instead of leaving hard spots at the screws.
componentRecords.maintenance: Coat or sleeve the threads before grouting so that grout does not bond to them, and follow the installation procedure for backing them off after cure. Protect exposed threads from corrosion.
componentRecords.notes: Some installations use wedges or shim packs instead of levelling screws. Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Thin plates placed under machine feet, mainly the motor, to adjust height and correct angular misalignment in the vertical plane during alignment.
componentRecords.construction: Pre-cut slotted shims in a range of thicknesses, commonly stainless steel, sized to cover the foot contact area.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A shim pack must be solid. Too many thin shims, or dirty, burred, bent or painted shims, act like a spring (soft foot) and let alignment drift. Corroding shims can swell and change alignment over time.
componentRecords.maintenance: Use the fewest practical number of clean, flat, burr-free shims, combining thin shims into a thicker one where possible. Record the final shim pack at each foot. Replace corroded or damaged shims and re-check soft foot after changes.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation, spreading the load evenly, bonding the baseplate to the foundation so that they act as one stiff structure, adding damping and protecting the underside of the baseplate from moisture.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Properly placed grout makes full, void-free contact with both the baseplate and the foundation, so static and dynamic loads pass into the concrete over a large area instead of through a few points. This greatly increases the effective stiffness of the baseplate and raises the natural frequencies of the installed unit.
componentRecords.construction: Epoxy or non-shrink cementitious grout is poured or pumped through grout holes, within formwork, with vent holes so that air can escape. The concrete surface is first prepared to sound material and cleaned, pre-wetted for cementitious grout or kept dry for epoxy, as the grout manufacturer specifies.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Voids under the baseplate reduce stiffness, allow vibration and can let the baseplate distort when bolts are tightened. Poor surface preparation or curing causes delamination and cracking. Epoxy grouts generally offer higher strength, better bond and chemical resistance but are more sensitive to temperature during placement and cure; cementitious grouts are cheaper and simpler but need careful curing.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for cracks, edge breakaway, separation from the baseplate and oil soaking, since oil attacks cementitious grout and concrete. Tap-test the baseplate for hollow areas. Repair voids or delamination by the method the grout manufacturer recommends, typically injection.
componentRecords.notes: Grouting materials, thicknesses and procedures follow the OEM, the grout manufacturer and the project specification. The model shows grout as a simple layer.

componentRecords.function: Fix the baseplate to the foundation, resist sliding, overturning and dynamic loads, and clamp the baseplate firmly onto the grout.
componentRecords.construction: Cast-in bolts, often in sleeves that allow small lateral adjustment and provide a free stretch length, or post-installed mechanical or chemical anchors, with nuts and washers.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Loose anchor bolts allow the baseplate to move and are a common cause of foundation-related vibration. They should be tightened only after the grout has cured, and tightening a baseplate that has voids beneath it can distort it.
componentRecords.maintenance: Tighten as the project specification or OEM requires, after grout cure. Check periodically for looseness, corrosion and cracking of the concrete around the bolts.
componentRecords.notes: Shown simplified.

componentRecords.function: Supports the whole pump set, resists its static and dynamic loads, keeps the baseplate stable so that alignment holds, and limits the vibration passed to the surrounding structure.
componentRecords.construction: Typically a reinforced concrete block, in many installations separated from the surrounding floor slab by an isolation joint. It is designed by a civil or structural engineer using the OEM's loading data and allowed to cure fully before grouting.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A foundation that is too light, too flexible, cracked or settling allows movement and vibration; one whose natural frequency is close to running speed or a multiple of it can resonate. Foundation problems show up as alignment that will not hold and vibration that persists after the machine has been corrected.
componentRecords.maintenance: Inspect for cracks, spalling, oil soaking and signs of settlement, and check baseplate level over time. During vibration surveys, compare readings on the machine, baseplate, foundation and surrounding floor.
componentRecords.notes: Shown as a simple block. Foundation design is site-specific.

componentRecords.function: Joins the larger suction pipe to the smaller pump suction nozzle without creating a high point where air or vapour could collect.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: With the flat side on top, the crown of the pipe stays continuous into the nozzle, so there is no pocket for air. A concentric reducer, or an eccentric reducer installed flat side down, leaves a pocket at the top where air can accumulate, reducing the flow area, disturbing the flow into the impeller and sometimes releasing into the pump as a slug of air.
componentRecords.construction: A flanged or welded eccentric reducer installed directly at, or close to, the suction flange.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Air pockets in suction lines cause noisy, unsteady operation, reduced performance and possible loss of prime. Under suction lift, flange leaks on the suction side draw air in rather than letting liquid out.
componentRecords.maintenance: Verify orientation (flat side up) during installation and after any piping work. Check flanged joints for leaks, remembering that leaks under vacuum may not be visible.
componentRecords.notes: Illustrative spool for the installation lessons; hidden by default. The flat-side-up orientation is the arrangement most guidance shows for horizontal suction lines; particular layouts should follow the system designer's and OEM's instructions.

componentRecords.function: Delivers liquid to the pump with a steady, uniform flow and enough pressure (net positive suction head available) to avoid cavitation.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: For a double-suction pump, the flow arriving at the suction nozzle should be as uniform as possible so that both impeller eyes receive equal flow. An elbow close to the suction nozzle lying in a plane parallel to the shaft (a horizontal plane for this pump) can bias flow towards one eye, causing unequal loading, additional axial thrust, noise and cavitation at one eye. Guidance from the OEM and the Hydraulic Institute typically calls for a straight run before the nozzle and, where an elbow is unavoidable close to the pump, orienting it in the plane perpendicular to the shaft.
componentRecords.construction: A pipe run sized for low velocity, laid without high points where air could collect, with an isolating valve that is kept fully open in service and, during commissioning, often a temporary strainer.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check joints for leaks, supports for load and condition, and any strainer's pressure drop. Never throttle the pump on the suction valve.
componentRecords.notes: Illustrative spool for the installation lessons; hidden by default. Required straight lengths and layout come from the OEM, the system designer and the applicable guidance.

componentRecords.function: Joins the pump discharge nozzle to the larger discharge pipe, lowering velocity and so reducing friction losses in the downstream pipework.
componentRecords.construction: A concentric flanged or welded reducer. Concentric is acceptable here because the discharge runs at positive pressure and any high points in the system can be vented.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: It is commonly followed by the non-return valve and then the isolating valve. Like all piping at the nozzle, it must fit up without forcing so that no strain is transmitted to the casing.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check flange fit-up and joints for leaks, and make sure the reducer and the valves after it are independently supported.
componentRecords.notes: Illustrative spool for the installation lessons; hidden by default.

componentRecords.function: Carries the pumped liquid away from the pump and accommodates the non-return valve, isolating valve and pressure measurement points.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The non-return valve prevents reverse flow and reverse rotation when the pump stops, and the isolating valve allows maintenance. Where the pump may run against a closed or nearly closed system, a minimum-flow bypass may be needed to prevent overheating and unstable operation. Rapid valve closure can cause pressure surges (water hammer).
componentRecords.construction: A pipe run sized for the system, with supports close to the pump and at valves, and tappings for pressure gauges.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check supports, joints, valve operation and pressure gauge condition. Confirm that the isolating valve position at start-up follows the commissioning procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Illustrative spool for the installation lessons; hidden by default.

componentRecords.function: Carry the weight of the pipes, valves and liquid, and control thermal movement, so that the pump nozzles are not loaded beyond what the OEM allows.
componentRecords.construction: Fixed supports and anchors, guides, adjustable supports and spring hangers as the piping design requires, with supports placed close to the pump. Expansion joints, where used, need tie rods or anchors to restrain the pressure thrust.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Pipe strain, from poor fit-up, unsupported weight or thermal expansion, distorts the casing and pushes the pump out of alignment, leading to bearing, seal and coupling problems and, in a split case pump, possible joint leakage. An unrestrained expansion joint exerts a force equal to the pressure times its effective area on the nozzle.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that supports are carrying load (no gaps, correct spring hanger settings) and are undamaged. When flanges are disconnected or reconnected, watch dial indicators on the coupling for movement as a check on pipe strain.
componentRecords.notes: Illustrative supports for the installation lessons; hidden by default. Allowable nozzle loads come from the OEM.

componentRecords.function: Lifts the upper casing half off the lower half, after the joint nuts and dowels have been removed, and lowers it again during reassembly, keeping it level so that it does not strike the rotor, wear rings or joint faces.
componentRecords.construction: Certified slings, shackles and a hook on a crane or hoist, attached at the upper casing's lifting lugs. Jacking screws, where provided, are used first to break the joint evenly.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The upper casing is heavy and its centre of gravity may be offset. A tilted or swinging lift can damage the impeller, wear rings, gasket faces and joint. The casing lifting lugs are designed for the upper half only, never for lifting the whole pump.
componentRecords.maintenance: Use only gear that is inspected and within its certification, with capacity for the weight stated by the OEM. Follow the site lifting plan, with competent riggers. Lift slowly and vertically, and never place any part of the body under a suspended load or between the casing halves.
componentRecords.notes: Generic lifting gear for the maintenance animations; synthetic slings are also common but are not a family in the material library.

componentRecords.function: Lifts the complete rotating element (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals or packing parts and, in many designs, the bearings and housings) out of the lower casing, and lowers it back, level and without bending the shaft.
componentRecords.construction: A spreader beam with two slings placed at the points the OEM designates, using soft slings or protective wrapping where they contact the shaft so that journals, sleeves and seal surfaces are not marked.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: The rotor must come out level so that the impeller and wear rings clear the casing. Slinging on precision surfaces can damage them, lifting by the impeller can distort it, and a single-point lift can tilt the rotor. The spreader beam keeps the slings vertical and the load shared.
componentRecords.maintenance: Use inspected, certified gear sized for the rotor weight stated by the OEM, follow the site lifting plan, and lift slowly while watching the clearances at both ends.
componentRecords.notes: Generic lifting gear for the maintenance animations; synthetic slings are not a family in the material library.

componentRecords.function: Support the removed rotor horizontally for inspection, measurement (for example shaft and impeller runout) and dismantling.
componentRecords.construction: A pair of stable steel stands with V-blocks, sometimes with rollers or soft liners, positioned under the points the OEM specifies, often the bearing journals or bearing housings.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Supporting the rotor at the correct points avoids bending it and lets it be turned for runout checks with dial indicators. Hard, dirty or burred V-blocks can mark precision surfaces, and an unsecured rotor can roll.
componentRecords.maintenance: Keep V-faces clean and burr-free, set the stands level on firm ground, use protective material where they contact precision surfaces, lower the rotor gently and secure it against rolling.
componentRecords.notes: Generic stands for the maintenance animations.

componentRecords.function: Jacking screws are threaded through tapped holes in the upper split flange and bear on the lower flange face. Turning them evenly breaks the casing joint and lifts the upper half off the gasket and dowels without forcing tools into the joint.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: After every joint nut has been removed, the screws are advanced a little at a time and in turn, so the upper half rises squarely.
