This overcomes the adhesion of the gasket and the grip of the dowel pins while keeping the joint faces parallel, so the dowels are not bent and the faces are not marked.
componentRecords.construction: Typically two or more hexagon-head set screws in tapped holes near opposite corners of the upper flange, clear of the bolt circle and the gasket seating area (where they pass the gasket, the gasket is cut clear of them). In this model two screws sit at diagonal corners of the upper flange.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: Prying the joint open with wedges or chisels damages the machined joint faces and the gasket seat, which can cause casing joint leakage later. Lifting the half unevenly can bind it on the dowels or let it swing into the impeller and wear rings once it is free.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check that the threads turn freely before use and that the tips are clean and undamaged. Back the screws off fully before the upper half is refitted, so they do not hold the joint open when the nuts are tightened. Follow the OEM manual for the joint-breaking procedure.
componentRecords.notes: Position, number and size of jacking screws are design specific. Some designs use tapped jacking holes in the lower flange or dedicated jacking bosses instead; the OEM manual governs.

componentRecords.function: Hold-down bolts fasten the casing feet and the motor feet to their machined pads on the baseplate, so pump and motor keep their aligned positions under hydraulic forces, torque reaction, pipe loads and vibration.
componentRecords.workingPrinciple: Clamping the feet to the pads through the shim packs makes the machine, shims and baseplate act as one stiff support. Alignment is set by shimming and lateral adjustment before final tightening, and is rechecked after tightening because tightening can move the shaft if a foot does not sit flat (soft foot).
componentRecords.construction: Studs or bolts screwed into tapped holes in the pads (or through-bolted), passing through clearance holes in the foot plates, with washers and nuts on top. The clearance holes allow small lateral moves of the machine during alignment.
componentRecords.engineeringImportance: A soft foot, a loose bolt or uneven tightening distorts the casing or motor frame, which changes the alignment, loads the bearings and can raise vibration. Pipe strain that is "held" by the hold-down bolts shows up as misalignment when they are released, which is why alignment checks are often repeated with pipework connected and disconnected.
componentRecords.maintenance: Check for soft foot before final alignment, tighten in a consistent sequence to the values in the OEM manual, and recheck alignment afterwards. Inspect for looseness and corrosion during routine checks, especially where vibration is reported.
componentRecords.notes: In this model each casing foot plate has two studs and each motor foot one, drawn with washers and nuts on top of the plates. Sizes and numbers are illustrative.

failures.title: Cavitation
failures.definition: The formation of vapour cavities (bubbles) in the liquid wherever the local static pressure falls to or below the vapour pressure of the liquid at the pumping temperature, followed by their rapid collapse when they are carried into regions of higher pressure. In a double-suction pump it normally starts at the impeller inlet, close to the leading edges of the vanes in one or both eyes.
failures.mechanism:
Liquid entering the pump accelerates through the suction nozzle, the suction passages and the two side chambers into the impeller eyes, and accelerates again locally as it flows around the leading edges of the vanes. Each increase in velocity, and each friction loss on the way, lowers the static pressure. The lowest pressure in the whole pump therefore occurs just inside the impeller eye, on the low-pressure (suction) side of the vanes a short distance behind the leading edge.

If the local static pressure there falls below the vapour pressure of the liquid at its actual temperature, the liquid boils locally and vapour bubbles form, even though the bulk liquid may be cold to the touch. The bubbles are swept along the vane passage into regions where the impeller has already raised the pressure. There they become unstable and collapse (implode) in a very short time. A bubble collapsing close to a metal surface produces a micro-jet of liquid and a pressure pulse concentrated on a very small area. Repeated over an enormous number of collapses, these impacts fatigue and tear out the surface, producing the rough, pitted, sponge-like damage typical of cavitation erosion.

Vapour also occupies passage volume and disturbs the flow, so as cavitation develops the head, flow and efficiency fall; when it is severe the head can collapse altogether. The engineering criterion is that the net positive suction head available from the system (NPSHa) must exceed the net positive suction head required by the pump (NPSHr) with an adequate margin. The NPSHr published by manufacturers is usually NPSH3, the value at which the head has already fallen by 3 %, so some cavitation is already present at NPSH3. The margin needed is given by the OEM and by guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.1.

Cavitation can also occur at flows well below the best efficiency point (BEP), when the eye can no longer accept the flow smoothly and recirculating vortices form at the eye; the low-pressure cores of these vortices can cavitate and damage the pressure side of the vanes and the shrouds near the inlet. In a double-suction pump each eye handles roughly half of the total flow, which helps to keep NPSHr lower than for a comparable single-suction impeller, but if the inflow is unequal the eye that receives more, or more disturbed, flow can cavitate first.
causes: Insufficient NPSH available: low suction source level, excessive suction lift, or high suction-side friction losses from a long, undersized or fouled suction line.
Partly closed suction valve, or blocked suction strainer or intake screen, adding loss immediately upstream of the pump.
Liquid temperature higher than the design basis, which raises the vapour pressure and reduces NPSH available.
Operation well to the right of the best efficiency point, where both the suction losses and the NPSH required increase.
Operation well below the best efficiency point, where suction recirculation at the impeller eyes can cause cavitation even when NPSH available appears adequate.
Distorted or unequal inflow to the two eyes from poor suction piping layout, for example an elbow in the plane of the shaft close to the suction nozzle.
Increased wear-ring clearances, which return a larger leakage flow with swirl into the eyes and can raise the NPSH required.
Speed higher than design (for example a variable-speed drive setpoint), since NPSH required rises with speed.
warningSigns: Crackling, rattling or gravel-like noise from the casing near the suction side, often changing with flow.
Fluctuating discharge pressure, flow and motor current.
Increased broadband vibration at the bearing housings compared with the baseline.
Head and flow lower than the performance curve at the same speed and valve setting.
Suction pressure lower than normal for the flow, or liquid temperature higher than normal.
inspection: Measure suction pressure, liquid temperature and flow, calculate NPSH available and compare it with the OEM NPSH required curve at that flow, applying the margin recommended by the OEM or applicable guidance.
Check the suction source level, the suction valve position (confirm the valve is actually open, not only indicated open) and the condition of the suction strainer.
Listen at the casing with a stethoscope or acoustic instrument and take vibration spectra; compare with the commissioning baseline and note whether the noise changes with flow.
Review the suction piping layout for elbows, valves, reducers or tees close to the suction nozzle.

At a planned outage, after isolation, lock-out/tag-out (LOTO), depressurising and draining, remove the upper casing using approved lifting arrangements and inspect the vane inlet edges on both sides of the impeller. Record which side and which vane surface is damaged: damage on the low-pressure side near the leading edge points to insufficient NPSH, while damage on the pressure side, or on one side of the impeller only, points towards recirculation or unequal inflow.
consequences: Pitting and material loss on vanes and shrouds, eventually leading to perforated or broken vanes.
Reduced head, flow and efficiency; in severe cases the pump may vapour-lock and lose delivery.
Vibration and unsteady hydraulic loads that shorten bearing and shaft seal life.
Rotor unbalance from uneven material loss.
corrective: Increase NPSH available: raise the suction level or pressure, reduce suction losses (clean strainers, fully open suction valves, modify the suction line) or reduce the liquid temperature.
Return operation to the OEM preferred or allowable operating region by adjusting system demand, throttling or speed within approved limits.
Correct the suction piping layout so that both eyes receive uniform inflow, following the OEM instructions and recognised pump piping guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.6.
Restore wear-ring clearances to OEM values.
Repair or replace the damaged impeller; where the root cause cannot be fully removed, discuss a more cavitation-resistant impeller material with the OEM.
preventive: Verify the NPSH margin across the whole operating range, including the lowest source level and highest liquid temperature, at selection and after any process change.
Keep suction strainers clean and suction valves fully open in service.
Trend suction pressure, flow, liquid temperature and vibration so that a falling margin is noticed early.
Avoid prolonged operation outside the OEM allowable operating region.

scene.label: Cavitation damage usually starts near the vane inlet edges in the eyes

failures.title: Air or gas ingress
failures.definition: Entry of air or other gas into the pumped liquid, either drawn in through leaks wherever the suction side is below atmospheric pressure, or carried in from the process by vortices, entrainment or release of dissolved gas.
failures.mechanism:
An impeller adds energy to each kilogram of fluid it handles. The head it develops is broadly similar for gas and for liquid, but because gas has a very low density the pressure it can produce on gas is tiny. Gas therefore cannot be pushed out effectively and, being lighter, it is driven towards the low-pressure centre of the impeller, where it collects in the eyes, and it accumulates at the high points of the upper casing half.

Small amounts of gas reduce the effective passage area and disturb the flow onto the vanes, so head and efficiency fall and the pump runs noisily; the noise can resemble cavitation. Larger amounts form a gas pocket that blocks the eye (gas binding or air lock) and the pump loses prime.

Wherever the suction pipework, the stuffing boxes or the seal chambers are below atmospheric pressure, a leak draws air in rather than letting liquid out, so leaks on a suction lift are often invisible. In a double-suction pump both shaft seals are normally exposed to a pressure close to suction pressure; with gland packing on a suction lift, the sealing water supplied to the lantern ring is what prevents air being drawn in along the shaft sleeve. Gas can also enter from free-surface vortices at an intake with insufficient submergence, from pockets trapped at high points of the suction line, or from return flows that cascade into the sump close to the intake.
causes: Leaking suction flanges, gaskets, valve stem packing or instrument connections where the suction is below atmospheric pressure.
Insufficient submergence at the suction source, allowing surface vortices to draw air into the suction pipe.
Air pockets at high points of the suction line, or an eccentric suction reducer fitted flat side down instead of flat side up.
Loss of sealing water to the packing lantern rings, or a worn mechanical seal, while the stuffing box or seal chamber is below atmospheric pressure.
Incomplete venting of the casing and seal chambers during filling and priming.
Return or overflow lines discharging into the sump near the intake and entraining air.
Process liquids containing entrained or dissolved gas that comes out of solution as the pressure falls in the suction.
warningSigns: Erratic or falling discharge pressure and flow, with the gauge needle fluctuating.
Noise resembling cavitation (crackling or gurgling) that does not clearly follow NPSH conditions.
Fluctuating motor current.
Loss of prime after start or during operation.
Visible vortices at the intake, or gas released when the casing vents are opened.
inspection: Check the suction source level and look for surface vortices around the intake at the lowest operating level.

Inspect the suction pipework for leaks; on a suction lift leaks may not drip, so use a method approved by site procedure, such as a soap-solution check while running or a pressure test of the isolated line.
Confirm the suction reducer orientation and look for high points where gas can accumulate.
Check the sealing-water or flush supply to the lantern rings or seal chambers: pressure, flow and that the supply valve is open.
Open the upper casing vent connections, after assessing the hazard of the pumped liquid, and observe whether gas is released.
consequences: Reduced head and flow, or complete loss of delivery.
Dry running after loss of prime, which can rapidly damage mechanical seal faces, packing and wear rings.
Vibration and unsteady loads on bearings and seals.
Pressure surges when gas pockets move through the system.
corrective: Seal suction-side leaks; replace defective gaskets and valve packing.
Raise the minimum source level or improve the intake, for example with anti-vortex arrangements, following pump intake design guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.8.
Remove high points from the suction line or add venting; fit eccentric reducers flat side up.
Restore sealing water to the packing or flush to the mechanical seals.
Re-prime and vent the casing completely before restarting.
preventive: Include suction-side leak checks and intake inspections in routine rounds.
Verify intake submergence for the lowest expected level at the design stage.
Maintain sealing-water and flush systems with flow or pressure indication.
Use a documented filling, venting and priming procedure before every start.

scene.label: Air can enter wherever the suction side is below atmospheric pressure

failures.title: Low suction pressure (insufficient NPSH available)
failures.definition: Suction pressure below the design basis, so that the net positive suction head available (NPSHa) is reduced and the margin above the NPSH required by the pump is eroded or lost.
failures.mechanism:
NPSH available is the absolute pressure head at the pump suction, plus the velocity head, minus the vapour pressure head of the liquid, all referred to the impeller centreline datum. Seen from the suction source, it equals the pressure head acting on the liquid surface, plus or minus the static height between the liquid surface and the datum, minus the friction losses in the suction line, minus the vapour pressure head.

Anything that lowers the source pressure or level, increases the suction losses, or raises the liquid temperature (and therefore its vapour pressure) reduces NPSH available. Friction losses rise approximately with the square of the flow, while the NPSH required also rises at high flow, so the margin is usually smallest at high flow; this is why run-out operation is a common route to cavitation.

Low suction pressure has a second effect in a double-suction pump: in many designs both stuffing boxes or seal chambers sit close to suction pressure. If this falls below atmospheric pressure, air can be drawn in at the packing or past a worn seal, and in a mechanical seal chamber the margin between chamber pressure and the vapour pressure of the liquid falls, which can allow the liquid film between the seal faces to flash to vapour.
causes: Falling level in the suction tank or sump, or reduced pressure in the suction vessel.
Blocked suction strainer, foot valve or intake screen.
Partly closed or failed suction isolation valve, for example a gate detached from its stem.
Suction line that is undersized, too long, fouled or has too many fittings.
Higher flow than design, increasing suction friction losses.
Higher liquid temperature than design, which lowers NPSH available even when the suction gauge reading is unchanged.
Several pumps drawing from a common suction header beyond its design capacity.
warningSigns: Suction gauge reading lower than normal for the same flow.
Cavitation noise and fluctuating discharge pressure.
Falling flow and head.
Air drawn in at the packing, or seal faces running hot or spitting vapour, when the seal area is below atmospheric pressure.
inspection: Read suction pressure at the suction pressure tapping with a calibrated gauge, noting flow and liquid temperature, and compare with design and commissioning records.
Calculate NPSH available from the measured values and compare it with the OEM NPSH required at the same flow, applying the recommended margin.
Check strainer differential pressure where fitted, or inspect the strainer after isolation and draining.
Confirm the suction valve is fully open and that its indicator matches the actual gate or disc position.
Check source level instrumentation, level control setpoints and low-level alarms.
consequences: Cavitation damage to the impeller.
Loss of head and flow, and possible loss of prime.
Air ingress at the shaft seals or packing when the seal-area pressure is below atmospheric.
Vibration and unsteady loading affecting bearings and seals.
corrective: Clean strainers and screens; open or repair the suction valve.
Restore the source level or pressure and review level control setpoints.
Reduce flow to within the allowable operating region.
Modify the suction piping (diameter, length, number of fittings) after an engineering review.
Reduce the liquid temperature or raise the suction pressure where vapour pressure is the limiting factor.
preventive: Provide low-suction-pressure or low-level alarms and trips according to the site protection philosophy.
Monitor strainer differential pressure and clean strainers according to site procedure.
Re-check the NPSH margin whenever process conditions, liquid temperature or system layout change, through management of change.
Record suction pressure at commissioning as a reference for later troubleshooting.

scene.label: Suction conditions set the NPSH available

failures.title: Impeller blockage
failures.definition: Partial or complete obstruction of one or both impeller eyes, the vane passages or the casing suction passages by debris, fibrous material, solids or deposits.
failures.mechanism:
Debris carried into the pump tends to lodge on the leading edges of the vanes at the eyes, where the passages are narrow and the flow turns; fibrous material can wrap around the hub and vane edges, and solids or scale can pack the passages. A blockage reduces the effective flow area, raises local velocities and losses, and changes the inflow angle onto the vanes, so head, flow and efficiency fall and the NPSH required can rise.

In a double-suction pump the casing divides the incoming flow between two side chambers feeding two eyes. If one eye or one side is obstructed more than the other, more of the flow is forced through the clear side. The two halves of the impeller then operate at different flows and pressures, so the axial forces on the two halves no longer cancel as intended and the residual thrust on the locating bearing increases. Debris trapped in the vane passages also creates mass unbalance and uneven hydraulic forces, raising vibration. Hard debris can jam in the wear-ring clearance or between the impeller and the volute tongue, damaging the rings or locking the rotor.
causes: Missing, damaged or unsuitable suction strainer or intake screen.
Construction or maintenance debris left in the pipework, such as rags, gasket offcuts, welding debris or tools.
Fibrous or solids-laden liquid beyond the solids-handling capability of the pump.
Scale, biological growth or deposits from the process liquid.
Fragments from failed upstream equipment such as valve parts or linings.
Fragments from failed pump internals, for example a broken wear ring.
warningSigns: Gradual or sudden drop in flow and head at the same valve setting and speed.
Increased vibration, often with a once-per-revolution (unbalance-type) component.
Change in motor current, commonly a reduction as flow falls, although the direction depends on the pump curve and the nature of the blockage.
Rough running or noise, sometimes cavitation-like when an eye is restricted.
Rotor hard to turn by hand when debris has jammed.
inspection: Compare running data (suction and discharge pressure, flow, power) with the performance curve and the commissioning baseline.
After isolation, lock-out/tag-out, depressurising and draining, inspect and clean the suction strainer and intake screen.
With the motor isolated and locked out, turn the rotor by hand to check for obstruction or rubbing.
At an outage, remove the upper casing using approved lifting arrangements and inspect both eyes, the vane passages and both suction side chambers; note whether the blockage is on one side only.
If fragments are found, identify their origin and inspect the equipment they came from.
consequences: Loss of flow and head, and failure to meet duty.
Unbalance and vibration that load bearings and seals.
Increased residual axial thrust on the locating bearing when one side is blocked.
Overheating if flow falls very low.
Damage to vanes, wear rings or the volute tongue from hard debris.
corrective: Remove the debris, clean the impeller and passages, and inspect the vanes for damage.
Check impeller balance, rotor run-out and wear-ring clearances before reassembly.
Repair or fit a suitable strainer or screen.
Identify and eliminate the source of the debris.
preventive: Fit and maintain a suction strainer or screen suitable for the liquid and the pump.
Flush new or modified pipework before commissioning, using temporary strainers according to site practice.
Apply water treatment or process controls to limit scaling and biological fouling.
Trend flow, head and vibration to detect gradual fouling.

scene.label: Debris usually lodges at the eyes and vane inlet edges

failures.title: Impeller erosion
failures.definition: Progressive loss of material from impeller surfaces by the mechanical action of the flowing liquid, mainly the solid particles it carries. It is distinct from cavitation erosion, although the two can occur together.
failures.mechanism:
Erosion is the mechanical removal of material by particles striking or sliding along a surface. The wear rate rises steeply with the velocity of the particles relative to the surface, and it also depends on particle concentration, size, hardness and angularity, on the angle of impact, and on the hardness and toughness of the impeller material.

The most affected areas are those where relative velocities are highest or the flow changes direction sharply: the vane leading edges at the two eyes, the vane tips and shroud edges at the impeller outlet, and the wear-ring surfaces, where the leakage flow passes through a narrow gap at high velocity. The volute tongue (cutwater) and the casing wear rings wear in the same way. Off-design operation increases turbulence and recirculation and can concentrate wear in particular regions.

Where the liquid is also corrosive, the flow continually strips the protective oxide or passive film and exposes fresh metal, so erosion and corrosion reinforce each other (erosion-corrosion). Erosion changes vane geometry and opens clearances, so head and efficiency fall; uneven wear also unbalances the rotor. Erosion damage is typically smooth, polished, grooved or wavy and aligned with the flow, which distinguishes it from the rough pitting of cavitation.
causes: Abrasive solids such as sand, silt or scale in the pumped liquid.
Intake design or low sump levels that draw settled sediment into the suction.
Operation away from the best efficiency point, increasing local velocities, turbulence and recirculation.
Impeller material not suited to the solids loading or velocity.
Enlarged wear-ring clearances, which increase the leakage velocity and the wear rate at the rings.
Erosion-corrosion where the flow removes protective surface films.
warningSigns: Gradual decline in head, flow and efficiency over months of service.
Rising vibration as the impeller becomes unbalanced.
Increasing wear-ring clearances found at successive inspections.
Abrasive particles evident in liquid samples or strainer debris.
inspection: Trend head, flow and power against the commissioning baseline to estimate the rate of deterioration.
Sample the liquid to determine solids content and particle characteristics.

At an outage, after isolation, lock-out/tag-out, depressurising and draining, remove the upper casing with approved lifting arrangements and inspect the vane inlet edges, outlet tips, shrouds and the volute tongue; distinguish smooth, flow-aligned erosion from rough cavitation pitting.
Measure wear-ring clearances on both the drive-end and non-drive-end sides and compare with OEM values.
Check the impeller balance condition if significant material has been lost.
consequences: Loss of head, flow and efficiency, with higher energy consumption.
Increased internal leakage across the wear rings.
Unbalance and vibration that shorten bearing and seal life.
Eventual thinning, perforation or breakage of vanes and shrouds.
corrective: Repair or replace the impeller and wear rings, and balance the repaired rotor according to OEM requirements.
Discuss more erosion-resistant materials, hard facings or coatings with the OEM.
Reduce solids at source, for example by settling, screening or intake improvements.
Return operation closer to the best efficiency point.
preventive: Select materials appropriate to the expected solids loading at the design stage.
Control the solids entering the suction.
Trend performance and record wear-ring clearances at every overhaul.
Operate within the OEM preferred operating region.

scene.label: Erosion concentrates where relative velocity is highest

failures.title: Impeller corrosion
failures.definition: Chemical or electrochemical attack of the impeller material by the pumped liquid. It may be general (uniform thinning) or localised, for example pitting, crevice corrosion, galvanic corrosion or selective leaching of an alloy constituent.
failures.mechanism:
Most aqueous corrosion is electrochemical: at anodic areas metal dissolves into the liquid, while at cathodic areas a reduction reaction, usually of dissolved oxygen or hydrogen ions, consumes the released electrons. The rate depends on the liquid chemistry (pH, chlorides, dissolved oxygen, temperature and other species), on the flow velocity and on the material.

Stainless steels and some other alloys resist corrosion through a thin passive film. Chlorides and stagnant, oxygen-depleted conditions can break this film down locally, producing pitting, or crevice corrosion in tight gaps such as under wear rings, at the impeller bore and key, or under deposits. When two dissimilar metals are in electrical contact in the liquid, the less noble one corrodes faster (galvanic corrosion), and the effect is worst when a small anodic area is coupled to a large cathodic area. Some alloys suffer selective leaching, such as dealloying of certain copper alloys or graphitic corrosion of grey cast iron, which leaves a weak, porous structure that can look almost intact.

Corrosion combines with other mechanisms: with flow it becomes erosion-corrosion, and with the cyclic stresses in the vanes it can cause corrosion-fatigue cracking, often starting at vane roots or other stress concentrations. Standby pumps left full of stagnant, aggressive liquid can corrode faster than running pumps.
causes: Pumped liquid chemistry outside the design basis (pH, chlorides, dissolved oxygen, temperature) or changed process conditions.
Impeller material not compatible with the liquid.
Galvanic couples between dissimilar metals in the casing, impeller, wear rings or fasteners.
Stagnant liquid in the pump during idle or standby periods.
Chemical dosing upsets or aggressive cleaning chemicals.
High local velocities causing erosion-corrosion.
warningSigns: Discoloured liquid, or corrosion products in strainers and drains.
Gradual decline in performance.
Rising vibration from uneven material loss.
Corrosion visible on accessible wetted surfaces such as nozzle bores or drain connections.
inspection: Review liquid chemistry records and any process or dosing changes.

At an outage, after isolation, lock-out/tag-out, draining and any decontamination required for hazardous liquids, remove the upper casing with approved lifting arrangements and inspect the impeller and casing surfaces.
Measure the remaining vane and shroud thickness where accessible and compare with previous records.
Inspect the fits at the impeller bore, key and wear-ring seats for crevice corrosion.
Where cracking is suspected, arrange non-destructive testing (for example dye penetrant) by competent personnel.
consequences: Loss of material and strength, leading to vane cracking or breakage.
Reduced head, flow and efficiency.
Unbalance and vibration.
Seized or corroded fits that make dismantling difficult.
Contamination of the pumped product.
corrective: Repair or replace the impeller in a material approved by the OEM for the actual liquid.
Correct the liquid chemistry or dosing.
Eliminate galvanic couples through material changes agreed with the OEM.
Flush and drain, or lay up correctly, pumps that stand idle.
preventive: Select materials for the full range of expected liquid chemistry, with corrosion specialist input where needed.
Monitor liquid chemistry.
Apply a lay-up or periodic run procedure for standby pumps according to site practice and OEM advice.
Inspect wetted parts at planned outages and keep thickness records.

scene.label: Corrosion can be general or concentrated in crevices and at vane roots

failures.title: Unequal flow distribution between the two eyes
failures.definition: A condition in a double-suction pump in which the two impeller eyes do not receive equal and uniform flow, usually because the velocity profile arriving at the suction nozzle is skewed or swirling.
failures.mechanism:
The suction nozzle feeds a casing passage that divides the flow and turns it into two side chambers, one on each side of the impeller, feeding the drive-end and non-drive-end eyes. The casing is designed on the assumption that the flow arriving at the suction flange is reasonably uniform.

An elbow close to the suction nozzle skews the velocity profile: the faster flow moves towards the outside of the bend and secondary (swirling) flows develop. If the plane of the elbow is perpendicular to the shaft, the skew is upwards or downwards and is shared roughly equally between the two side chambers. If the elbow lies in the plane of the shaft, so that it turns the flow horizontally alongside the pump, the faster flow is thrown towards one end of the casing and one side chamber and eye receive more flow than the other. This layout is commonly cited in OEM installation instructions and in pump piping guidance (for example ANSI/HI 9.6.6) as one to avoid; how much it matters depends on the casing design, the distance to the nozzle and the operating point.

The eye receiving more flow behaves as if it were operating at a higher flow, with a higher NPSH required and a greater risk of cavitation; the other behaves as if at a lower flow and moves closer to recirculation. The pressure distributions on the two halves of the impeller then differ, so the residual axial thrust increases and may fluctuate, loading the locating bearing at the non-drive end. Noise, vibration and cavitation damage concentrated on one side of the impeller are commonly reported consequences. Swirl from two elbows in different planes, or a partly open valve near the nozzle, can produce similar effects.
causes: Suction elbow lying in the plane of the shaft, installed close to the suction nozzle.
Insufficient straight pipe upstream of the suction nozzle compared with the OEM recommendation or pump piping guidance.
Partly open valve, strainer or other fitting close to the suction nozzle.
Two or more elbows in different planes producing pre-swirl.
Tees, branch connections or poorly arranged reducers that distort the velocity profile.
Partial blockage of one side chamber or one eye.
Asymmetry in the casing suction passages or between the impeller halves from manufacturing (less common).
warningSigns: Cavitation-type noise, sometimes louder towards one end of the casing.
Non-drive-end (locating) bearing running warmer than its own baseline, or its temperature fluctuating.
Increased vibration, possibly with a larger axial component.
Cavitation or wear damage found on one side of the impeller only.
Repeated bearing or seal problems at one end of the pump.
inspection: Review the as-built suction piping: identify every elbow, valve, reducer, tee and strainer, its orientation relative to the shaft and its distance from the suction nozzle, and compare with the OEM instructions and pump piping guidance.
Take vibration readings at both bearing housings in all three directions, including axial, and compare with the baseline.
Trend the non-drive-end bearing temperature against the operating point.

At overhaul, after safe isolation and removal of the upper casing with approved lifting arrangements, compare the condition of the drive-end and non-drive-end halves of the impeller and of the wear rings on each side.
consequences: Cavitation damage on one side of the impeller.
Increased residual axial thrust, raising locating-bearing temperature and shortening its life.
Increased vibration and noise, which also shorten seal life.
Reduced efficiency and performance.
corrective: Modify the suction piping after an engineering review, for example by re-orienting the elbow into a plane perpendicular to the shaft, adding straight pipe or relocating valves.
Where re-piping is impractical, evaluate flow-conditioning devices with the OEM or a piping specialist.
Remove any partial blockage from the affected side.
Repair cavitation damage and inspect the locating bearing for thrust-related damage.
preventive: Check suction piping designs against the OEM instructions and recognised pump piping guidance before construction.
Include a suction layout check in the installation and commissioning checklists.
Record baseline axial vibration and non-drive-end bearing temperature at commissioning.

scene.label: Skewed inflow can feed one eye more than the other

failures.title: Hydraulic instability at off-design flow
failures.definition: Unsteady flow inside the pump, including flow separation, suction and discharge recirculation, rotating stall and pressure pulsation, usually caused by operation far from the best efficiency point or by interaction between the pump and the system.
failures.mechanism:
Near the best efficiency point (BEP) the liquid meets the vane leading edges at close to the design angle and leaves the impeller in step with the volute. As flow is reduced, the incidence angle at the vane inlet changes and the flow separates from the vanes. Below a certain flow, which depends on the impeller design, the eye can no longer accept the flow smoothly and part of it reverses at the outer region of the eye: this is suction recirculation. It forms strong rotating vortices whose low-pressure cores can cavitate, typically damaging the pressure side of the vanes near the inlet. A similar reversal at the impeller outlet (discharge recirculation) can damage the pressure side of the vanes near the outlet and the shrouds.

At every flow, each vane tip passing the volute tongue (cutwater) produces a pressure pulse, so the pump generates pressure pulsation at vane-pass frequency, the number of vanes multiplied by the running speed. The amplitude grows when the radial gap between the impeller and the tongue is small or the flow is far from BEP. Some double-suction impellers stagger the vanes of the two halves to reduce this excitation.

Pump-system interaction can also cause instability. A pump whose head curve droops towards shut-off, or pumps in parallel with mismatched curves, can hunt between operating points (surging). Pulsations that coincide with acoustic or structural natural frequencies of the piping are amplified.
causes: Prolonged operation well below or well above the BEP flow.
Pump oversized for the actual duty.
Parallel operation of pumps with mismatched head curves, or a pump with a drooping head curve in a system that allows hunting.
Distorted inflow from poor suction piping.
Reduced gap between the impeller tips and the volute tongue, for example after fitting a larger-diameter impeller.
Acoustic or structural resonance of the piping at pulsation frequencies.
warningSigns: Fluctuating discharge pressure and flow, or surging.
Rumbling, crackling or random noise at low flow.
Vibration with broadband, sub-synchronous or vane-pass components.
Rising bearing temperatures and recurring seal problems.
inspection: Establish the actual operating point (flow and head) and compare it with BEP and with the OEM preferred and allowable operating regions (see also ANSI/HI 9.6.3).
Analyse vibration spectra for vane-pass frequency, sub-synchronous components and broadband energy, and compare with a baseline taken at a similar flow.
Measure pressure pulsations where suitable instruments are available.
Review parallel-pump control logic and compare the head curves of the pumps involved.
At overhaul, examine where damage appears on the vanes and the volute tongue; pressure-side damage near the vane inlet or outlet points towards recirculation.
consequences: Cavitation erosion from recirculation vortices.
Vibration and cyclic loads that damage bearings, seals and couplings and can fatigue the shaft or piping.
Reduced efficiency.
Noise and process upsets from unstable flow.
corrective: Move operation back into the preferred operating region by adjusting system demand, speed or control strategy, or by providing a minimum-flow bypass.
Re-rate, trim or replace the impeller, or replace the pump, in consultation with the OEM where the pump is mismatched to the duty.
Correct parallel-operation control so that no pump is pushed back towards shut-off.
Improve suction conditions where distorted inflow contributes.
preventive: Select pumps for the real duty range, not only a single rated point.
Define and enforce the operating envelope in the control system and in operator training.
Monitor vibration and performance and compare with the commissioning baseline.

scene.label: Vane tips passing the volute tongue generate pressure pulses

failures.title: Excessive residual axial thrust
failures.definition: A net axial force on the rotor larger than the locating bearing is intended to carry. A double-suction impeller balances most of the axial hydraulic force by symmetry, but it does not eliminate it: a residual thrust always remains, and some conditions increase it considerably.
failures.mechanism:
Axial force on an impeller comes from the pressures acting on the outer faces of the shrouds (in the side spaces between the shrouds and the casing), from the lower pressure acting over the eye areas, and from the change of momentum as liquid enters axially and leaves radially. In a single-suction impeller these do not balance and produce a large net force towards the suction.

A double-suction impeller consists of two mirror-image halves back to back, so the forces on the two halves nominally oppose each other and largely cancel. In practice they are never exactly equal. Residual thrust arises from casting and machining differences between the halves, an impeller not centred axially in the volute, unequal wear-ring clearances (which change the leakage and therefore the pressure distribution in each side space), unequal inflow to the two eyes, cavitation or recirculation on one side, and any difference between the shaft or sleeve diameters exposed to pressure at the two shaft seals. Forces transmitted through the coupling, for example from incorrect shaft-end spacing or from a motor rotor seeking its magnetic centre, add to the hydraulic thrust.

In this arrangement the paired angular-contact bearings at the non-drive end locate the rotor and carry the net axial load in either direction, while the drive-end ball bearing is a floating radial bearing intended to carry radial load only and to slide axially in its housing to accommodate thermal expansion. If the residual thrust becomes excessive, the locating bearing runs hotter, its lubricant degrades faster and its life shortens. If the drive-end bearing is prevented from floating, thermal expansion of the shaft imposes an additional axial load on both bearings.
causes: Unequal wear-ring clearances on the two sides, from uneven wear or incorrect replacement.
Impeller not centred axially in the volute after reassembly, for example from an incorrect sleeve-nut setting.
Unequal inflow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping layout.
Partial blockage, cavitation or recirculation affecting one side more than the other.
Axial force from the coupling: incorrect distance between shaft ends, a motor not running on its magnetic centre with a coupling that transmits axial load, or a stiffened or damaged coupling element.
Drive-end bearing prevented from floating, so that thermal expansion loads both bearings.
Casting or machining differences between the two impeller halves or the casing passages.
Operation far from the best efficiency point.
warningSigns: Non-drive-end bearing temperature rising relative to its own baseline (the two bearings are different and do not necessarily run at the same temperature).
Increased axial vibration at the bearing housings.
Abnormal noise from the locating bearing.
Evidence of axial rubbing at wear rings or shrouds found at inspection.
Repeated, premature failures of the locating bearing.
inspection: Trend the drive-end and non-drive-end bearing temperatures and the axial vibration against the operating point.
With isolation and lock-out/tag-out, check the distance between shaft ends and the coupling element condition and, with the motor uncoupled according to site procedure, the motor magnetic centre.
At overhaul, measure the wear-ring clearances on both sides and compare them with each other and with OEM values.
Check the axial position of the impeller relative to the volute centreline using the OEM method.
When the locating bearing is removed, examine the raceway load paths; a load band displaced towards one side of the raceways on one row indicates heavy axial load in that direction.
Confirm that the drive-end bearing outer ring is free to slide in its housing.
consequences: Overheating and premature failure of the locating bearing.
Accelerated lubricant degradation.
Axial rubbing damage to the impeller, wear rings or shrouds if the rotor moves.
Changes in mechanical seal working length if the rotor shifts axially, leading to seal leakage.
corrective: Restore the wear-ring clearances on both sides to OEM values.
Re-centre the impeller in the volute following the OEM procedure.
Correct the shaft-end spacing and coupling condition, and check the motor magnetic centre.
Correct suction piping that causes unequal inflow.
Replace the locating bearing with the correct matched pair in the correct orientation, and confirm that the drive-end bearing can float.
preventive: Follow the OEM reassembly procedure and record the impeller axial position and the wear-ring clearances.
Replace wear rings so that the two sides have matched clearances.
Baseline and trend the non-drive-end bearing temperature and axial vibration.
Review the suction piping layout at design and after modifications.

scene.label: Residual axial thrust is carried by the locating bearing at the non-drive end

failures.title: Bearing overheating
failures.definition: A bearing running hotter than is normal for that bearing, its lubrication method and its duty, as defined by the OEM limits, site criteria or the bearing's own temperature trend. It is often the first sign of a developing bearing failure.
failures.mechanism:
Heat in a rolling bearing comes from rolling friction, sliding at the cage and at the rolling contacts (greater in angular-contact bearings under axial load), viscous shearing and churning of the lubricant, and friction at the housing seals. It is removed by conduction through the shaft and housing, by convection to the surroundings and, with oil lubrication, by the oil itself. The temperature settles where the heat generated equals the heat removed; anything that increases generation or reduces removal raises it.

Too much lubricant causes churning: a housing over-filled with oil, or a bearing packed too full of grease, can run hotter than one with the correct quantity. Too little lubricant, the wrong viscosity, or contaminated or oxidised lubricant allows metal-to-metal contact. Higher loads, whether from residual axial thrust on the locating bearing, misalignment, unbalance or pipe strain, increase contact friction. Fits that are too tight, or a temperature difference between the inner and outer rings, use up the internal clearance and can create a preload that generates more heat, which reduces the clearance further in a self-reinforcing process. If the floating drive-end bearing cannot slide in its housing, shaft thermal expansion loads both bearings axially.

Rising temperature lowers the lubricant viscosity and thins the oil film, and it accelerates oil oxidation and grease degradation, so overheating tends to accelerate itself. A newly relubricated grease bearing commonly runs warmer for a period until excess grease is expelled; watching the trend distinguishes this from a genuine problem. The drive-end and non-drive-end bearings in this pump are different types carrying different loads, so they need not run at the same temperature.
causes: Over-lubrication: oil level too high or too much grease, causing churning.
Under-lubrication: low oil level, an empty or incorrectly set constant-level oiler, or missed regreasing.
Wrong lubricant type or viscosity, or mixing of incompatible greases.
Contaminated or degraded lubricant (water, pumped liquid, dirt, oxidation).
Excessive load from residual axial thrust, misalignment, unbalance or pipe strain.
Incorrect fits or internal clearance, or a drive-end bearing that cannot float.
Paired angular-contact bearings installed in the wrong orientation or with incorrect preload.
Rubbing housing lip seals, high ambient temperature, or heat conducted from a hot pumped liquid.
warningSigns: Bearing housing temperature rising above its normal trend or above the limit given by the OEM or site procedure.
Darkened oil, burnt odour, or grease purging from the housing.
Change of oil level in the sight glass.
New or louder bearing noise.
Rising vibration, especially at bearing defect frequencies.
inspection: Measure the housing temperature at a consistent location with a contact probe or calibrated infrared thermometer; compare the drive-end and non-drive-end readings with their own baselines and with OEM limits.
Check the oil level in the sight glass and the constant-level oiler setting as described by the OEM, or verify the grease type, quantity and relubrication records.
Take an oil sample and check it for water, discolouration and particles.
Check alignment, coupling condition and vibration spectra for bearing, misalignment and unbalance signatures.
Check for pipe strain and, on dismantling, confirm that the drive-end bearing can float axially.
consequences: Lubricant breakdown and accelerated bearing wear.
Bearing seizure and damage to shaft journals and housing bores.
Heat transfer into nearby seals, reducing their life.
Unplanned shutdown.
corrective: Correct the lubricant quantity and type according to the OEM manual.
Drain, flush and refill contaminated oil, or purge and replace contaminated grease, according to OEM instructions.
Correct alignment and remove sources of excessive load (thrust, unbalance, pipe strain).
Replace damaged bearings, correcting fits and arrangement.
Replace worn or rubbing housing seals.
preventive: Follow the OEM lubrication schedule, quantities and lubricant specification.
Trend bearing temperature, vibration and, for oil-lubricated bearings, oil condition.
Keep housing seals, deflectors and breathers in good condition to exclude contamination.
Maintain good alignment and correct installation practice.

scene.label: Check lubricant level, lubricant condition and the load on the bearing

failures.title: Rolling bearing failure
failures.definition: Loss of a rolling bearing's ability to support and locate the rotor smoothly, through fatigue, wear, corrosion, indentation, smearing, electrical erosion or fracture, progressing to noise, vibration, heat and ultimately seizure.
failures.mechanism:
Every revolution, each rolling element passes through the load zone and creates very high, cyclic contact stresses in the raceways. Under clean, well-lubricated, correctly loaded conditions, the eventual failure mode is rolling contact fatigue: cracks start below the surface and grow until material flakes out (spalling). Bearing rated life is a statistical value based on this mechanism. In practice many pump bearings fail earlier from other causes.

Contaminant particles are rolled into the raceways and leave dents whose edges become starting points for surface fatigue. Water, whether from the pumped liquid, washdown or condensation, reduces the load-carrying ability of the lubricant film and causes corrosion. Inadequate lubrication allows surface distress and smearing. Misalignment, unbalance, pipe strain and excessive axial thrust increase or redistribute the contact loads. Incorrect mounting, for example hammering on a ring so that the mounting force passes through the rolling elements, causes dents (brinelling); wrong fits let a ring creep or fret. Standby pumps exposed to vibration while stationary can suffer false brinelling. Current passing through a bearing, more commonly a motor-bearing issue with variable-speed drives, causes electrical erosion and fluting.

The two pump bearings fail differently because they are different: the drive-end floating bearing carries radial load and must be free to slide in its housing, while the non-drive-end paired angular-contact bearings carry radial load plus residual axial thrust in either direction and must be fitted as a matched set in the correct orientation. Reading the damage pattern on a failed bearing is the key to finding the root cause.
causes: Lubrication problems: wrong quantity or type, or degraded or contaminated lubricant.
Contamination by water, by pumped liquid leaking from the seal or packing, or by dust, through worn housing seals or missing deflectors.
Excessive or abnormal load from residual axial thrust, misalignment, unbalance, pipe strain or soft foot.
Incorrect installation: wrong fits, impact damage, an angular-contact pair reversed or unmatched, or a locknut over-tightened or not locked.
False brinelling of standby pumps subject to vibration while stationary.
Overheating from any of the causes of bearing overheating.
End of normal fatigue life.
warningSigns: Rising vibration, particularly at bearing defect frequencies or in high-frequency (envelope) measurements.
Rising bearing temperature.
Grinding, rumbling or clicking noise from the bearing housing.
Metallic particles, discolouration or water in the oil or grease.
Increased shaft movement leading to seal leakage.
inspection: Analyse vibration, including envelope (demodulation) techniques, and compare with the baseline, OEM limits and applicable standards such as the ISO 10816 / ISO 20816 series or ANSI/HI 9.6.4.
Review temperature and lubricant analysis trends.
After isolation and lock-out/tag-out, remove the bearings with suitable pullers or the OEM method, never by striking the rolling elements, and keep the parts for examination.
Examine raceways, rolling elements and cages and record the damage pattern (load path, spalling, dents, corrosion, discolouration, smearing) to identify the root cause.

Check shaft journals and housing bores for wear, fretting and fits against OEM values; confirm that the drive-end outer ring can float, and check the orientation and locking of the non-drive-end pair.
consequences: Bearing seizure and damage to the shaft journals.
Rotor movement causing contact at the wear rings, impeller and seals.
Mechanical seal or packing damage and leakage.
Overheating, which may present a fire risk with some lubricants or pumped liquids.
Unplanned outage and secondary damage.
corrective: Replace the bearings with the type and arrangement specified in the OEM parts list, using correct mounting methods such as controlled heating.
Repair or replace worn journals and housings to OEM dimensions.
Correct the root cause found from the damage pattern (lubrication, contamination, alignment, thrust).
Replace housing seals and deflectors and refill with the specified lubricant.
Recheck alignment after reassembly.
preventive: Control lubricant quality, quantity and cleanliness.
Use condition monitoring: vibration, temperature and lubricant analysis.
Train personnel in correct bearing handling and mounting, with the correct tools.
Run or rotate standby pumps according to site procedure and OEM advice.
Carry out root-cause analysis on every bearing failure.

scene.label: The DE floating bearing and the NDE locating pair carry different loads and fail differently

failures.title: Shaft deflection and bent shaft
failures.definition: Bending of the pump shaft under load in operation (elastic deflection), or a permanent bend (bow), so that the rotor runs off its geometric centre at the impeller, the wear rings and the shaft seals.
failures.mechanism:
The shaft of a between-bearings pump behaves like a beam supported at the two bearings and loaded mainly by the weight of the rotor and the hydraulic radial force on the impeller. For a given load, beam theory shows that deflection increases very steeply with bearing span and falls very steeply with shaft diameter, which is why shaft stiffness is a key design parameter.

In a single-volute casing the pressure around the impeller periphery is close to uniform only near the best efficiency point. Away from it, and especially towards low flow, the pressure becomes non-uniform and produces a net radial force on the impeller; in many single-volute designs this force grows as flow falls towards shut-off. A double volute, with a splitter rib, reduces this force but does not remove it completely. The resulting deflection moves the impeller towards the casing wear rings on one side and tilts the shaft in the seal chambers, so the seal faces must follow a moving shaft and the wear-ring clearances can close on one side.

A permanent bend can come from poor handling, storage or transport, from a rub that heated one side of the shaft, or from a previous seizure. A bent shaft or an unbalanced rotor makes the shaft centre orbit at running speed, producing once-per-revolution vibration. The cyclic bending stress at every revolution, concentrated at keyways and shoulders, can eventually initiate fatigue cracks.
causes: Prolonged operation far from the best efficiency point, particularly at low flow in a single-volute casing.
Bent shaft from handling, storage, transport, a rub or a previous seizure.
Rotor unbalance from impeller wear, deposits or unbalanced repairs.
Coupling reaction forces from misalignment.
Thermal bow from a local rub or uneven heating.
Replacement shaft not meeting the OEM specification.
warningSigns: Once-per-revolution vibration that increases at low flow or after a rub.
Mechanical seals leaking repeatedly, or packing wearing quickly.
Rubbing noise from the wear rings.
Uneven, one-sided wear on sleeves or wear rings found at inspection.
inspection: With the pump isolated and locked out, measure shaft run-out at accessible locations with a dial indicator while turning the shaft by hand, and compare with OEM limits.
With the rotor removed using approved lifting gear and supported on stands at the bearing journals, measure run-out along the shaft and at the impeller wear-ring diameters.
Inspect the wear rings and sleeves for one-sided rubbing.
Compare the operating point with BEP and the OEM operating region.
Analyse vibration amplitude and phase at running speed.
consequences: Wear-ring contact, galling and increased clearances.
Mechanical seal or packing failure.
Increased bearing loads.
Fatigue cracking of the shaft, typically at keyways or shoulders.
corrective: Replace a bent shaft, or straighten it only where the OEM permits and by a qualified workshop.
Balance the rotor according to OEM requirements.
Correct the operating point to reduce the hydraulic radial load.
Renew wear rings, sleeves and seals damaged by deflection.
preventive: Operate within the OEM allowable operating region and provide minimum-flow protection.
Store and transport spare rotors correctly supported, following OEM storage advice.
Check run-out and balance at every overhaul.
Maintain good alignment.

scene.label: The between-bearings shaft bends under rotor weight and hydraulic radial force

failures.title: Pump-to-motor shaft misalignment
failures.definition: The pump and motor shaft centrelines are not collinear under operating conditions. The error may be a parallel offset, an angle, or a combination of both, in the vertical and horizontal planes.
failures.mechanism:
A flexible coupling can tolerate some misalignment, but only by flexing its elements every revolution. The reaction forces and moments this creates grow with misalignment and are passed into the bearings of both machines. Typical consequences are vibration at once and twice running speed (angular misalignment often shows a high axial component), heating and fatigue of the coupling elements, and higher loads on the pump drive-end bearing and the motor drive-end bearing.

With a spacer coupling, misalignment is measured between the two shaft ends across the spacer length. Alignment achieved at installation can be lost through pipe strain when the piping is connected, soft foot (a foot that does not sit flat, so that tightening its bolt distorts the frame), thermal growth when the pump or motor reaches operating temperature, foundation or grout deterioration, and disturbance during maintenance. Alignment tolerances, and any cold offsets that allow for thermal growth, come from the OEM or the coupling manufacturer.
causes: Inadequate initial alignment, or alignment not rechecked after the piping was connected.
Pipe strain from misaligned or poorly supported suction or discharge piping.
Soft foot under the pump or motor feet.
Thermal growth not allowed for in the cold alignment.
Foundation settlement, grout deterioration or baseplate distortion.
Loose hold-down or anchor bolts.
Bearings, coupling or motor replaced without realignment.
warningSigns: Vibration at once and twice running speed, often with high axial readings.
Coupling element wear debris, or heat under the guard.
Higher temperatures at the pump drive-end and motor drive-end bearings.
Repeated seal or bearing problems at the drive end.
inspection: With isolation and lock-out/tag-out, remove the coupling guard and measure alignment with dial indicators or a laser system, comparing the result with OEM or coupling-manufacturer tolerances.
Check for soft foot at every foot before correcting alignment.
Check for pipe strain, for example by monitoring alignment indicators while flange bolts are slackened according to site procedure.
Inspect the coupling elements, hubs and spacer bolts.
Check hold-down bolts, shims and grout; where required, check alignment hot or estimate thermal growth.
consequences: Coupling element fatigue and failure.
Bearing failures in the pump and the motor.
Shaft seal wear and leakage, particularly at the drive end.
Shaft fatigue in severe cases.
Higher vibration and energy consumption.
corrective: Correct soft foot, then realign within tolerance.
Eliminate pipe strain by correcting the piping and its supports.
Replace damaged coupling elements and bearings.
Tighten hold-down bolts to the specified values in the specified sequence.
preventive: Use precision alignment methods and record the as-left readings.
Recheck alignment after piping work and, where required, after the first run to operating temperature.
Check alignment periodically according to site procedure.
Design pipe supports so that nozzle loads stay within the OEM allowable values.

scene.label: Alignment is measured between the shaft ends across the spacer

failures.title: Mechanical seal failure
failures.definition: Loss of a mechanical seal's ability to contain the pumped liquid within acceptable leakage. A pump fitted with mechanical seals has one at each shaft exit, and the drive-end and non-drive-end seals can fail independently. This failure mode applies only to pumps fitted with mechanical seals; many split case pumps use gland packing instead.
failures.mechanism:
A mechanical seal seals across two flat, lapped faces: a rotating face that turns with the shaft and a stationary face (seat) held in the gland plate. Springs and the liquid pressure hold the faces together. A very thin liquid film between them lubricates and cools the faces, and the small leakage of a healthy seal is the flow across this film. Secondary seals (elastomers) seal the faces to the shaft sleeve and the gland, and allow the flexible element to move axially as the faces wear.

Seal life depends on keeping that film stable. If it is lost, through dry running, vaporisation of the film from too much heat or too little pressure margin in the seal chamber, or a missing flush, the faces overheat, wear quickly and can crack or blister. If the faces are pushed apart or distorted, through excessive vibration, shaft deflection, misalignment, bearing wear, axial rotor movement, a secondary seal that hangs up, or uneven gland tightening, leakage increases. Solids in the liquid wear the faces and clog the springs; chemical attack or heat degrades the elastomers.

In a double-suction pump both seal chambers usually operate close to suction pressure, so low suction pressure leaves a reduced margin between the chamber pressure and the vapour pressure of the liquid. The flush arrangement, defined by the seal manufacturer, removes heat and keeps solids away from the faces.
causes: Dry running: loss of prime, or a start with a closed suction valve or an unvented seal chamber.
Inadequate, blocked or unsuitable flush arrangement.
Abrasive solids, or crystallising or polymerising liquids.
Excessive shaft movement from vibration, deflection, misalignment, bearing wear or excessive axial float.
Installation errors: incorrect setting length, damaged or dirty faces, cut or rolled O-rings, sleeve or retainer not locked, or uneven gland tightening.
Elastomers or face materials incompatible with the liquid or the temperature.
Operation outside the seal's pressure or temperature limits, or thermal shock.
warningSigns: Visible leakage at a seal gland, increasing over time.
Squealing noise, heat or vapour at the gland.
Leakage when the pump is stationary but not when running, or the reverse.
Abnormal flush line temperature or pressure.
Liquid appearing at the bearing housing deflector.
inspection: Identify which end is leaking and trace the leak path: across the faces, at the gland gasket or O-rings, along the sleeve, or from the casing joint near the seal housing. Do not assume the faces have failed.
Check the flush supply (pressure, flow, temperature, open valves) against the seal arrangement drawing.
Check vibration, alignment, bearing condition, shaft run-out and end play.
Review the operating history for dry running, low-flow operation, frequent starts or process upsets.

After isolation, lock-out/tag-out, depressurising, draining and decontamination where needed, remove the seal and examine the faces (wear track, heat checking, chipping, blistering), the elastomers (swelling, hardening, extrusion) and the springs (clogging, breakage).
consequences: Release of pumped liquid, which is a safety and environmental hazard with hot, toxic or flammable liquids.
Liquid entering the bearing housing, leading to bearing failure.
Unplanned outage.
Sleeve damage if the failure is not addressed promptly.
corrective: Replace or repair the seal; repair is normally carried out by the seal manufacturer.
Correct the root cause found during inspection (flush, alignment, bearings, operating point, venting).
Install the seal with the correct setting and cleanliness according to the seal manufacturer's instructions.
Review the seal type, materials and flush arrangement with the seal manufacturer if failures recur.
preventive: Vent the casing and seal chambers fully before every start.
Maintain flush systems and their instruments.
Protect against dry running and low-flow operation.
Use trained installers, setting tools and clean working conditions.
Where specified, select seals to recognised standards such as ISO 21049 / API 682.

scene.label: The seal faces run on a very thin liquid film

failures.title: Gland packing leakage or overheating
failures.definition: Leakage from a packed stuffing box above the controlled rate the packing needs, or packing running hot because the leakage is too low. Packing is designed to leak a small, controlled amount for lubrication and cooling, so zero leakage is not the target. This failure mode applies to pumps fitted with gland packing.
failures.mechanism:
Braided packing rings are squeezed axially by the gland follower. The packing converts this axial compression into radial pressure against the shaft sleeve and the stuffing box bore, which restricts leakage. The compression is not uniform: the rings nearest the gland follower carry most of the load and the rings deepest in the box carry least.

The controlled leakage flows along the sleeve and carries away the friction heat generated between the packing and the rotating sleeve. If the gland is over-tightened, the leakage is squeezed off, friction rises, the packing overheats, hardens and glazes, and the sleeve is scored; leakage then increases sharply and can no longer be controlled. If the gland is too loose, the packing is worn or the sleeve is scored, leakage is excessive.

A lantern ring positioned under the packing flush connection distributes clean sealing water into the packing. This lubricates and cools the rings, keeps abrasive solids out and, where the stuffing box is below atmospheric pressure, prevents air being drawn into the pump along the shaft. Both stuffing boxes of a double-suction pump are usually close to suction pressure, so on a suction lift this sealing function is essential.
causes: Gland over-tightened (packing runs hot) or under-tightened (excessive leakage).
Worn, hardened or incorrectly installed packing: wrong size, joints not staggered, or rings cut incorrectly.
Lantern ring not aligned with the flush connection.
Scored or worn shaft sleeve.
Sealing water absent, insufficient or dirty.
Shaft run-out, vibration, misalignment or bearing wear.
Packing material unsuitable for the liquid, speed or temperature.
Abrasive solids in the pumped liquid.
warningSigns: Leakage visibly above the controlled rate recommended by the OEM, or no leakage at all.
Gland or stuffing box hot, smoking or steaming.
Gland follower near the end of its adjustment.
Air drawn in and loss of prime on a suction lift.
Liquid spraying onto the bearing housing.
inspection: Observe the leakage rate and gland temperature and compare them with OEM guidance.
Check the gland follower position and remaining adjustment, and that the follower is square to the shaft.
Check the sealing-water pressure and flow at the packing flush connection.
Check shaft run-out and vibration.
After isolation and lock-out/tag-out, remove the packing and examine the rings (glazing, burning, extrusion), the sleeve surface, the lantern ring position and the stuffing box bore.
consequences: Sleeve scoring and wear.
Liquid spray contaminating the bearing housing and its lubricant.
Air ingress and loss of prime on a suction lift.
Product loss and slip hazards.
corrective: Adjust the gland evenly and gradually according to the OEM manual; adjust a running pump only where the site procedure permits, with guards in place and away from rotating parts.
Repack with the correct material and size, with joints staggered and the lantern ring aligned with the flush connection.
Replace scored sleeves.
Restore a clean sealing-water supply.
Correct mechanical causes such as run-out, vibration or bearing wear.
preventive: Train personnel in correct packing installation and run-in.
Monitor the sealing-water supply.
Adjust packing periodically according to the OEM manual rather than over-tightening to stop all leakage.
Consider conversion to mechanical seals where justified and approved by the OEM.

scene.label: Packing needs a small controlled leakage to stay cool

failures.title: Excessive vibration
failures.definition: Vibration of the pump, motor or bearing housings above the acceptable level for that machine, as defined by the OEM, site criteria or applicable standards, or a significant increase from its own baseline.
failures.mechanism:
Vibration is the response of the machine and its supports to dynamic forces. The size of the response depends both on the force and on the stiffness, mass and damping of the structure; when a forcing frequency is close to a natural frequency of the rotor, bearing housings, baseplate or piping, the response is amplified (resonance).

Different sources produce characteristic frequencies, which is why spectrum analysis is used for diagnosis. Unbalance and a bent shaft produce mainly once-per-revolution vibration. Misalignment produces once and twice per revolution vibration, often with high axial readings. Mechanical looseness produces many harmonics of running speed. Rolling bearing defects produce non-synchronous frequencies determined by the bearing geometry. Hydraulic sources include vane-pass frequency from the vanes passing the volute tongue, broadband random vibration from cavitation and recirculation, and unsteady forces from unequal inflow to the two eyes. Motor electrical faults produce their own characteristic frequencies.

Vibration is both a symptom and a cause: it accelerates the wear of bearings, seals and couplings and loosens fasteners, which in turn increases vibration. Measurement methods and evaluation criteria are given in standards such as the ISO 10816 / ISO 20816 series and ANSI/HI 9.6.4, and in the OEM documentation.
causes: Rotor unbalance from impeller wear, corrosion, deposits, blockage or unbalanced repairs.
Misalignment and pipe strain.
Worn or damaged bearings.
Hydraulic excitation: off-design operation, cavitation, recirculation, air ingress or unequal flow to the two eyes.
Bent shaft or rubbing at the wear rings.
Mechanical looseness at hold-down bolts, bearing housing bolts or worn fits.
Soft foot, deteriorated grout or foundation problems.
Resonance of the rotor, structure or piping.
warningSigns: Rising trend in measured vibration.
Change in noise, or visible movement of piping and baseplate.
Loosening fasteners and fretting marks.
Increasing seal leakage and bearing temperature.
inspection: Measure vibration at both pump bearing housings and on the motor in the horizontal, vertical and axial directions, using a consistent method and locations; compare with the baseline and the acceptance criteria.
Use spectrum and phase analysis to identify the dominant frequencies (once and twice per revolution, vane pass, bearing defect frequencies, broadband).
Correlate vibration with the operating point by noting flow and pressures at each reading.
Check fasteners, soft foot, grout and pipe supports.
Check alignment and coupling condition; at overhaul, check rotor balance and run-out.
Where resonance is suspected, arrange specialist tests such as impact testing.
consequences: Bearing, seal and coupling failures.
Fatigue cracking of the shaft, piping, baseplate welds or brackets.
Loosened fasteners and loss of alignment.
Noise and unplanned outages.
corrective: Correct the identified root cause: balance, align, replace bearings, correct the operating point or rectify looseness.
Correct soft foot and repair the grout or foundation.
Where resonance is confirmed, modify stiffness, mass or supports under engineering guidance.
Repair secondary damage to seals, bearings and coupling.
preventive: Record a vibration baseline at commissioning.
Monitor vibration periodically or continuously and act on trends.
Operate within the OEM operating region.
Maintain balance and alignment quality during maintenance.

scene.label: Measure vibration at both bearing housings in three directions

failures.title: Casing split-joint leakage
failures.definition: Leakage of pumped liquid through the horizontal joint between the upper and lower casing halves. This joint is the main static seal of an axially split casing and runs the full length of the casing, including around the seal housings at each end.
failures.mechanism:
The machined flanges of the two casing halves are clamped together by the casing studs and nuts, compressing a thin joint gasket (some designs use other joint arrangements; the joint design is OEM-specific). Dowel pins locate the upper half on the lower half. Internal pressure acts over the projected area of the casing and tries to push the halves apart; the bolt load must overcome this separating force and still leave enough compressive stress on the gasket at every point along the joint.

Leakage starts where the local contact stress becomes too low: midway between bolts, where the flange is less stiff, near the seal housing bores and corners, or where the faces are not flat because of distortion, corrosion, damage or residues of old gasket or sealant. Gasket stress also falls over time as the gasket creeps and relaxes. Rapid temperature changes heat the halves unevenly and distort the flanges. Pressure surges, or operation above the casing design pressure, increase the separating force. Once a leak starts, high-velocity liquid can cut grooves across the joint face (often called wire drawing), making the leak worse and the repair more extensive.

The gasket thickness and material are specified by the OEM because the joint also forms part of the bores that hold the casing wear rings and the seal housings. A gasket of the wrong thickness can change the clamping of these parts and the roundness of the bores, as well as the sealing performance.
causes: Gasket deterioration: ageing, compression set, chemical attack, damage during handling, or reuse of an old gasket.
Uneven or damaged joint surfaces: distortion, corrosion pitting, erosion grooves from previous leaks, nicks, or residues of old gasket or sealant.
Improper bolt tightening: incorrect torque, incorrect sequence, uneven tightening, damaged or unlubricated threads, or bolts not retightened when the OEM requires it.
Thermal distortion from rapid temperature changes or uneven heating of the casing.
Excessive casing pressure: operation above design pressure, pressure surges (water hammer) or speed higher than rated.

Incorrect assembly: wrong gasket material or thickness, gasket misplaced or incorrectly trimmed at the bores, dowels not engaged, or wear rings or seal housings not seated so that they hold the halves apart.
External loads from piping that distort the casing.
warningSigns: Weeping or dripping along the joint line.
Staining, corrosion or crystalline deposits along the flange.
Wet lagging or liquid pooling under the casing.
Leakage appearing only at certain pressures or temperatures, or after start-up and shutdown.
Spray from the joint, which must be treated as a pressurised leak.
inspection: Treat a spraying joint as a pressurised leak: keep clear, assess the hazard of the liquid (hot, toxic, flammable) and isolate if required. Do not tighten bolts on a pressurised casing unless the site procedure explicitly allows it.
Map the leak location along the joint (between which studs, near the seal housings, near the nozzles) and record the operating conditions when it occurs.
Compare recorded discharge pressures and any pressure transients with the casing design pressure.

After isolation, lock-out/tag-out, depressurising, draining and cooling, check the fasteners, then remove the upper casing using approved lifting arrangements; examine the gasket imprint for uneven compression and the joint faces for flatness, erosion and damage using the OEM method.
Verify the gasket material and thickness against the OEM parts list.
Check nozzle loads and pipe supports for strain on the casing.
consequences: Loss of liquid and a safety hazard from hot or hazardous spray.
Erosion of the joint faces, making the repair more extensive.
Corrosion of studs and nuts.
Environmental release and housekeeping problems.
corrective: Fit a new gasket of the OEM-specified material and thickness; do not reuse old gaskets.
Clean the joint faces without damaging them; where faces are not flat or are eroded, have them repaired only according to OEM instructions, because machining affects internal dimensions.
Replace damaged studs and nuts.
Tighten in the OEM sequence, in stages, to the OEM-specified values.
Correct the cause of over-pressure or surges, and relieve pipe strain.
preventive: Follow the OEM assembly procedure and record the tightening values used.
Protect the joint faces during maintenance and storage.
Control start-up and thermal transients according to the OEM manual.
Provide surge protection where the system needs it.
Check the joint for leakage on routine rounds.

scene.label: The split joint runs the full length of the casing

failures.title: Wear-ring wear
failures.definition: Increase in the running clearance between the impeller wear rings and the casing wear rings on either side of the double-suction impeller, through wear, erosion, corrosion or contact.
failures.mechanism:
Each side of the impeller has a pair of wear rings, one rotating with the impeller and one fixed in the casing, separated by a small running clearance. Each pair restricts the leakage of liquid from the high-pressure region around the impeller outlet back to the low-pressure eye on that side. The leakage increases with the clearance and with the pressure difference across the rings.

The leakage is recirculated through the impeller, which must pump the delivered flow plus the leakage. As clearances open, the net delivered flow and head at a given speed fall, efficiency falls and the power needed for the useful output rises. The leakage jet also re-enters the eye with swirl and disturbs the inlet flow, which can raise the NPSH required and promote cavitation.

In a double-suction pump the two ring pairs also influence axial balance. The leakage through each pair affects the pressure distribution in the side space between that shroud and the casing.
