If one side wears more than the other, the pressure distributions on the two halves differ and the residual axial thrust on the locating bearing increases. Close-clearance rings also provide some hydrodynamic stiffness and damping to the rotor; as clearances open, this support reduces and vibration may increase in some designs. Contact between the rings, from shaft deflection, misalignment, bearing wear or dry running, can cause rapid wear or galling.
causes: Abrasive solids in the pumped liquid.
Contact caused by shaft deflection (for example low-flow operation in a single-volute casing), misalignment, bearing wear or a bent shaft.
Dry running or gas entrainment, removing the liquid film in the clearance.
Thermal transients causing differential expansion.
Corrosion or erosion-corrosion.
Galling-prone material pairing, or incorrect clearances on replacement rings.
Casing distortion from pipe strain or an incorrect joint gasket.
warningSigns: Gradual fall in flow and head at the same speed and valve setting.
Higher power for the same useful output (falling efficiency).
Change in non-drive-end bearing temperature or axial vibration as the axial balance changes.
Rising vibration or rubbing noise.
inspection: Trend performance (flow, head, power) against the curve and the baseline; a fall in head and flow with stable suction conditions is consistent with wear-ring wear, but can also come from impeller damage, blockage or air.
Where available, use performance or thermodynamic testing to estimate internal losses.

At overhaul, after isolation, lock-out/tag-out, draining, removal of the upper casing and lifting of the rotor with approved lifting gear, measure the impeller ring outside diameters and the casing ring bores at several positions on both sides; calculate the clearances and compare them with OEM values and with each other.
Look for galling, scoring and one-sided contact, which point to deflection or misalignment.
Check the seating and anti-rotation features of the casing wear rings.
consequences: Loss of performance and higher energy consumption.
Increased residual axial thrust on the locating bearing.
Higher NPSH required and increased cavitation risk.
Galling or seizure if the rings make contact.
corrective: Renew ring pairs to OEM clearances, restoring both sides.
Correct the root cause (deflection, misalignment, solids, dry running).
Review ring materials with the OEM if wear is rapid or galling occurs.
Check the impeller axial position and bearing condition at the same time.
preventive: Trend performance so that ring renewal is planned before losses become large.
Record the clearances on both sides at every overhaul.
Operate within the operating region and avoid dry running.
Control solids in the pumped liquid.

scene.label: A wear-ring pair on each side controls leakage back to the eye

failures.title: Coupling failure
failures.definition: Failure of the flexible spacer coupling between pump and motor: wear, cracking or fatigue of the flexible elements, loose or damaged hubs and keys, failure of the spacer bolts, or loss of the coupling's ability to accommodate misalignment.
failures.mechanism:
A flexible coupling transmits torque while accommodating small misalignment and axial movement by flexing its elements, which may be elastomeric or metallic depending on the coupling type. Any misalignment makes the elements flex once per revolution. In elastomeric elements this cyclic flexing generates heat through internal friction (hysteresis); in metallic elements it produces fatigue stress. Element life therefore falls with misalignment, with excessive axial displacement from incorrect shaft-end spacing, with torque peaks at start-up or from seizure, and with heat, oil, chemicals, ozone or age attacking elastomers.

The spacer allows the pump bearings and seals to be serviced without moving the motor, but its bolts must be correctly tightened and locked. The hubs depend on their fits, keys and retainers; a loose hub frets and wears the shaft end and the key. Worn elastomer elements often leave a fine powder under the guard, which is a useful early sign.
causes: Misalignment beyond the OEM or coupling-manufacturer tolerance.
Incorrect distance between shaft ends or incorrect axial positioning.
Torque overload from seizure, large solids or severe starting transients.
Elements degraded by heat, oil, chemicals, ozone or age.
Loose hubs, worn keys or keyways, or incorrect fits.
Spacer bolts incorrectly tightened, unlocked or missing.
Coupling selection unsuited to the duty.
warningSigns: Element debris or powder under the coupling guard.
Knocking at start-up or noise from the coupling.
Rising vibration at once and twice running speed.
Visible cracks, deformation or play when inspected during isolation.
inspection: With isolation and lock-out/tag-out, remove the guard and inspect the elements for cracks, wear, deformation and heat discolouration.
Check hubs, keys, retainers and spacer bolts for tightness, fretting and damage.
Measure alignment and the distance between shaft ends.
Check axial float and bearing condition on both machines.
Confirm that the guard is undamaged and clear of rotating parts before refitting it.
consequences: Loss of drive and unplanned shutdown.
Fragments released inside the guard.
Damage to shaft ends, keyways and bearings.
Vibration damage to seals and bearings.
corrective: Replace the elements or the complete coupling with parts approved by the OEM or the coupling manufacturer.
Realign and set the correct shaft-end spacing.
Repair hub fits and keys, and tighten and lock the spacer bolts to the specified values.
Refit the coupling guard before any restart.
preventive: Inspect the coupling at the intervals defined by site procedure.
Maintain alignment within tolerance.
Confirm the coupling selection whenever the duty or the driver changes.
Never run the pump without the coupling guard in place.

scene.label: Flexible elements flex every revolution when the shafts are misaligned

failures.title: Low discharge pressure
failures.definition: Discharge pressure lower than expected. It needs careful interpretation: the pump may be generating less head than its curve at the actual flow (an internal or drive problem), the system may be drawing more flow so that the pump has moved along its curve, or the suction pressure may have fallen.
failures.mechanism:
A centrifugal pump operates where its head-flow curve crosses the system curve, and the discharge pressure equals the suction pressure plus the pressure rise generated by the pump. A low discharge reading therefore has three broad explanations.

First, the pump may be producing less head than its curve at that flow because of internal deterioration (wear-ring leakage, impeller erosion or blockage), gas in the liquid, cavitation, low speed, the wrong direction of rotation, or an impeller fitted the wrong way round on the shaft after maintenance. A double-suction impeller looks symmetrical, but its vanes are curved for one direction of rotation, so reversing the impeller on the shaft, or reversing the motor, still produces some head but considerably less.

Second, the system resistance may have fallen (an open bypass, a burst pipe, extra users), so the operating point moves to a higher flow and lower head along the normal curve; this can also overload the motor and reduce the NPSH margin. Third, if suction pressure falls, discharge pressure falls with it even though the pump is healthy. Measuring suction pressure, discharge pressure, flow and speed together, and plotting the result on the OEM curve, separates these cases.
causes: Wear-ring wear increasing internal recirculation.
Impeller erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage or partial blockage.
Air or gas in the liquid, or cavitation.
Wrong direction of rotation, or impeller reversed on the shaft after maintenance.
Speed lower than rated (motor, supply or variable-speed drive setting).
System resistance lower than design, so that the pump runs out on its curve.
Low suction pressure.
Instrument error or a blocked gauge tapping.
warningSigns: Discharge gauge reading below normal for the operating condition.
Flow higher or lower than expected, depending on the cause.
Change in motor current.
Noise associated with cavitation or air.
inspection: Verify the instrument: use a calibrated gauge and check that the tapping is clear.
Measure suction pressure, discharge pressure, flow and speed at the same time, calculate the head and plot it on the OEM curve.
Check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing; after electrical work, check it with the motor uncoupled according to site procedure.
Vent the casing and check for gas.
Check the system for open bypasses, leaks or valve changes.
At overhaul, check the impeller orientation and condition and the wear-ring clearances.
consequences: Inadequate supply to the process.
Possible run-out with high power and cavitation.
Continued internal deterioration if the cause is wear.
corrective: Correct the specific cause identified: renew wear rings, repair or clean the impeller, vent the pump or seal air leaks.
Correct the direction of rotation or the impeller orientation.
Restore the rated speed.
Restore the system resistance to design, for example by closing unintended bypasses.
preventive: Record a performance baseline at commissioning.
Check the direction of rotation, uncoupled, after any motor electrical work.
Mark and record the impeller orientation during dismantling and check it at reassembly.
Trend suction and discharge pressure together with flow.

scene.label: Read suction and discharge pressure together with flow

failures.title: No discharge
failures.definition: The pump is running but delivers no flow to the system.
failures.mechanism:
A centrifugal pump generates head only when its impeller passages are full of liquid. The head developed depends on the impeller tip speed and is broadly independent of the fluid, but the pressure produced is the head multiplied by the density and gravity. With air in the impeller the pressure generated is only a tiny fraction of that with liquid, far too little to lift liquid into the pump or to open the discharge check valve. Horizontal split case pumps are normally not self-priming, so the casing must be flooded and vented before starting.

Even when the pump is primed, there is no flow if the head the system requires at zero flow, for example the static head plus the pressure holding a check valve shut, is higher than the shut-off head of the pump. This can happen with an incorrect speed or impeller, reversed rotation or a reversed impeller, or when a stronger parallel pump holds the common check valve closed. Finally, the flow path may be blocked, or the drive may not be turning the impeller (broken coupling, sheared key).

A pump running with no flow converts nearly all its input power into heat in the liquid trapped in the casing. The liquid temperature rises quickly, seals and wear rings can be damaged, and if both suction and discharge are closed the trapped liquid can heat and pressurise to a hazardous level.
causes: Pump not primed or casing not vented; gas lock.
Closed suction or discharge valve, or a check valve stuck closed.
Suction source empty, suction lift too high, or a leaking foot valve allowing the suction line to drain.
System static head above the shut-off head of the pump, or a parallel pump holding the common check valve closed.
Wrong direction of rotation, or impeller reversed on the shaft.
Broken coupling, sheared key, or impeller loose on the shaft.
Blocked strainer, suction line or impeller.
warningSigns: Discharge pressure at or near shut-off with zero indicated flow, or near zero pressure if the pump is not primed.
Motor current lower than normal.
Casing heating up.
Noise from gas, or from a pump running against a closed valve.
inspection: Stop the pump promptly if flow is not established, because running with no flow heats the liquid rapidly.
Check the valve line-up, the check valve operation and the suction source level.
Vent the casing at the upper vent connections, after assessing the hazard of the liquid, and confirm that liquid rather than gas is present.
Check the direction of rotation and, after isolation, the coupling, and confirm that turning the shaft turns the impeller.
Compare the measured shut-off pressure with the OEM curve and the system static head.
Inspect the strainers and the suction line.
consequences: Rapid heating and vaporisation of the liquid in the casing.
Damage to mechanical seals or packing and to wear rings from dry running.
Hazardous pressure and temperature rise if the pump runs with both suction and discharge closed.
Loss of supply to the process.
corrective: Prime and vent the pump fully before restarting.
Open the valves, and repair or replace faulty check valves.
Correct the direction of rotation or the impeller orientation.
Repair the coupling or replace sheared keys.
Clear blockages.
preventive: Use a pre-start checklist covering valve line-up, priming and venting.
Provide no-flow or low-flow protection, such as flow, power or temperature monitoring, according to the site protection philosophy.
Check the direction of rotation, uncoupled, after motor electrical work.
Maintain foot valves and check valves.

scene.label: The impeller must be full of liquid before it can generate pressure

failures.title: Excessive motor current
failures.definition: Motor current above the motor's rated value, or above normal for the operating point, causing overheating and protective tripping.
failures.mechanism:
Motor current depends mainly on the mechanical power the pump demands, the motor losses and the supply voltage. Pump shaft power is proportional to density, flow and head divided by efficiency, and under the affinity laws it varies approximately with the cube of speed. For the radial-flow impellers usually found in split case pumps, the absorbed power typically rises with flow towards and beyond the best efficiency point, so running out to high flow increases power; the OEM power curve shows the actual shape for a given pump.

Power also rises if the liquid is denser or more viscous than the design basis, if the speed is higher than rated, or if the impeller diameter is larger than the duty requires. Mechanical drag adds torque: rubbing wear rings, over-tightened packing, failing bearings, a bent shaft or severe misalignment. On the electrical side, low voltage or phase imbalance increases the current for the same power, and loss of a phase can cause rapid overheating. Separating pump-side causes from motor and supply causes is the first step.
causes: Operation at higher flow than design because the system resistance is lower than expected (run-out).
Liquid density or viscosity higher than design.
Speed higher than rated, or impeller diameter larger than the duty requires.
Mechanical drag from rubbing wear rings, over-tightened packing, failing bearings or misalignment.
Electrical supply problems: low voltage, phase imbalance or loss of a phase.
Motor faults such as winding or bearing defects.
Wrong motor, incorrect connection or incorrect protection settings.
warningSigns: Current reading higher than normal for the operating point.
Motor frame running hotter than usual.
Overload trips, particularly after start-up or at high flow.
Humming, burning odour or a discoloured terminal box.
inspection: Have authorised electrical personnel measure the current on all phases and the supply voltage.
Establish the operating point (flow, head) and compare the expected power with the OEM power curve.
Confirm the liquid properties (density, viscosity, temperature).
With isolation and lock-out/tag-out, turn the pump by hand to check for drag and, where needed, run the motor uncoupled according to site procedure to separate the motor from the pump.
Check packing gland tightness, bearing condition and alignment.
Check the overload protection settings against the motor data.
consequences: Motor overheating and insulation degradation.
Repeated trips and loss of supply.
Reduced motor life.
Pump damage if the cause is run-out (cavitation) or mechanical drag.
corrective: Return operation to the design point by correcting the system resistance or the control.
Correct the liquid conditions or speed; trim the impeller only in consultation with the OEM.
Remove sources of mechanical drag.
Repair electrical supply or motor faults.
Set the protection to the motor rating; never raise the settings above the rating just to stop trips.
preventive: Size the motor for the full operating range and the worst-case liquid properties.
Monitor current and power trends.
Carry out periodic electrical inspections.
Maintain packing, bearings and alignment.

scene.label: Separate pump-side load from motor and supply problems

failures.title: Low-flow operation and overheating
failures.definition: Operation at flows well below the best efficiency point, down to shut-off, causing a temperature rise in the liquid, internal recirculation and, in a single-volute casing, increased radial load on the rotor.
failures.mechanism:
At low flow, much of the power absorbed by the pump is not converted into useful hydraulic work. Disc friction, recirculation and leakage losses become heat in the relatively small amount of liquid passing through. The temperature rise across the pump is approximately the power lost divided by the product of the mass flow and the specific heat of the liquid, so it increases sharply as flow falls; at shut-off nearly all the input power heats the liquid trapped in the casing. A higher temperature raises the vapour pressure, reducing the NPSH margin and the margin against vaporisation in the seal chambers.

Hydraulically, low flow causes suction and discharge recirculation, with noise, pressure pulsation and possible cavitation damage. In a single-volute casing the pressure distribution around the impeller becomes increasingly non-uniform as flow falls below BEP, creating a radial force that in many designs is greatest near shut-off. This deflects the shaft, can close the wear-ring clearances on one side, makes the mechanical seals follow a moving shaft and increases bearing loads. A double volute reduces this radial force but does not eliminate it.

The OEM defines the minimum continuous stable flow and any thermal minimum flow for a particular pump; these values are pump-specific and should not be assumed.
causes: Discharge valve heavily throttled or closed, or system demand far below the pump capacity.
Pump oversized for the actual duty.
Parallel pumps with mismatched curves, pushing the weaker pump back towards shut-off.
Minimum-flow bypass closed, blocked or failed.
Variable-speed drive reducing the flow below the minimum.
Blocked downstream path, or a check valve failing to open.
warningSigns: Casing and discharge pipe hotter than normal.
Rumbling or crackling noise and fluctuating pressure.
Increased vibration.
Seal leakage, or packing running hot.
Motor current lower than normal for the pump.
inspection: Measure the flow and compare it with the OEM minimum continuous flow and allowable operating region.
Measure the liquid temperature at suction and discharge to establish the temperature rise.
Check the minimum-flow bypass valve and its control.
Review parallel operation and the control logic.
At overhaul, inspect the impeller for recirculation damage, the wear rings for rub marks and the shaft for run-out.
consequences: Vaporisation in the casing or seal chambers, and loss of delivery.
Seal and wear-ring damage.
Shaft deflection, fatigue and increased bearing loads.
Hazardous temperature and pressure rise if the pump runs with closed valves.
corrective: Increase the flow through the pump by adjusting the system or opening the bypass.
Repair or restore the minimum-flow bypass.
Resize the impeller or select a smaller pump in consultation with the OEM.
Correct the control logic for parallel and variable-speed operation.
preventive: Provide minimum-flow protection (bypass, flow monitoring or power monitoring) according to OEM requirements.
Select pumps for the real duty range.
Train operators on minimum-flow limits and on limiting operation against a closed discharge valve to the time permitted by the OEM.

scene.label: Away from BEP a single volute produces a net radial force on the impeller

failures.title: Foundation and baseplate vibration
failures.definition: Excessive vibration or movement of the baseplate, grout or foundation block, usually caused by inadequate stiffness or support, voids, loose anchors or structural resonance.
failures.mechanism:
The baseplate, grout and foundation form a stiff, heavy support that holds the pump and motor in alignment and limits their response to dynamic forces. The grout transfers load from the baseplate to the concrete and adds stiffness and damping; the anchor bolts clamp the assembly together.

If there are voids under the baseplate (incomplete grouting, shrinkage, or debonding of the grout from the baseplate or the concrete), cracked grout, grout degraded by oil or chemicals, or loose anchor bolts, the support becomes less stiff and less damped. The natural frequencies of the structure fall and may move close to running speed or vane-pass frequency, so vibration is amplified by resonance. A flexible baseplate also lets the alignment change in operation. Unsupported piping can transmit forces and vibration into the baseplate, and foundation settlement can distort it.

Comparing the vibration of the bearing housings, the pump and motor feet, the baseplate and the foundation, including phase, shows where relative movement occurs and therefore which joint or element is weak.
causes: Voids under the baseplate from incomplete grouting or grout shrinkage.
Cracked or debonded grout, or grout attacked by oil or chemicals.
Loose, corroded or failed anchor bolts.
Foundation too small, poor soil, cracking or settlement.
Structural natural frequency close to running speed or vane-pass frequency.
Forces and vibration transmitted from unsupported piping.
Levelling screws left carrying load where the installation procedure requires them to be released after grouting.
warningSigns: Visible baseplate movement, or vibration felt on the baseplate.
Hollow sound when the baseplate is tapped, indicating voids.
Cracks or gaps in the grout.
Alignment repeatedly drifting.
Loosening anchor or hold-down bolts.
inspection: Measure vibration on the bearing housings, the pump and motor feet, the baseplate and the foundation, and compare amplitudes and phase to find where relative movement occurs.
Tap-test the baseplate to locate voids and inspect the grout for cracks and debonding.
Check the anchor bolts according to site procedure.
Review the soft foot and alignment history.
Check the pipe supports near the pump.
Where resonance is suspected, arrange specialist impact testing to identify natural frequencies.
consequences: Misalignment and the resulting bearing, seal and coupling failures.
Fatigue cracking of the baseplate, welds or piping.
Loosening of fasteners.
Noise and reduced reliability.
corrective: Fill voids (for example by epoxy injection) or re-grout following a specialist procedure.
Replace or re-tighten anchor bolts according to the design.
Stiffen or detune the structure where resonance is confirmed, under engineering guidance.
Correct the pipe supports.
Realign the pump and motor after foundation repairs.
preventive: Follow correct grouting practice at installation, using the OEM instructions and recognised guidance such as API 686 where applicable.
Inspect the grout and anchor bolts periodically.
Protect the grout from oil and chemical leakage.
Record baseline vibration on the baseplate as well as on the bearing housings.

scene.label: Grout and anchors give the baseplate its stiffness

symptoms.title: Casing joint leakage
symptoms.description: Liquid weeping, dripping or spraying from the horizontal split joint between the upper and lower casing halves. Joint leakage has several possible causes, often acting together, so the gasket, the joint faces, the bolting, the operating conditions and the assembly history should all be checked before a repair is chosen. A spraying joint is a pressurised leak: keep clear and isolate if the liquid is hazardous.

investigationPoints.detail: Ageing, compression set, chemical attack or damage during assembly reduces the gasket's ability to seal, and a reused gasket rarely seals reliably. At dismantling, examine the gasket for hardening, cracking, extrusion and an uneven imprint, and confirm the material is compatible with the liquid and temperature.

Distortion, corrosion pits, erosion grooves from a previous leak, nicks or residues of old gasket or sealant leave paths the gasket cannot close. Check the faces for flatness and damage using the OEM method; any repair that removes material must follow OEM instructions because it changes internal dimensions.

Incorrect torque, the wrong tightening sequence, uneven tightening, damaged or dry threads, or relaxation without the retightening the OEM requires all leave areas of low gasket stress, typically midway between studs. Check the fastener condition and the tightening records against the OEM values and sequence.

Rapid heating or cooling, or uneven temperature across the casing, distorts the flanges and can open the joint, sometimes only during start-up, shutdown or after running against a closed valve. Compare when the leak occurs with temperature changes and with the warm-up guidance in the OEM manual.

Operation above the casing design pressure, pressure surges (water hammer) or a speed higher than rated increase the force separating the halves. Review discharge pressure records and transient events against the casing design pressure.

Wrong gasket material or thickness, a gasket misplaced or incorrectly trimmed at the bores, dowels not engaged, or casing wear rings or seal housings not fully seated so that they hold the halves apart. Check the gasket against the OEM parts list and the seating of internal parts at reassembly.

Misaligned or poorly supported suction and discharge piping can distort the casing and unload part of the joint; the same pipe strain often disturbs shaft alignment. Check pipe supports and flange alignment at the nozzles.

symptoms.title: Noisy pump / crackling noise
symptoms.description: Crackling, rattling, gravel-like, rumbling or grinding noise from the pump. A crackling noise is often attributed to cavitation, but entrained air, recirculation at low flow, unequal inflow to the two eyes, debris and mechanical sources such as bearings, rubbing parts or the coupling can sound similar. Locate where the noise comes from and note how it changes with flow before concluding on a cause; more than one cause may be present.

investigationPoints.detail: Check suction pressure, liquid temperature and flow against the NPSH available calculation and the OEM NPSH required curve. Noise that grows as flow increases or as the suction level falls points this way.

investigationPoints.point: Air or gas in the liquid
investigationPoints.detail: Look for vortices at the intake, suction-side leaks, loss of sealing water and gas at the casing vents. Air noise is easily mistaken for cavitation.
Noise that appears or grows as flow is reduced, typically a rumbling or random crackle, suggests recirculation. Compare the flow with the OEM minimum flow and allowable operating region.

investigationPoints.point: Unequal inflow to the two eyes
investigationPoints.detail: A suction elbow in the plane of the shaft close to the nozzle is commonly cited as a cause of uneven inflow and noise, sometimes louder at one end of the casing. Review the suction layout.
Rattling or knocking together with falling performance can indicate debris in the eyes or passages. Check the strainer and, after safe isolation, inspect internally.
Grinding, rumbling or clicking from a bearing housing, often with rising temperature and vibration at bearing defect frequencies, points to a bearing problem rather than a hydraulic one.

Metallic rubbing at the wear rings or seals, or knocking from a worn coupling, can be confused with hydraulic noise. With the pump isolated and locked out, turn the rotor by hand and inspect the coupling.

symptoms.title: High vibration
symptoms.description: Vibration at the bearing housings, motor or piping above the acceptable level or rising from its baseline. Vibration has many possible sources, mechanical, hydraulic, electrical and structural, and more than one can be present at the same time; spectrum analysis and correlation with the operating point are needed to identify them.

investigationPoints.detail: Dominant once-per-revolution vibration, mainly radial, suggests unbalance from impeller wear, corrosion, deposits, debris or a repair that was not balanced. Check the rotor balance at overhaul.
Once and twice per revolution vibration with high axial readings suggests misalignment. Check alignment, soft foot and pipe strain.

Non-synchronous frequencies matching bearing defect frequencies, or rising envelope values, indicate bearing damage. The drive-end and non-drive-end bearings are different types with different defect frequencies.
Broadband vibration, vane-pass components, or vibration that changes markedly with flow point to cavitation, recirculation, air or unequal inflow. Record flow and pressures with every reading.
Once-per-revolution vibration that does not improve with balancing, or that changes after a rub, suggests a bent shaft or excessive deflection. Measure the shaft run-out.
Many harmonics of running speed, or high vibration on the baseplate relative to the bearing housings, point to looseness, soft foot, or grout and anchor problems.
Vibration that peaks sharply at a particular speed, or is much higher in one direction, may be resonance of the rotor, structure or piping. Specialist testing is needed to confirm it.
Uncouple and run the motor on its own, according to site procedure, to establish whether the vibration originates in the motor.

symptoms.title: Bearing housing running hot
symptoms.description: A bearing housing temperature above its normal trend, or above the limit given by the OEM or site procedure. The heat can come from the lubricant, the load on the bearing, the bearing's condition or external sources, so several causes need to be considered. The drive-end and non-drive-end bearings are different types and need not run at the same temperature; compare each with its own baseline.

investigationPoints.detail: Too much oil or grease causes churning and heat; too little allows metal contact. Check the oil level in the sight glass, the constant-level oiler setting, or the grease quantity and relubrication records against the OEM manual.
Wrong viscosity, mixed greases, water, dirt or oxidation reduce the lubricating ability. Take an oil sample or inspect the grease.

investigationPoints.point: Residual axial thrust on the locating bearing
investigationPoints.detail: A non-drive-end bearing running hotter than its baseline may be carrying more axial load, for example from unequal wear-ring clearances, unequal inflow to the eyes or coupling forces.
These increase the radial loads, particularly at the drive end. Check alignment, vibration spectra and pipe supports.
A damaged bearing runs hotter and noisier; check vibration at bearing defect frequencies.
Tight fits, a drive-end bearing that cannot float, or a reversed angular-contact pair generate extra heat; these are checked at dismantling against OEM requirements.
Rubbing housing lip seals, a high ambient temperature or heat conducted from a hot pumped liquid can raise the housing temperature without any bearing defect.

symptoms.title: Seal leaking
symptoms.description: Visible leakage at a mechanical seal gland at the drive end or the non-drive end (this applies to pumps fitted with mechanical seals; for packed pumps see the packing symptom). The leak may come from the seal faces, the secondary seals, the gland gasket or even the casing joint near the seal housing, and face leakage itself has many possible causes; trace the leak path and review the operating history before replacing the seal.

investigationPoints.detail: Determine which end leaks and whether the liquid comes from between the faces, from the gland gasket or O-rings, along the sleeve, or from the casing joint close to the seal housing.
Loss of prime, or a start with an unvented seal chamber or a closed suction valve, can destroy the faces in a short time.
Check that the flush required by the seal arrangement is flowing at the correct pressure and temperature, and that its valves and orifices are clear.
Vibration, deflection, misalignment, bearing wear or excessive end float make the faces open and close. Check vibration, run-out and bearing condition.
Low suction pressure, low-flow operation or a high liquid temperature reduce the margin against vaporisation in the seal chamber.
An incorrect setting, damaged faces, cut O-rings, unlocked sleeves or elastomers unsuitable for the liquid often show up soon after a repair.

symptoms.title: Packing leaking excessively or running hot
symptoms.description: A packed stuffing box at either end leaking well above the controlled rate recommended by the OEM, or running hot with little or no leakage (this applies to pumps fitted with gland packing). Some leakage is normal and necessary. Excessive leakage and overheating can each result from adjustment, installation, sealing-water, sleeve or mechanical causes, and often from a combination of them.

investigationPoints.detail: An over-tightened gland runs hot; a loose one leaks. Adjust evenly and gradually according to the OEM manual, and adjust a running pump only where the site procedure allows it.
Look for hardened, glazed or burnt rings, the wrong size, joints that are not staggered, or a lantern ring out of position under the flush connection.
Absent, insufficient or dirty sealing water removes the cooling and lubrication; on a suction lift it also allows air to be drawn in.
A scored or worn sleeve cannot be sealed by new packing; inspect it whenever the pump is repacked.
Run-out, vibration, misalignment or bearing wear work the packing loose and wear it unevenly.
Abrasive solids, or a packing material unsuited to the liquid, speed or temperature, shorten packing life.

symptoms.title: Low discharge pressure
symptoms.description: The discharge gauge reads lower than normal. This does not by itself mean the pump is faulty: the pump may be producing less head, the system may be drawing more flow, or the suction pressure may have fallen, and several of these can combine. Always read suction pressure, discharge pressure and flow together.

investigationPoints.detail: Confirm the gauge is calibrated and the tapping is not blocked before investigating further.
If suction pressure has fallen by a similar amount, the pump may be healthy and the problem lies upstream.

Plot head and flow on the OEM curve. Low pressure with high flow indicates the system resistance has fallen (open bypass, leak, extra users); low pressure with low flow indicates the pump is under-performing.
Wear-ring wear, impeller erosion, corrosion or blockage reduce the head at a given flow.
Fluctuating pressure with noise points to air ingress or cavitation.
Check the speed and the direction of rotation; after maintenance, also confirm that the impeller was not refitted the wrong way round on the shaft.

symptoms.title: No flow after start
symptoms.description: The pump starts but no flow reaches the system. Possible causes range from priming and valve line-up to system head, rotation and mechanical failure of the drive, so work through them systematically. Stop the pump promptly if flow is not established, because a pump running without flow heats its liquid rapidly.

investigationPoints.detail: Confirm that the casing and suction line are full of liquid; vent at the upper casing vents after assessing the hazard of the liquid.
Check that the suction and discharge valves are open and that the check valve is not stuck closed.
Check the source level, the suction lift and the foot valve; an empty source or a drained suction line prevents priming.
Compare the measured shut-off pressure with the OEM curve and the system static head; a parallel pump may be holding the common check valve shut.
Wrong rotation, or an impeller reversed on the shaft, reduces the head, possibly below the system static head.
After isolation and lock-out/tag-out, check the coupling and keys and confirm that turning the shaft turns the impeller.
Check the strainers, the suction line and, if necessary, the impeller.

symptoms.title: Motor drawing high current / tripping
symptoms.description: Motor current above normal for the operating point, or overload trips. The cause may lie in the operating point, the liquid, the mechanical condition of the pump, the motor or the electrical supply, and often more than one contributes. Electrical checks must be carried out by authorised personnel.

investigationPoints.detail: High flow because the system resistance is lower than expected increases the power drawn by the radial-flow impellers usual in split case pumps. Compare with the OEM power curve.
A higher density or viscosity than the design basis raises the power required.
A speed above rated, or an impeller larger than the duty requires, raises the power required.
With the pump isolated and locked out, turn it by hand; rubbing wear rings, tight packing, failing bearings or misalignment add load.
Measure voltage and current on all phases; low voltage, imbalance or a lost phase raise the current. Run the motor uncoupled, according to site procedure, where needed to isolate motor faults.
Check that the overload settings match the motor data; never raise them above the motor rating to stop trips.

symptoms.title: Flow lower than expected
symptoms.description: Delivered flow below the design value, or below the previous normal value at the same conditions. Reduced flow may come from the pump (wear, damage, blockage, gas, speed), from the suction conditions or from increased system resistance; measure suction and discharge pressure together with flow to see whether the pump or the system has changed.

investigationPoints.detail: First confirm the flowmeter reading. If the discharge pressure is higher than normal, the system has become more restrictive (throttled valves, fouled lines, blocked filters) and the pump has moved back along its curve towards low flow.
Increased internal recirculation lowers the net delivered flow and head at the same speed.
Erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage or blockage of one or both eyes reduces head and flow.
A blocked strainer, a partly closed suction valve or a low source level reduces flow and may cause cavitation.
Entrained gas reduces the delivered flow and makes the readings fluctuate.
Low speed, wrong rotation or a reversed impeller reduce the flow.

symptoms.title: Pump loses prime
symptoms.description: The pump delivers normally after priming but then loses flow as gas accumulates, or it cannot be primed at all. Gas can enter at several places or come out of the liquid itself, so suction-side leaks, intake conditions, shaft sealing and the suction layout all need checking.

investigationPoints.detail: Where suction pressure is below atmospheric, leaking flanges, valve glands or instrument fittings draw air in without visible drips.
Insufficient submergence at a low source level lets surface vortices draw air into the suction.

investigationPoints.point: Shaft sealing on a suction lift
investigationPoints.detail: Loss of sealing water to the packing lantern rings, or a worn mechanical seal, lets air in along the shaft when the seal area is below atmospheric pressure.
Air pockets form at high points of the suction line, or under an eccentric reducer fitted flat side down.

investigationPoints.point: Foot valve or check valve leakage
investigationPoints.detail: A leaking foot valve lets the suction line drain when the pump stops.
A low NPSH margin or a high liquid temperature can produce vapour that blocks the eyes.

symptoms.title: Shaft hard to turn by hand
symptoms.description: With the pump isolated, the rotor is stiff, rough or binds when turned by hand. Turn the shaft only after isolation and lock-out/tag-out, once it is confirmed that the motor cannot start. Stiffness can come from the packing or seals, internal contact, debris, the bearings, the coupling or a distorted casing, so check one source at a time, for example with the coupling spacer removed.

investigationPoints.detail: Newly packed or over-tightened glands can make the rotor stiff; set them according to the OEM run-in instructions.
Rings in contact because of deflection, a bent shaft, casing distortion or incorrect clearances cause binding at one position or all the way round.
Debris trapped in the eyes, the passages or the wear-ring clearances can jam the impeller.
Rough or notchy rotation points to damaged bearings or lubricant failure.

Pipe loads, an incorrect joint gasket or uneven bolt tightening can distort the casing and close internal clearances; check whether the rotor frees when the pipe flange bolts are slackened under site procedure.
Remove the coupling spacer to establish whether the stiffness is in the pump or in the motor, and check the coupling elements for binding.
Liquid that has crystallised or solidified at the mechanical seals or in the casing after shutdown, or corrosion products in tight clearances, can lock the rotor.

symptoms.title: Coupling wear / element debris
symptoms.description: Powder, fragments or visible wear of the flexible coupling elements, or play, cracks and fretting at hubs and keys. Coupling wear is often a consequence of conditions elsewhere, most commonly misalignment, but it has other causes too, so replacing the elements without finding the cause usually leads to repeat failures.

investigationPoints.detail: The most common cause of element wear; measure alignment and check soft foot and pipe strain.
An incorrect distance between shaft ends imposes axial strain on the elements and can add axial load on the locating bearing.
Seizure, debris in the impeller or severe starting transients overload the elements.
Heat, oil, chemicals or age degrade elastomer elements.
Loose hubs or worn keys cause fretting, play and knocking.
Baseplate or foundation problems can allow the alignment to change in service.

symptoms.title: Foundation or baseplate vibration
symptoms.description: Noticeable vibration or movement of the baseplate, grout or foundation. It may be caused by weak support (voids, cracked grout, loose anchors), by resonance, or by high forces from the machines or the piping, alone or in combination; comparing the vibration on the machines, the baseplate and the foundation shows where the problem lies.

investigationPoints.detail: Tap-test the baseplate for hollow areas and inspect the grout for cracks, debonding and oil damage.
Loose or corroded anchor bolts, or loose machine mountings, allow rocking and alignment changes.
If baseplate vibration is much higher than expected for the forces involved, especially at a particular speed, structural resonance may be the cause.
Unbalance, misalignment and hydraulic excitation generate the forces the structure must resist; check the machines as well as the structure.
Unsupported or poorly supported piping transmits forces and vibration into the baseplate.
Levelling screws left carrying load where the procedure requires them to be released, or poor shimming, change how the load passes into the foundation.

symptoms.title: Pump casing or discharge pipe running hot
symptoms.description: The casing or discharge pipe is noticeably hotter than normal for the liquid being pumped. The most common cause is too little flow through the pump, but internal rubbing and changes in the incoming liquid temperature can also be responsible, so confirm the flow before drawing conclusions.

investigationPoints.detail: Check the flow against the OEM minimum continuous flow; a throttled or closed discharge valve converts the input power into heat.
Confirm that the bypass valve opens when required and that its control works.
A weaker pump running in parallel with others may be operating near shut-off.
Contact at the wear rings generates local heat and may be accompanied by noise and a higher current.
A higher suction temperature makes the whole pump hotter and reduces the NPSH margin even if the pump itself is healthy.

symptoms.title: Fluctuating discharge pressure / surging
symptoms.description: Discharge pressure and flow that hunt, surge or fluctuate. Fluctuation can result from gas in the liquid, cavitation, recirculation at low flow, pump-system interaction in parallel operation or control-system behaviour, so consider the whole system as well as the pump.

investigationPoints.detail: Gas pockets passing through the impeller cause irregular pressure; check the intake, suction leaks and vents.
Fluctuation with crackling noise and low suction pressure suggests insufficient NPSH margin.
Fluctuation that appears at reduced flow and disappears at higher flow points to recirculation.
Pumps with mismatched curves, or a pump with a drooping head curve, can hunt between operating points; review the curves and control logic.
Skewed or swirling inflow from the suction piping can make the flow through the two eyes unsteady.
An undamped gauge, a hunting control valve or a variable-speed drive control loop can produce fluctuations unrelated to the pump hydraulics.

symptoms.title: Bearing oil or grease discoloured, milky or contaminated
symptoms.description: Oil in a bearing housing sight glass that is milky, darkened or contains particles, or an oil level that changes unexpectedly; grease-lubricated bearings show similar signs as discoloured, watery or hardened grease. Contamination may enter from outside, come from seal or packing leakage, or be generated inside by bearing wear or overheating, so more than one source may need to be ruled out.

investigationPoints.detail: Milky oil usually indicates water from seal or packing leakage, washdown, rain or condensation entering past worn housing seals or missing deflectors.
Dark oil with a burnt odour suggests the bearing or the oil has overheated.
Metallic particles indicate bearing wear; analyse the oil and check the vibration.
Check the lubricant type against the OEM specification and the maintenance records.
A falling level may indicate leaking housing seals or gaskets; a rising level may indicate water ingress. Check the constant-level oiler setting.

materials.name: Grey cast iron
materials.description: An iron-carbon-silicon casting alloy in which most of the carbon is present as graphite flakes. The flakes give excellent castability, machinability and vibration damping, but they act as internal notches, so grey iron has low ductility and low toughness compared with ductile iron or steel. It is the traditional, economical material for casings, bearing housings and some baseplates in clean-water service.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good compressive strength but limited tensile strength and very little elongation. Because the graphite flakes concentrate stress, the material is brittle and can fracture with little warning under impact, shock, overpressure, water hammer, excessive pipe loads or uneven bolt loads. Properties vary with section thickness and cooling rate, so different sections of a heavy casting may not have identical strength.
materials.corrosionResistance: Similar to other unalloyed irons: rusts in aerated water, is generally acceptable in clean, near-neutral water, and is limited in seawater, acidic or otherwise aggressive water unless coated or protected. Long exposure to some waters causes graphitic corrosion, a selective loss of iron that leaves a weak graphite-rich network which may not be obvious from the surface.
materials.wearResistance: Fair sliding behaviour because graphite acts as a solid lubricant, but grey iron is not normally used as a wear-ring or sleeve material against hard counterfaces.
materials.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate. Erodes readily in water carrying hard solids, especially in high-velocity zones such as the volute tongue, the impeller inlet region and around wear-ring clearances.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for ambient and moderately elevated water temperatures. Sensitive to thermal shock and rapid temperature change. The allowable pressure-temperature combinations are set by the applicable casting and pump standards and the OEM design, not by the material family alone.
materials.costConsiderations: Usually the lowest-cost casting material for pump casings, widely available from foundries, with established pattern equipment for many standard pump ranges.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Excellent fluidity and castability allow complex suction and volute passages; very good machinability. Weld repair is difficult and is frequently restricted or prohibited on pressure-containing parts; where permitted it needs preheat, suitable consumables and an approved procedure. A stress-relief heat treatment may be applied for dimensional stability before final machining of the split joint and bores.
advantages: Excellent castability for complex hydraulic passages
Adequate corrosion behaviour in clean, near-neutral water
limitations: Brittle: low ductility and impact resistance because of the graphite flakes
Weld repair is difficult and often not permitted on pressure parts
Limited resistance to seawater, acidic or aggressive water
Susceptible to graphitic corrosion over long service
Excluded by many process-industry specifications for flammable or hazardous liquids
suitableService: Cooling water in treated or closed systems
Irrigation and fire water where the governing specification allows it

materials.name: Ductile (spheroidal graphite) iron
materials.description: Cast iron in which the graphite is present as spheroids (nodules) rather than flakes, achieved by treating the molten iron, typically with magnesium, before casting. Nodular graphite does not act as a sharp notch, so ductile iron keeps much of the castability of grey iron while offering significantly higher strength, ductility and toughness.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Higher tensile strength, elongation and impact toughness than grey iron, giving much better tolerance of overpressure, water hammer, nozzle loads and handling impacts. The grade (ferritic, pearlitic or mixed matrix), nodularity and section size determine the actual properties, which should be confirmed from the material certificate.
materials.corrosionResistance: Broadly similar to grey iron: rusts in aerated water, acceptable in clean near-neutral water, and limited in seawater and acidic media without protection. Internal coatings are often applied to extend life in water service.
materials.wearResistance: Fair for sliding contact, similar to grey iron. Not normally used for wear rings without surface treatment.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Somewhat better than grey iron because of its toughness, but it still erodes in high-velocity, solids-laden flow.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures, with better thermal-shock tolerance than grey iron. Low-temperature impact toughness depends on the grade. Pressure-temperature limits come from the applicable standards and the OEM design.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderately more expensive than grey iron because of the nodularising treatment and tighter process control; usually well below cast steel and stainless steels.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Good castability, although it shows a greater shrinkage tendency than grey iron and needs careful feeding and metallurgical control to maintain nodularity. Good machinability. Weld repair is possible with qualified procedures but can alter the microstructure near the weld, so repairs on pressure parts need OEM and specification approval. Heat treatment can be used to adjust the matrix and properties.
advantages: Much greater ductility and toughness than grey iron
Higher strength allows lighter or higher-pressure casings
Better tolerance of pipe loads, water hammer and handling impact
Cost remains well below steel and stainless alloys
limitations: Corrosion resistance broadly similar to grey iron
Properties depend on nodularity and must be verified
Weld repair requires qualified procedures and approval
Not suitable for seawater or acidic service without protection
suitableService: Municipal and potable water, with approved coatings where required
Cooling water and general industrial water
Fire protection pumping where the specification allows it
Higher-pressure water service where grey iron is not acceptable

materials.name: Cast carbon steel
materials.description: Steel castings with low to moderate carbon content and no significant alloying additions. Cast steel is chosen for pressure-containing parts when higher strength, toughness and weldability than cast iron are required, for example at higher pressures or temperatures, or where specifications exclude cast iron for flammable or hazardous liquids.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High strength and toughness with good ductility; tolerates pressure transients and external loads well. Low-temperature toughness depends on composition and heat treatment and is verified by impact testing where required.
materials.corrosionResistance: Limited. Rusts in water and lacks the graphite-rich surface layer that helps cast iron in some waters, so designs typically include a corrosion allowance and may be coated. Not suitable for seawater or corrosive chemicals without protection.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate. Not used as a wear-ring or sleeve material without surface hardening or overlay.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Tougher than cast iron but of similar hardness, so erosion still occurs in solids-laden flow; extra wall thickness or liners are used where wear is expected.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for higher temperatures than cast iron within the pressure-temperature ratings of the applicable standard. Low-temperature duties need impact-tested material.
materials.costConsiderations: Higher than cast iron because of higher pouring temperatures, more feeding metal, heat treatment and inspection; usually below stainless and duplex alloys.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: More demanding to cast than iron: higher pouring temperature, greater shrinkage and a greater tendency to casting defects, so castings are commonly inspected by non-destructive testing and repaired by welding under qualified procedures. Normally heat treated (for example normalised) after casting. Good weldability and machinability.
advantages: Weldable, so casting defects can be repaired under qualified procedures
Accepted by many higher-pressure and hazardous-fluid specifications
Better thermal-shock tolerance than cast iron
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance in water without coating or corrosion allowance
More expensive and slower to produce than iron castings
Castability inferior to cast iron for thin, complex passages
Requires heat treatment and inspection
suitableService: Hot water duties within the applicable ratings
Hydrocarbon or hazardous liquids where cast iron is excluded
typicalUse: Casing nozzles as part of the casing casting

materials.name: Cast austenitic stainless steel
materials.description: Cast chromium-nickel stainless steels, with or without molybdenum, for example compositions related to the molybdenum-bearing 316-type family. Cast grades have their own designations and often contain some ferrite in their microstructure, so they should not be treated as identical to wrought grades. Corrosion resistance comes from a thin, self-repairing chromium-rich passive film.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength with good ductility and toughness, including at low temperatures. Strength is lower than that of duplex stainless steels and cannot be increased by heat treatment.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good general corrosion resistance in many waters and chemicals. Susceptible to pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride-containing water, especially where flow is stagnant, temperature is raised, or oxidisers such as chlorine are present; molybdenum-bearing grades perform better than molybdenum-free grades. Chloride stress corrosion cracking is possible at elevated temperatures.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate. Austenitic stainless steels have a strong tendency to gall when rubbing against similar stainless alloys, which matters at wear rings and threaded parts.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate. Better than cast iron where corrosion and erosion act together, but not a wear-resistant material for heavy solids.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Wide range from low to elevated temperatures within code ratings. The risk of chloride stress corrosion cracking increases with temperature.
materials.costConsiderations: Significantly higher than cast iron; sensitive to nickel and molybdenum market prices.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Good castability with appropriate foundry practice; solution heat treatment after casting is normally applied to restore full corrosion resistance. Weldable with qualified procedures. Machining is slower than for iron because the material work-hardens, so tooling and cutting parameters must suit it.
advantages: Weldable and repairable under qualified procedures
Suitable for potable and high-purity duties where approved
No rust contamination of the pumped liquid
limitations: Pitting and crevice corrosion in chloride environments
Chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperature
Galling tendency in stainless-on-stainless sliding contact
Lower strength than duplex alloys
Higher cost than cast iron
suitableService: Many dilute chemical solutions, subject to corrosion data
Brackish water only after careful assessment of chlorides and temperature
typicalUse: Casing halves for corrosive or high-purity service

materials.name: Duplex stainless steel
materials.description: Stainless steels with a mixed ferritic-austenitic microstructure, generally higher in chromium than common austenitic grades and alloyed with molybdenum and nitrogen. The two-phase structure gives substantially higher strength than austenitic stainless steels and improved resistance to chloride pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking. Available as castings for casings and impellers and as wrought bar for shafts and sleeves.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Substantially higher strength than austenitic stainless steels with good toughness, which supports stiff, compact shafts and good fatigue performance. Toughness depends on a correct ferrite-austenite balance and the absence of embrittling phases.
materials.corrosionResistance: Better chloride pitting and crevice corrosion resistance than common austenitic grades and much better resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking. The Pitting Resistance Equivalent Number (PREN) is a calculated index based on chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen content, with molybdenum and nitrogen weighted more heavily than chromium. It is used to rank alloys comparatively; several formula variants exist, and PREN alone does not predict performance in a specific fluid, temperature or crevice geometry.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate to good; harder than austenitic grades, but galling is still possible against similar alloys, so wear-ring pairs need attention.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good where corrosion and erosion act together, generally better than austenitic grades; not a substitute for hard wear materials in heavy slurries.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good from low to moderately elevated temperatures. Prolonged exposure in an intermediate elevated temperature range causes embrittlement, which limits the upper service temperature; the limit is set by the applicable codes and material supplier.
materials.costConsiderations: Typically higher than austenitic stainless castings, although higher strength can reduce section sizes. Fewer foundries are qualified, which can affect lead time.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Casting and welding require close control of chemistry, cooling rate and solution annealing to achieve the correct phase balance and to avoid intermetallic phases (such as sigma phase) that reduce toughness and corrosion resistance. Weld repairs need qualified procedures and often ferrite measurement and corrosion testing. Machinability is lower than that of austenitic grades.
advantages: High strength allows compact, stiff designs
Improved resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion
High resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking
One alloy family can cover casing, impeller, shaft and sleeves
limitations: Sensitive to incorrect heat treatment and welding (intermetallic phases)
Upper service temperature limited by embrittlement
Fewer qualified foundries and longer lead times
Still susceptible to crevice corrosion in warm, chlorinated or stagnant seawater
More difficult to machine than austenitic grades
suitableService: Brackish water and many seawater duties after assessment
Desalination and reverse osmosis feed pumping
Mildly acidic or chemical service, subject to corrosion data

materials.name: Super duplex stainless steel
materials.description: Highly alloyed duplex stainless steels with higher chromium, molybdenum and nitrogen than standard duplex grades. This gives a higher PREN as a comparative index and stronger resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion. Commonly considered for seawater, brines and other aggressive chloride service.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very high strength for a stainless steel with good toughness when correctly heat treated; generally comparable to or above standard duplex grades.
materials.corrosionResistance: One of the most resistant stainless steel families in chloride environments, with high resistance to pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking. It is not immune: crevice corrosion can still occur in warm, chlorinated or stagnant seawater, under deposits and in tight crevices, so design details and operating practice still matter.
materials.wearResistance: Good; harder than austenitic grades, but galling precautions are still needed for sliding pairs.
materials.abrasionResistance: Good resistance to erosion-corrosion in clean or lightly laden seawater; not a slurry material.
materials.temperatureSuitability: As for standard duplex grades: suitable from low to moderately elevated temperatures, with an upper limit set by embrittlement and code rules.
materials.costConsiderations: High; one of the more expensive pump alloy families, with limited foundry sources and longer lead times.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Even more sensitive than standard duplex to intermetallic phase formation during casting, heat treatment and welding, and heavy sections are difficult to cool quickly enough. Qualified procedures, solution annealing and testing (for example microstructure and corrosion tests) are commonly specified. Machining is demanding.
advantages: High resistance to chloride pitting and crevice corrosion
Good resistance to chloride stress corrosion cracking
Avoids the velocity limits of copper alloys in seawater
Long life in seawater when correctly specified and manufactured
limitations: High material and manufacturing cost
Very sensitive to casting, heat treatment and welding quality
Limited foundry capability for large castings
Not immune to crevice corrosion in severe conditions
Accelerates galvanic corrosion of less noble metals coupled to it
suitableService: Seawater intake, cooling and fire water
Reverse osmosis high-pressure and brine duties

materials.name: Tin bronze and gunmetal (low-zinc copper alloys)
materials.description: Copper-tin casting alloys, including leaded and zinc-containing gunmetal variants, long used for water pump impellers, wear rings and small parts. Because they contain little or no zinc, they resist dezincification, the selective leaching of zinc that weakens high-zinc brasses in many waters. Where brass-type alloys are considered for water service, dezincification-resistant compositions are normally required.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength and good ductility; adequate for impellers and wear rings at moderate peripheral speeds, but lower than steels and stainless steels.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to fresh water and many treated waters and, in suitable compositions, to seawater at moderate velocities. Susceptible to erosion-corrosion at high local velocities, to stress corrosion cracking in the presence of ammonia, and to attack in sulphide-polluted water and some oxidising chemicals.
materials.wearResistance: Good sliding and anti-galling behaviour, which makes bronze a common wear-ring partner against stainless steel or against a bronze of different hardness.
materials.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate; soft relative to sand and other hard particles, so it erodes in solids-laden water.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated water temperatures; strength reduces as temperature rises.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high and sensitive to copper and tin prices; scrap value is high.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Very good castability for impellers and rings and excellent machinability, especially in leaded grades. Weld repair of leaded grades is difficult. Lead content may be restricted by drinking-water regulations, so low-lead or lead-free alloys with national approvals may be required for potable water.
advantages: Good corrosion resistance in fresh water
Good anti-galling behaviour as a wear-ring material
Long, well-documented service history in water pumps
limitations: Limited strength at high peripheral speeds
Erosion-corrosion at high local velocity
Attacked by ammonia, sulphides and some chemicals
Lead content may conflict with potable water rules
Galvanic interaction with iron and steel parts must be considered
suitableService: Municipal and potable water (with approved alloys)
Seawater at moderate velocity in suitable compositions, after assessment
typicalUse: Shaft sleeves in older or low-duty water pumps

materials.name: Aluminium bronze (including nickel-aluminium bronze)
materials.description: Copper-aluminium alloys, usually with iron and often nickel additions. They combine higher strength than tin bronzes with good resistance to seawater corrosion and cavitation erosion, and are widely used for seawater pump impellers, casings and wear parts. Behaviour varies significantly between grades and heat-treatment conditions, so the specific grade matters.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High strength and good toughness for a copper alloy, with good fatigue resistance in seawater.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to seawater and brackish water, with a velocity tolerance generally better than tin bronze, although velocity limits still apply. Some grades and heat-treatment conditions are susceptible to selective phase corrosion (de-aluminification), particularly in crevices, under deposits and in stagnant or polluted seawater, so grade, heat treatment and design detail must address it. Not suitable for many acids, ammonia or sulphide-polluted water.
materials.wearResistance: Good; often used for wear rings, though pairings with stainless steel still need attention to galling and hardness difference.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate; better than tin bronze, but still limited in sandy or slurry flows.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Ambient to moderately elevated temperatures typical of seawater and cooling duties.
materials.costConsiderations: High and sensitive to copper and nickel prices.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Castable, but more demanding than tin bronze because of oxide film and dross formation, so good foundry practice is essential. Weldable with qualified procedures; a post-weld heat treatment may be specified to restore resistance to selective phase corrosion. Machinability is moderate.
advantages: High strength for a copper alloy
Some natural resistance to marine biofouling
limitations: Selective phase corrosion in some grades and conditions
Velocity limits still apply
Sensitive to sulphide-polluted seawater
Galvanic effects when coupled to stainless steel or carbon steel
Higher foundry complexity than tin bronze
suitableService: Fire water drawn from the sea
typicalUse: Casing halves in some seawater designs
Shaft sleeves in some marine designs

materials.name: High-chromium white cast iron
materials.description: Abrasion-resistant cast irons with high chromium content in which the carbon forms very hard chromium carbides instead of graphite. Hardened by heat treatment, they are the standard metallic wear material for dedicated slurry pump impellers, liners and throatbushes, and are rarely used in standard split-case pumps.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very hard but brittle, with low tensile ductility and low impact resistance. Components must be designed, handled and installed to avoid impact, point loading and thermal shock.
materials.corrosionResistance: Moderate in near-neutral slurries. Resistance falls in low-pH or high-chloride slurries, where corrosion and erosion combine and wear accelerates; specialised compositions exist for such duties.
materials.wearResistance: Very good in sliding abrasion.
materials.abrasionResistance: Excellent against hard and coarse particles. For fine particles at low impact angles, rubber linings can outperform it in some duties.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for normal slurry temperatures; thermal shock can crack castings.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate material cost but higher processing cost because of heat treatment and grinding; generally justified by wear life in abrasive duties.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Castable with careful foundry control. Essentially not machinable by conventional turning, so designs minimise machined surfaces and finish them by grinding. Practically not weldable, so worn parts are replaced rather than repaired. Heat treatment develops the hard matrix.
advantages: Established material for replaceable slurry wear parts
Moderate cost relative to wear life
limitations: Brittle; sensitive to impact and thermal shock
Very difficult to machine and not weld repairable
Limited corrosion resistance in acidic slurries
Rarely offered in standard split-case pumps

materials.name: Natural rubber and elastomer linings
materials.description: Soft natural rubber or other elastomer compounds, moulded or bonded as replaceable liners in slurry pumps. The resilient surface deforms elastically and absorbs the energy of fine particles, so it can outlast hard metals with fine, rounded particles. Used in dedicated slurry pump designs rather than standard split-case pumps.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Low structural strength; relies on the metal casing or support behind it. Integrity of the bond or mechanical retention to the backing is critical.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to many aqueous slurries, including many acidic ones. Natural rubber is attacked by oils, hydrocarbons, strong oxidisers and some solvents, so the compound must match the liquid.
materials.wearResistance: Good for low-angle, fine-particle abrasion.
materials.abrasionResistance: Excellent for fine particles; vulnerable to cutting and tearing by large, sharp or tramp particles, and to high tip speeds that cause heat build-up.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Limited to relatively low temperatures; heat build-up and ageing shorten life.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate; liners are consumables with reasonable replacement cost.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded and vulcanised; bonded liners require careful surface preparation and controlled bonding. Damaged liners are normally replaced rather than repaired.
advantages: Good resistance to many acidic slurries
limitations: Damaged by oversized or sharp particles
Attacked by oils and hydrocarbons
Temperature limited
Tip speed limited
Not normally used in standard split-case pumps
suitableService: Acidic slurries compatible with the compound
Flue gas desulphurisation slurries in dedicated designs
typicalUse: Impeller coverings in dedicated slurry pumps

materials.name: Wrought carbon steel
materials.description: Hot-rolled, cold-drawn or forged plain carbon steels, from low-carbon grades to medium-carbon grades that can be hardened. Used for shafts in non-corrosive service where sleeves protect the wetted length, and for keys, coupling hubs, levelling screws, anchor bolts and general fasteners.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate to good strength depending on carbon content and heat treatment; good fatigue performance when stress raisers such as keyways and shoulders are well designed and finished.
materials.corrosionResistance: Poor in water: rusts readily. Wetted shaft surfaces are normally protected by sealed sleeves, and external surfaces by coatings or lubricant films.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate; can be surface hardened (for example by induction hardening) where wear resistance is needed.
materials.abrasionResistance: Low to moderate.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Satisfactory over the temperature range of most water pumping duties; low-temperature toughness depends on grade.
materials.costConsiderations: Low and widely available.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Excellent machinability and availability as bar. Low-carbon grades weld easily; medium-carbon grades need preheat and controlled procedures. Normalising or quenching and tempering adjusts strength.
advantages: Adequate strength for many shafts and hubs
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance
Requires sleeves or coatings where wetted
Lower fatigue strength than alloy steels
Corrosion at keyways and journals reduces fatigue life
suitableService: Clean water where the shaft is fully sleeved

materials.name: Low-alloy steel (quenched and tempered)
materials.description: Steels with chromium and molybdenum and sometimes nickel additions (for example the 4140-type chromium-molybdenum family, given only as an illustration) that are hardened and tempered to high strength and toughness. Used for highly loaded shafts, casing joint studs and nuts, and coupling components.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High strength and fatigue resistance after quenching and tempering, with good toughness when the heat treatment is controlled.
materials.corrosionResistance: Similar to carbon steel; requires protection in wetted areas and in corrosive atmospheres. High hardness combined with hydrogen or sour (hydrogen sulphide) environments can cause environmental cracking, so hardness limits are specified for such service.
materials.wearResistance: Good when hardened; journals and seats can be surface hardened.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate when hardened.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Retains strength at moderately elevated temperatures better than carbon steel. Bolting grades for elevated temperature are specified by the relevant bolting standards.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate; higher than carbon steel because of alloying and heat treatment.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Good machinability in the annealed or quenched and tempered condition. Welding is difficult: preheat, low-hydrogen practice and post-weld heat treatment are needed, and weld repair of shafts is not normally accepted without OEM approval. Heat treatment response depends on section size.
advantages: Allows smaller shaft diameters for the same torque
limitations: Poor corrosion resistance
Difficult to weld or repair
Risk of hydrogen embrittlement and environmental cracking at high hardness
Requires controlled heat treatment
suitableService: Clean water duties with sleeved shafts
Casing bolting in most pump designs

materials.name: Martensitic and precipitation-hardening stainless steel
materials.description: Stainless steels with enough chromium to form a passive film and a composition balanced so that they can be hardened by heat treatment. The family includes straight-chromium grades (for example 410-type and 420-type), cast martensitic grades with nickel used for impellers, and precipitation-hardening grades. They offer higher strength and hardness than austenitic stainless steels at the expense of some corrosion resistance.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High strength and hardness after hardening and tempering, with good fatigue properties. Toughness depends strongly on the tempering treatment.
materials.corrosionResistance: Moderate: generally lower than austenitic grades, adequate for fresh water and many mild duties, but prone to pitting in chloride water. Highly hardened conditions are susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement and sulphide stress cracking, so hardness limits apply in sour service.
materials.wearResistance: Good. The hardened condition resists galling better than austenitic grades, so martensitic rings are used in wear-ring pairs with a specified hardness differential.
materials.abrasionResistance: Good when hardened; used for impellers, rings and sleeves in mildly abrasive water such as sandy river or bore water.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good strength retention at moderately elevated temperatures; suitable grades are used in hot water and condensate duties.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate; usually lower than austenitic or duplex grades of similar form.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Machinable in the annealed or tempered condition; hardened parts may need grinding. Welding requires preheat and post-weld heat treatment to avoid cracking. Heat treatment is essential and must be controlled to balance hardness, toughness and corrosion resistance.
advantages: Better galling resistance than austenitic grades
Good erosion and cavitation resistance in water
Well suited to shafts and sleeves
limitations: Lower corrosion resistance than austenitic grades
Pitting in chloride water
Hydrogen embrittlement and sulphide stress cracking at high hardness
Welding needs strict preheat and post-weld heat treatment
suitableService: Clean and mildly abrasive fresh water
Duties where shaft strength and moderate corrosion resistance are both needed

materials.name: Wrought austenitic stainless steel
materials.description: Rolled or forged chromium-nickel stainless steels, with or without molybdenum (for example the 304-type and 316-type families, given only as examples). Widely used for shafts, sleeves, wear rings, fasteners, springs and shims where corrosion resistance matters more than high strength.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength in the annealed condition with high ductility and toughness. Cannot be hardened by heat treatment; strength can only be raised by cold work. Lower strength than alloy or martensitic steels, which shaft design must take into account.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good general resistance in water and many chemicals; molybdenum-bearing grades have better pitting resistance. Susceptible to pitting and crevice corrosion in chlorides, particularly under gaskets and sleeves and in stagnant zones, and to chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperatures.
