materials.wearResistance: Poor in self-mated sliding. Stainless-on-stainless contact galls readily (adhesive transfer leading to seizure), which is critical for wear rings, sleeve nut threads and stainless fasteners.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Very wide temperature range, including low temperatures; stress corrosion cracking risk in chloride environments increases with temperature.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high; sensitive to nickel and molybdenum prices.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Good weldability. Machining is slower than for carbon steel because of work hardening. Solution treatment restores corrosion resistance after hot work where needed. Threaded stainless parts need anti-seize compounds to avoid galling during assembly.
advantages: Good corrosion resistance in water and many chemicals
Readily available as bar, plate, sheet and shim
limitations: Strong galling tendency in sliding contact with itself
Pitting and crevice corrosion in chlorides
Chloride stress corrosion cracking at elevated temperature
Lower strength than alloy or martensitic steels
Cannot be hardened by heat treatment
suitableService: Mild chemical service, subject to corrosion data
typicalUse: Wear rings paired with a dissimilar or harder ring
Fasteners, seal springs and gland plates

materials.name: Hardfacing overlays and hard coatings
materials.description: Wear-resistant surface layers applied to a tougher base metal. They include weld-deposited or laser-clad cobalt-chromium and nickel-based alloys and thermally sprayed coatings such as tungsten carbide-based cermets or chromium oxide ceramics. They put a hard surface where it is needed without making the whole part brittle.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Strength comes from the substrate; the layer itself is hard but has limited ductility. Bond strength and coating integrity are critical, and thick or brittle layers can crack or spall under impact, bending or thermal cycling.
materials.corrosionResistance: Depends on the overlay chemistry; cobalt-chromium and nickel-based alloys generally have good corrosion resistance. Sprayed coatings can contain porosity that lets corrosive liquid reach the substrate and undermine the coating unless the coating is sealed or otherwise suitable for the duty.
materials.wearResistance: Very good to excellent; used to resist galling, fretting and sliding wear on sleeves, wear rings and seal sleeves.
materials.abrasionResistance: Very good to excellent, depending on carbide or ceramic content.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Generally good. Differential thermal expansion between coating and substrate can cause cracking under thermal cycling.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high per part; often cost-effective because it extends the life of sleeves and rings.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Requires qualified application procedures, correct surface preparation and control of dilution (weld overlays) or porosity (sprayed coatings). Hard surfaces are usually finished by grinding rather than turning. Weld overlays can distort parts and may require stress relief. Rotating parts must be rebalanced after application. Use on shafts and pressure parts needs OEM approval.
advantages: Very high wear and abrasion resistance where needed
Can restore worn sleeves and rings where approved
Improves galling resistance at running clearances
limitations: Bond failure, cracking or spalling under impact or thermal shock
Porosity of sprayed coatings in corrosive service
Requires grinding to finish
Application quality is critical and difficult to inspect
Repairs on shafts and pressure parts need OEM approval

materials.name: Galling-resistant stainless alloys
materials.description: Nitrogen-strengthened austenitic stainless steels with raised manganese and silicon content, developed specifically for resistance to galling and wear in metal-to-metal sliding contact and often sold under proprietary names. They are used where stainless wear-ring pairs, bushings or sleeves would otherwise be at risk of seizure.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Higher strength than standard austenitic stainless steels because of nitrogen strengthening, with good ductility.
materials.corrosionResistance: Broadly in the range of common austenitic stainless steels in many waters, but performance varies by composition and must be confirmed against the specific fluid, especially in chloride service.
materials.wearResistance: Very good galling resistance compared with standard austenitic grades, including against itself and against other stainless steels.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good over a wide temperature range, with galling resistance retained at moderately elevated temperatures.
materials.costConsiderations: Higher than standard austenitic grades; usually limited to small parts such as rings and bushings.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Machinable with similar precautions to other austenitic stainless steels and weldable with suitable procedures. Usually supplied as bar or ring forgings. Property data must come from the alloy supplier because compositions differ.
advantages: Higher strength than standard austenitic grades
Good corrosion resistance in many waters
Reduces seizure risk at tight running clearances
limitations: Higher cost than standard stainless steel
Corrosion resistance must be confirmed for chloride service
Proprietary compositions vary, so supplier data is essential
Not a substitute for hard materials in abrasive service
suitableService: Clean and corrosive water where stainless rings are required
Duties with a risk of contact at running clearances
Start-up or transient conditions with marginal lubrication

materials.name: Engineered polymers and polymer composites
materials.description: High-performance thermoplastics and fibre-reinforced polymer composites, for example carbon-fibre-reinforced PEEK-type compounds and filled PTFE compounds. In pumps they are used mainly for stationary wear rings and bushings because they resist galling and seizure, and in some designs as composite coupling spacers or lantern rings.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Lower stiffness and strength than metals. Creep under sustained load and temperature must be considered, and rings must be positively retained by the design (interference fit and mechanical locking as specified by the OEM).
materials.corrosionResistance: Excellent in water and many chemicals; some compounds are affected by particular solvents, strong acids or oxidisers, so compatibility must be checked for the actual fluid.
materials.wearResistance: Good; non-galling against metal counterparts and tolerant of brief contact during start-up or transients.
materials.abrasionResistance: Limited to moderate; abrasive solids can wear polymer rings quickly.
materials.temperatureSuitability: More limited than metals. Thermal expansion is much higher than that of metals and fluid absorption may cause swelling, both of which change fits and clearances, so the ring design is temperature dependent.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high per part.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Machined from moulded stock; dimensional stability, fluid absorption and thermal expansion must be allowed for in the design. Not weldable; damaged parts are replaced.
advantages: Can allow reduced running clearances where the OEM permits
limitations: Temperature limits and high thermal expansion
Creep and retention must be designed for
Limited abrasion resistance
Chemical compatibility must be verified
Any clearance reduction must be OEM approved
suitableService: Duties where seizure risk is high
Upgrades carried out with OEM agreement
typicalUse: Composite coupling spacers in some designs

materials.name: Through-hardened bearing steel
materials.description: High-carbon chromium steels of very high cleanliness, through-hardened and tempered for rolling contact fatigue resistance, used for the rings and rolling elements of ball and roller bearings. Corrosion-resistant martensitic bearing steels and case-hardened steels are used in special designs. Cages may be pressed steel, machined brass or polymer, depending on bearing design.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very high hardness and rolling contact fatigue strength. Actual bearing life depends on lubrication, load, alignment, fits, temperature and contamination control rather than on the steel alone.
materials.corrosionResistance: Poor. Water in the lubricant or condensation in the housing causes corrosion pitting and early failure, so housing seals and lubricant condition are critical.
materials.wearResistance: Excellent under correct lubrication.
materials.abrasionResistance: Sensitive to particle contamination, which causes indentations and accelerated wear.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Suitable for normal bearing operating temperatures; special dimensional stabilisation is used for higher temperatures. In practice the lubricant and cage material usually set the limit.
materials.costConsiderations: Bearings are bought-in components; cost depends on bearing type, precision and design rather than on the steel alone.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Produced by specialist bearing manufacturers and not repaired in the field. Mounting requires the fits, heating methods and tools specified by the bearing manufacturer and the pump OEM.
advantages: Long fatigue life when correctly lubricated
limitations: Sensitive to water and particle contamination
Corrodes readily
Susceptible to electrical erosion from stray shaft currents, for example with variable speed drives
Easily damaged by incorrect mounting
suitableService: Rolling bearings in all pump services
Electric motor bearings, with insulated or hybrid designs where current passage is a risk

materials.name: Silicon nitride (bearing ceramic)
materials.description: A dense engineering ceramic used for the rolling elements of hybrid bearings (ceramic balls or rollers running in steel rings) in selected designs. It is lighter and harder than bearing steel and electrically insulating.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very hard and stiff with high compressive strength; lower fracture toughness than steel, so it is sensitive to impact and tensile stress concentrations.
materials.corrosionResistance: Excellent; the rolling elements do not corrode, although the steel rings still can.
materials.wearResistance: Excellent, and more tolerant of marginal lubrication than steel-on-steel contact.
materials.abrasionResistance: Good.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good high-temperature capability; bearing limits are usually set by the lubricant and the steel rings.
materials.costConsiderations: High compared with all-steel bearings.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Made by powder processing and sintering, then precision finished; supplied only as part of a complete bearing from the bearing manufacturer.
advantages: Electrically insulating, which protects against damage from current passage
Lower mass reduces centrifugal loads at speed
limitations: High cost
Lower toughness and sensitivity to impact
Different contact stiffness requires correct bearing selection
Availability may be limited in some sizes
suitableService: Drives with a risk of bearing current passage, such as variable speed drives
typicalUse: Motor bearings where electrical insulation is required

materials.name: Carbon-graphite (seal face grades)
materials.description: Mixtures of carbon and graphite that are pressed, baked and usually impregnated with resin or metal to close their porosity. Widely used as the softer face of a mechanical seal pair running against a hard face such as silicon carbide or tungsten carbide. Carbon is self-lubricating, conforms well and tolerates brief marginal lubrication better than hard-on-hard pairs.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Low strength and stiffness compared with ceramics and carbides; brittle, so it must be protected from impact, chipping and distortion.
materials.corrosionResistance: Carbon itself resists most chemicals. The impregnant (resin or metal) governs compatibility with some solvents, strong oxidisers and alkaline media, and may also affect approvals for drinking water.
materials.wearResistance: Good as the soft face of a pair when a stable fluid film exists.
materials.abrasionResistance: Poor. Abrasive particles embed in or erode carbon faces, so carbon is avoided in solids-laden liquids unless clean flushing keeps solids away from the faces.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Stable over a wide temperature range; oxidising atmospheres at high temperature attack carbon, and resin impregnants have their own limits.
materials.costConsiderations: Low to moderate.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded, machined and lapped flat; faces must be handled, stored and installed carefully to avoid chipping and contamination.
advantages: Self-lubricating; tolerant of brief marginal lubrication
Good conformability to the mating face
limitations: Poor abrasion resistance
Brittle and easily chipped
Impregnant may limit chemical compatibility
Blistering can occur in some conditions, for example with viscous liquids
suitableService: Clean water and many clean liquids
Hot water in suitable seal designs
typicalUse: Mechanical seal rotating or stationary face

materials.name: Silicon carbide
materials.description: A very hard ceramic seal face material with high thermal conductivity. The main types are reaction-bonded silicon carbide, which contains free silicon, and sintered silicon carbide, which does not and therefore has broader chemical resistance. It runs against carbon in clean liquids, or against itself or tungsten carbide where abrasives are present.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very hard and stiff but brittle, with low fracture toughness; sensitive to mechanical impact and, in some grades, to thermal shock.
materials.corrosionResistance: Excellent. Sintered grades resist most acids and alkalis; reaction-bonded grades can be attacked by strong alkalis and some acids because of their free silicon phase.
materials.wearResistance: Excellent.
materials.abrasionResistance: Excellent; preferred in solids-laden service, usually as part of a hard-vs-hard pair with suitable flushing.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Very good; high thermal conductivity helps carry frictional heat away from the seal faces.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high, depending on grade.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Produced by sintering or reaction bonding, then diamond ground and lapped. Faces can sometimes be relapped within the seal manufacturer limits but cannot otherwise be repaired.
advantages: Very high hardness and abrasion resistance
Broad chemical resistance in sintered grades
limitations: Brittle; sensitive to impact and thermal shock
Hard-vs-hard pairs are very sensitive to dry running and marginal lubrication
Reaction-bonded grades are limited in strong alkalis and some acids
Requires careful handling
suitableService: Abrasive or solids-laden liquids as a hard-vs-hard pair with flushing
typicalUse: Sleeves and bushings in product-lubricated bearings

materials.name: Cemented tungsten carbide
materials.description: Tungsten carbide particles held in a metallic binder, typically cobalt or nickel. Very hard and tougher than ceramics, it is used as a seal face material where abrasive solids or high pressures are present and as a thermally sprayed coating. Nickel-bound grades are generally preferred in corrosive water because cobalt binder can be leached out.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Very hard with higher fracture toughness than silicon carbide; high stiffness and density help faces resist distortion.
materials.corrosionResistance: Governed by the binder. The binder can be attacked in acidic or corrosive media, leaving unsupported carbide grains (binder leaching); nickel-bound grades are more corrosion resistant than cobalt-bound grades.
materials.wearResistance: Excellent.
materials.abrasionResistance: Excellent.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good, though thermal conductivity is lower than silicon carbide; heat checking (surface cracking) can occur under poor lubrication.
materials.costConsiderations: High; heavier and generally more expensive than silicon carbide.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Powder metallurgy: pressed, sintered, then ground and lapped. Faces can be relapped within the seal manufacturer limits.
limitations: Binder leaching in corrosive media
High cost and density
Heat checking and dry-running sensitivity in hard-vs-hard pairs
Lower thermal conductivity than silicon carbide
typicalUse: Thermally sprayed coatings on sleeves and rings

materials.name: Nitrile rubber (NBR)
materials.description: Acrylonitrile-butadiene elastomer: a general-purpose O-ring and secondary seal material with good resistance to mineral oils, greases and water at moderate temperatures. Hydrogenated nitrile (HNBR) is a related family with improved heat and ozone resistance.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good tensile strength, tear resistance and compression set for a general-purpose elastomer.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good with mineral oils, aliphatic hydrocarbons and water at moderate temperatures. Poor resistance to ozone and weathering, ketones, esters, aromatic and chlorinated solvents, strong acids and oxidisers, and it may degrade over time in chlorinated or chloraminated water.
materials.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
materials.abrasionResistance: Good for an elastomer.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Moderate; not suitable for hotter water or steam. Low-temperature flexibility depends on the acrylonitrile content of the compound.
materials.costConsiderations: Low.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded and easily compounded. Store away from ozone sources such as electric motors and from sunlight; observe shelf-life guidance from the supplier.
advantages: Good resistance to mineral oils and greases
limitations: Poor ozone and weathering resistance
Limited temperature range
Poor with ketones, esters and aromatic or chlorinated solvents
Limited with oxidisers and some disinfectants

materials.name: Ethylene propylene diene rubber (EPDM)
materials.description: An elastomer with excellent resistance to water, steam, glycols, ozone and weathering and to many dilute acids and alkalis. Widely used for secondary seals in water services, including potable water where an approved compound is selected.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good general mechanical properties and compression set; peroxide-cured compounds have better heat resistance.
materials.corrosionResistance: Excellent with hot water, steam, glycols, ozone and many dilute acids and alkalis. Not compatible with mineral oils, hydrocarbon fuels, petroleum-based greases or many solvents, which cause severe swelling; water, a soap solution or a lubricant approved by the seal supplier should be used during assembly instead of mineral grease.
materials.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate to good for an elastomer.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Good; suitable for hot water and steam within the limits of the specific compound.
materials.costConsiderations: Low.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded. Drinking-water approvals are specific to the compound, not to EPDM in general, and must be confirmed for each part.
advantages: Good resistance to many dilute acids and alkalis
limitations: Swells severely in mineral oils and hydrocarbons
Must not be assembled with petroleum-based greases
Unsuitable for many solvents
Oil contamination of the pumped water can damage seals

materials.name: Fluorocarbon rubber (FKM)
materials.description: A fluoroelastomer with broad resistance to hydrocarbons, oils, fuels and many acids and chemicals, including at elevated temperatures. Several types exist with different fluorine contents and cure systems, which change both chemical and temperature behaviour, so the grade must be specified, not just the family.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good; typically firmer than NBR and EPDM, with reduced flexibility at low temperatures.
materials.corrosionResistance: Excellent resistance to mineral oils, fuels, aromatic hydrocarbons and many acids. Resistance to hot water and steam is limited depending on grade and cure system (some types swell or harden), and resistance to ketones, low-molecular-weight esters, amines and strong alkalis is poor.
materials.wearResistance: Good for an elastomer.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
materials.temperatureSuitability: High temperature capability in air and oils; reduced flexibility at low temperatures. Limits in hot water and steam depend on the grade.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate to high compared with NBR and EPDM.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded; grade selection is critical and should be confirmed with the seal or elastomer supplier.
limitations: Limited in hot water and steam depending on grade
Poor with ketones, amines and some esters
Poor low-temperature flexibility
More expensive than NBR and EPDM
suitableService: Many corrosive chemicals, subject to compatibility data
Water at moderate temperature in suitable grades
typicalUse: Bearing housing lip seals for higher temperatures

materials.name: Perfluoroelastomer (FFKM)
materials.description: A fully fluorinated elastomer with the widest chemical resistance of the elastomer families, approaching that of PTFE while retaining elasticity. Used where no other elastomer is compatible or where chemistry varies widely.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate; some grades show higher compression set and lower resilience than other elastomers, and low-temperature flexibility is limited.
materials.corrosionResistance: Very wide chemical resistance, including many acids, alkalis, solvents and oxidisers. Specific grades still have limitations in particular media, such as hot water, steam or amines, so the grade must be checked against the actual fluid.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate for an elastomer.
materials.temperatureSuitability: High temperature capability in many media; limited at low temperatures.
materials.costConsiderations: Very high; usually justified only where other elastomers are not compatible.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Specialist manufacture with long lead times; parts must be handled carefully. Higher thermal expansion may require groove dimensions specified by the seal manufacturer.
advantages: Widest chemical resistance of the elastomers
One material can cover mixed or variable chemistry
Long life in aggressive service when correctly selected
limitations: Very high cost
Grade-specific chemical limitations still exist
Limited low-temperature flexibility
May need modified groove designs
typicalUse: O-rings and secondary seals in chemical service

materials.name: PTFE (polytetrafluoroethylene)
materials.description: A fluoropolymer that is chemically inert to almost all chemicals and has very low friction. Used in virgin, filled (for example glass, carbon or graphite) or expanded form for gaskets, secondary seal wedges and V-rings, encapsulated O-rings, packing yarns and lantern rings. It is not an elastomer and has little elastic recovery.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Low strength and stiffness. PTFE creeps and cold-flows under sustained load, so gaskets can lose bolt load; fillers and expanded structures are used to reduce this.
materials.corrosionResistance: Essentially inert to almost all chemicals; only a few highly reactive substances, such as molten alkali metals and elemental fluorine, attack it.
materials.wearResistance: Very low friction; virgin PTFE wears quickly, and fillers improve wear resistance.
materials.abrasionResistance: Poor in virgin form, improved by fillers.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Wide range from very low to elevated temperatures; creep increases with temperature.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Sintered and machined, or skived into sheet; it cannot be moulded like an elastomer. Expanded PTFE is produced by stretching, which improves conformability and creep resistance.
advantages: Approved forms available for food and drinking-water duties
limitations: Creep and cold flow under load
Little elastic recovery
Poor abrasion resistance in virgin form
Higher thermal expansion than metals

materials.name: Compressed non-asbestos fibre (CNAF) sheet
materials.description: Gasket sheet made from fibres (for example aramid, glass, carbon or mineral fibres) and fillers bound with an elastomer binder such as NBR and compressed into sheet. It replaced former asbestos-based sheets in water and general services and is often used for split-case casing joint gaskets cut to the joint shape.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good crush resistance over a useful sealing stress range. Performance depends on thickness, bolt load and flange stiffness; thinner gaskets generally relax less under load.
materials.corrosionResistance: Depends on fibre and binder. Generally good in water, oils and many mild chemicals; limited in strong acids, strong alkalis and some solvents.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Moderate. The safe envelope is defined by the combination of pressure, temperature and thickness in the gasket manufacturer data; the binder ages at elevated temperature and in steam.
materials.costConsiderations: Low.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Cut from sheet. For split-case joints the OEM specifies gasket material and thickness, because thickness affects the relative position of the casing halves, bore roundness and the clamping of wear rings and seal housings. Gaskets are not reused.
advantages: Low cost and easily cut to shape
Good sealing in water and oils
limitations: Pressure, temperature and thickness limits must be respected
Binder degrades at high temperature and in steam
Limited resistance to strong chemicals
Incorrect thickness alters internal fits in split-case pumps
suitableService: General industrial service at low to moderate pressure

materials.name: Spiral wound gaskets
materials.description: Semi-metallic gaskets made by winding a preformed metal strip (often stainless steel) together with a soft filler such as flexible graphite, PTFE or a mineral-based material, usually with an outer centring ring and often an inner ring. Used on circular bolted flanges at higher pressures and temperatures or where blow-out resistance is required.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High resilience and blow-out resistance; needs adequate bolt load and a suitable flange surface finish.
materials.corrosionResistance: Depends on the winding metal and filler, both of which must be compatible with the fluid.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material; it is a static seal.
materials.temperatureSuitability: High; limited by the filler and winding metal selected.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Manufactured to suit standard flange dimensions; not normally used on the irregular split joint of a casing. Must be handled carefully to avoid damaging or unwinding the spiral.
limitations: Needs high bolt load and stiff flanges
Unsuitable for irregular split-joint shapes
Easily damaged by poor handling
Single use
suitableService: Higher pressure or temperature nozzle flanges
typicalUse: Seal gland plate gaskets in some designs

materials.name: Flexible (exfoliated) graphite
materials.description: Expanded graphite formed into sheet, tape or rings. Used for gaskets (often with a metal reinforcing insert), as the filler of spiral wound gaskets, and as die-formed packing rings or braided graphite packing.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Low strength on its own; reinforced sheets add handling strength. Conforms well to flange surfaces and shows low stress relaxation.
materials.corrosionResistance: Wide chemical resistance except to strongly oxidising media. In the presence of an electrolyte it can promote galvanic corrosion of some metals, and low-impurity grades are used against stainless steel.
materials.wearResistance: Self-lubricating when used as packing.
materials.abrasionResistance: Limited; abrasive solids damage graphite packing.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Very wide temperature range in inert or non-oxidising conditions; oxidises in air at high temperature.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Unreinforced sheet is fragile; reinforced variants are easier to cut and handle. Die-formed packing rings must be sized to the stuffing box.
limitations: Oxidises in air at high temperature
Attacked by strong oxidisers
Can promote galvanic corrosion of some metals
Fragile and easily damaged in handling

materials.name: Braided compression packing
materials.description: Square-section braided rings made from yarns impregnated with lubricants and blocking agents and compressed in the stuffing box by the gland follower. Yarn families include PTFE (virgin or graphite-filled), expanded graphite, carbon and graphite fibres, aramid, acrylic and other synthetic fibres, glass fibre, and traditional vegetable fibres such as cotton or flax for low-duty water. Packing needs a small, controlled leakage to lubricate and cool its contact with the sleeve.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Varies by yarn: aramid is strong and abrasion resistant but can wear sleeves; PTFE is soft and conformable; carbon and graphite conduct heat well.
materials.corrosionResistance: Depends on yarn and impregnant. PTFE and graphite have broad chemical resistance, aramid and acrylic are more limited, and vegetable fibres are limited to water.
materials.wearResistance: Packing wears and consolidates gradually and needs periodic gland adjustment.
materials.abrasionResistance: Aramid and some blends tolerate abrasives better, but solids in the stuffing box rapidly wear packing and sleeves unless clean flush water is supplied through the lantern ring.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Depends on the yarn; carbon and graphite tolerate higher temperatures. Heat generated at the sleeve must be removed by leakage or flush.
materials.costConsiderations: Low per ring; adjustment labour, leakage and sleeve wear add to lifecycle cost.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Cut to length on a mandrel or supplied as die-formed rings; joints are staggered and rings are installed and seated one at a time, following the OEM and packing manufacturer instructions.
limitations: Requires continuous controlled leakage
Causes sleeve wear
Needs periodic adjustment
Higher friction power loss than mechanical seals
Leakage may be unacceptable for hazardous liquids
suitableService: Abrasive water when a clean flush is provided
typicalUse: Stuffing box packing rings at both shaft exits

materials.name: Coupling elastomers
materials.description: Flexible elements of jaw, tyre, pin-and-bush and similar couplings, made from rubbers (natural rubber, polychloroprene, NBR), polyurethanes or thermoplastic polyester elastomers. They transmit torque while accommodating small misalignments and damping torsional vibration and shock.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Lower torque capacity for a given size than all-metal designs; elements degrade by fatigue, heat and misalignment.
materials.corrosionResistance: Depends on compound: some rubbers are attacked by oil, ozone or ultraviolet light, and some polyurethanes can degrade by hydrolysis in hot, humid conditions.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate; rapid wear or debris under the guard usually indicates misalignment or overload.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not relevant in normal service.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Limited; heat build-up from misalignment accelerates degradation.
materials.costConsiderations: Low; elements are consumables.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Moulded; replaced rather than repaired.
limitations: Temperature and chemical sensitivity
Ageing from ozone, ultraviolet light and oils
Not a substitute for correct alignment
Some designs are not fail-safe if the element fails
suitableService: General pump and motor drives within the coupling rating
Drives that benefit from torsional damping or shock absorption
Installations where the element compound suits the ambient temperature and any oil or ozone exposure

materials.name: Structural steel (fabricated)
materials.description: Weldable rolled sections and plate used to fabricate baseplates, motor pedestals, coupling guards and pipe supports.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Adequate strength; for a baseplate the stiffness of the fabricated and grouted structure matters more than material strength for keeping alignment.
materials.corrosionResistance: Poor without protection; requires a paint system or galvanising, especially in wet pump rooms. Surfaces to be grouted need preparation or primer compatible with the grout manufacturer instructions.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Ambient conditions of pump rooms and outdoor installations.
materials.costConsiderations: Low material cost; fabrication and machining dominate.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Good weldability, but welding causes distortion; stress relief before final machining of mounting pads may be specified. Pads are machined coplanar. Grout fill holes, vent holes and lifting points are provided in the design.
advantages: Flexible design for any pump and motor combination
limitations: Requires corrosion protection
Welding distortion must be controlled
Lower damping than cast iron
Relies on correct grouting to achieve stiffness

materials.name: Reinforced concrete
materials.description: Concrete with embedded steel reinforcement, used for the foundation block that supports the grouted baseplate. It provides mass and stiffness, resists vibration and transmits loads to the ground or structure.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High compressive strength but low tensile strength; reinforcement carries tension and controls cracking.
materials.corrosionResistance: Durable in normal pump room conditions. Prolonged oil contamination softens concrete, and chlorides or carbonation can corrode reinforcement.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Ambient conditions; must be protected from freezing during curing.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate; part of the civil works.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Designed by a qualified civil or structural engineer using the OEM loading data. Must be adequately cured before grouting and loading; the top surface laitance is removed by chipping to sound concrete before grouting. Anchor bolt sleeves or pockets are set during construction. Isolation from surrounding structures may be specified to limit vibration transmission.
advantages: Damps vibration transmitted to the building
limitations: Long curing time before loading
Degraded by long-term oil contamination
Cracking if poorly reinforced or cured
Difficult to modify after construction
suitableService: Indoor and outdoor installations with suitable concrete cover and drainage

materials.name: Epoxy grout
materials.description: A resin and hardener system filled with graded aggregate, poured between the baseplate and the foundation. It bonds the baseplate to the foundation so that the two act as one stiff unit, and is widely used for machinery baseplates in industrial plants.
materials.mechanicalStrength: High compressive and tensile strength compared with cementitious grout, and good bond to properly prepared steel and concrete. Its thermal expansion is higher than that of concrete, and creep at elevated temperature must be considered.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good resistance to oils, water and many chemicals.
materials.wearResistance: Good surface abrasion resistance.
materials.abrasionResistance: Good surface abrasion resistance.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Placement and cure are temperature sensitive. Service temperature limits are set by the grout manufacturer; strength reduces and creep increases at elevated temperature.
materials.costConsiderations: Higher material cost than cementitious grout and requires trained installers.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Mixing ratio, pot life, pour depth and ambient conditions follow the grout manufacturer instructions. The cure is exothermic, so thick pours can crack unless poured in layers or with expansion joints. Concrete and steel surfaces must be clean, dry and prepared; formwork is waxed or lined; the baseplate primer must be compatible with the grout.
advantages: High strength and bond to steel
Resistant to oils and many chemicals
Low shrinkage and relatively fast strength gain
Improves baseplate stiffness when voids are avoided
limitations: Higher cost
Exothermic cure and pour depth limits
Temperature-sensitive placement
Higher thermal expansion than concrete
Requires dry, clean, prepared surfaces
suitableService: Areas exposed to oil or chemical spillage
Machinery where baseplate stiffness is critical

materials.name: Cementitious (non-shrink) grout
materials.description: A Portland cement-based grout with additives that compensate for shrinkage and give a flowable consistency. A traditional and economical alternative to epoxy grout, common in water and wastewater pump stations.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Good compressive strength; lower tensile strength and much lower bond to steel than epoxy grout.
materials.corrosionResistance: Attacked over time by oils and acids; adequate in clean, dry pump rooms.
materials.wearResistance: Moderate.
materials.abrasionResistance: Moderate.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Tolerant of normal ambient temperatures; must be protected from freezing and from rapid drying during curing.
materials.costConsiderations: Lower material cost than epoxy grout and familiar to civil contractors.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: The concrete surface is usually pre-soaked to a saturated surface-dry condition before placement. Mixed with the specified water quantity, placed continuously and moist-cured as the manufacturer instructs. Excess water causes bleeding, shrinkage and voids.
limitations: Lower bond to steel
Lower resistance to oils and chemicals
Requires moist curing before loading
Sensitive to excess mixing water
suitableService: General industry with low oil exposure

materials.name: Electrical (lamination) steel
materials.description: Silicon-alloyed steel sheet with an insulating surface coating, stacked into laminated stator and rotor cores. The laminations carry magnetic flux while limiting eddy current losses.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Adequate for stacked cores; mechanical stress, burrs and damage from rubbing increase core losses and can cause local hot spots.
materials.corrosionResistance: The insulating coating gives some protection, but exposed edges rust in damp conditions or during poor storage.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material; rotor-to-stator contact damages laminations.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Motor temperature limits are set by the winding insulation class rather than by the core steel.
materials.costConsiderations: Part of the motor cost; higher-grade low-loss steels improve efficiency at higher cost.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Punched or laser cut, stacked and sometimes annealed to restore magnetic properties. Core damage generally needs specialist motor repair.
limitations: Lamination damage increases losses and creates hot spots
Corrosion during damp storage
Repair requires specialist motor workshops
suitableService: Motors started direct on line or fed from variable speed drives

materials.name: Copper (electrical conductor)
materials.description: High-conductivity copper used for enamelled stator windings, connections and, in some motors, rotor bars and end rings.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength and high ductility; conductors are supported by insulation, slot wedges and bracing.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good in normal environments; insulation integrity, not copper corrosion, is usually the limiting factor. Moisture and contamination degrade winding insulation.
materials.wearResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.abrasionResistance: Not a wear material in this application.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Governed by the insulation class of the winding system.
materials.costConsiderations: Significant part of motor cost and sensitive to copper prices.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Drawn, enamelled and wound; rewinding is carried out by specialist motor repair workshops.
limitations: Cost
Insulation can be damaged by moisture, heat and voltage stress
Heavier than aluminium

materials.name: Aluminium alloys
materials.description: Light alloys used for die-cast squirrel-cage rotor windings in induction motors, frames and end shields of smaller motors, cooling fans, terminal boxes, and in some designs coupling spacers or guards.
materials.mechanicalStrength: Moderate strength with low density; lower stiffness than steel.
materials.corrosionResistance: Good in normal atmospheres because of its natural oxide film; galvanic corrosion can occur when coupled to steel or copper in wet conditions, and some alloys are attacked in marine or alkaline environments.
materials.wearResistance: Low; soft against steel.
materials.abrasionResistance: Low.
materials.temperatureSuitability: Normal motor operating temperatures; strength reduces at elevated temperatures.
materials.costConsiderations: Moderate; lower weight reduces handling and shipping cost.
materials.manufacturingConsiderations: Excellent die-castability and machinability. In potentially explosive atmospheres, light alloys may be restricted for exposed parts because of sparking risks, so hazardous-area requirements must be checked.
limitations: Lower strength and stiffness than steel
Galvanic corrosion with dissimilar metals
May be restricted in hazardous areas
Soft; prone to damage by impact
suitableService: Motor rotors, frames and end shields
Light drive parts such as coupling spacers where hazardous-area rules permit

componentMaterials.label: Upper and lower casing
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The casing is the main pressure-containing part, so its material must meet the pressure-temperature rating, hydrostatic test and code requirements as well as resisting corrosion and erosion. Grey cast iron is common for clean water at moderate pressure; ductile iron gives much better toughness against water hammer, nozzle loads and handling impact; cast carbon steel is used where higher pressure or temperature, weldability or hazardous liquids require it; austenitic, duplex and super duplex stainless castings are used for corrosive, high-purity or chloride-bearing water, and aluminium bronze is used in some seawater designs. Both halves are normally made of the same material and machined together at the split joint and bores. Iron casings may be internally coated for water service. Final selection depends on fluid chemistry, temperature, solids content, pressure, velocity, OEM and material-supplier specifications and the applicable standards.

componentMaterials.label: Impeller
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The impeller sees the highest relative velocities in the pump, so erosion, cavitation and corrosion resistance govern, together with castability of the vane passages and the ability to be dynamically balanced. Bronze alloys are traditional for clean water and seawater; cast iron is a low-cost option in clean water but erodes and corrodes faster; austenitic and martensitic stainless grades improve erosion and cavitation resistance; duplex and super duplex grades are used in chloride-bearing or more aggressive water. The impeller is usually specified as equal to or more noble than the casing so that it is not the corroding anode of a galvanic couple. Copper alloy velocity limits must be respected. Impellers that are trimmed, repaired or hardfaced must be rebalanced to the OEM requirement.

componentMaterials.label: Shaft
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The shaft transmits torque and carries the impeller and bearing loads, so fatigue strength, stiffness and notch sensitivity at keyways, threads and shoulders are key. In clean water, carbon or alloy steel shafts are common, protected from the liquid by sealed sleeves and sleeve nuts. Martensitic and precipitation-hardening stainless grades combine strength with moderate corrosion resistance; austenitic or duplex stainless shafts are used where the shaft may be wetted by corrosive liquid. A lower-strength material may need a larger diameter for the same duty, which is an OEM design decision. Weld repair or metal spraying of journals and seats generally needs OEM approval because it can reduce fatigue life.

componentMaterials.label: Shaft sleeve
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Sleeves protect the shaft from the liquid and, with gland packing, from wear at the packing contact. Stainless grades are usual; under packing, a hard surface such as hardened martensitic stainless or a hardfaced or ceramic-coated zone reduces grooving. Sleeve and sleeve nut threads can gall if both are austenitic stainless, so dissimilar materials or anti-seize compounds are used as the OEM specifies. The sleeve-to-shaft joint is sealed (for example with an O-ring or gasket) so that liquid cannot reach the shaft, which also prevents crevice corrosion under the sleeve. The sleeve material must also be compatible with the seal or packing selected.

componentMaterials.label: Casing wear rings
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The stationary ring forms the running clearance with the impeller wear ring and limits internal leakage from discharge back to suction. The ring pair must resist galling if contact occurs; common approaches are bronze against stainless steel, a hardness differential between two stainless or martensitic rings as required by the applicable pump standard or the OEM, galling-resistant stainless alloys, or hardfaced surfaces. Engineered polymer composite rings are used in some designs for seizure resistance and, only where the OEM permits, reduced clearance. Clearance values must come from the OEM manual, not from material tables. Thermal expansion of the chosen materials affects the running clearance at operating temperature.

componentMaterials.label: Impeller wear rings
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The rotating ring is fitted to the impeller hub by the OEM method (for example interference fit with locking), or the impeller may have integral wear surfaces. It must form a galling-resistant pair with the casing ring and should be galvanically compatible with the impeller. Replaceable rings allow clearance to be restored without replacing the impeller. Hard or hardfaced rotating rings are used in abrasive water. Rotating and stationary rings are normally replaced together so that the clearance specified by the OEM is restored. Polymer materials are generally used for the stationary ring rather than the rotating ring.

componentMaterials.label: Bearing housing
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Bearing housings locate the bearings, hold the lubricant and carry the housing seals. Grey cast iron offers good damping, machinability and low cost; ductile iron is chosen for higher toughness or where the specification excludes grey iron. Bore accuracy and dimensional stability matter more than strength. Housings are outside the pumped liquid, so the main concerns are the external atmosphere, water spray from packing leakage and contamination of the lubricant.

componentMaterials.label: Bearing elements
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Rolling bearings are bought-in components; through-hardened bearing steel is standard. Hybrid bearings with silicon nitride rolling elements are used in selected designs, for example to resist damage from electrical current passage with variable speed drives or to tolerate marginal lubrication. Bearing type, arrangement, internal clearance class and cage material follow the pump OEM specification. Water ingress, particle contamination and incorrect mounting are the main threats regardless of material.

componentMaterials.label: Mechanical seal faces
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: One face rotates with the shaft and the other is stationary; together they must run on a very thin liquid film. Carbon-graphite against silicon carbide or tungsten carbide is a common pairing for clean liquids because carbon tolerates brief marginal lubrication and conforms well. In abrasive service, hard-vs-hard pairs (silicon carbide against silicon carbide or tungsten carbide) are used with suitable flushing, but they are more sensitive to dry running and can be damaged quickly if the film is lost. Compatibility of the carbon impregnant, the silicon carbide type and the carbide binder must be checked against the liquid. Seal selection, including arrangement and flush plan, should follow the seal manufacturer and the applicable seal standard.

componentMaterials.label: Secondary seals
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: O-rings, bellows and wedges in the mechanical seal must be compatible with the pumped liquid, any flush or barrier fluid, cleaning chemicals and the temperature. NBR suits mineral oils and cold to warm water but is poor with ozone and many chemicals; EPDM suits water, steam and glycols but swells in mineral oils and greases; FKM suits many hydrocarbons and chemicals but some grades are limited in hot water and steam; FFKM covers very wide chemistry at high cost; PTFE is used where elastomers are not compatible but has little elasticity. Compatibility charts are only a starting point and must be confirmed with the seal or elastomer supplier for the actual fluid, concentration and temperature. Assembly lubricants must also be compatible with the elastomer.

componentMaterials.label: Gaskets
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The casing joint gasket is usually cut from sheet (for example CNAF) to the material and thickness specified by the OEM. Changing material or thickness can alter internal fits, wear-ring and seal housing clamping and bore alignment in a split-case pump, and some designs use a metal-to-metal joint with a sealant or O-ring instead of a gasket. Bearing housing gaskets see low pressure. PTFE-based gaskets suit corrosive service; spiral wound gaskets are used at circular flanged connections in higher pressure or temperature service; flexible graphite suits high temperatures and many chemicals. Gasket choice must suit pressure, temperature, fluid, bolt load and flange finish, and gaskets are not reused.

componentMaterials.label: Coupling
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Coupling hubs are usually steel, cast iron or ductile iron, keyed or interference fitted to the shafts; spacers are steel or, in some designs, aluminium alloy or fibre-reinforced composite. Flexible elements are either elastomeric (rubber, polyurethane or polyester elastomer) or metallic disc packs, often stainless steel. The coupling type and size are selected for torque, speed, misalignment capacity, service factor and environment; a flexible coupling is not a substitute for accurate alignment. Guards are usually sheet steel or mesh; in potentially explosive atmospheres the coupling and guard materials must satisfy the hazardous-area requirements, which may restrict light alloys and some non-metallic materials.

componentMaterials.label: Baseplate
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The baseplate keeps the pump and motor in alignment; stiffness and the flatness and coplanarity of the mounting pads matter more than material strength. Fabricated structural steel is the most common construction; cast iron baseplates appear in some smaller or standardised designs. Pads are machined after fabrication, sometimes after stress relief. Shims are normally stainless steel so that corrosion does not change alignment over time; levelling screws are steel. Surfaces in contact with grout need preparation compatible with the grout manufacturer instructions.

componentMaterials.label: Gland packing
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Packing yarn is chosen for the liquid, temperature, shaft surface speed and presence of solids: PTFE-based yarns for chemical resistance, carbon and graphite yarns for heat dissipation and higher temperatures, aramid and blends for abrasive service (with attention to sleeve wear), and traditional fibres only for low-duty water. Lantern rings, often bronze, stainless steel or PTFE, distribute flush water; gland followers are commonly cast or ductile iron, bronze or stainless steel. A suitably hard sleeve surface and a small controlled leakage are essential. In abrasive service, clean flush water at a pressure above the stuffing box pressure keeps solids out of the packing. Ring size, number and installation follow the OEM and packing manufacturer instructions.

componentMaterials.label: Grout and foundation
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: The reinforced concrete foundation provides mass and stiffness and must be designed by a qualified civil or structural engineer using the OEM loading data. Grout fills the space between baseplate and foundation, transfers load and stiffens the baseplate. Epoxy grout offers high strength, good bond to prepared steel, oil and chemical resistance and low shrinkage, but costs more, has an exothermic cure, is temperature sensitive during placement and has pour depth limits set by its manufacturer. Cementitious non-shrink grout costs less and is familiar to civil contractors but has lower bond to steel and lower oil and chemical resistance, and needs moist curing. Anchor bolts are typically carbon steel, often set in sleeves to allow small adjustments. The concrete must be cured and its surface prepared by removing laitance before grouting.

componentMaterials.label: Casing bolting
componentMaterials.selectionNotes: Casing joint studs and nuts clamp the split joint against internal pressure and gasket reaction. Quenched and tempered alloy steel is the usual choice for strength; carbon steel may be used in lower-duty designs; austenitic or duplex stainless bolting is used where external corrosion, for example seawater spray, requires it, taking account of the lower strength of some grades and the galling tendency of stainless threads. Bolting grade, coating, lubricant, tightening method and sequence must follow the OEM manual, because thread lubricant and coating change the preload achieved at a given torque. Dowel pins locate the two halves and must be refitted correctly.

serviceExamples.title: Clean water service: municipal, cooling water and general industrial water
serviceExamples.summary: Municipal supply, cooling water and general industrial water are the classic duties of horizontal split case pumps. The water is usually clean and near neutral, but it is never chemically inert: hardness, chlorides, dissolved oxygen, residual disinfectant and occasional sand all influence material life. Iron casings with bronze or stainless internals are common, well-proven combinations. The combinations below are examples only; final selection depends on the water analysis, temperature, solids content, pressure, velocity, OEM and material-supplier specifications, the applicable standards and any drinking-water regulations.

factors.explanation: Hardness, alkalinity, pH, chlorides, dissolved oxygen and conductivity determine whether iron and copper alloys corrode slowly or rapidly and whether stainless steels are at risk of pitting. A water analysis should be obtained rather than assuming that water is clean.
Chlorine, chloramine and other disinfectants can increase corrosion of some metals and degrade some elastomers over time, which affects secondary seal, gasket and coating selection.
Materials in contact with potable water, including coatings, elastomers, lubricants and lead-containing copper alloys, often require national approvals or certification.

High peripheral speeds, high local velocities or operation with a small NPSH margin increase erosion-corrosion and cavitation damage. Cast iron and tin bronze are less tolerant than stainless steels or aluminium bronze.
River intakes and raw water may carry sand intermittently, accelerating wear at wear rings, sleeves under packing and impeller inlet edges.
Duty and standby pumps that stand idle full of water can suffer tuberculation of iron, crevice corrosion of stainless steel and microbiologically influenced corrosion.

Combining iron casings with bronze or stainless internals is usually acceptable because the large iron area acts as the anode, but increased corrosion of the iron next to the more noble parts should be expected and inspected.
Initial cost, expected life, spares availability and retention of efficiency as wear-ring clearances open up should be compared over the life of the asset, not only purchase price.

options: grey-cast-iron
ductile-iron
combinations.rationale: Economical, readily cast and adequate in clean near-neutral water; ductile iron is chosen where higher toughness against water hammer, nozzle loads or handling is needed. Internal coatings may be applied for potable or more aggressive water.

options: tin-bronze
austenitic-stainless-cast
ductile-iron
combinations.rationale: Bronze is the traditional choice for corrosion resistance in water; cast stainless offers better erosion and cavitation resistance; iron impellers are lower in cost but wear and corrode faster.

options: carbon-steel
alloy-steel
martensitic-stainless
combinations.rationale: Carbon or alloy steel shafts are acceptable when the wetted length is fully covered by sealed sleeves; martensitic stainless adds corrosion margin where the shaft may be exposed.

options: austenitic-stainless-wrought
martensitic-stainless
hardfaced-overlay
combinations.rationale: Stainless sleeves protect the shaft from the water; with gland packing, hardened or hard-coated sleeves reduce grooving at the packing contact.

options: tin-bronze
austenitic-stainless-wrought
galling-resistant-stainless
combinations.rationale: Bronze against stainless steel, or stainless pairs with a hardness differential or a galling-resistant alloy, reduce the risk of seizure if the rings touch during start-up or transients.

options: carbon-graphite
silicon-carbide
combinations.rationale: Carbon against silicon carbide is a common clean-water pairing: carbon tolerates brief marginal lubrication and conforms well, while silicon carbide conducts frictional heat away from the faces.

options: epdm
nbr
combinations.rationale: EPDM suits water and many disinfectants and is available in drinking-water approved compounds; NBR is used where contact with mineral oil is possible. Compatibility with the disinfectant and assembly lubricants should be confirmed.

options: braided-packing
ptfe
combinations.rationale: PTFE-based or graphite-PTFE yarns with clean flush water through the lantern ring are common in water service; a small controlled leakage is required for cooling and lubrication.

options: cnaf
combinations.rationale: CNAF sheet cut to the OEM specified thickness is common; the thickness affects internal fits and must not be changed without OEM agreement.

cautions: Clean water is not chemically inert; obtain a water analysis before confirming materials.
Lead-containing copper alloys may not be acceptable for drinking water; check national regulations and approvals for all wetted materials, coatings and lubricants.
Do not use mineral-oil-based grease on EPDM components during assembly; use a lubricant approved by the seal supplier.
Mechanical seals must not run dry during priming or venting; carbon tolerates brief marginal lubrication but not sustained dry running.
Stainless-on-stainless contact at wear rings and sleeve nut threads can gall; follow the OEM material pairing and anti-seize recommendations.

These are typical examples, not specifications. No combination is universally acceptable; final selection depends on fluid chemistry, temperature, solids content, pressure, velocity, OEM and material-supplier specifications and the applicable standards.

serviceExamples.title: Corrosive service: seawater, brackish water and chemical solutions
serviceExamples.summary: Corrosive service covers seawater and brackish water, chloride-bearing process water, acidic or alkaline solutions and liquids containing oxidisers. Selection is driven by the specific corrosion mechanisms that the fluid can cause rather than by a single ranking of alloys, and the whole wetted assembly, including fasteners, elastomers and gaskets, must be assessed together. Selection should be based on the fluid analysis, corrosion data, service experience or testing, the recommendations of the material supplier and the OEM, and the applicable standards.

factors.explanation: Chlorides drive pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking in stainless steels. Progressively more highly alloyed grades (molybdenum-bearing austenitic, duplex, super duplex) are considered as chloride content and temperature rise. PREN is a useful comparative index for ranking alloys but does not guarantee performance in a particular fluid.

Acidic liquids dissolve protective films and attack iron, copper alloys and some carbide binders; alkaline liquids attack some ceramics (such as reaction-bonded silicon carbide), aluminium and some elastomers. Material behaviour can change sharply across the pH range.

factors.factor: Dissolved chemicals, oxidisers and dissolved oxygen
factors.explanation: Chlorine, hypochlorite and other oxidisers raise the pitting risk of stainless steels; reducing acids behave differently, so each chemistry needs its own assessment. Dissolved oxygen accelerates corrosion of iron and copper alloys, while stainless steels need oxygen to maintain their passive film and are most at risk in oxygen-depleted crevices.

Corrosion rates usually increase with temperature, and the onset of pitting, crevice corrosion and stress corrosion cracking depends on temperature, so a material that performs well cold may fail in warm or hot service.

Copper alloys have velocity limits above which erosion-corrosion accelerates sharply. Stainless steels generally benefit from flowing conditions and are more at risk in stagnant liquid. Very high local velocities near the impeller inlet and volute tongue can still damage any material.

Dissimilar metals in electrical contact in a conductive liquid cause the less noble metal to corrode faster. A small anode coupled to a large cathode, for example a small steel or iron part inside a stainless or bronze assembly, is particularly harmful; critical small parts such as impellers, rings and fasteners should be equal to or more noble than the surrounding material.

Gasket faces, wear-ring fits, sleeve-to-shaft interfaces, impeller bores and the internals of idle standby pumps create oxygen-depleted zones where crevice corrosion starts. Design details, sealing of crevices and operating practice (draining or periodic running) matter as much as alloy choice.

O-rings, bellows, gaskets, packing and coatings must be compatible with the fluid, its concentration, the temperature and any cleaning or flushing chemicals. Swelling, hardening or chemical attack of a secondary seal can cause seal failure even when the metals are fully resistant.

options: austenitic-stainless-cast
duplex-stainless
super-duplex-stainless
aluminium-bronze
combinations.rationale: Selected progressively as chloride content, temperature and oxidiser levels increase. Aluminium bronze is an established seawater option within its velocity limits and with grade and heat treatment chosen to resist selective phase corrosion.

options: duplex-stainless
super-duplex-stainless
austenitic-stainless-cast
aluminium-bronze
combinations.rationale: The impeller is normally equal to or more noble than the casing so that it is not the corroding member of a galvanic couple; duplex grades also provide good erosion-corrosion resistance at the high velocities the impeller experiences.

options: duplex-stainless
super-duplex-stainless
austenitic-stainless-wrought
combinations.rationale: The high strength of duplex grades suits shafts; austenitic shafts may need a larger diameter. Where the shaft is fully sleeved and sealed, a less highly alloyed shaft may be acceptable subject to OEM approval.

options: duplex-stainless
super-duplex-stainless
hardfaced-overlay
combinations.rationale: Sleeves are wetted and contain crevices at the seal and shaft interfaces, so they are often specified in an alloy at least as resistant as the casing; coatings must be suitable for corrosive service and free of through-porosity.

options: galling-resistant-stainless
duplex-stainless
engineered-polymer-composite
aluminium-bronze
combinations.rationale: Ring pairs must resist both corrosion and galling; galling-resistant alloys, hardness differentials or polymer composite stationary rings are used, with corrosion resistance confirmed for the actual fluid.

options: silicon-carbide
carbon-graphite
tungsten-carbide
combinations.rationale: Sintered silicon carbide is widely used for its broad chemical resistance; carbon faces need an impregnant compatible with the fluid; nickel-bound tungsten carbide is preferred over cobalt-bound grades where binder leaching is a risk.

options: fkm
ffkm
epdm
ptfe
combinations.rationale: Chosen for the specific chemistry and temperature: EPDM for many aqueous solutions and seawater, FKM for many acids and hydrocarbons, FFKM for very aggressive or mixed chemistry, and PTFE where no elastomer is compatible.

options: ptfe
flexible-graphite
spiral-wound
combinations.rationale: PTFE-based gaskets for broad chemical resistance; flexible graphite for higher temperatures except in oxidising media, using low-impurity grades against stainless steel; spiral wound gaskets with compatible winding and filler at circular flanges.

options: duplex-stainless
austenitic-stainless-wrought
alloy-steel
combinations.rationale: External corrosion from seawater spray or chemical atmospheres may require stainless or duplex bolting; coated alloy steel bolting is also used. Strength, galling and the effect of lubricants and coatings on preload must be considered.

cautions: A more highly alloyed or more expensive material is not automatically better for every fluid; alloys that perform well in chlorides may perform poorly in certain acids, and the reverse.
PREN values and published compatibility charts are screening tools only; confirm suitability with material-supplier corrosion data, service experience or testing.
Avoid unfavourable galvanic couples, especially small less noble parts within a large noble assembly; match materials or insulate where needed.
Drain, flush or periodically run standby pumps so that stagnant liquid does not promote crevice and pitting corrosion.
Weld repairs of stainless, duplex and aluminium bronze castings require qualified procedures and, where specified, post-weld heat treatment and testing.

No combination is universally acceptable; final selection depends on fluid chemistry, temperature, solids content, pressure, velocity, OEM and material-supplier specifications and the applicable standards.

serviceExamples.title: Abrasive service: sandy water, suspended solids and light slurries
serviceExamples.summary: Abrasive service covers raw water carrying sand, mine water, process water with suspended solids and light slurries. Wear is concentrated where velocity and particle impingement are highest, and life is extended by hard or hardened materials, hard seal faces with clean flushing, and replaceable wear parts. A standard split-case pump can handle water with modest solids when suitably specified, but dedicated slurry pump designs, with thick hard-metal or rubber-lined wetted parts and features for wear adjustment and replacement, are often preferred for heavy, coarse or high-concentration slurries. Final selection depends on particle characteristics, concentration, fluid chemistry, temperature, pressure, velocity and OEM and material-supplier specifications.

factors.explanation: Hard, angular and coarse particles cause much faster wear than soft, rounded or fine particles. The hardness of the particles relative to the wear surface is critical: a surface softer than the solids wears rapidly.
Wear increases with solids concentration. Heavy slurries also change pump performance and are often outside the intended scope of a standard split-case design.

Wear rate rises steeply with local velocity, so peripheral speed and the operating point strongly influence life. Operation well away from the best efficiency point increases recirculation and local velocities, accelerating wear.

Impeller inlet edges and vane tips, wear-ring clearances, the volute tongue, side walls and the stuffing boxes wear first. Designs with replaceable rings, sleeves and liners allow performance to be restored at lower cost.

Hard, brittle materials resist sliding abrasion but can crack under impact from large particles or tramp material; resilient elastomer linings resist fine-particle erosion but are cut by sharp or large solids.
Corrosive slurries continually remove protective surface films, so the combined wear rate can exceed that of either mechanism alone; the material must resist both.

Solids reaching seal faces or packing destroy them quickly. Hard seal faces, an appropriate flush plan with a clean external flush where necessary, and seal chamber design that keeps solids away from the faces are required.
Wear-ring and other internal clearances increase as wear proceeds, reducing head and efficiency. Performance monitoring helps plan replacement of wear parts before efficiency loss becomes costly.

options: martensitic-stainless
duplex-stainless
high-chrome-white-iron
hardfaced-overlay
combinations.rationale: Hardened martensitic stainless and duplex grades improve erosion resistance in sandy water; high-chrome white iron gives the highest abrasion resistance but is mainly found in dedicated slurry pumps; hardfacing or hard coatings can protect local high-wear zones where the OEM approves.

options: ductile-iron
cast-carbon-steel
high-chrome-white-iron
natural-rubber-liner
combinations.rationale: Ductile iron or steel casings may be given additional wear allowance or replaceable liners; hard-metal or rubber liners are typical of dedicated slurry designs rather than standard split-case pumps.

options: martensitic-stainless
hardfaced-overlay
combinations.rationale: Hardened or hardfaced replaceable rings slow clearance growth; rings are replaced as matched sets to restore the OEM clearance.

options: hardfaced-overlay
martensitic-stainless
combinations.rationale: Hard coatings such as tungsten carbide-based or ceramic coatings, or hardened stainless sleeves, resist grooving under packing and in seal areas exposed to solids.

options: silicon-carbide
tungsten-carbide
combinations.rationale: Hard-vs-hard pairs (silicon carbide against silicon carbide or tungsten carbide) resist abrasion, but must be combined with a suitable flush plan, often a clean external flush, and must never run dry.

options: epdm
fkm
nbr
combinations.rationale: Chosen by fluid chemistry and temperature; flushing keeps solids away from dynamic O-rings, where packed solids can prevent the seal face from following shaft movement.

options: braided-packing
ptfe
flexible-graphite
combinations.rationale: Abrasion-tolerant yarn blends with clean flush water injected through the lantern ring keep solids out of the packing; hard-surfaced sleeves are needed to limit sleeve wear.

cautions: For heavy, coarse or high-concentration slurries a dedicated slurry pump design is usually preferred to a standard split-case pump.
Very hard materials such as high-chrome white iron and hard coatings are brittle, difficult to machine and generally not weld repairable; handle and install them with care.
Hard-vs-hard seal faces are very sensitive to dry running and loss of flush; monitor or interlock the flush supply where appropriate.
Operating away from the best efficiency point increases recirculation and local velocities, accelerating wear.
Rebalance impellers after hardfacing or repair, and replace wear rings as matched sets to the OEM clearance.

No combination is universally acceptable; final selection depends on particle size, hardness and concentration, fluid chemistry, temperature, pressure, velocity and OEM and material-supplier specifications.

standards.fullTitle: Technical specifications for centrifugal pumps — Class II
standards.edition: 2002 edition, published 2002-03-14. It replaced ISO 5199:1986, which is withdrawn. No amendment was found in the ISO catalogue data checked. Adopted in Europe as EN ISO 5199:2002.
standards.status: Published (current). The ISO catalogue data show the systematic review at stage 90.60 "Close of review", dated 2023-06-05. No revision project was found.
standards.technicalScope:
ISO 5199 sets Class II technical requirements for centrifugal pumps for general application. That covers single-stage and multistage pumps, horizontal and vertical, with any type of drive and any installation arrangement. It was written with chemical-process pumps (for example those built to ISO 2858 dimensions) as typical examples, but it is not limited to them.

It deals with the design features that affect installation, maintenance and safe operation of the pump unit, including the baseplate, the coupling and the auxiliary piping. It also covers materials, shop inspection and testing, and the information that passes between purchaser and supplier, including a pump data sheet. The driver is outside its scope except for its rated power output. A supplier may offer a pump that does not meet every requirement, as long as each deviation is declared in the offer.
standards.applicability:
For a general-industry horizontal split case pump (water, cooling water, process water, general services), ISO 5199 is a common international reference when the purchaser wants a defined Class II level of mechanical quality without calling up API 610. It applies to a between-bearings, axially split, double-suction pump in the same way as to other centrifugal configurations. Its requirements are organised by function (pressure-containing parts, shaft and bearings, shaft sealing, coupling, baseplate, inspection, testing and documentation), not by casing type.

In this module it is the reference for general Class II expectations in the casing, shaft, bearing, sealing, coupling and baseplate topics. Hydraulic acceptance testing is normally specified separately, for example to ISO 9906.
standards.limitations:
Being a split case pump does not make a pump compliant with ISO 5199, and neither does a mention of the standard in a catalogue. Conformance has to be written into the purchase specification. The data sheet must be completed, the supplier must declare any deviations and the purchaser must accept them, and compliance must be shown through the documents, inspections and tests the order requires.

ISO 5199 is a Class II specification. For more severe services, such as petroleum, petrochemical or natural gas process duty, the purchaser may require API 610 or ISO 13709 instead. This module only summarises the purpose of the standard. It does not reproduce its requirements, values or text, which are copyright of ISO, so always work from the purchased current edition.
standards.verificationNote: Checked online on 2026-11-06, but not on iso.org itself: iso.org returned HTTP 403 to automated access. The reference, title, publication date (2002-03-14), owner committee (ISO/TC 115/SC 1), withdrawn predecessor and review stage come from ISO catalogue records (ISO project 31945) republished by two ISO national members, the Institute for Standardization of Montenegro and the General Directorate of Standardization of Albania. A search-engine index of iso.org confirmed the page title and URL. Those records show no confirm/revise decision after the review closed in June 2023. Open the iso.org page in a browser before publication to confirm the status and check whether a revision has started.

standards.fullTitle: Rotodynamic pumps — Hydraulic performance acceptance tests — Grades 1, 2 and 3
standards.edition: 2012 edition, published 2012-04-26. It replaced ISO 9906:1999 (now withdrawn), which covered Grades 1 and 2 only. No amendment was found in the ISO catalogue data checked. Adopted in Europe as EN ISO 9906:2012.
standards.status: Published (current). The ISO catalogue data show the systematic review at stage 90.60 "Close of review", dated 2022-12-03. No revision project was found.
standards.technicalScope:
ISO 9906 defines the hydraulic performance tests used when a customer accepts a rotodynamic pump (centrifugal, mixed-flow or axial) of any size. The test liquid must behave like clean cold water. The tests are meant to be run at a pump test facility, such as the manufacturer's works or an independent laboratory. They can be run on the bare pump or with some or all of its inlet and outlet fittings in place.

The standard covers which quantities are measured (flow rate, pump total head, power input and efficiency, and NPSH), the measurement methods and their uncertainty, the test arrangements, and how test results are converted to the guarantee conditions. It defines three acceptance grades: Grade 1 has the narrowest tolerances and Grade 3 the widest. Sub-grades with letter suffixes (B, E, U) set how the tolerance band is applied around the guarantee point.
standards.applicability:
For a horizontal split case pump, ISO 9906 is the international reference for the factory performance test. The test shows that the pump meets its guaranteed duty point (flow and head), its power and efficiency, and, if specified, its NPSH3 at the agreed flows. The purchaser selects the acceptance grade in the specification. A tighter grade means tighter tolerances and more demanding instrumentation. Large split case pumps can exceed the capacity of the test bed. In that case, reduced-speed testing or another arrangement, and the method for converting the results, must be agreed before the order is placed.

In this module it supports the hydraulic performance, NPSH and acceptance testing topics, alongside ANSI/HI 14.6 for North American practice.
standards.limitations:
Passing an ISO 9906 test shows that the pump met the agreed hydraulic guarantees on a test stand with clean cold water. It does not show mechanical integrity, vibration, or seal and bearing behaviour. It also does not show performance in the installed system, where inlet conditions and fluid properties are different. Field tests are generally less accurate than shop tests and cannot directly replace them. The standard does not apply automatically: the order must state the grade, guarantee points, witness requirements and test procedure.

Tolerance values, formulae and tables are not reproduced here. Use the purchased current edition, which is copyright of ISO.
