standards.verificationNote: Checked online on 2026-11-06, but not on iso.org itself: iso.org returned HTTP 403 to automated access. The reference, title, publication date (2012-04-26), owner committee (ISO/TC 115/SC 2), withdrawn predecessor (ISO 9906:1999) and review stage come from ISO catalogue records (ISO project 41202) republished by the Institute for Standardization of Montenegro. The Standards Council of Canada and AFNOR listings agree. Those records show no confirm/revise decision after the review closed in December 2022. Open the iso.org page in a browser before publication to confirm the status.

standards.fullTitle: Rotodynamic Pumps for Hydraulic Performance Acceptance Tests
standards.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 14.6-2016, and HI's version history also lists earlier editions (2011, 2000).
standards.status: Current. The Hydraulic Institute product page marks it as the current version and mentions no newer edition or revision in progress.
standards.technicalScope: HI 14.6 sets out how rotodynamic pumps (centrifugal, mixed-flow and axial-flow) are tested and accepted. It covers four test types: hydraulic performance, NPSH, hydrostatic pressure and mechanical integrity. It also covers instrumentation, test arrangements and procedures, and the acceptance criteria for the results. Acceptance uses three grade levels with different tolerance bands and measurement-accuracy demands. The grade structure parallels the one in ISO 9906.
standards.applicability:
HI 14.6 is used for factory acceptance testing of horizontal split case pumps when the purchase specification calls up HI standards, which is typical of North American water, HVAC, power and general-industry projects. Besides hydraulic performance and NPSH, it gives the method for hydrostatic testing of the pressure-containing casing halves and for mechanical integrity (running) tests. That makes it the reference for what a test witness should expect to see. The grade, the test types, the basis for the NPSH test and the witness points must all be specified.

In this module it supports the performance, NPSH, hydrostatic test and acceptance testing topics. Purchasers normally specify either HI 14.6 or ISO 9906 for the hydraulic test, not both, so the order must say which.
standards.limitations: A pump has only been tested to HI 14.6 if the test was ordered, carried out and reported to the standard at the agreed grade. A catalogue curve is not an acceptance test. Shop tests use clean cold water and the test stand's own piping, so installed performance can be different. HI standards are copyright publications. This module only paraphrases their purpose and does not reproduce tolerances, tables or text.
standards.verificationNote: Verified on 2026-11-06 on the Hydraulic Institute product page (pumps.org). The page marks this as the current version, says it supersedes the 2016 edition, and HI's standards listing shows 2022 for this title. The HI page gives no ANSI approval date, and the ANSI Webstore returned HTTP 403, so that date is not verified. The statement that the grade structure parallels ISO 9906 is based on HI's published descriptions. Check it, and any changes made in 2022, against the purchased edition.

standards.edition: 2022 edition. It supersedes ANSI/HI 9.6.6-2016; the earlier edition was 2009.
standards.status: Current. The Hydraulic Institute product page marks it as the current version.
standards.technicalScope:
HI 9.6.6 covers the piping immediately upstream and downstream of rotodynamic pumps and how that piping affects pump performance and reliability. On the inlet side it deals with pipe size and velocity, swirl generated by the piping, minimum straight pipe lengths after fittings that disturb the flow, and suction elbows, including their orientation at double-suction pumps. It also says when a physical model study or CFD is appropriate. On the outlet side it covers piping, valves and water hammer. For both sides it covers pipe-to-nozzle alignment and nozzle loads, pipe supports, anchors and expansion joints, and parallel operation. A final part explains how to assess and fix existing piping that does not conform.

It does not cover piping that discharges into tanks, vessels or intake structures. Intake design is covered by ANSI/HI 9.8.
standards.applicability:
HI 9.6.6 matters directly for a horizontal split case pump, because a double-suction impeller is sensitive to uneven inlet flow. The HI guidance, including its figures for between-bearings split case pumps, deals with a classic mistake: an elbow close to the suction flange lying in a plane parallel to the shaft. That elbow sends more flow to one impeller eye than the other. The result is unbalanced hydraulic axial thrust and a higher risk of noise, vibration and cavitation.

The standard is also the reference for keeping pipe loads off the casing flanges. Pipe strain can distort the split casing and pull the pump out of alignment with its driver. In this module it supports the suction and discharge piping, installation, unequal flow distribution and pipe strain topics. Where the pump manufacturer's instructions are more restrictive, they take precedence.
standards.limitations: Following the principles of the standard does not guarantee good pump inlet conditions on every site. Unusual layouts may need a model study or a review by the manufacturer. Straight-length numbers and other requirements depend on the fitting type, the pump type and the suction energy, so read them from the purchased current edition. This module gives no numeric values and reproduces no HI text. Conformance only applies where a project specification calls up the standard and the as-built piping is checked against it.
standards.verificationNote: Verified on 2026-11-06 in two places on the HI site. The product page (pumps.org) marks it as the current version and says it supersedes the 2016 edition. HI's public table of contents (pumps.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/9.6.6-Table-of-Contents.pdf, copyright 1997–2022) confirms the 2022 content outline, including the figures on elbows at double-suction pumps. The exact approval or publication date is not on the HI page. A reseller gives a 2022 publication date and the same ISBN, but HI has not confirmed the date.

standards.organisation: AWWA (American Water Works Association) — American National Standard
standards.fullTitle: Horizontal Centrifugal and Vertical Line Shaft Pumps
standards.edition: 2021 edition (E103-21). It revises E103-15, which was titled "Horizontal and Vertical Line-Shaft Pumps" in reseller listings. That in turn revised the first edition, E103-07, approved by the AWWA Board of Directors in June 2007.
standards.status: Appears to be current. The AWWA store and ANSI Webstore listings, as indexed by a search engine, show it as the latest edition, and resellers list E103-15 as superseded by it. This could not be confirmed on a readable AWWA page.
standards.technicalScope: AWWA E103 sets minimum requirements for horizontal centrifugal pumps and vertical line-shaft pumps installed in water utility service: wells, water treatment plants, and water transmission and distribution systems. It is a purchasing standard. It sets baseline requirements for the pump and relies on the purchaser to state the duty and to choose among the options it allows.
standards.applicability: AWWA E103 is relevant to horizontal split case pumps in water utility service, such as raw water, treated water transmission, booster and distribution pumping. North American utility specifications commonly call up AWWA standards. In this module it gives the water-utility context: what a utility purchaser typically specifies and expects to check. It applies only when the utility's specification calls it up.
standards.limitations: A split case pump does not comply with AWWA E103 just because of its type. The purchaser has to call up the standard and provide the information it asks for. The manufacturer then has to meet and document each requirement that applies. E103 sets minimum requirements, and project specifications commonly add more. Other standards and regulations may govern contact with drinking water, the motor and the controls. No AWWA text is reproduced here, and the scope summary above does not come from reading the standard itself.
standards.verificationNote: NOT VERIFIED against a readable AWWA page. The AWWA store pages (store.awwa.org) load their content in the browser, so the fetch tool received no content, and the ANSI Webstore returned HTTP 403. The edition (E103-21) and title come from the store.awwa.org listing as indexed by a search engine (SKU 45103-2021). Reseller listings mark ANSI/AWWA E103:2021 as current and the 2015 edition as superseded. Reseller dates differ (October 2021 in one record, a 2022 publication date in another). The scope summary comes from the descriptions on those listings, not from the standard. Before publication, check the exact title (the 2021 title shows no hyphen in "Line Shaft"), approval date, status and scope in the AWWA store and in the standard's foreword.

standards.organisation: API (American Petroleum Institute); ISO for ISO 13709
standards.fullTitle: Centrifugal Pumps for Petroleum, Petrochemical, and Natural Gas Industries (API Std 610); Centrifugal pumps for petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industries (ISO 13709)
standards.edition: API Std 610 Thirteenth Edition, June 2026, superseding the Twelfth Edition (January 2021). ISO 13709:2009 (second edition) is identical only to API 610 Eleventh Edition (2010). The 12th and 13th Editions are API-only documents and are not identical to ISO 13709.
standards.status: API Std 610 13th Edition is reported as current: BSI Knowledge lists API STD 610:2026 as current, published 2026-06-29. ISO 13709:2009 is published, and the ISO catalogue data show it reconfirmed (stage 90.93) on 2026-10-08.
standards.technicalScope:
API 610 specifies requirements for centrifugal pumps used in petroleum, petrochemical and natural gas industry process services, including pumps run in reverse as hydraulic power recovery turbines. It classifies pumps by configuration: overhung (OH), between-bearings (BB) and vertically suspended (VS). A single-stage, axially split, between-bearings pump is the BB1 type. The standard sets requirements for design, pressure casings, rotors and rotordynamics, and for bearings and lubrication. It covers shaft sealing, with mechanical seals generally specified to API 682, as well as couplings, baseplates and auxiliary piping. It also covers materials, inspection and testing (including performance, NPSH and vibration acceptance), data sheets and documentation.

According to trade press (not the standard itself), the 13th Edition revises rotordynamics, casing pressure rating and joint bolting, seal chamber dimensions, NPSH reference points and margin, auxiliary piping connections, coupling sizing and baseplate requirements.
standards.applicability:
API 610 applies to a horizontal split case pump only when the purchaser's specification or the service requires it. Typical cases are refinery, petrochemical, gas processing, pipeline and offshore duties, and other hazardous, high-temperature or high-pressure services. General water, HVAC and utility split case pumps are normally specified to ISO 5199, AWWA E103 or the manufacturer's standard design instead. Where API 610 is called up, the pump is a BB1 design and must meet API's heavier-duty requirements for the casing, rotor, bearings, sealing, baseplate, testing and documentation, as set out on the API data sheet.

In this module API 610 is cited for comparison, to show what a more demanding specification adds. It is not a requirement for the generic pump that is modelled.
standards.limitations: An axially split double-suction pump is not an API 610 pump because of its configuration. Compliance requires the specification to call up a stated edition, the data sheets to be completed, exceptions to be listed and agreed, and compliance to be demonstrated by inspection, test and documentation. The specification must also state which document applies, because API 610 13th Edition and ISO 13709:2009 are no longer technically identical. Projects still working to the 11th or 12th Edition must say so. Requirements change between editions, so do not assume that a clause in one edition exists in another. No API or ISO text is reproduced here.
standards.verificationNote: NOT VERIFIED against the issuing organisation. The API Webstore (apiwebstore.org) loads its product data in the browser and returned only an empty product template, so the URL above must be confirmed in a browser. The Accuris store listing for API publications returned HTTP 403. Two sources confirm the 13th Edition (June 2026): BSI Knowledge (API STD 610:2026, current, published 29 June 2026) and a Hydrocarbon Processing news item (17 August 2026). One reseller gives 1 June 2026, so check the exact date with API. The ISO 13709:2009 status comes from ISO catalogue records (ISO project 41612; ISO page https://www.iso.org/standard/41612.html) republished by ISO national members: reconfirmed 2026-10-08, owner committee shown as ISO/TC 115/SC 3. One training site cites an "ISO 13709:2024". The ISO catalogue data do not support that edition, so do not cite it. The list of 13th Edition changes comes from trade press only.

sources.title: Improving Pumping System Performance: A Sourcebook for Industry, Second Edition (May 2006)
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy (Office of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy), in cooperation with the Hydraulic Institute
sources.usedFor: Pumping system basics: system curves and the operating point, best efficiency point, effects of oversizing and throttling, flow control and variable speed, energy and life-cycle cost, and common pumping-system problems and their symptoms. Full text is also hosted at https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2014/05/f16/pump.pdf.

sources.title: Pumping Systems Tip Sheet #6: Match Pumps to System Requirements (October 2005)
sources.publisher: U.S. Department of Energy, Industrial Technologies Program
sources.usedFor: Energy context for the hydraulics and troubleshooting topics: operating far from BEP, oversized and throttled pumps, imbalance between the system and the pump, and impeller trimming or replacement as corrective measures.

sources.title: The Basics of NPSH & Pump Operating Regions
sources.usedFor: Definitions of NPSHA, NPSHR and NPSH3, the meaning of NPSH margin, and preferred and allowable operating regions (POR/AOR). Explains why more margin is needed away from BEP. Points to ANSI/HI 9.6.1 (NPSH margin) and ANSI/HI 9.6.3 (operating regions).

sources.title: Reliability Basics: Understanding NPSH, POR, and AOR
sources.usedFor: Cavitation mechanism and impeller damage, BEP as the practical reference for the shock-free inlet flow, reasons to run inside the POR, and why the AOR limits must be confirmed with the pump supplier. Used for the cavitation, low-flow and operating-point topics.

sources.title: ANSI/HI 9.6.6 Rotodynamic Pumps for Pump Piping — published table of contents (2022 edition)
sources.usedFor: Scope of the HI piping guidance (straight lengths, swirl, suction elbows, nozzle loads, supports and anchors, expansion joints, water hammer), including the figures on elbow orientation at between-bearings double-suction split case pumps. Also confirms the 2022 edition outline cited in STANDARDS.

sources.title: Piping requirements for rotodynamic pumps: an overview of the updated ANSI/HI 9.6.6 standard (P. Gaydon, Hydraulic Institute)
sources.publisher: Processing Magazine (article by Hydraulic Institute technical staff), 10 August 2016
sources.usedFor: Why uniform inlet flow matters, an elbow mounted directly on the suction flange as a poor arrangement, pipe supports and restraint, and the effects of excessive nozzle loads (casing distortion, coupling misalignment, bearing heating, seal or packing failure). It describes the 2016 edition, which the 2022 edition has superseded, so use it for principles only.

sources.title: Axially split design (KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon)
sources.usedFor: Definition of an axially (horizontally) split casing divided along the shaft centreline, compared with radially split designs. Used for the overview and casing topics.

sources.title: Double-entry impeller (KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon)
sources.usedFor: Double-entry (double-suction) impeller with an inlet on both sides, and its purpose in reducing axial thrust and NPSHR. Used for the impeller and working-principle topics.

sources.title: Axial thrust (KSB Centrifugal Pump Lexicon)
sources.usedFor: Sources of axial thrust on a pump rotor, balancing by a double-entry impeller, and residual thrust at low-flow and overload conditions that a thrust (locating) bearing must carry. Used for the axial thrust lesson and the residual-thrust caution.

sources.title: LS Horizontal split case pump — Installation and operating instructions
sources.usedFor: Typical OEM practice for a horizontal split case pump. Covers receiving and storage, foundation, base frame and grouting, piping and inlet pipe guidelines (eccentric reducers, elbows, pipe strain), soft foot, prestart checks, priming, start-up and final alignment. Also covers stuffing box/packing and mechanical shaft seal notes, operating checks, maintenance, and fault finding (no flow, low pressure, high power, vibration, cavitation noise, bearing overheating). Used for the installation, commissioning, checklist and troubleshooting topics. Values in the manual are model-specific and are not reproduced.

sources.title: Wilo Mather and Platt Horizontal Split Case Pumps — Installation and operating instructions (HSC_20131001_03)
sources.publisher: Wilo Mather and Platt Pumps Pvt. Ltd. (Wilo group)
sources.usedFor: A second OEM view of split case practice. Covers lifting (including lifting points for the top casing only), storage, grouting, alignment, the sealing system (gland packing and mechanical seal), a pre-commissioning checklist, filling and venting, start-up, dismantling and reassembly, wear rings, and troubleshooting. Used for the procedure, sealing and commissioning topics. Values in the manual are model-specific and are not reproduced.

sources.title: Technical Insight: Choosing the Right Bearing and Arrangement — a step-by-step guide
sources.usedFor: Locating/non-locating bearing arrangements: the locating bearing fixes the shaft axially and carries axial load, while the non-locating bearing carries radial load and lets the shaft grow axially with temperature. Also covers paired angular-contact (back-to-back and face-to-face) arrangements and the effect of shaft temperature on clearance. Used for the drive-end and non-drive-end bearing and thrust bearing topics.

sources.title: BURGMANN ABC lexicon — Mechanical seal
sources.usedFor: How a mechanical seal works: rotating and stationary seal faces, secondary seals on the shaft and housing sides, spring loading, and the thin lubricating film between the faces. Used for the mechanical seal component and sealing topics.

sources.title: API Piping Plan Guide for Mechanical Seals
sources.usedFor: Controlling the seal environment: flush, recirculation, quench and barrier/buffer piping plans, and why seal life depends on conditions at the seal faces. Used for the seal flush / auxiliary piping and mechanical-seal-failure topics.

procedures.title: Upper casing removal
procedures.intro:
This procedure takes the pump from service to an open casing, with the upper half set down on a prepared laydown area. In this arrangement the suction and discharge nozzles are cast in the lower half, so the upper half can be lifted without disturbing the main suction and discharge piping, the lower half or the rotor.

The sequence shown is a generic, illustrative one for training. Not every manufacturer designs or handles the casing joint identically: the number and type of fasteners, the use of dowels and jacking screws, gasketed or metal-to-metal joints, and the way the seal glands and stuffing box halves are released all vary between designs. The OEM manual and the site-approved procedure govern every step.
procedures.oemNote: Illustrative sequence only. The fastener loosening sequence, jacking arrangement, lifting points, rigging method and component weights are design specific. Always follow the OEM manual, the site permit-to-work system and the approved lifting plan. Where the OEM instructions differ from this training sequence, the OEM instructions apply.

steps.title: Confirm isolation and the safe maintenance condition
tools: Permit to work and isolation certificate
Personal lock, tag and hasp (lock-out / tag-out kit)
Approved voltage indicator and proving unit (authorised electrical personnel only)
Personal protective equipment as identified in the risk assessment
steps.purpose: Make sure the pump cannot start, rotate, be pressurised or release hazardous liquid while people work on it. The motor is electrically isolated and locked off, the suction and discharge isolation valves are closed and secured, and the absence of energy is verified before any fastener is touched.
inspectionPoints: The permit covers the exact pump tag number and the work scope (casing opening and lifting), together with any hot-work or restricted-area requirements.
The motor main supply is isolated at the designated isolation point, and locked and tagged by every person working on the pump as the site rules require.
Separate supplies are also isolated where fitted: motor anti-condensation heaters, auxiliary lubrication or seal support systems, and remote or automatic start circuits.
A start attempt from the local and remote controls (try-out) is made in line with the site procedure, and the controls are returned to off.
Suction and discharge isolation valves are closed, locked or chained, and tagged; bypass, minimum-flow or warm-up lines that could pressurise the casing are also isolated.
The shaft is stationary. A passing check valve can let reverse flow drive the rotor backwards, so the discharge isolation must be positive.
The liquid and casing temperature is safe to work on, and the safety data sheet for the pumped liquid has been reviewed.
commonMistakes: Isolating only the control circuit (stop button or control fuse) instead of the main power supply.
Forgetting separate heater, instrument or auxiliary supplies on the motor and the seal support system.
Relying on a check valve as a means of isolation.
Assuming that another crew has already locked off the pump.
Starting work on a hot or recently stopped pump without allowing it to cool.
safety: No work starts without a valid permit and verified isolation.
Electrical isolation and voltage verification are carried out only by authorised personnel.
Treat every system as live and pressurised until it has been proven otherwise.
Where a variable-speed drive is fitted, follow the drive manufacturer and site rules for stored electrical energy before any work on the motor circuit.

steps.title: Isolate and depressurise the casing
tools: Installed or temporary calibrated pressure gauges
Spanners for vent valves and plugs
Hose or tubing to a safe collection point
Collection container or connection to a closed drain system
steps.purpose: Release the pressure trapped between the closed isolation valves so that no stored hydraulic energy remains in the casing before the joint is disturbed.
inspectionPoints: The suction and discharge pressure gauges fall to zero (atmospheric) and stay there.
Vents are opened slowly, directed away from people, and discharged to a safe location or a closed system.
Pressure is watched after venting: a pressure rise indicates a passing isolation valve. Stop and re-isolate if this happens.
For hot, toxic, flammable or corrosive liquids, the site requirements for venting to a closed system are followed.
commonMistakes: Opening a vent quickly and being sprayed with pressurised or hot liquid.
Trusting a gauge without confirming that its isolation valve is open and that it is working.
Ignoring a slow pressure build-up from a passing valve.
safety: Stand to one side of any vent or plug being opened, never in line with it.
Wear face and hand protection suitable for the pumped liquid.
Never loosen casing joint nuts to relieve pressure.

steps.title: Drain the casing
tools: Spanners or hexagon keys for drain plugs
Drain hose and collection container, or connection to the closed drain
Decontamination materials where the liquid is hazardous
steps.purpose: Empty the casing so that liquid does not spill when the joint is broken and the internal parts can be inspected. Opening the high-point vent while draining lets air in so the casing drains fully.
inspectionPoints: All drain connections on the lower half are opened, including drains serving more than one low point where the casing has them.
The casing vent on the upper half is open so that liquid is not held up by vacuum.
Flow from the drains stops completely; continued flow indicates a passing isolation valve.
The drained liquid is checked for solids, rust, oil or unusual colour, and the observation is recorded.
Where the permit requires it, the casing is flushed or decontaminated before it is opened.
commonMistakes: Leaving liquid trapped in the lower half or the seal chambers, which then floods the work area when the joint is broken.
Discharging hazardous liquid to an open drain.
Losing drain plugs or damaging their threads.
safety: Handle and dispose of the drained liquid in line with its safety data sheet and the environmental rules.
Clean up spills immediately to prevent slips around the baseplate.

scene.label: Drain at the lower half, vent at the top

steps.title: Disconnect or make safe the auxiliary connections
tools: Clean bags or caps for instrument connections
steps.purpose: Free the upper casing half from everything attached to it: vent piping, seal-flush or packing-flush lines and any instrumentation mounted on the upper half. Every connection is tagged so that it can be reconnected correctly.
inspectionPoints: Vent piping on the upper half is disconnected and supported so that it is not bent or strained.
Seal-flush or packing-flush tubing is disconnected and both ends are capped to keep dirt out.
Pressure gauges, transmitters or other instruments on the upper half are disconnected or removed by the responsible discipline and protected.
Each connection is tagged with its location to prevent mix-ups at reassembly.
Where the design requires it, gland nuts or other fasteners that tie the seal glands or stuffing box parts to the upper half are released as the OEM manual describes.
commonMistakes: Lifting the upper half with a small-bore line still attached and tearing out the fitting.
Leaving tubing ends open so that dirt enters the flush circuit.
Reconnecting flush lines to the wrong ports at reassembly because they were not tagged.
safety: Small-bore lines can still hold pressure or liquid: open them slowly.
Instrument and electrical disconnections are made only by authorised personnel.

steps.title: Identify the casing joint fasteners
tools: Paint marker for match marks (no punch marks on fitted or sealing faces)
steps.purpose: Locate every fastener and locating feature on the split joint before loosening starts: the joint studs and nuts, the dowel pins, the jacking-screw holes and the lifting lugs. Match-mark the casing halves so that their relative position can be confirmed at reassembly.
inspectionPoints: All joint nuts are identified, including any near the seal housings or bearing brackets and any hidden by insulation.
Dowel pin positions and type (parallel or tapered, fixed or withdrawable) are confirmed from the OEM drawing.
The jacking-screw holes in the upper flange are located and their threads are clean.
The OEM loosening sequence for the joint is available at the pump.
Exposed stud threads are cleaned and treated with penetrating oil where corrosion is present.
Conditions worth recording before disassembly, such as corrosion, leakage marks at the joint or damaged nuts, are noted and photographed.
commonMistakes: Missing a nut and then trying to jack or lift against it.
Confusing jacking-screw holes with other tapped holes.
Marking parts with a punch or chisel on sealing or fitted surfaces.
safety: Use spanners and sockets of the correct size; worn or adjustable spanners slip and cause hand injuries.

scene.label: Joint fasteners: nuts, studs and dowels

steps.title: Loosen the casing joint nuts incrementally
tools: Correctly sized sockets or ring spanners
Torque multiplier or hydraulic bolting tool where the OEM specifies one
steps.purpose: Release the clamping load evenly across the whole joint. Each nut is eased a small amount in turn, following the pattern given by the OEM (typically the reverse of the tightening pattern), so that the casing unloads evenly and does not distort.
inspectionPoints: The nuts are loosened in stages in the specified pattern, not one nut fully at a time.
Any nut that is unusually loose or unusually tight is recorded, as it may indicate a joint problem or incorrect previous tightening.
A nut that will not turn is not forced to the point of damaging the stud; the approved method for seized fasteners is used.
commonMistakes: Removing the nuts completely one at a time around the flange, which can distort the casing.
Using impact tools on joint nuts without OEM approval.
Bending or stripping studs by using excessive leverage.
safety: Keep fingers clear of the pinch point between spanner and flange.
Use a stable stance and footing when breaking tight nuts loose.

scene.label: Loosen all nuts in stages, in the OEM pattern

steps.title: Remove the casing joint nuts in sequence
tools: Labelled parts tray for nuts and washers
steps.purpose: Once the joint has been unloaded evenly, remove the nuts and washers in the removal sequence and store them so that they can be inspected and, where the OEM requires it, refitted in the same positions.
inspectionPoints: Nut and washer condition: thread damage, galling, corrosion, flattened or cracked washers.
Stud condition: stretched, necked, bent or corroded studs and damaged threads.
The studs remain in the lower half. They are not removed unless they are damaged or the OEM requires it.
commonMistakes: Dropping nuts into the drip rim or drain openings.
Mixing nuts and washers of different grades.
safety: Keep the area tidy; loose nuts on the baseplate are a slip and trip hazard.

steps.title: Complete nut removal and release the dowels
tools: Dowel extractor or jacking nut where withdrawable dowels are fitted
steps.purpose: Remove the remaining nuts and release the dowel pins as the design requires, so that nothing holds the upper half to the lower half except the gasket or joint adhesion.
inspectionPoints: All joint nuts (16 in this model) are removed and accounted for.
Withdrawable dowels are removed with the correct extractor; fixed dowels stay in the lower half and the upper half lifts off them.
No fasteners remain at the seal housings, bearing brackets or any other attachment between the two halves.
commonMistakes: Hammering dowels out and damaging the dowel holes, which then lose their locating accuracy.
Overlooking a dowel and then jacking the casing unevenly.
safety: Use the correct tools for dowel removal; hardened drifts and punches can shatter.

scene.label: All joint nuts removed; studs stay in the lower half

steps.title: Separate the casing joint with the jacking screws
tools: Jacking screws of the size and length specified by the OEM
Steel rule or feeler gauges to confirm the gap is even all round
steps.purpose: Break the gasketed or metal-to-metal joint by turning the jacking screws evenly, raising the upper half slightly and level. This parts the joint without damaging the machined faces.
inspectionPoints: The jacking screws are turned evenly in small steps so that the upper half rises level.
The gap is watched all round the flange. If one area will not release, stop and look for a missed fastener or dowel.
The rotor does not move with the casing, and wear rings and seal parts are not dragged upwards.
commonMistakes: Driving wedges, chisels or screwdrivers into the joint, which damages the sealing faces and creates leakage paths.
Jacking on one side only, which cocks the upper half and can damage studs, dowels or wear ring seats.
Continuing to tighten jacking screws against a missed fastener.
safety: Never place hands or fingers in the joint gap.
Never use wedges, chisels or pry bars in the joint faces.

scene.label: Joint separated with jacking screws only

steps.title: Rig the upper casing at the designated lifting points
tools: Certified overhead crane, hoist or other approved lifting equipment
Certified slings, shackles and accessories rated for the load
Approved lifting plan with the upper-half weight taken from the OEM documentation
steps.purpose: Attach certified lifting gear only to the lifting lugs or other lifting points designated by the OEM on the upper half, so that it can be lifted vertically and level.
inspectionPoints: The weight of the upper half is known from the OEM documentation and the gear is rated for it.
The hoist, slings and shackles carry current inspection and certification marks.
Sling arrangement and angles follow the lifting plan and keep the upper half level.
The lifting lugs are free from cracks, corrosion and damage.
A laydown area with timber bearers or other soft supports is prepared so that the machined joint face is protected.
commonMistakes: Lifting the whole pump, or the pump with its baseplate, by the upper-half lugs. These lugs are designed for the upper half only.
Slinging around nozzles, flanges or bosses instead of using the designated lifting points.
Using uncertified or damaged slings and shackles.
safety: Only trained and competent persons rig loads and signal lifts.
Set up an exclusion zone; never stand or reach under a suspended load.
Never lift the complete pump by the upper-half lifting lugs.

scene.label: Designated lifting lugs and certified gear only

steps.title: Lift the upper casing vertically
steps.purpose: Raise the upper half slowly and vertically, guiding it clear of the studs and dowels and never letting it swing into or touch the rotor.
inspectionPoints: The upper half rises level; the lift is stopped and corrected if it tilts.
The casing clears the studs and dowels without binding.
The impeller, wear rings, sleeves and seals are not struck or dragged.
The gasket is observed as the joint opens; note which half it stays on and avoid tearing it, so that its condition can still be read.
commonMistakes: Lifting too fast or at an angle so that the casing jams on the studs.
Letting the upper half swing and strike the impeller or shaft.
Dragging the casing sideways with the crane hook instead of lifting vertically.
safety: Keep hands off the casing while it is above the rotor; control it with tag lines.
Stop the lift at once if binding, unexpected weight or any problem with the gear is noticed.
Protect the exposed rotor once the casing is clear.

scene.label: Lift vertically, clear of studs and dowels

steps.title: Set down the upper casing and inspect the internals
steps.purpose: Land the upper half on the prepared laydown area with its joint face protected, then record the as-found condition of the internal components before anything is cleaned or disturbed, and cover the open casing.
inspectionPoints: The upper half is stable on its supports and cannot roll or tip.
As-found photographs of the rotor, wear rings, gasket and joint faces are taken before cleaning.
Deposits, debris, foreign objects, corrosion products and wear particles are noted and sampled where useful.
The open casing and exposed rotor are covered to keep out dirt and dropped objects.
Detailed checks then follow the internal inspection procedure.
commonMistakes: Setting the upper half directly on its machined joint face on concrete or steel.
Cleaning parts before recording their as-found condition, which destroys evidence of the failure cause.
Leaving the casing open and unattended without covers.
safety: Land the load fully and confirm it is stable before removing the slings.
Keep the laydown area barriered and clear of walkways.

scene.label: Upper half on the laydown area; record as found

procedures.title: Internal inspection
procedures.intro:
With the upper casing removed, the rotor, wear rings, sleeves and seal areas in the lower half are exposed. The aim is to record the condition of each component, measure the critical clearances and compare the results with the OEM limits, so that a sound repair decision can be made. Many findings are clues to how the pump has been operated or installed, so record the as-found condition before cleaning.

Some checks can be made with the rotor in place; others, such as full bearing, seal and shaft inspection, need the rotor removed (see the rotor removal procedure). Measured values are always compared with the OEM manual; no limits are given in this module.
procedures.oemNote: All acceptance criteria, including wear ring clearances, impeller axial position, shaft run-out, sleeve wear, bearing condition and joint face flatness, come from the OEM manual and site standards. Record every measurement with the instrument used and the measurement position.

steps.title: Prepare and record the as-found condition
tools: Lint-free cloths and approved cleaning agents
steps.purpose: Create a record of the as-found condition, then clean the parts enough to inspect them properly. The pattern of deposits and wear is often the best evidence of how the pump has been running.
inspectionPoints: Photographs of the whole rotor and lower half from fixed reference views before cleaning.
Type and location of deposits: scale, sludge, fibres, or debris lodged in the impeller eyes or vane passages.
Any foreign objects, broken pieces or missing material.
The equipment history: running hours, recent vibration, temperature and leakage trends, and previous repairs.
commonMistakes: Wire-brushing or blasting surfaces before inspection, removing evidence and damaging fitted surfaces.
Using cleaning agents that attack elastomers, coatings or seal faces.
safety: Treat deposits as hazardous until the pumped liquid and its residues are known.
Wear gloves and eye protection when cleaning.

scene.label: Record the as-found condition before cleaning

steps.title: Inspect the impeller
tools: Inspection light and mirror or borescope
Dye-penetrant or other approved crack-detection method (qualified personnel)
steps.purpose: Assess the double-suction impeller for cavitation, erosion, corrosion, cracking, blockage and rubbing, and compare the two halves of the impeller with each other.
inspectionPoints: Cavitation pitting: a rough, sponge-like pitted surface, typically on the low-pressure (suction) side of the vanes a short distance downstream of the inlet edges, seen by looking into each impeller eye.
Pitting on the pressure side of the vanes near the inlet can point to suction recirculation from prolonged operation at low flow.
Damage near the vane outlet tips and shrouds can point to operation well away from the design flow or to interaction with the volute tongue.
Erosion: smooth, polished or grooved wear from solids, often at the inlet edges, the shroud surfaces and the outlet tips.
Corrosion: general wastage, pitting with corrosion products, or selective attack of the material.
Cracks at the vane-to-shroud junctions, the hub and the outlet tips; any suspected crack is confirmed by an approved non-destructive test.
Rubbing marks on the outer faces of the shrouds or on the hub, indicating contact with the casing or wear rings.
Blockage of vane passages or eyes by debris, fibres or deposits.

Uneven wear or damage between the two eyes. Heavier damage on one side is a clue to asymmetric flow to the two eyes (for example from an elbow in the plane of the shaft close to the suction nozzle), a partly blocked suction passage, an impeller not centred in the volute, or misalignment.
Orientation: the vane direction must match the direction of rotation shown on the casing.
commonMistakes: Looking only at the outlet tips and missing cavitation damage inside the eyes.
Treating heavy pitting as a material defect without investigating suction conditions and operating flow.
Ignoring a small crack; cracks in rotating parts can grow and release fragments into the casing.
safety: Do not turn the rotor while fingers or tools are near the impeller and casing.
Apply penetrant chemicals in a ventilated area and follow their safety data sheets.

scene.label: Impeller: compare both eyes and vane passages

steps.title: Inspect the impeller wear rings
steps.purpose: Check the rotating wear rings at both eyes (or the wear surfaces of the impeller where no separate rings are fitted) for wear, damage and security on the impeller.
inspectionPoints: Scoring, grooving, galling or smearing of the running surface.
Rub pattern: all round (concentric wear) or on one side only, which suggests shaft deflection, misalignment or casing distortion.
Difference in wear between the DE and NDE rings, which can point to unequal flow, an off-centre impeller or misalignment.
Security: the ring is tight on the impeller and its retention method (for example interference fit, pins, set screws or tack welds, as designed) is intact.
Outside diameter measured at several angular positions and recorded for the clearance calculation.
commonMistakes: Measuring at one position only and missing ovality or taper.
Assuming both rings have worn equally.
safety: Worn rings can have sharp edges; wear cut-resistant gloves.

scene.label: Impeller wear rings at both eyes

steps.title: Inspect the casing wear rings
steps.purpose: Check the stationary wear rings for wear and damage, correct seating in the casing, and engagement of their anti-rotation feature.
inspectionPoints: Scoring, grooving, galling or pick-up of material in the bore.
Location of rub marks (top, bottom or one side), which helps to diagnose shaft deflection, bearing wear, misalignment or pipe strain.
The anti-rotation pin, tongue or tab is intact and the ring has not turned in its seat.
The seating diameters on the ring and in both casing halves are free from fretting, erosion and corrosion.
Bore diameter measured at several positions, in more than one plane, by the method in the OEM manual.
commonMistakes: Missing a ring that has turned in its seat because the anti-rotation feature has sheared.
Measuring a ring bore while the ring is unsupported and distorted, instead of following the OEM method.
safety: Do not lever rings out with screwdrivers; use the correct removal method and lifting aids for heavy rings.

scene.label: Casing wear rings: wear, seating, anti-rotation

steps.title: Measure the impeller clearances
tools: Depth gauge for axial position checks
steps.purpose: Determine the running clearance between the impeller and casing wear rings at both eyes and check the axial position of the impeller in the volute, then compare the results with the OEM values for new and worn condition.
inspectionPoints: Diametral clearance is calculated from the measured casing ring bore and impeller ring outside diameter at matching positions, not estimated with feeler gauges alone.
Clearances at the DE and NDE eyes are recorded separately and compared with each other.
The impeller axial position relative to the volute centreline or the OEM reference faces is measured and recorded.
Rotor axial float between the locating bearing limits is checked only where the OEM procedure calls for it.
Results are compared with the OEM values; rings beyond the limits are renewed or the parts repaired as the OEM specifies.
commonMistakes: Comparing measurements with figures remembered from a different pump.
Measuring mating parts at very different temperatures.
Recording a single clearance for both eyes.
safety: Keep fingers clear when the rotor is turned to take readings.

scene.label: Measure and compare with OEM values

steps.title: Inspect the shaft sleeves
steps.purpose: Check the sleeves that protect the shaft through the seal or stuffing box areas for wear, corrosion and leakage paths.
inspectionPoints: Gland packing: grooving or scoring under the packing rings, which also suggests over-tightened packing or abrasive solids.
Mechanical seals: fretting or damage under the secondary seal, and marks from the seal drive collar set screws.
Corrosion or erosion at the sleeve ends next to the impeller hub.
Signs of leakage under the sleeve (staining or corrosion of the shaft), which indicate a failed sleeve-to-hub seal or O-ring.
Sleeve nuts are tight and their locking arrangement is intact.
commonMistakes: Polishing a grooved sleeve instead of renewing or repairing it as the OEM specifies.
Overlooking shaft corrosion hidden under a sleeve.
safety: Sleeve nut threads can be right- or left-handed depending on the design; check the OEM drawing before applying force.

steps.title: Inspect the shaft
steps.purpose: Inspect the accessible parts of the shaft and, where the OEM procedure allows, check run-out with a dial indicator while the rotor is turned slowly by hand. A complete shaft inspection is made with the rotor removed.
inspectionPoints: Coupling end: keyway edges, fretting under the hub and the condition of the hub retainer threads.
Corrosion, pitting or erosion on exposed sections and at the sleeve ends.
Discolouration from overheating near the bearings or seals.
Run-out: the total indicator reading at the positions the OEM specifies, compared with the OEM limit.
With the rotor removed: bearing journals and shoulders for wear, fretting and marks from a bearing that has turned on the shaft.
commonMistakes: Taking run-out readings on a damaged or dirty surface and misreading the result.
Mistaking movement from bearing looseness for a bent shaft.
safety: Turn the rotor only by hand with the motor isolated; never use the motor to turn it.

steps.title: Inspect the shaft seals (mechanical seal or gland packing)
steps.purpose: Assess the sealing arrangement at both shaft exits. Not all split case pumps use mechanical seals; many use gland packing, and the inspection differs.
inspectionPoints: Mechanical seal: leakage history, crystallised or carbonised deposits on the atmospheric side, and the condition of the flush connection.
Mechanical seal faces, when the seal is removed as the seal manufacturer describes: chips, cracks, heat checking, grooves and uneven wear tracks. Lapped faces are not touched with bare fingers.
Mechanical seal secondary seals and O-rings: hardening, swelling, cracking, extrusion or chemical attack.
Mechanical seal springs and drive collar: corrosion, clogging, broken springs or slipped set screws.
Gland packing: glazing, burning, extrusion, loss of lubricant and uneven compression between rings.
Gland packing: lantern ring position relative to the flush connection, and the condition of the gland follower and studs.
Seal chamber or stuffing box bores in both casing halves: erosion, corrosion and damage.
commonMistakes: Refitting a disturbed mechanical seal without the inspection or refurbishment the seal manufacturer requires.
Replacing packing without finding out why it failed (sleeve wear, flush failure, misalignment).
Assuming both shaft exits are in the same condition.
safety: Carbon, silicon carbide and tungsten carbide seal faces can chip and leave sharp edges.
Flush systems may hold residual liquid; handle them with the same precautions as the pumped liquid.

steps.title: Inspect the bearing assemblies
tools: Operating records of bearing temperature and vibration
steps.purpose: Assess the lubrication and condition of both bearing assemblies. The DE floating radial bearing and the NDE locating bearings differ in type and duty, so they are assessed separately.
inspectionPoints: Oil lubrication: level history, colour, cloudiness (water), sludge, and metal particles in the sample or on the drain plug.
Grease lubrication: colour, consistency, hardening, contamination and excess grease in the housing.
Housing seals (lip or labyrinth): wear, damage and evidence of water or dirt ingress.
Operating records: temperature and vibration trends at each bearing before the shutdown.
Bearings, where covers or caps are removed as the design permits or with the rotor removed: discolouration, pitting, spalling, brinelling, corrosion, cage damage and roughness when turned by hand.
NDE locating bearings: correct type and arrangement (paired angular-contact, back-to-back, in this model) and signs of axial overload.
DE floating bearing: free to move axially in its housing as designed; any marks of binding or outer-ring creep are recorded.
commonMistakes: Assuming the DE and NDE bearings are identical or interchangeable.
Spinning a dry bearing with compressed air, which damages it and is a safety hazard.
Letting dirt into an open bearing housing.
safety: Never spin bearings with compressed air.
Hot oil can scald; allow housings to cool before draining.

scene.label: DE floating bearing and NDE locating pair differ

steps.title: Inspect the casing joint surfaces
tools: Straight edge or other flatness check method given by the OEM
steps.purpose: Check the split flange faces of both casing halves for damage that could cause external leakage, or internal leakage across the joint from the high-pressure volute to the suction side.
inspectionPoints: Old gasket material is removed completely with a non-metallic scraper and solvent, without scratching the faces.
Erosion channels (wire drawing) across the joint, especially between the volute and the suction chambers, which indicate internal leakage.
Scratches, dents, corrosion or tool marks across the sealing width.
Flatness or distortion checked by the OEM method where there is a history of joint leakage.
Stud threads, nut seating faces, dowel holes and jacking-screw holes are in good condition.
commonMistakes: Using a grinder, file or wire wheel on the joint faces.
Leaving gasket fragments in stud holes, dowel holes or wear ring seats.
safety: Use solvents with adequate ventilation and the protection stated on their safety data sheets.

scene.label: Joint faces: no wire drawing, no tool marks

steps.title: Inspect the casing passages
tools: Coating thickness gauge where coatings are applied
steps.purpose: Inspect the suction chambers, impeller chamber and volute in both casing halves for erosion, corrosion, cavitation damage and cracking.
inspectionPoints: Volute tongue (cutwater): erosion or cavitation damage, which can be linked to operation away from the design flow.
Suction chambers on both sides: debris, erosion or uneven deposits that would disturb the flow to one eye.
Coatings or linings: blistering, disbondment or wear.
Casing walls: corrosion wastage, and cracks near ribs, nozzles and bosses.
Double-volute splitter rib, where fitted: erosion and cracking.
commonMistakes: Inspecting only the lower half and forgetting the upper half on the laydown area.
safety: Wear gloves when reaching past sharp eroded edges inside the casing.

steps.title: Record the results and decide on corrective action
steps.purpose: Bring the findings together, compare every measurement with the OEM values, identify root causes and decide which parts to repair or renew before reassembly.
inspectionPoints: Each measurement is recorded with its position, instrument, OEM limit and result.
Patterns are considered together: for example one-sided ring rubs with bearing wear and misalignment, or cavitation at one eye with the suction piping layout.
Required spares are confirmed against the OEM parts list and material specification.
Findings that point to operating or installation causes, such as low-flow operation, poor suction conditions or pipe strain, are reported to operations and engineering.
commonMistakes: Replacing worn parts without finding out why they wore.
Fitting parts of a different material or dimension from those specified.
safety: Label and store damaged parts kept for failure analysis safely.

scene.label: Compare with OEM limits; find the root cause

procedures.title: Rotor removal
procedures.intro:
In a between-bearings split case pump the complete rotor (shaft, impeller, wear rings, sleeves, seals and, in this model, the bearing housings) can be lifted out of the lower casing once the upper half has been removed, without disturbing the suction and discharge piping. The sequence below is illustrative and suited to the configuration in this module.

Rotor removal procedures differ between designs and manufacturers. Some bearing housings are split and their caps are removed, others are solid and lift out with the rotor; some seals must be set, locked or removed before lifting; and the designated lifting and support points differ. The OEM manual governs.
procedures.oemNote: Illustrative sequence only. Rotor removal procedures differ between designs. The OEM manual, the seal manufacturer instructions and the site lifting plan govern every step, including slinging points, rotor weight, support points and the dismantling sequence.

steps.title: Confirm the prerequisites and plan the lift
tools: Permit to work, confirmed still valid
OEM manual with the rotor weight and slinging points
steps.purpose: Confirm that the upper casing is off under a valid permit and that isolation is still in place, and prepare the equipment, supports and laydown area for the rotor lift.
inspectionPoints: Motor and process isolation is still in place and has been re-verified.
Bearing housing oil is drained (oil-lubricated pumps), and the drain plugs are refitted or kept safe.
Bearing housing instrumentation (temperature and vibration sensors) is disconnected by authorised personnel and protected.
The rotor weight, slinging points and lifting equipment are confirmed in the lifting plan.
V-block stands are set level on a firm surface beside the baseplate, at the support spacing the OEM designates, with soft protection on the contact faces.
As-found coupling alignment readings are taken if they are needed for diagnosis.
commonMistakes: Spilling oil because the bearing housings were not drained.
Tearing sensor cables when the rotor is lifted.
Setting the stands at the wrong spacing for the rotor support points.
safety: Re-confirm isolation before starting each new stage of work, especially after a shift change.

steps.title: Disconnect the coupling and remove the spacer
tools: Spanners and sockets for the coupling bolts
Clean storage for the spacer, bolts and flexible elements
steps.purpose: Remove the coupling guard and the coupling spacer so that the pump shaft is free of the motor shaft. With a spacer coupling, the motor and its hub can stay in place.
inspectionPoints: Hubs, spacer and bolts are match-marked so that their orientation and positions can be restored.
Flexible elements (discs, membranes, elastomer elements or grid, depending on type) are inspected for cracks, wear, deformation or fatigue.
Coupling bolts are checked for wear, elongation and thread damage; their replacement policy follows the coupling manufacturer.
Hub keys and bores show no sign of fretting or movement.
commonMistakes: Losing the orientation or bolt positions of a balanced coupling spacer.
Replacing coupling bolts with ordinary bolts of a different grade.
Letting the spacer drop when the last bolt is removed.
safety: The guard is removed only under the permit with the motor isolated, and is refitted before any run.
Support the spacer before removing the last bolts.

steps.title: Release the seal glands and confirm the flush lines are disconnected
tools: Seal setting plates or clips (cartridge seals)
steps.purpose: Free the mechanical seal glands, or the packing gland followers, from their studs and slide them outboard along the shaft so that the rotor can be lifted without the glands catching on the casing.
inspectionPoints: Cartridge mechanical seals: setting plates or clips are refitted before the drive collar set screws and gland nuts are released, as the seal manufacturer requires.
Component mechanical seals: the position of the seal parts on the sleeve is recorded or marked before anything is moved.
Gland packing: gland nuts are removed and the followers slid outboard; the packing is removed now or after rotor removal as the OEM describes.
Seal-flush or packing-flush connections are confirmed disconnected and capped.
Glands are supported so that they cannot slide onto the seal faces or drop.
commonMistakes: Releasing a cartridge seal without its setting plates, so that the faces separate or the spring setting is lost.
Letting a gland plate slide and strike the seal faces.
safety: Seal parts can hold residual liquid; follow the precautions for the pumped liquid.

scene.label: Glands slid outboard; flush lines disconnected

steps.title: Remove the bearing housing hold-down bolts and caps
tools: Dowel extractor where the bearing housings are dowelled
Clean covers for the bearing housings
steps.purpose: Release the bearing housings from their supports on the lower casing. In this model the housings stay on the shaft and lift with the rotor; other designs remove split bearing caps so that the bearings lift out on the shaft, or withdraw the housings separately.
inspectionPoints: Each housing is match-marked to its bracket, and any shims or adjusting pieces are recorded and kept with that housing.
Housing dowels, where fitted, are removed with the correct extractor.
Where split bearing caps are used, each cap stays with its own housing and is never interchanged.
Housing support faces and hold-down bolts are in good condition.
commonMistakes: Losing or mixing shims under the bearing housings, which changes rotor centring and alignment.
Interchanging DE and NDE parts, which are not identical.
safety: Keep hands clear of the gap between housing and bracket when a housing is moved.

steps.title: Attach the rotor lifting gear
tools: Certified soft slings (web or round slings) and shackles
steps.purpose: Sling the rotor at the points designated by the OEM, using a spreader beam so that the slings hang vertically and the rotor stays level, with the shaft protected where the slings bear on it.
inspectionPoints: Slings bear only on the OEM-designated points, such as specified shaft sections or bearing housings.
No sling touches seal faces, bearing journals, sleeve sealing surfaces, wear rings or the impeller.
The spreader beam keeps the slings near vertical and the rotor level.
The rotor centre of gravity is known and the hook is positioned over it.
Slings are protected from sharp edges such as keyways and shoulders.
commonMistakes: Slinging around the impeller or across the seal glands.
Using wire rope slings directly on the shaft.
Lifting from a single point without a spreader beam so that the rotor tilts.
safety: Only competent riggers sling the rotor, and the lift follows the lifting plan.
Never stand under or reach beneath the rotor during the lift.

steps.title: Lift the rotor vertically and level
tools: Second person watching the wear rings and seals at both ends
steps.purpose: Raise the complete rotor straight up out of the lower casing, keeping it level so that the wear rings, seals and bearing housings come clear of their seats without binding or striking the casing.
inspectionPoints: The rotor rises level and evenly at both ends.
The casing wear rings, which in many designs stay on the impeller and lift with the rotor, come clear of their seats and anti-rotation slots without binding.
Bearing housings, glands and seal parts clear the casing and brackets.
The impeller does not touch the casing or the volute tongue.
commonMistakes: Lifting one end first so that the rotor binds in the wear ring or seal housing seats.
Allowing the rotor to swing into the casing or the motor.
safety: Stop the lift if any binding is felt; never use the crane to pull the rotor free.
Keep the exclusion zone in force until the rotor is set down.

steps.title: Set the rotor on V-block stands
tools: Chocks or restraints to prevent rolling
steps.purpose: Land the rotor on the prepared V-block stands at the OEM support points, with soft protection between the shaft and the blocks, and secure it so that it cannot roll.
inspectionPoints: Support points are on plain shaft sections or other OEM-designated points, never on seal faces, journals or sleeve sealing surfaces.
The rotor is level and stable and cannot roll off the stands.
The open lower casing is covered to keep out dirt and dropped objects.
commonMistakes: Resting the rotor on the impeller or on the bearing journals.
Using bare steel V-blocks that mark the shaft.
safety: Confirm stability before releasing the slings.
Barrier off the rotor laydown area.

scene.label: Rotor on V-block stands with soft protection

steps.title: Rotor dismantling (general notes)
tools: Controlled induction heater, only where the OEM permits heating
Hook or C-spanners for sleeve nuts and bearing locknuts
steps.purpose: Where further work is needed, dismantle the rotor in the order given by the OEM, keeping every part identified by position and protecting fitted surfaces. The outline below is general and does not replace the OEM sequence.
inspectionPoints: A typical order, which depends on the design: coupling hub, bearing housing end covers, bearing locknuts and locking washers, bearings, bearing housings, seals (cartridge seals as complete units), sleeve nuts, sleeves, impeller and impeller key.
Impeller orientation relative to the shaft and the direction of rotation is marked before removal; a double-suction impeller can physically be refitted the wrong way round.
Thread directions of sleeve nuts and bearing locknuts are checked on the OEM drawing.
Pullers act on the bearing ring being removed; force is never passed through the rolling elements.
Positions of spacers and shims, and the impeller axial position on the shaft, are recorded.
Fits and surfaces are inspected as each part comes off, and measurements are compared with the OEM values.
commonMistakes: Hammering bearings, hubs or the impeller off the shaft.
Heating with an uncontrolled flame where the OEM does not permit it, damaging materials or seals.
Mixing DE and NDE parts.
safety: Pullers under load store energy; fit covers and stand out of line with the puller.
Wear heat-resistant gloves when handling heated parts.

procedures.title: Reassembly
procedures.intro:
Reassembly returns the pump to a fully assembled, aligned and guarded condition. It broadly reverses the dismantling sequence, with inspection and measurement at each stage. Clean, correct parts and the OEM settings matter more than speed: many early failures after maintenance are traced to dirt, incorrect fits, the wrong gasket, seal setting errors, misalignment or pipe strain.

The sequence below is illustrative. All dimensions, settings, tightening values and patterns come from the OEM manual and from the seal, bearing and coupling manufacturers.
procedures.oemNote: Illustrative sequence only. Fits, clearances, run-out limits, gasket specification, bolting pattern and tightening values, the rotor centring method and alignment tolerances are design specific and must be taken from the OEM manual and the relevant component manufacturers. No values are given in this module.

steps.title: Inspect and prepare all components
tools: Lint-free cloths and approved cleaning agents
steps.purpose: Make sure every part to be fitted is the correct part, clean, undamaged and within the OEM dimensional limits, and that all single-use items are new.
inspectionPoints: New parts match the OEM part numbers and material specification.
Fitted surfaces, threads and keyways are clean and free from burrs.
New gaskets, O-rings, locking washers and other single-use items are available.
Measurements of new and reused parts are recorded and compared with the OEM values.
The work area and the open lower casing are clean, and covered when not being worked on.
commonMistakes: Reusing locking washers, O-rings or gaskets.
Fitting non-OEM parts without engineering approval.
safety: Handle heavy parts with suitable lifting aids.

steps.title: Verify the bearing condition and fitting method
tools: Induction bearing heater with temperature control
Fitting sleeves that bear on the ring being fitted
steps.purpose: Confirm that each end receives bearings of the correct type, arrangement and condition, and that they are fitted by a controlled method at the point in the rotor build the OEM specifies, so that the DE bearing can float and the NDE bearings locate the rotor as designed.
inspectionPoints: Bearing designations match the OEM parts list for each end; DE and NDE bearings are not interchanged.
The paired angular-contact bearings at the NDE are a matched set, fitted in the arrangement the OEM specifies (back-to-back in this model).
Bearings are heated only by a controlled method, to no more than the temperature the bearing manufacturer allows, and fitted fully against their shoulders.
Locknuts and locking washers are new or in good condition and correctly locked.
The DE floating bearing has the axial freedom in its housing that the design requires.
Fitted bearings turn smoothly by hand, and housings and covers are clean before lubricant is added.
commonMistakes: Hammering bearings onto the shaft or pressing through the wrong ring.
Fitting an angular-contact pair in the wrong arrangement.
Overfilling with grease, which causes overheating.
Refitting a used bearing whose condition has not been verified.
safety: Wear heat-resistant gloves; heated bearings stay hot for some time.
Follow the heater instructions, including demagnetisation where applicable.

scene.label: Correct bearing type and arrangement at each end

steps.title: Inspect the shaft and check run-out
tools: V-block stands, or a lathe between centres
steps.purpose: Confirm that the shaft is straight, its fitted diameters are within the OEM limits, and its keyways and threads are sound before parts are built onto it.
inspectionPoints: Run-out (total indicator reading) is measured while the shaft is turned slowly, at the positions the OEM specifies, typically including the impeller seat, seal areas, bearing journals and coupling end.
Run-out readings are compared with the OEM limit. A shaft outside the limit is not straightened without OEM or engineering approval.
Bearing journal, impeller seat and coupling seat diameters are measured and compared with the OEM values.
Keyways are free from cracks, burrs and deformation, and threads are undamaged.
Shoulders are square and undamaged.
commonMistakes: Measuring run-out with the shaft resting on damaged surfaces or dirty V-blocks.
Mistaking surface damage for run-out.
safety: Secure the shaft so that it cannot roll off its supports.

scene.label: Shaft run-out and fits per OEM

steps.title: Verify the impeller condition, orientation and position
steps.purpose: Confirm that the impeller is sound, balanced where required after any repair, fitted the right way round for the direction of rotation, and located on the shaft in the axial position the OEM requires.
inspectionPoints: Repairs, trimming or wear ring renewal are followed by balancing where the OEM requires it.
Vane direction matches the rotation arrow on the casing; a reversed double-suction impeller still fits, but performs poorly.
The impeller key fits correctly in both keyways without rocking.
Impeller wear rings are secure and their outside diameters are recorded.
The impeller axial position on the shaft is set by the sleeves and sleeve nuts as the OEM specifies, and is recorded.
Seals between the sleeves and the impeller hub (O-rings or gaskets) are fitted where the design uses them.
commonMistakes: Fitting the impeller reversed.
Over-tightening sleeve nuts so that the impeller or sleeves distort.
safety: Use lifting aids for heavy impellers.

steps.title: Install the shaft seals
tools: Seal manufacturer instructions and setting drawing
Lint-free wipes and approved cleaning fluid
Elastomer-compatible lubricant specified by the seal manufacturer
Fitting sleeves or tape to protect O-rings over keyways and threads
steps.purpose: Fit the mechanical seals at both shaft exits with complete cleanliness and to the setting defined by the seal manufacturer, or prepare the packing for installation once the casing is closed.
inspectionPoints: Mechanical seal faces are clean, undamaged and free from fingerprints, and are not lubricated unless the seal manufacturer specifies it.
O-rings and secondary seals are of the correct material, lubricated only with a compatible product, and protected from cuts as they pass keyways and threads.
Cartridge seals are fitted with their setting plates in place; the plates are removed only after the rotor is located and the glands are secured, as the seal manufacturer instructs.
Component seals are set to the working length or setting dimension on the seal drawing, measured from the stated reference.
Glands are placed on the shaft outboard of the seal chambers, ready for final positioning.
Gland packing is normally installed after the casing is closed, as the OEM describes: rings cut to suit the sleeve, joints staggered and the lantern ring aligned with the flush connection.
commonMistakes: Touching seal faces or wiping them with a dirty cloth.
Using a lubricant that attacks the elastomer.
Removing cartridge setting plates before the seal is secured, or forgetting to remove them before start-up.
Winding packing in as a continuous spiral instead of separate rings.
safety: Seal faces can chip; handle and store them with care.

scene.label: Seals fitted clean, set per seal manufacturer

steps.title: Prepare the lower casing
steps.purpose: Make the lower half ready to receive the rotor: clean joint faces and seats, sound threads and nothing left inside the casing.
inspectionPoints: The joint face, wear ring seats, seal chamber or stuffing box seats and bearing bracket faces are clean and undamaged.
The anti-rotation slots for the casing wear rings are clean and undamaged.
Drain plugs and connections are refitted.
No tools, rags, gasket debris or packing pieces remain in the suction chambers or volute.
Bearing housing shims and dowels are ready at their recorded positions.
commonMistakes: Leaving foreign objects in the suction chambers, where they will be drawn into the impeller eyes.
safety: Keep a count of the tools and materials used inside the casing.

steps.title: Lift the rotor into the lower casing
tools: Certified spreader beam, soft slings and shackles
steps.purpose: Lower the rotor vertically and level into the lower casing, guiding the wear rings, seal parts and bearing housings into their seats.
inspectionPoints: Slings bear only on the OEM-designated points, with shaft protection in place.
The rotor descends level, and the anti-rotation features of the casing wear rings are lined up with their slots before the rings touch the casing.
Glands, seals and bearing housings come down square to their seats.
commonMistakes: Landing a wear ring on its anti-rotation pin so that it sits high; the upper half will then pinch and distort it.
Dropping the rotor the last distance onto its seats.
safety: Never place hands between the rotor and the casing seats while the load is suspended.

scene.label: Lower the rotor vertically and level

steps.title: Position the rotor: seat the wear rings and centre the impeller
steps.purpose: Seat the rotor so that the wear rings and seal parts sit fully in their casing seats with the anti-rotation features engaged, and the impeller is centred axially in the volute as the OEM requires.
inspectionPoints: Casing wear rings are fully seated in the lower half, with their anti-rotation pins or tongues engaged in the slots.

Impeller axial centring in the volute is checked by the OEM method (for example from reference faces) and adjusted by the means the design provides, such as sleeve nut positions or bearing housing shims and covers.
The rotor turns freely by hand with no rub at the wear rings.
The seal chambers or stuffing boxes are concentric with the shaft, as far as can be checked.
commonMistakes: Assuming the impeller is centred because the parts went back in the same order.
Correcting the impeller position by forcing the rotor axially against the locating bearing.
safety: Remove the lifting gear only when the rotor is fully supported in the casing.

scene.label: Wear rings seated; impeller centred in the volute

steps.title: Secure the bearing housings
tools: Spanners and calibrated torque wrench (values per OEM)
steps.purpose: Refit the bearing housing hold-down bolts, dowels, shims and any caps in their original positions so that the rotor is held in its correct radial and axial position.
inspectionPoints: Shims and dowels are refitted at their recorded positions.
Bolts are tightened to the OEM values in the specified sequence.
The rotor still turns freely by hand after the housings are secured.
Impeller centring is re-checked after the housings are tightened.
commonMistakes: Swapping shims between the DE and NDE.
Not re-checking free rotation after tightening.
safety: Use the torque wrench within its calibrated range.

steps.title: Install the casing joint gasket
tools: New gasket of the OEM-specified material and thickness
Sharp knife or gasket cutter for trimming as the OEM describes
Gasket adhesive or jointing compound, only if the OEM specifies it
steps.purpose: Fit a new joint gasket of the correct material and thickness. The thickness is part of the design: it sets how the casing halves clamp the wear rings and the seal chamber or stuffing box seats, so the wrong thickness can leave parts loose or distorted and change the running clearances.
inspectionPoints: Gasket material and thickness are confirmed against the OEM specification before fitting.
The gasket is cut or trimmed to the shape and at the positions the OEM specifies, especially where it meets the wear ring and seal chamber or stuffing box bores.
The gasket lies flat, without wrinkles or overlaps, and does not protrude into bores or the volute.
Adhesive or jointing compound is used only where and as the OEM specifies.
Joint faces are clean and dry immediately before fitting.
commonMistakes: Cutting a gasket from sheet material of the wrong thickness or type.
Fitting two gaskets, or adding liquid sealant on top of a gasket.
Leaving gasket material overhanging into wear ring or seal bores.
safety: Wear cut-resistant gloves when trimming gaskets with a knife.

scene.label: Gasket material and thickness per OEM

steps.title: Lift the upper casing into position
tools: Certified lifting equipment and slings at the designated lifting lugs
Guide studs or alignment aids where the OEM provides them
steps.purpose: Lift the upper half from the laydown area and bring it vertically over the lower half, level and aligned with the studs and dowels.
inspectionPoints: The upper half joint face and internal surfaces are clean and have been inspected before lifting.
The upper half hangs level and is aligned with the studs and dowels before it is lowered.
The rotor, seals and gasket are protected from contact as the casing comes down.
commonMistakes: Lowering at an angle so that the casing drags the gasket out of position.
safety: Keep hands out from between the casing halves.
Never stand under the suspended upper half.

steps.title: Guide the upper casing onto the dowels
steps.purpose: Bring the upper half down the last distance slowly so that the dowels engage and locate the two halves accurately, then land it fully on the gasket.
inspectionPoints: The dowels engage without binding; the casing is not forced down onto them.
The gasket stays in place and is not pinched or displaced.
The upper halves of the wear ring and seal seats close over their parts without contact.
The match marks made at dismantling line up.
Jacking screws are fully retracted before the casing is landed.
commonMistakes: Hammering the upper half down onto the dowels.
Using the joint nuts to pull the halves together over a misaligned dowel or a ring sitting high.
safety: Keep fingers clear of the closing joint at all times.

steps.title: Check casing alignment and rotor freedom
steps.purpose: With the upper half landed and the dowels engaged, confirm that the halves are correctly aligned and that the rotor still turns before the joint is bolted.
inspectionPoints: The flanges sit evenly all round, with no gap that suggests a wear ring or seal part is trapped high.
The rotor turns freely by hand.
Nuts and washers are clean, and threads are lubricated only as the OEM specifies.
commonMistakes: Ignoring a tight spot, which often means a part is not seated.
safety: Remove the lifting gear only after the casing is fully landed and stable.

scene.label: Halves located by dowels; rotor free

steps.title: Tighten the casing joint in the specified pattern and stages
tools: Calibrated torque wrench, or hydraulic tensioning or torque equipment where the OEM specifies it
Thread lubricant of the type the OEM specifies
steps.purpose: Clamp the joint uniformly by tightening the nuts in the OEM pattern over several stages up to the final value in the OEM manual, so that the gasket compresses evenly and the casing does not distort.
inspectionPoints: The OEM tightening pattern is followed. A common approach starts near the middle of the casing and works outwards alternately on both sides of the shaft, but the OEM pattern governs.
Tightening is done in several stages of increasing value, followed by a final check pass at full value.
Thread and nut-face lubrication is as specified, because lubrication changes the clamping load achieved for a given torque.
Rotor rotation by hand is checked between stages; any new tight spot stops the work.
The final values and sequence are recorded.
commonMistakes: Tightening each nut to full value one at a time.
Using a torque figure from another pump or a general table.
Skipping the final check pass.
safety: Position yourself so that a slipping wrench cannot cause a fall or hand injury.

scene.label: Pattern, stages and final values per OEM

steps.title: Set the seals, refit the glands and reconnect the auxiliaries
tools: Packing rings and packing tools (packed pumps)
steps.purpose: Bring the glands up to the seal chambers or stuffing boxes, secure and set the mechanical seals or install the packing, and reconnect the vent, flush and instrument connections at their tagged positions.
inspectionPoints: Mechanical seal gland nuts are tightened evenly so that the gland is square to the shaft.
Cartridge seal drive collar set screws are tightened and the setting plates removed and stored, as the seal manufacturer requires.
Gland packing: rings installed one at a time with joints staggered and the lantern ring aligned with the flush port; gland nuts left finger-tight so that leakage can be adjusted at start-up.
Flush and vent lines are reconnected to the correct ports and are leak-tight.
Instruments removed from the upper half are refitted by the responsible discipline.
commonMistakes: Leaving cartridge setting plates in place.
Over-tightening packing glands before start-up.
Swapping flush lines between ports.
safety: Make up small-bore connections properly to avoid leaks when the system is pressurised.

steps.title: Carry out the hand-rotation check
tools: Strap wrench or turning tool that does not mark the shaft
steps.purpose: With the casing bolted and the seals set, turn the pump rotor by hand through several revolutions to confirm there is no rubbing, binding or tight spot before the coupling is connected.
