inspectionPoints: The rotor turns smoothly and evenly through complete revolutions.
There is no scraping or rubbing noise from the wear rings, seals or bearing housings.
The effort needed is consistent around each revolution; any tight spot is investigated before proceeding.
commonMistakes: Skipping the check because the rotor turned freely before bolting.
Using pipe wrenches on the shaft and damaging the coupling seat.
safety: The motor stays isolated and the coupling spacer is still removed.

steps.title: Check and correct the coupling alignment
tools: Laser alignment system or dial indicators (reverse-indicator or rim-and-face method)
OEM and coupling manufacturer alignment tolerances
steps.purpose: Confirm that the pump and motor shafts are aligned within the tolerances given by the OEM or the coupling manufacturer, correct the motor position where needed, and record the final readings.
inspectionPoints: Soft foot is checked and corrected before alignment readings are taken.
Offset and angularity are measured in both the vertical and horizontal planes with the hold-down bolts tightened.
Any thermal growth offsets specified by the OEM are applied to the target values.
The distance between shaft ends matches the coupling specification.
Where piping was disturbed, shaft movement is monitored while the flange bolts are released and retightened; movement beyond the site criterion is corrected at the piping, not at the pump.
The final as-left readings are recorded.
commonMistakes: Taking readings with the hold-down bolts loose and then tightening them.
Moving the pump instead of the motor without OEM guidance, which disturbs the piping.
Using a stack of many thin, dirty or damaged shims.
safety: Alignment is done with the motor isolated; turn the shafts by hand only.

scene.label: Alignment within OEM or coupling tolerances

steps.title: Refit the coupling spacer and guard
tools: Coupling bolts and fittings as specified
Calibrated torque wrench (values per coupling manufacturer)
steps.purpose: Install the coupling spacer in its match-marked orientation, tighten its bolts to the coupling manufacturer values, and refit the coupling guard so that no rotating part is exposed.
inspectionPoints: The spacer and bolts are refitted in their match-marked positions.
The flexible elements are not pre-stressed or twisted by the installation.
The guard is complete and secure, and does not touch any rotating part.
commonMistakes: Leaving the guard off for a test run.
Mixing coupling bolts of different grades or weights.
safety: The pump must never run without the coupling guard fitted.

steps.title: Restore lubrication and auxiliaries and hand back
steps.purpose: Return the pump to an operable condition: fill the bearing housings with the specified lubricant, confirm all connections, remove blanks and tools, close the work under the permit, and hand over for restart following the pre-commissioning and commissioning guidance.
inspectionPoints: Bearing housings are filled to the correct level with the OEM-specified lubricant, and constant-level oilers are set as the OEM directs.
All drain plugs are fitted, vents are closed or set for priming, and blanks are removed.
Tools, rags and materials are removed and accounted for.
The maintenance record includes measurements, parts replaced, bolting values used and as-left alignment readings.
Isolations are removed only through the permit system, and restart follows the pre-commissioning and commissioning guidance.
commonMistakes: Starting the pump with empty bearing housings.
Removing locks before every person has signed off the work.
safety: The pump must be filled and vented before any start; it must never run dry.

guidance.title: Installation
guidance.intro: Much of the long-term reliability of a split case pump is decided at installation. A rigid, well-grouted foundation, a level baseplate, good suction piping, unstrained pipe connections and accurate alignment protect the bearings, seals and wear rings for years. The topics below explain what to check and why.
guidance.disclaimer: General training guidance only. All installation activities must be checked against the particular OEM installation manual, the project specifications and the site-approved procedures. Tolerances, tightening values, grout curing requirements and alignment limits are not given here and must be taken from those documents.

topics.title: Foundation design
topics.body: The foundation supports the weight of the pump, motor and baseplate, resists the forces from the piping and from operation, and absorbs vibration. It is normally a reinforced concrete block designed by a civil or structural engineer, using the loads and mass data supplied by the OEM. The foundation must be stiff enough that its natural frequencies are well separated from the running speed and its multiples; otherwise resonance can amplify vibration. It should rest on properly prepared ground or structure and, where specified, be separated from surrounding floors so that vibration is not transmitted. Before the baseplate is set, the concrete must have cured as specified, surface laitance must be removed and the top surface chipped or roughened so that the grout bonds. Anchor bolt pockets or sleeves must be at the positions shown on the OEM foundation drawing.
checks: Foundation designed using the OEM loads and foundation drawing.
Concrete curing complete as specified before grouting.
Top surface roughened, clean and free of oil, laitance and standing water.
Anchor bolt positions and projections match the OEM drawing.
pitfalls: Setting the baseplate on a smooth, uncured or oily concrete surface.
A foundation or support structure with a natural frequency close to running speed.
Mounting on a flexible steel structure without a dynamic assessment.

topics.title: Baseplate setting
topics.body: The baseplate holds the pump and motor in fixed relative positions. It is lifted at its designated lifting points, set on the foundation on levelling screws or wedges and packers at the positions the OEM recommends, and adjusted until the machined mounting pads are level and in the same plane within the OEM tolerances. A baseplate that is twisted or bowed during setting will be locked in that shape by the grout, which makes alignment difficult and causes soft foot. Many OEMs recommend removing the pump and motor, or at least loosening them, while the baseplate is levelled and grouted, and checking the pads with a precision level or an optical method. The baseplate underside must be clean, and any surface that will be in contact with grout must be prepared as the grout manufacturer specifies.
checks: Machined pads level and coplanar within the OEM tolerances.
Levelling screws or packers positioned as the OEM recommends.
Baseplate underside clean and prepared for the chosen grout system.
Baseplate lifted only as the OEM permits, with or without the machines fitted.
pitfalls: Using anchor bolt tension to pull a twisted baseplate flat.
Levelling on the baseplate frame instead of the machined pads.
Lifting a loaded baseplate by unsuitable points and distorting it.

topics.title: Grouting
topics.body: Grout fills the space between the baseplate and the foundation, transferring load evenly and making the baseplate and foundation act as one stiff unit. The grout type, epoxy or cementitious, is selected by the project specification and placed exactly as the grout manufacturer instructs, including surface preparation, temperature limits during placing and curing time. Forms are built tightly around the baseplate, and grout is poured continuously from one side so that air is pushed out through the vent holes, with grout holes in the baseplate used to fill the cavity. Voids left under the baseplate reduce stiffness and can lead to vibration and alignment changes. After curing, the baseplate is tapped (sounded) to find hollow areas, which are repaired as the grout manufacturer recommends. Levelling screws are backed off or removed after curing if the specification requires it, so that the grout carries the load.
checks: Grout type matches the project specification.
Placing and curing as the grout manufacturer instructs.
Sounding test after curing; voids recorded and repaired.
Levelling screws dealt with as specified after curing.
pitfalls: Pouring grout from several sides and trapping air.
Grouting outside the temperature limits given by the grout manufacturer.
Carrying out final alignment before the grout has cured.

topics.title: Anchor bolts
topics.body: Anchor (foundation) bolts hold the baseplate down and resist overturning and sliding forces. They are positioned with a template to the OEM foundation drawing and either cast in or set in sleeves or pockets, so that small adjustments are possible during baseplate setting. They must project far enough to engage the full nut with its washer. Sleeves are filled or sealed as the specification requires; where a free stretch length is specified, grout must not bond the bolt over that length. Anchor bolts are normally tightened only after the grout has cured, to the values in the project specification or OEM manual and in a pattern that does not distort the baseplate. Level and alignment are checked again after tightening, because a baseplate that moves when the anchor bolts are tightened was not properly supported.
checks: Bolt positions set with a template before the concrete is placed.
Projection and thread condition correct; threads protected during grouting.
Bolts tightened after grout cure as specified; level re-checked afterwards.
pitfalls: Tightening anchor bolts before the grout has cured.
Bending bolts to fit misplaced baseplate holes.
Letting grout fill sleeves where a free stretch length is required.

topics.title: Pump and motor levelling
topics.body: Once the baseplate is grouted, the pump is set on its mounting pads and checked for level at the reference surfaces named by the OEM, which for a split case pump may include the casing joint flange, the nozzle faces or machined bosses. The motor is then set on its pads with shims so that its shaft height and position allow alignment. Shims should be clean, flat, corrosion resistant, of full contact size and as few in number as practical. Before alignment, every foot is checked for soft foot: a foot that does not sit flat distorts the casing or motor frame when its bolt is tightened. Soft foot is corrected with shims at the affected foot, not by over-tightening. The pump is normally treated as the fixed machine and the motor is moved to achieve alignment, because the pump is connected to the piping.
checks: Pump level checked at the OEM reference surfaces.
Soft foot checked at every foot and corrected.
Shims clean, flat, full size and few in number.
pitfalls: Correcting soft foot by tightening the hold-down bolts harder.
Using many thin or damaged shims.
Moving the pump after the piping has been connected.

scene.label: Level the pump; check soft foot

topics.title: Coupling alignment
topics.body: Misalignment between the pump and motor shafts creates cyclic loads on the coupling, bearings and seals, and is a frequent cause of vibration and premature failure. Alignment is checked for both offset and angularity in the vertical and horizontal planes, using a laser system or dial indicators (reverse-indicator or rim-and-face methods). A preliminary alignment is made before grouting and piping, and the final alignment after the grout has cured and the piping is connected, because both can move the machines. Where the pump or motor grows thermally in service, the OEM may specify cold offsets so that the shafts come into line at operating temperature. With a spacer coupling, the distance between shaft ends must also match the coupling specification. Tolerances come from the OEM or the coupling manufacturer. A flexible coupling can accept misalignment without failing immediately, but that does not mean the bearings and seals tolerate it.
checks: Soft foot corrected before alignment.
Offset and angularity in both planes within the OEM or coupling tolerances.
Thermal offsets applied where specified.
Distance between shaft ends correct for the spacer.
Final readings recorded after the piping is connected.
pitfalls: Aligning only with a straight edge across the hubs.
Doing the final alignment before the piping is connected.
Ignoring specified thermal growth offsets.

scene.label: Offset and angularity in both planes

topics.title: Suction piping arrangement
topics.body: A double-suction impeller takes nominally half the flow through each eye, so the flow arriving at the suction nozzle should be uniform. An elbow close to the suction nozzle lying in the plane of the shaft (for this horizontal pump, an elbow turning in the horizontal plane) throws more flow towards the outside of the bend, and therefore towards one eye. The resulting unequal flow distribution makes one side run closer to its cavitation limit, increases residual axial thrust, and raises noise, vibration and bearing and seal loads. ANSI/HI 9.6.6, Rotodynamic Pumps for Pump Piping, recommends a straight, uniform run of pipe ahead of the suction nozzle and advises against elbows in the plane of the shaft close to double-suction pumps; it expresses the run in pipe diameters, so consult the current edition. An elbow in the vertical plane, perpendicular to the shaft, disturbs both eyes symmetrically and is less harmful, but straight-run guidance still applies. Keep the suction line short, direct, generously sized and free of high points where air can collect.
checks: Straight run ahead of the suction nozzle as recommended by ANSI/HI 9.6.6 and the piping design.
No elbow in the plane of the shaft close to the suction nozzle.
No high points or air traps in the suction line.
Suction isolation valve fully open in service and never used for throttling.
Temporary start-up strainer, where fitted, monitored and removed or replaced as the procedure directs.
pitfalls: A horizontal elbow bolted directly to the suction nozzle.
Throttling flow with the suction valve.
An undersized suction pipe with high velocity.
A suction line that rises and then falls, trapping air.

scene.label: Uniform flow to both impeller eyes

topics.title: Discharge piping arrangement
topics.body: The discharge line normally includes a concentric increaser at the nozzle, a non-return (check) valve to prevent reverse flow and reverse rotation when the pump stops, and an isolation valve for maintenance. The check valve is usually placed between the pump and the isolation valve so that it can be isolated for maintenance. Valve types and positions are chosen by the system designer, taking account of pressure surge (water hammer) when pumps start and stop. Pressure tappings near the discharge nozzle allow the discharge pressure to be measured for performance checks. Expansion joints, where used, must be restrained, for example with tie rods, or arranged so that pressure thrust is not transmitted to the pump nozzle; an unrestrained bellows can apply a large force to the casing. Air release valves are fitted at high points of the discharge line, and the piping is supported independently of the pump.
checks: Check valve and isolation valve installed as designed and accessible.
Expansion joints restrained as designed.
Pressure tapping and gauge near the discharge nozzle.
Air release valves at high points.
pitfalls: An unrestrained expansion joint next to the nozzle.
A check valve type unsuited to the surge conditions of the system.
Discharge pipe weight carried by the pump nozzle.

scene.label: Discharge: increaser, check and isolation valves

topics.title: Reducer orientation
topics.body: The suction pipe is often larger than the pump suction nozzle, so a reducer is needed. On the suction side an eccentric reducer is normally used, installed with its flat side up. With the flat side on top, the top of the pipe is continuous and any air or gas in the liquid is carried through to the pump instead of collecting. A concentric reducer, or an eccentric reducer installed flat side down, forms a pocket at the top of the pipe where air accumulates. The pocket reduces the flow area, can release slugs of air into the impeller, and can cause loss of prime, noise, vibration and unstable performance. Some arrangements, for example where the supply drops from above, may justify a different orientation, but any departure must be justified by the piping designer against ANSI/HI 9.6.6. On the discharge side a concentric increaser is usual.
checks: Suction eccentric reducer installed flat side up unless the design justifies otherwise.
No concentric reducer on a horizontal suction line at the pump.
Discharge increaser installed as designed.
pitfalls: An eccentric reducer installed upside down.
A concentric reducer at the suction nozzle trapping air.

topics.title: Pipe supports
topics.body: The pump casing is not designed to carry the weight of the piping, valves and liquid. Suction and discharge piping is supported independently, with supports close to the pump nozzles so that the nozzles carry as little load as possible. Supports, guides and anchors are arranged by the piping designer to carry the weight and to control thermal expansion so that growth is directed away from the pump. Heavy valves and fittings near the pump need their own supports, and spring supports may be needed where thermal movement is significant. Supports must be installed and adjusted before the piping is connected to the pump, and temporary construction supports must be replaced by the permanent ones. After installation, each support is checked to confirm that it actually carries load rather than simply touching the pipe, and that spring supports have had their travel stops removed.
checks: Supports close to both nozzles carry the pipe weight.
Valves and fittings near the pump are supported.
Thermal movement directed away from the pump as designed.
Spring supports set to their design positions, with travel stops removed.
pitfalls: Removing temporary supports and relying on the pump nozzle.
Supports installed but not adjusted to carry load.
Spring support travel stops left in place after commissioning.

scene.label: Piping supported independently of the pump

topics.title: Pipe strain
topics.body: Pipe strain is force or moment applied to the pump by the piping, because the pipe flanges do not line up with the pump nozzles or because the piping is not properly supported. Even moderate strain can distort the casing, shift the pump on its baseplate and spoil the coupling alignment, leading to bearing overload, seal leakage, wear ring rubbing and, in a split case pump, casing joint leakage. Pipe flanges should meet the pump flanges square, concentric and at the correct gap without force before any bolt is inserted. Flange bolts must never be used to pull the piping into position. A common check is to set dial indicators on the coupling hubs, or use the laser alignment system, and watch for shaft movement while the flange bolts are tightened or released; movement beyond the site criterion means the piping must be corrected. Alignment is re-checked after the piping is finally connected.
checks: Flanges parallel, concentric and correctly gapped before bolting.
Shaft movement monitored while the flange bolts are tightened.
Alignment re-checked after the piping is connected.
pitfalls: Pulling piping into place with flange bolts or chain blocks.
Correcting a piping misfit by moving the pump.
Connecting the piping before the grout has cured.

topics.title: Nozzle loading
topics.body: Even well-fitted piping applies some forces and moments to the pump nozzles in service, from pressure, the weight of pipe and liquid, thermal expansion and transient events. The OEM states the allowable nozzle forces and moments for the pump, sometimes by reference to an industry standard, and the piping designer must show by analysis that the loads in all operating cases, hot and cold, stay within them. Loads above the allowables distort the casing and baseplate, move the pump shaft relative to the motor and can overload the casing feet and hold-down bolts. In this arrangement both nozzles are on the lower casing half, so the lower half and its feet carry the nozzle loads. The upper half can therefore be removed without disconnecting the piping, which is an important maintenance advantage, but it does not reduce the loads the lower half must carry.
checks: Allowable nozzle loads obtained from the OEM.
Piping analysis covers all operating and transient cases.
Supports installed exactly as analysed.
pitfalls: Assuming the pump can accept whatever load the piping applies.
Changing supports in the field after the analysis was completed.

topics.title: Vent and drain arrangement
topics.body: Vents let air or gas escape when the pump is filled and primed, and drains allow the casing to be emptied for maintenance or to protect it from freezing. The casing vent is at the high point of the upper half and the drain connections are at the low points of the lower half. Vent and drain valves should be accessible and, where the liquid is hazardous or hot, piped to a safe location or a closed system as the site requires. High points of the suction and discharge piping also need vents, and low points need drains. Seal and packing leakage is collected by the baseplate drip rim and routed to a suitable drain. Vent and drain connections are closed or plugged in operation, and their piping must not load the casing or prevent the upper half from being lifted.
checks: Casing vent at the upper-half high point is accessible.
Drains at the lower-half low points, piped as the site requires.
High-point vents and low-point drains fitted on the piping.
Drip rim drain clear and routed to a suitable drain.
pitfalls: Vent piping fixed rigidly to structure so that the upper half cannot be lifted.
Hazardous liquid drained to an open drain.
Plugs left out after maintenance.

scene.label: Vent at the top, drains at the bottom

guidance.title: Pre-commissioning
guidance.intro: Pre-commissioning checks confirm that the installation is complete and correct, and that the pump can be filled, rotated and started safely. Each check is recorded and signed off. Many first-start failures, such as seized bearings, burnt seals and reverse rotation, are prevented at this stage.
guidance.disclaimer: General training guidance only. All pre-commissioning checks must be verified against the particular OEM manual, the seal, coupling and motor manufacturer instructions, and the site-approved procedures. Electrical tests are carried out only by qualified and authorised personnel. No acceptance values are given here.

topics.title: Foundation and grouting checks
topics.body: Before the first start, confirm that the foundation and grout have reached the strength required by their specifications and that the baseplate is fully supported. If the grout was not sounded after curing, sound it now and repair any hollow areas. Check the grout edges and the foundation for cracks, and confirm that the anchor bolts have been tightened to the specified values and are complete with nuts, washers and any locking devices. Confirm that the levelling screws have been dealt with as the specification requires. Check that the baseplate drip rim drain is clear and that the area around the foundation drains freely, because standing liquid can damage grout and corrode the baseplate. Record the final level and alignment readings taken after grouting as the reference for later checks.
checks: Grout cured as specified; sounding test done and voids repaired.
No cracks in grout edges or foundation.
Anchor bolts tightened as specified and complete.
Drip rim and foundation drainage clear.
pitfalls: Starting before the grout has reached its specified strength.
Ignoring hollow-sounding areas under the baseplate.

topics.title: Casing inspection
topics.body: Inspect the outside of the casing and confirm that it is complete and ready for filling. The casing joint nuts must be fully tightened to the OEM values, with records available, especially if the casing was opened on site. Drain plugs and vent valves are fitted and closed, gauge connections are made, and any transport covers or blanks on the nozzles were removed before the piping was connected. Find out whether preservation compounds were applied inside the casing for storage, and whether the OEM requires them to be removed or flushed out before service. Check that the casing hold-down bolts are tight and that nothing on the casing is being used to support piping, cables or access platforms. Look for damage from transport or installation, such as cracked bosses or bent small-bore connections.
checks: Casing joint bolting tightened and recorded.
Drains plugged; vents closed and accessible.
Preservation removed or flushed where the OEM requires it.
Casing hold-down bolts tight; no external loads hung on the casing.
pitfalls: Leaving a transport blank in a flange.
Starting with storage preservative still inside a casing where the OEM requires its removal.

topics.title: Shaft rotation by hand
topics.body: Before the motor is ever started, the pump rotor is turned by hand to prove that it is free. With the coupling spacer removed, the pump and motor can each be checked on their own, which shows clearly which machine is responsible for any tightness. The rotor should turn smoothly through complete revolutions without rubbing, scraping, tight spots or noise from the wear rings, seals or bearings. A pump that is stiff to turn must not be started; the cause may be pipe strain distorting the casing, an incorrectly set seal, debris in the casing or a bearing problem. A few turns by hand are normally acceptable with a mechanical seal fitted, but follow the seal manufacturer guidance on turning a seal dry. Turn the shaft with a strap wrench or at the coupling hub, never with tools that mark the shaft or the hub fits.
checks: Pump rotor turns freely through complete revolutions, uncoupled.
Motor rotor turns freely, uncoupled.
No rubbing, scraping or tight spots.
pitfalls: Starting a pump that is stiff to turn.
Using pipe wrenches on the shaft.

scene.label: Turn the pump rotor by hand, uncoupled

topics.title: Bearing lubrication
topics.body: Pumps are often shipped without oil in the bearing housings, so never assume the bearings are lubricated. For oil lubrication, fill each housing with the oil type and grade specified by the OEM to the level shown at the sight glass, and set any constant-level oiler to the height the OEM gives; an incorrect oiler setting is a common cause of bearing problems. For grease lubrication, confirm that the grease is the type specified and compatible with any grease already in the bearings, and that the housings contain the quantity the OEM specifies; overfilling with grease causes churning and overheating. The DE and NDE housings may have different lubricant quantities and arrangements, so check each one separately. Breathers, drains and plugs should be fitted and clean. Motor bearings are checked as the motor manufacturer instructs.
checks: Lubricant type and grade as the OEM specifies.
Oil level correct at both housings; oilers set as the OEM directs.
Grease quantity as specified; no overfilling.
Motor bearings lubricated as the motor manufacturer instructs.
pitfalls: Assuming oil was filled at the factory.
Mixing incompatible greases.
Setting a constant-level oiler at the wrong height.

scene.label: Correct lubricant at both bearing housings

topics.title: Seal installation
topics.body: Confirm that the shaft sealing at both ends is completely installed and ready to run. For mechanical seals, check that the cartridge setting plates or clips have been removed after the seal was secured, the drive collar set screws are tight and the gland nuts are evenly tightened. Seal support systems, such as flush, quench, barrier or buffer arrangements, must be connected to the correct ports shown on the seal arrangement drawing, with valves set and any reservoirs filled and pressurised as specified. For gland packing, confirm that the correct number of rings has been fitted with staggered joints, that the lantern ring lines up with the flush connection and that the gland nuts are only finger-tight, ready for adjustment while running. Packing needs a controlled leakage to cool and lubricate it. Check that the flush or seal water supply is available and the drip rim drain is clear.
checks: Cartridge seal setting plates removed.
Seal support system connected per the seal arrangement drawing and in service.
Packing gland nuts finger-tight; lantern ring aligned with the flush port.
Flush or seal water supply available.
pitfalls: Starting with setting plates still fitted.
Flush lines connected to the wrong ports.
Packing tightened hard before the first start.

scene.label: Seals complete and support systems connected

topics.title: Coupling alignment
topics.body: Final alignment is confirmed after the grout has cured, the piping is fully connected and supported, and the pump has been filled if the OEM procedure requires it. The readings of offset and angularity in both planes, and the distance between shaft ends, are compared with the OEM or coupling manufacturer tolerances and any specified thermal offsets. Soft foot is checked again at all pump and motor feet. The hold-down bolts are tightened before the final readings are taken, and the readings are repeated if any bolt is adjusted. Record the as-left alignment, the method and the instrument used, because these readings become the baseline for later checks. Where the OEM recommends it, plan a hot alignment check once the pump has reached normal operating temperature, because thermal growth of the pump and motor can change the alignment.
checks: Final alignment within tolerance after piping connection.
Soft foot re-checked.
As-left readings, method and instrument recorded.
Hot alignment check planned where the OEM recommends it.
pitfalls: Accepting alignment readings taken before the piping was connected.
Adjusting a hold-down bolt after the final readings without repeating them.

topics.title: Coupling guard installation
topics.body: The coupling guard prevents contact with the rotating coupling and shaft ends. It must be complete, securely fixed and positioned so that it does not touch any rotating part, while still allowing access to lubrication and inspection points where the design provides them. Openings and gaps must comply with the applicable machinery safety requirements. Before the guard is closed, the coupling bolts and fasteners are confirmed as tightened to the coupling manufacturer values and the spacer is fitted in its marked orientation. Where an uncoupled motor run is needed, the site procedure defines how the motor half-coupling and key are secured or removed and how the shaft end is guarded during that run. The pump must never be run with the coupling guard removed or only partly fitted.
checks: Guard complete, secure and clear of rotating parts.
Coupling bolts tightened to the coupling manufacturer values before closing the guard.
Guarding arrangement for any uncoupled motor run defined in the procedure.
pitfalls: Running briefly without the guard "just to check".
A guard that rubs on the coupling.

topics.title: Motor checks
topics.body: Check that the motor suits the duty: the nameplate voltage, frequency, power, speed and enclosure must match the supply and the pump data sheet. The motor hold-down bolts must be tight and the feet shimmed as in the final alignment. Confirm that the cooling air path is clear, the fan cover is fitted and nothing obstructs the air inlet. The motor bearings are lubricated as the motor manufacturer specifies. If the motor has been stored, check whether the anti-condensation heaters were energised and whether bearing re-greasing or other storage recovery steps are required. Terminal box connections, cable glands and earthing are checked by qualified electrical personnel, and protection settings such as overload, earth fault and any winding or bearing temperature sensors are set by the electrical discipline in line with the motor data and site procedures.
checks: Nameplate data matches the supply and the pump data sheet.
Hold-down bolts tight; cooling air path clear.
Motor bearings lubricated as specified.
Terminations, earthing and protection settings checked by qualified personnel.
pitfalls: Overlooking storage recovery requirements for a motor that has stood idle.
Obstructing the fan inlet with cables or covers.

topics.title: Electrical insulation checks
topics.body: An insulation resistance test confirms that the motor windings and cables are dry and undamaged before they are energised, especially after storage, transport or exposure to moisture. The test is carried out only by qualified and authorised electrical personnel, under the site electrical safety rules, using the test voltage and acceptance criteria given by the motor manufacturer and the applicable electrical standards. Electronic equipment such as variable-speed drives, soft starters and sensors must be disconnected or protected before testing as their manufacturers require, because the test voltage can damage them. Results are corrected for temperature where the procedure requires and recorded for trend comparison. A low or falling result is investigated, for example by drying the motor as the manufacturer recommends, before any attempt to energise it. Pump maintenance staff do not carry out these tests unless they are authorised to do so.
checks: Test carried out by qualified, authorised personnel.
Electronic equipment disconnected or protected before testing.
Results recorded and compared with the motor manufacturer criteria.
pitfalls: Testing with a variable-speed drive still connected.
Energising a motor with an unexplained low result.

topics.title: Correct rotation verification
topics.body: Running a centrifugal pump in the wrong direction gives low head and flow and, in some designs, can loosen threaded parts such as sleeve nuts. The required direction is shown by the arrow on the casing. It is verified on the motor alone, with the coupling spacer removed, by a short bump (jog) start carried out by authorised personnel under the site procedure. Before the bump test, the motor half-coupling and key are secured or removed as the procedure requires so that nothing can be thrown off, the guarding arrangement for the test is in place and everyone stands clear. If the direction is wrong, the supply connections are changed by qualified electrical personnel and the test is repeated. The pump itself must never be bump tested to check rotation unless it is full of liquid and the procedure permits it, because the seals and wear rings can be damaged very quickly without liquid.
checks: Direction arrow on the casing identified.
Bump test performed uncoupled, under the site procedure.
Motor half-coupling and key secured or removed before the test.
Correct direction confirmed and recorded before coupling up.
pitfalls: Bump testing with a loose key in the motor shaft keyway.
Checking rotation with the pump coupled and dry.

topics.title: Suction line inspection
topics.body: Debris left in new or modified piping is a common cause of damage at first start: welding rod, slag, rags, bolts and gasket pieces can be drawn into the impeller eyes and wear rings. The suction line should be cleaned or flushed as the site procedure requires before it is connected to the pump. A temporary start-up strainer is often fitted in the suction line, with differential pressure monitoring so that a blocking strainer is detected before it starves the pump; it is removed or replaced with a permanent strainer as the procedure directs. Check that the suction isolation valve can open fully and that flange gaskets are centred and do not protrude into the bore. Confirm that the eccentric reducer is flat side up and that the line has no unintended high points. For a suction tank or sump, check the liquid level and the intake arrangement.
checks: Suction line cleaned or flushed as required.
Temporary strainer fitted with differential pressure monitoring where specified.
Gaskets centred; no protrusion into the bore.
Eccentric reducer flat side up; no air traps.
Suction source level adequate.
pitfalls: Connecting unflushed piping to the pump.
Leaving a blocked temporary strainer unmonitored.

topics.title: Priming and venting
topics.body: A centrifugal pump of this type cannot pump air and must be completely full of liquid before it is started. With a flooded suction, the pump is filled by opening the suction valve and venting the casing at the high-point vent until a steady flow of liquid without air comes out. Where the liquid level is below the pump (suction lift), a priming method designed for the installation is needed, such as a foot valve with a filling connection or a vacuum priming system. On a horizontal split case pump the top of the volute and the upper part of each seal chamber or stuffing box can trap air; vent them as the OEM and seal manufacturer describe, because mechanical seal faces must be surrounded by liquid before rotation. Turning the rotor by hand during venting can help release trapped air. Hot or hazardous liquids are vented to a safe location.
checks: Casing vented until liquid flows free of air.
Seal chambers or stuffing boxes vented as described by the OEM.
Priming system in service where the installation has a suction lift.
Vents closed after priming.
pitfalls: Starting with air trapped at the top of the casing or seal chambers.
Assuming a flooded suction has vented itself.

scene.label: Fill and vent before any start

topics.title: Instrumentation checks
topics.body: Instruments allow the start-up to be monitored and the pump to be protected. Suction and discharge pressure gauges or transmitters should be installed at the tappings, calibrated and fitted with open isolation valves. The flow meter, where provided, should be commissioned with a range suited to the expected flow. Bearing temperature and vibration sensors at both bearing housings should be installed, connected and giving sensible readings before the start. Protective functions such as low suction pressure, low flow or minimum-flow valve operation, high bearing temperature, high vibration and seal leakage alarms are set to the values in the site documentation and function tested by the responsible discipline. Confirm that the control system shows the correct pump tag and units, and that readings will be recorded during the first run.
checks: Pressure instruments calibrated and isolation valves open.
Flow meter commissioned where fitted.
Temperature and vibration sensors at both bearings reading correctly.
Protective trips and alarms set and function tested.
pitfalls: Gauge isolation valves left closed.
Protective trips bypassed and not restored.

guidance.title: Commissioning
guidance.intro: Commissioning is the first controlled operation of the pump in its system. The aims are to start safely, confirm that the pump performs as expected and record baseline readings for future condition monitoring. Every reading is compared with the OEM data and the site acceptance criteria; none are given here. If any reading is abnormal, stop the pump in a controlled way and investigate before restarting.
guidance.disclaimer: General training guidance only. Start-up sequences, valve positions, operating limits and acceptance criteria must be checked against the particular OEM manual, the system design and the site-approved commissioning procedures. No limits for temperature, vibration, pressure, flow or current are given here.

topics.title: Start-up sequence
topics.body: The start-up follows a written procedure agreed between operations, maintenance and the system owner. Before the start, all pre-commissioning checks are signed off, the pump is primed and vented, lubrication and seal support systems are in service, valves are in the positions the procedure specifies, protective trips are active, and everyone not needed is clear of the coupling and the piping. Communication between the control room and the field team is confirmed. After the start, the pump should reach speed and build pressure promptly; if it does not, stop it. Valves are then moved to their running positions in the sequence the procedure gives, while suction pressure, discharge pressure, flow, motor current, bearing temperatures, vibration, noise and seal leakage are watched. The first run is often kept short, followed by a stop and checks, before a longer run to stable temperatures.
checks: Pre-commissioning sign-off complete.
Pump primed and vented; auxiliaries in service.
Valves positioned as the procedure specifies.
Communication established and area clear.
Pump reaches speed and builds pressure promptly.
pitfalls: Starting before all pre-commissioning items are closed.
Continuing to run when pressure does not build.

topics.title: Discharge valve arrangements
topics.body: There is no single universal rule for the discharge valve position at start-up: it depends on the pump characteristics and the system, and is set by the pump and system procedure. For many radial-flow centrifugal pumps, such as this split case pump, power rises with flow, so starting against a closed or partly open discharge valve reduces the starting power and helps limit pressure surges; the valve is then opened promptly and in a controlled way to the running position. Running against a closed valve for more than a short time overheats the liquid, so the OEM limits it. Other systems start with the valve open or partly open, for example into a pressurised system behind a check valve, with automatically sequenced valves, with a minimum-flow bypass in service, or on long pipelines where slow valve movement is needed to avoid water hammer. Pumps operating in parallel need a coordinated sequence. Always follow the approved procedure for the specific pump and system.
checks: Discharge valve start position taken from the approved procedure.
Time at closed or near-closed valve kept within the OEM limit.
Valve movement rate suitable for surge control.
pitfalls: Applying a rule from a different pump or system.
Leaving the pump running against a closed valve while other tasks are done.

scene.label: Valve sequence per the approved procedure

topics.title: Minimum flow and dry running cautions
topics.body: A centrifugal pump must never run dry and must not run below the minimum continuous flow stated by the OEM. Without liquid, mechanical seal faces lose their lubricating film and can crack or burn very quickly, packing overheats, and the close-clearance wear rings can rub and seize. At very low flow or against a closed valve, most of the input power becomes heat in a small volume of liquid, which can then boil. Low flow also causes internal recirculation at the impeller eyes and outlet, leading to vibration, noise, higher radial loads and cavitation damage. Protection may include a minimum-flow bypass line or valve, low-flow and low-suction-pressure trips, and seal leakage or temperature alarms, as designed for the system. Operators should know the allowable operating region from the OEM curve and avoid prolonged operation at its edges, including run-out at very high flow.
checks: Pump confirmed full of liquid before start.
Minimum-flow arrangement in service where fitted.
Operating point inside the OEM allowable operating region.
Low-flow and low-suction-pressure protection active.
pitfalls: Running with the discharge closed and no minimum-flow path.
Bump testing a dry pump.
Prolonged operation at the extremes of the curve.

scene.label: Never dry; never below minimum flow

topics.title: Suction pressure
topics.body: Suction pressure shows whether the pump is receiving liquid at sufficient pressure to avoid cavitation. It is read at the suction tapping close to the pump and compared with the design value. From it, the net positive suction head available (NPSHA) can be estimated and compared with the NPSH required by the pump at the operating flow, with the margin specified for the application. A falling suction pressure during the run may indicate a clogging strainer, a partly closed suction valve, a falling tank level or air ingress. Fluctuating suction pressure can point to vortices at the intake or air entrainment. Low suction pressure combined with a crackling noise and unsteady discharge pressure suggests cavitation. The strainer differential pressure is monitored closely during early operation and the strainer cleaned when needed.
checks: Suction pressure compared with the design value.
NPSH margin confirmed at the operating flow.
Strainer differential pressure monitored.
pitfalls: Ignoring a steadily falling suction pressure.
Reading a gauge mounted far from the pump without correcting for losses and elevation.

topics.title: Discharge pressure
topics.body: Discharge pressure, together with suction pressure and flow, shows whether the pump is delivering the expected head. The differential pressure is converted to head using the liquid density and compared with the OEM performance curve at the measured flow and speed, allowing for gauge elevations and velocity effects where the procedure requires. A discharge pressure that is too low may indicate reverse rotation, air in the casing, a blocked impeller, excessive wear ring clearance, the wrong impeller diameter or a system drawing more flow than expected. A higher-than-expected pressure with low flow suggests a restricted discharge, such as a partly closed valve. Readings should be steady at a steady operating point; strong fluctuation suggests cavitation, air, or operation in an unstable part of the curve.
checks: Differential head compared with the OEM curve at the measured flow.
Readings steady at a steady operating point.
pitfalls: Comparing discharge pressure alone with the curve, without suction pressure.
Ignoring liquid density when converting pressure to head.

scene.label: Discharge pressure versus the OEM curve

topics.title: Flow monitoring
topics.body: Flow measurement shows where the pump is operating on its curve. The operating point should lie within the allowable operating region given by the OEM, and preferably near the best efficiency point for long life. Operating well to the left of the curve (low flow) increases recirculation, radial loads, vibration and temperature rise. Operating well to the right (high flow, towards run-out) increases the NPSH required, risks cavitation and can overload the motor. Where no permanent flow meter is fitted, flow may be estimated with temporary instruments, from system data, or with care from the pump curve using differential head and motor power, as the site procedure allows. Flow, pressure and power readings are taken at the same time so that the pump performance can be compared with the OEM test curve.
checks: Operating point within the OEM allowable operating region.
Flow, pressures and power recorded together.
pitfalls: Accepting operation at run-out because the flow looks good.
Estimating flow from one reading without cross-checking.

topics.title: Bearing temperature
topics.body: Bearing temperatures rise after start-up and should settle at a steady value once the pump, lubricant and surroundings reach equilibrium. They are monitored at both bearing housings, by installed sensors or contact instruments, and trended until stable. The acceptable values come from the OEM and the site procedures, not from a general rule. The DE and NDE bearings are different: the NDE locating bearings carry the residual axial thrust as well as radial load, so the two housings may run at different temperatures. A newly greased bearing may run warmer for a period while excess grease is expelled. A temperature that keeps rising, or rises suddenly, warns of incorrect lubrication, overfilled grease, incorrect oil level, misalignment, excessive thrust or incorrect bearing fitting. Stop and investigate rather than continuing to run.
checks: Temperatures at both housings trended until stable.
Stable values compared with the OEM and site limits.
DE and NDE assessed separately.
pitfalls: Assuming both bearings should run at the same temperature.
Continuing to run while a temperature is still climbing.

topics.title: Vibration monitoring
topics.body: Vibration readings are taken at both bearing housings in the horizontal, vertical and axial directions once the pump has reached a steady operating point, and repeated at the other operating conditions in the procedure. Acceptance criteria come from the OEM, the contract and the vibration standard named in the site documentation; no universal limit should be assumed. The first set of readings becomes the baseline for condition monitoring, so measurement positions are marked and the instrument and settings recorded. High vibration at start-up is commonly linked to misalignment, soft foot, pipe strain, an unbalanced or damaged rotor, poor grouting, resonance of the foundation or piping, or hydraulic causes such as cavitation, low-flow recirculation or unequal flow to the two impeller eyes. Frequency analysis by competent personnel helps to separate these causes.
checks: Readings in three directions at both bearing housings.
Results compared with the specified acceptance criteria.
Measurement positions marked; baseline recorded.
pitfalls: Using a limit from a different machine or standard than the one specified.
Taking readings before the operating point has stabilised.

topics.title: Seal leakage
topics.body: Seal behaviour is checked at both shaft exits during the first run. A mechanical seal may show slight weeping while the faces bed in; continuous dripping or a stream is not normal, and the pump should be stopped and the seal investigated, after checking that the flush is flowing and the seal chamber was vented. Gland packing, by contrast, needs a controlled leakage to lubricate and cool it. After start-up, the packing gland nuts are tightened gradually and evenly in small steps, allowing time for the leakage and temperature to settle after each adjustment, until the leakage given by the OEM or site procedure is reached. Packing must never be tightened to stop leakage completely, because it will overheat and wear the sleeve. Check the casing joint, flanges and auxiliary connections for leaks at the same time.
checks: Mechanical seals: no continuous leakage; flush flowing.
Packing: leakage adjusted gradually to the specified rate.
Casing joint, flanges and small-bore connections leak-free.
pitfalls: Tightening packing to zero leakage.
Adjusting glands on a running pump without the safe method and access required by the site procedure.

topics.title: Motor current
topics.body: Motor current, read from the control system or by qualified personnel, indicates the power the pump is absorbing. It is compared with the motor nameplate full-load current and with the power expected from the OEM curve at the measured flow and the actual liquid density. Current above expectation may mean the pump is running at higher flow than intended (towards run-out), the liquid is denser or more viscous than designed, the impeller diameter is larger than required, or there is mechanical rubbing or binding. Current below expectation may mean low flow, a closed valve, air in the pump or reverse rotation. The current in all three phases should be balanced. A motor that trips on overload must not be restarted repeatedly without investigation, and the motor manufacturer limits on the number of starts must be respected.
checks: Current compared with nameplate and expected power.
Phase currents balanced.
Start limits of the motor respected.
pitfalls: Repeated restarts after an overload trip.
Ignoring a low current that indicates air or low flow.

topics.title: Abnormal noise
topics.body: Listening to the pump during the first run gives early warning of problems. A crackling, gravel-like noise from the casing usually indicates cavitation, often linked to low suction pressure or operation far from the design flow. Surging or irregular noise with fluctuating pressure suggests air entrainment or unstable low-flow operation. A rumbling or high-pitched noise from a bearing housing indicates bearing damage, contamination or a lubrication problem. Scraping or squealing points to rubbing at the wear rings, seals or bearing housing seals, or to a seal running dry. Knocking or rattling near the coupling suggests misalignment, a loose coupling element or a loose guard. Any abnormal noise is investigated; if it suggests rubbing, dry running, cavitation or bearing distress, stop the pump in a controlled way and do not restart until the cause is understood.
checks: No cavitation, rubbing or bearing noise.
No knocking or rattling at the coupling or guard.
pitfalls: Treating cavitation noise as normal pump noise.
Restarting before the cause of an abnormal noise is found.

topics.title: Records and handover
topics.body: At the end of commissioning, record a complete set of baseline data at the agreed operating points: suction and discharge pressure, flow, motor current or power, bearing temperatures at both housings, vibration at the marked positions, seal or packing leakage and ambient conditions. Note any adjustments made, such as packing gland settings or valve positions. Where the OEM recommends a hot alignment check, carry it out after the pump has run at operating temperature, with the pump correctly isolated first. These records allow later readings to be compared with the as-commissioned condition, which is the basis of effective condition monitoring. Hand over to operations with the records, the OEM manual, the approved operating limits and any open punch-list items clearly listed.
checks: Baseline data recorded at the agreed operating points.
Adjustments recorded.
Hot alignment check done where the OEM recommends it.
Documentation and open items handed over.
pitfalls: Handing over without baseline readings.
Carrying out a hot alignment check without proper isolation.

lessons.title: Introduction to Horizontal Split Case Pump
lessons.objective: Name the main assemblies of a horizontal split case pump and state two reasons why it is chosen for large-flow duties.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: What is a split case pump?
chapters.narration: Welcome to this lesson on the horizontal split case pump. This is a centrifugal pump whose casing is divided into an upper half and a lower half. The two halves meet on a horizontal plane that passes through the centreline of the shaft. Because the joint runs along the shaft axis, this design is also called an axially split pump. The model in front of you is a single stage pump with one double suction impeller. The rotor is supported by a bearing at each end, so the impeller sits between the bearings. Please note that this is an educational model. It shows typical features, not one manufacturer's exact design.

chapters.title: Where it is used
chapters.narration: Split case pumps are widely used where large volumes of liquid must be moved reliably for long periods. Typical examples include municipal water supply, raw water intake, cooling water circulation in power and process plants, fire protection, irrigation and large building services systems. Most of these duties involve clean or lightly contaminated water, although suitable materials allow other liquids to be handled. The pump is usually driven by an electric motor through a flexible coupling. Both machines sit on a common steel baseplate, which is grouted onto a concrete foundation. The duty, size and materials of any real pump always come from its selection data and the manufacturer.

chapters.title: The main assemblies
chapters.narration: Let us separate the pump into its main assemblies. The casing forms the pressure boundary and the flow passages, including the volute. The impeller is the part that adds energy to the liquid. The shaft carries the impeller and transmits torque from the motor. A bearing housing at each end supports the shaft. Where the shaft leaves the casing, a shaft seal at each end limits leakage. This can be a mechanical seal or gland packing. Finally, the coupling connects the pump to the motor, and the baseplate holds everything in line.

chapters.title: Nozzles in the lower half
chapters.narration: Look at the suction and discharge nozzles. Both are cast into the lower half of the casing. They point horizontally, on opposite sides of the pump. This layout gives the split case pump its best known advantage. Once the pump is isolated and drained, the upper half can be lifted off without disconnecting the main suction and discharge pipes. The motor normally stays in place as well. This gives direct access to the impeller, wear rings and seals. The steps and precautions for this are covered in the upper casing removal lesson.

scene.label: Upper half lifted, main piping undisturbed

chapters.title: Double suction in brief
chapters.narration: Inside, the liquid enters the impeller from both sides at once. The suction chamber divides the incoming flow and guides it to two impeller eyes. The impeller then discharges into a single volute. This double suction arrangement allows a large flow through one impeller, with a lower velocity at each eye than a single suction impeller of the same flow would need. It also means that the axial forces from the two sides largely oppose each other. They do not cancel completely, so a locating bearing is still needed. Later lessons explain each of these ideas using the live model.

lessons.title: Difference Between Split Case and End Suction Pump
lessons.objective: Compare a horizontal split case pump with an end suction pump under five headings: rotor support, casing split, nozzle layout, maintenance access and typical application.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: The end suction pump
chapters.narration: An end suction pump is one of the most common types of centrifugal pump. Liquid enters along the shaft axis, straight into a single impeller eye. The impeller is mounted on the end of the shaft, beyond the bearings. This is called an overhung arrangement. The casing is usually split radially, across the shaft, so that the cover and rotor can be withdrawn from the back. The pump on screen differs in almost every one of these respects. Its suction enters from the side, not along the shaft. Let us compare the two designs feature by feature.

scene.label: Split case: side suction, not end suction

chapters.title: Overhung versus between bearings
chapters.narration: In the end suction pump, both bearings are on one side of the impeller. The impeller overhangs, so the shaft acts like a cantilever. In the split case pump, the impeller sits between two bearing housings, one at each end of the casing. The shaft is supported at both ends, like a beam. For a rotor of comparable size, this generally reduces shaft deflection at the impeller, which helps the wear rings and seals. The price is that the shaft passes through the casing twice, so two shaft seals are needed instead of one.

chapters.title: Radial split versus axial split
chapters.narration: Now compare the casing joints. A typical end suction casing is split in a plane at right angles to the shaft. The split case pump is split along the shaft axis, on the horizontal plane through the centreline. The two halves are bolted together through flanges, usually with a gasket between them and dowel pins to locate them. Many large pumps for water service use this axial split. For some high pressure, high temperature or hazardous services, purchasers and standards may require a radially split design instead. The choice depends on the duty and the applicable specification.

scene.label: Split plane through the shaft centreline

chapters.title: Nozzle layout
chapters.narration: The nozzle layout is also different. On an end suction pump, the suction is on the shaft axis and the discharge usually points upward. On this split case pump, the suction and discharge nozzles are on opposite sides of the lower casing and both point horizontally. This suits pipework that runs straight through a pump house at one level. It also means the pump set takes more floor space across its width. When planning a pump room, allow for both the piping route and the headroom needed to lift the upper casing.

chapters.title: Maintenance access
chapters.narration: Maintenance access differs too. Many end suction pumps use a back pull out design. The bearing frame, shaft and impeller are withdrawn as one unit, often with a spacer coupling so that the motor can stay in place. On the split case pump, the upper casing half is lifted instead. The rotor can then be lifted out, often with its bearing housings, while the lower half and the piping stay in place. Both approaches avoid disturbing the main pipework. The detailed sequence always depends on the manufacturer's design.

chapters.title: Choosing between them
chapters.narration: So when is each type chosen? End suction pumps are compact and usually economical for small and medium flows. Split case pumps are usually chosen for larger flows and long, continuous duty. For the same flow and speed, a double suction impeller often needs a lower net positive suction head, because each eye handles only part of the flow. However, these are tendencies, not rules. The final choice depends on the duty point, the suction conditions, the space available, the maintenance strategy, the cost over the life of the pump and the standard that applies.

lessons.title: Working Principle of Double Suction Pump
lessons.objective: Describe, in order, the five stages of flow through a double suction split case pump, from the suction nozzle to the discharge nozzle.

chapters.title: The complete flow path
chapters.narration: This lesson follows the liquid through the pump in five stages. Watch the particles moving through the cut away model. They show the direction and the general path of the flow. Please remember that this animation is qualitative. The speed, spacing and number of particles do not represent measured velocities, pressures or flow rates. Real flow inside a pump is three dimensional, and it changes with the operating point. With that in mind, let us follow the liquid from the suction nozzle to the discharge nozzle.

chapters.title: Stage one: suction entry and split
chapters.narration: Stage one is suction entry. Liquid arrives through the suction nozzle on the side of the lower casing. Inside, the suction chamber divides the flow into two streams. Each stream turns and travels around to one side of the impeller. The passages are shaped to deliver the liquid to the two eyes as evenly and smoothly as possible. In practice, the split is not always exactly equal. It depends on the casing design and, importantly, on the suction piping upstream of the pump. A poorly placed elbow can favour one side.

chapters.title: Stage two: through the impeller
chapters.narration: Stage two takes place inside the rotating impeller. The two streams enter the two eyes from opposite directions. The vanes pick up the liquid and turn it from an axial direction to a radial direction. As the impeller rotates, the vanes push the liquid outward and make it rotate with them. This is where energy from the motor is transferred to the liquid. Both the pressure and the velocity of the liquid increase as it moves from the eye towards the outer edge of the impeller.

scene.label: Stage 2: energy added by the impeller

chapters.title: Stage three: leaving the impeller
chapters.narration: Stage three is discharge from the impeller. The liquid leaves the outer edge of the impeller around its whole circumference. At this point it is moving fast, with a large component of velocity in the direction of rotation. The streams from the two halves of the impeller join as they leave it. Together they enter the volute, which surrounds the impeller. A large part of the energy at this point is kinetic energy. The casing must now convert much of it into useful pressure.

scene.label: Stage 3: from the impeller into the volute

chapters.title: Stage four: volute action
chapters.narration: Stage four is the action of the volute. The volute is a spiral passage whose cross section grows steadily around the impeller. It collects liquid from the whole impeller outlet. Because the area increases in the direction of flow, the liquid slows down in a controlled way. As it slows, much of its velocity energy is converted into pressure energy. The volute tongue, also called the cutwater, is the point where the spiral begins. It separates liquid leaving towards the discharge from liquid that continues around the casing.

chapters.title: Stage five: discharge
chapters.narration: Stage five is discharge. The volute leads into the discharge throat and the discharge nozzle, on the side opposite the suction. The widening passage continues to recover pressure before the liquid leaves the pump. From here, the liquid enters the discharge pipework. The actual flow and head depend on where the pump curve meets the system curve. So the same pump can deliver very different flows in different systems. Selecting and operating the pump close to its best efficiency point generally keeps loads and losses lower.

lessons.title: Double Suction Impeller Explained
lessons.objective: Identify the parts of a double suction impeller and explain how its two eyes, wear ring clearances and axial position affect performance.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Anatomy of the impeller
chapters.narration: Here the impeller has been isolated from the rest of the pump. It is a closed impeller, which means the vanes are enclosed between shrouds. At the centre is the hub, which is bored to fit the shaft. A central web divides the impeller into two halves. Each half has its own set of vanes, its own outer shroud and its own eye. Each eye also carries an impeller wear ring. You can think of it as two single suction impellers joined back to back on one hub.

chapters.title: An exploded view
chapters.narration: In this exploded view, the parts of the impeller move apart along the shaft axis. This is only a visual aid. In a real impeller, the hub, web, vanes and shrouds are normally cast as one piece. The wear rings are separate parts fitted at each eye. Notice that the vane passages on the two sides are mirror images of each other. Some designs stagger the vanes on one side relative to the other, which can reduce pressure pulsations. The arrangement used in a particular pump is shown on the manufacturer's drawings.

chapters.title: Why two eyes?
chapters.narration: Why use two eyes? The total flow is shared between them, so each eye carries only part of it. For the same total flow and speed, the velocity entering each eye can be lower than in a single suction impeller of similar duty. Lower inlet velocity generally means a lower net positive suction head required. That makes the pump more tolerant of the suction conditions available on site. It also allows a large flow to be handled in a single stage.

chapters.title: Is the flow shared equally?
chapters.narration: In an ideal, perfectly symmetrical pump, each eye would take half of the flow. In practice, the share is rarely exact. Differences in the suction passages, the impeller casting or the wear ring clearances all affect it. The biggest influence is often the suction pipework. An elbow close to the pump, turning in a plane parallel to the shaft, tends to push more liquid towards one eye. Uneven flow can increase noise, vibration, cavitation risk and residual axial thrust. That is why piping guidance for double suction pumps calls for a well conditioned suction flow.

scene.label: Equal sharing is an ideal, not a guarantee

chapters.title: Wear rings and clearances
chapters.narration: Look closely at each eye. A rotating impeller wear ring runs inside a stationary casing wear ring. Between them is a small running clearance. On one side of this gap is the high pressure liquid leaving the impeller. On the other side is the low pressure liquid at the eye. The clearance limits how much liquid leaks back from discharge to suction. As the rings wear, the clearance grows, the leakage increases and efficiency falls. The correct clearances, and the limits for replacement, are given by the manufacturer.

chapters.title: Locating the impeller on the shaft
chapters.narration: The impeller is fitted on a machined seat on the shaft and driven by a key. In this arrangement, its axial position is set by the shaft sleeves and sleeve nuts on each side. The aim is to centre the impeller in the volute, so that the two halves are as symmetrical as possible. During reassembly, the impeller must also be fitted the right way round. If it is reversed, the vanes face the wrong way for the direction of rotation, and performance falls sharply. Always check the rotation arrow on the casing and the manufacturer's instructions.

lessons.title: Complete Component Identification
lessons.objective: Locate and name at least twenty components of a split case pump set on the 3D model and state the purpose of each main assembly.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Casing exterior
chapters.narration: Start with the outside of the casing. The upper casing half carries the lifting lugs, and a vent connection at the high point. The lower casing half carries almost everything that connects to the outside world. That includes the suction and discharge nozzles, the casing feet, the drain connections and the pressure tappings used for gauges. The bearing housing supports, or brackets, are also cast onto the lower half at each end. Watch each feature as it is highlighted in the model.

chapters.title: The casing joint
chapters.narration: Next, the horizontal joint. The upper and lower halves each have a machined split flange. A casing joint gasket sits between them and seals the joint. Studs pass through the flanges, and nuts with washers clamp the halves together. In this model there are sixteen joint nuts. Two dowel pins locate the upper half accurately on the lower half, so that the bores for the wear rings and seals line up. The joint must seal against the full pressure inside the casing.

scene.label: Split flange, gasket, studs and dowels

chapters.title: Hydraulic internals
chapters.narration: Now the upper half becomes transparent. Inside you can see the double suction impeller, centred in the casing. Around it is the volute passage, with the volute tongue at its start. At each impeller eye there is a pair of wear rings, one on the impeller and one held in the casing. The suction passages wrap around both sides of the impeller to feed the two eyes. Some pumps use a double volute instead, with a splitter rib that divides the passage into two.

chapters.title: Shaft assembly
chapters.narration: With the casing hidden, the rotating parts are easy to see. The pump shaft runs the full length of the pump, from the coupling at the drive end to the bearing at the non-drive end. Shaft sleeves protect the shaft where it passes through the seal areas. Sleeve nuts lock the sleeves and help to locate the impeller. Water deflectors, also called flingers, sit on the shaft outside the seal areas. They throw off any leakage, so that it does not run along the shaft into the bearing housings.

chapters.title: Bearing assemblies
chapters.narration: Each end of the shaft runs in a bearing housing, bolted to its bracket on the lower casing. At the drive end, a radial ball bearing supports the shaft and is free to float axially. At the non-drive end, a pair of angular contact ball bearings locates the shaft and carries the residual axial thrust. Each housing has covers, gaskets and seals that keep lubricant in and contamination out. In the oil lubricated version shown here, you can also see a constant level oiler, a sight glass and a drain.

chapters.title: Shaft sealing
chapters.narration: The shaft passes through the casing at two places, so there is a shaft seal at each end. In the configuration shown, each end has a mechanical seal in a seal chamber. Its main parts are a rotating face, a stationary face, springs, secondary seals and a gland plate with a flush connection. The alternative configuration uses gland packing. That consists of packing rings, a lantern ring, a gland follower and gland studs, with a seal water connection. Both arrangements are covered in detail in the seal and packing lesson.

chapters.title: Coupling, motor and baseplate
chapters.narration: Finally, the drive train and the base. The pump coupling hub and the motor coupling hub are joined by a spacer and flexible elements. Removing the spacer leaves a gap, so that the pump rotor can be taken out without moving the motor. A guard covers the coupling for safety. The electric motor has a finned frame, a terminal box, and a cooling fan under its cowl. Both machines sit on mounting pads on a common baseplate. The baseplate is levelled, held by anchor bolts and grouted onto the concrete foundation.

lessons.title: Upper Casing Removal
lessons.objective: List, in the correct order, the isolation, preparation, unbolting and lifting steps needed to remove the upper casing half safely.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual
Site permit-to-work, isolation and lifting procedures

chapters.title: Safety first
chapters.narration: Before any tool touches the pump, it must be made safe. Follow your site permit to work system. Isolate and lock off the motor electrically, and prove that it cannot start. Close and secure the suction and discharge valves, and isolate any seal water, flush or cooling supplies. Then depressurise the casing, drain it through the drain connections, and vent it. Allow hot liquid to cool. Check whether the liquid is hazardous and what protective equipment is needed. Keep the manufacturer's manual for this exact pump at hand.

chapters.title: Disconnect auxiliaries and glands
chapters.narration: With the pump isolated and drained, prepare the joint. Disconnect any auxiliary piping that crosses the joint or is attached to the upper half. This can include vent lines, seal flush lines and instrument connections. Label everything, so that it goes back in the same place. On many designs, the seal glands or packing glands are bolted across the joint. These must be released and slid back along the shaft before the upper half can be lifted. The manufacturer's manual states which parts must be released on your pump.

chapters.title: Removing the joint nuts
chapters.narration: Now the casing joint nuts can be removed. In this model there are sixteen of them. Loosen them in the sequence given by the manufacturer. This is usually a balanced pattern, rather than working straight along one side. It avoids distorting the casing as the clamping load is released. Use the correct tools, and look out for seized or damaged threads. Keep the nuts and washers together, and note any that need replacing. The caption shows how many nuts have been removed so far.

chapters.title: All nuts removed
chapters.narration: All sixteen nuts are now off. The upper half still sits on the lower half, located by the dowel pins and held lightly by the gasket. Check that nothing else still connects the upper half to the rest of the pump. Depending on the design, look for remaining bolts at the seal housings, the bearing brackets or auxiliary connections. Do not try to lift until you are certain that the upper half is completely free. Lifting against a hidden fastener can damage the casing or overload the lifting gear.

chapters.title: Breaking the joint
chapters.narration: Next, the joint is separated. The gasket can make the two halves stick together. Where the upper flange has tapped holes for jacking screws, use the jacking screws evenly to break the joint. Do not drive wedges or chisels into the joint, because they can damage the machined faces. Raise the upper half evenly, so that it clears the dowel pins without binding. In the view, the upper half has now just separated from the lower half.

chapters.title: Lifting the upper half
chapters.narration: The upper half is heavy, so it must be lifted with approved, inspected lifting gear of adequate capacity. Its mass is given in the manufacturer's documentation. Use only the lifting points that the manufacturer designates. The lugs on the upper half are intended for the upper half alone. They must never be used to lift the complete pump. Lift slowly and keep the half level, so that it clears the studs, the impeller and the wear rings without contact. Nobody should stand or reach under a suspended load.

chapters.title: Setting it down and first look
chapters.narration: Move the upper half clear and set it down on timber or other suitable supports, with the joint face protected. Never rest it directly on its machined face. The impeller, the wear rings and the inside of the lower casing are now exposed. Before disturbing anything, record what you see. Look for erosion, corrosion, deposits, cavitation damage and rubbing marks. Remove the old gasket carefully, without scratching the joint faces. A new gasket of the specified material and thickness will be needed on reassembly.

lessons.title: Rotor Assembly and Dismantling
lessons.objective: Explain how the complete rotor is released, lifted and supported, and list the main checks made during rotor dismantling and reassembly.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual
Site permit-to-work, isolation and lifting procedures

chapters.title: What makes up the rotor
chapters.narration: The rotor is everything that turns, together with the parts that come out with it. At its core are the shaft and the double suction impeller, located by the key, the sleeves and the sleeve nuts. It also carries the impeller wear rings, the rotating parts of both shaft seals, the water deflectors, the bearings and the pump coupling hub. In many designs, the bearing housings and the casing wear rings come out with the rotor as one unit. Other designs differ, so always check the manufacturer's manual for your pump.

chapters.title: Before the rotor can move
chapters.narration: Rotor removal starts only after the pump has been isolated and drained, and the upper casing has been removed. Several more connections must then be released. The coupling spacer is removed, leaving a gap between the pump and motor hubs. All auxiliary piping is disconnected. The seal glands are released and slid back. If cartridge seals are fitted, their setting devices are normally refitted before the seal is released from the shaft, to protect the faces. Mark the relative positions of parts, so they can be reassembled exactly as they were.

chapters.title: Releasing the bearing housings
chapters.narration: The bearing housings are held to their brackets by hold down bolts. Some designs also use dowels to locate the housings. Before removing anything, mark the position of each housing relative to its bracket. Then remove the hold down bolts at both ends. Where shims are fitted under a housing, keep them with the housing they came from, because they help to set the height of the rotor. The rotor now rests in the lower casing, free of its fixings and ready to be lifted.

chapters.title: Lifting the rotor
