chapters.narration: The rotor is lifted with approved lifting gear, usually a spreader beam and slings. Sling it only at the points the manufacturer recommends, which are usually on the shaft. Never sling around the impeller vanes or the seal parts. Protect the shaft surfaces from damage by the slings. Lift slowly and keep the rotor level. If it tilts, the wear rings, sleeves or seal parts can strike the casing and be damaged. Once it is clear of the lower casing, move it to a clean work area.

chapters.title: Supporting the rotor
chapters.narration: Lower the rotor onto suitable stands, such as V blocks, placed under the shaft at the positions the manufacturer recommends. Do not rest the rotor on the impeller, the sleeves or the seal parts. With the rotor supported, it can be inspected before it is dismantled. A dial indicator can be used to check runout at the impeller wear rings, the sleeves and the shaft ends. Measure the wear ring diameters to work out the running clearances. Compare every reading with the manufacturer's limits, and record it for future comparison.

chapters.title: Dismantling the rotor
chapters.narration: Rotor dismantling follows the order in the manufacturer's manual, and that order varies between designs. Typically, the coupling hub comes off first, using a suitable puller. The bearing housings are removed, and then the bearings are taken off the shaft with their locknuts and washers. The seals, sleeve nuts and sleeves follow. Check the thread direction of each sleeve nut before turning it. Finally, the impeller is pressed or pulled off its seat. Mark which way round the impeller sits before removing it. If heat is needed, apply it only as the manual describes.

chapters.title: Reassembly principles
chapters.narration: Reassembly is broadly the reverse of dismantling, but it needs even more care. Work in a clean area and clean every part. Replace gaskets, O rings and other consumables, and any part that is outside the manufacturer's limits. Fit the bearings using the method that the bearing maker and pump maker specify. Centre the impeller in the volute, and check the axial position and end float of the rotor against the manual. Once the rotor is back in the casing, turn it by hand to confirm that it rotates freely. Then refit the upper casing and recheck the shaft alignment.

lessons.title: Bearing Arrangement
lessons.objective: Explain the different roles of the floating drive-end bearing and the locating non-drive-end bearing, and describe how each is lubricated and protected.
references: Bearing manufacturer mounting and lubrication guidance
OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Two bearings, two jobs
chapters.narration: The rotor of a split case pump is supported by two bearing assemblies, one at each end, outside the casing. Each carries part of the rotor weight and the radial hydraulic load. But the two bearings do not do the same job, and they are usually not identical. One bearing locates the shaft axially and carries the net axial thrust. The other supports radial load only, and lets the shaft move axially as it expands with temperature. The arrows in the view show this idea conceptually, not to scale.

chapters.title: The drive-end floating bearing
chapters.narration: In this arrangement, the drive-end bearing is a radial ball bearing. Its inner ring is clamped to the shaft by a locknut. Its outer ring can slide axially in the housing bore, within a small allowance. This is why it is called the floating bearing. As the shaft warms up and grows in length, the floating bearing moves with it. That stops the two bearings from fighting each other and creating extra axial load. The drive-end bearing is also nearest the coupling, so it feels most of any load caused by misalignment.

chapters.title: The non-drive-end locating bearing
chapters.narration: At the non-drive end, this pump has a pair of angular contact ball bearings, mounted back to back. Each bearing of the pair carries thrust in one direction. Together they carry thrust in both directions, as well as radial load. Their outer rings are clamped axially in the housing by the end cover. This fixes the axial position of the whole rotor. It is this locating bearing that carries the residual axial thrust that remains in a double suction pump.

chapters.title: Design variations
chapters.narration: Not every split case pump uses this exact arrangement. Some designs place the locating bearing at the drive end instead. Where the residual thrust is modest, a single deep groove ball bearing may be used as the locating bearing, as the model now shows. Larger or faster pumps may use other rolling bearing types, or hydrodynamic sleeve bearings. The bearing type, size, fits and arrangement are chosen by the manufacturer for the duty. Replacement bearings must match the manufacturer's specification exactly.

scene.label: Variant: deep groove ball locating bearing

chapters.title: Oil lubrication
chapters.narration: In the oil lubricated version, each housing holds an oil bath. A constant level oiler keeps the level steady, and the sight glass shows the level at a glance. Too little oil starves the bearing. Too much oil can cause churning, which raises the temperature. The correct oil grade, level and change interval come from the manufacturer. Some oilers must be fitted on a particular side, relative to the direction of rotation, so install them as instructed. Whenever the oil is drained, check it for water, discolouration or particles.

scene.label: Oil bath with constant level oiler

chapters.title: Grease lubrication
chapters.narration: Many split case pumps use grease lubricated bearings instead. Here, each housing has a grease nipple for adding grease and a relief plug that lets old grease escape. A common mistake is over greasing. Excess grease cannot escape, so it churns and the bearing runs hot. Too little grease leads to wear and early failure. Use the grease type, quantity and relubrication interval stated by the manufacturer. Keep the grease and the fittings clean, and never mix incompatible greases.

chapters.title: Keeping bearings clean and cool
chapters.narration: A bearing can fail quickly if water or dirt gets into it. Lip seals or labyrinth seals at the housing ends keep lubricant in and contamination out. The water deflectors on the shaft throw off any seal leakage before it can reach the housing. In service, bearings are checked by trending temperature, vibration and noise over time. A sudden rise, or a steady upward trend, is a signal to investigate. Acceptable limits come from the manufacturer and from the site condition monitoring programme.

lessons.title: Mechanical Seal and Packing
lessons.objective: Compare mechanical seals and gland packing in a split case pump, describing how each controls leakage and stating two key precautions for each.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Why two shaft seals?
chapters.narration: In a between bearings pump, the shaft passes through the casing at two places, one at each end. Each exit needs its own shaft seal. In a double suction pump, these seal areas sit beside the suction passages. So they usually see a pressure close to suction pressure, rather than discharge pressure. If the suction pressure is below atmospheric, air can be drawn in along the shaft. This is one reason why seal flushing or seal water is used. Not all pumps use the same arrangement. Some use mechanical seals, and others use gland packing.

scene.label: A shaft seal at each end

chapters.title: Mechanical seal parts
chapters.narration: Here is the mechanical seal at the drive end, shown in section. Its heart is a pair of flat, lapped faces. The rotating face turns with the shaft. The stationary face, or seat, is held in the gland plate. Springs push the faces together, so that they stay in contact as they wear. Secondary seals, usually elastomer rings, seal behind each face. A drive collar transmits rotation to the rotating parts. A flush connection in the gland supplies liquid to the seal area.

chapters.title: How a mechanical seal works
chapters.narration: When the pump runs, the rotating face slides against the stationary face. A very thin film of liquid forms between them. This film lubricates and cools the faces. Leakage across the faces is very small, and often escapes unseen as vapour. Because the faces depend on this liquid film, a mechanical seal must never run dry, even for a short time. The flush arrangement keeps the seal area full, cool and clean. The seal type, materials and flush arrangement are chosen by the seal supplier for the duty.

scene.label: Faces run on a thin liquid film

chapters.title: Gland packing parts
chapters.narration: Now the model switches to the gland packing configuration. The stuffing box holds several rings of braided packing around the shaft sleeve. Partway along, a lantern ring creates a space where seal water can be fed in through the flush connection. The gland follower sits at the outer end. Nuts on the gland studs push the follower inward, compressing the packing against the sleeve and the bore of the stuffing box. The same arrangement is fitted at the other end of the shaft.

chapters.title: How packing works
chapters.narration: Packing is designed to leak a little. That controlled leakage lubricates and cools the packing where it rubs on the sleeve. If the gland is tightened until leakage stops, the packing overheats, hardens and wears a groove into the sleeve. Adjust the gland nuts evenly and in small steps, as the manufacturer describes, taking great care near the rotating shaft. The acceptable leakage rate is set by the manufacturer. One advantage of packing is that, in many designs, it can be replaced with the pump isolated, without lifting the upper casing.

chapters.title: Choosing between them
chapters.narration: Which is better? It depends on the service. Mechanical seals give very low leakage and need no routine adjustment, which suits liquids that should not escape. However, replacing a conventional one piece seal on a split case pump usually means removing the upper casing and the rotor. Split seal designs exist to avoid this. Packing is simple, can be adjusted in service, and is still widely used on water duties. Its leakage must be drained away, and the sleeves wear over time. The choice is made by the purchaser and the manufacturer for each application.

lessons.title: Axial Thrust Explained
lessons.objective: Explain where axial thrust comes from, why a double suction impeller substantially balances it, and list at least four factors that leave a residual thrust for the locating bearing.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: What is axial thrust?
chapters.narration: Axial thrust is the net force on the rotor along the shaft axis. In a centrifugal pump, it comes mainly from pressure acting on the outside faces of the impeller shrouds. Liquid leaving the impeller fills the spaces between the shrouds and the casing at a high pressure. At the eye, however, the pressure is close to suction pressure. Changes in the momentum of the liquid entering the eye also contribute. The arrows in this view are conceptual. They show direction, not measured magnitude.

scene.label: Conceptual thrust arrows, not to scale

chapters.title: The single suction case
chapters.narration: Consider first a single suction impeller. On the eye side, the low suction pressure acts over the eye area, and the high pressure acts only on the part of the shroud outside the wear ring. On the back, the high pressure acts over almost the whole shroud. These forces do not balance, so a net thrust pushes the impeller towards the suction side. Designers reduce it with features such as back wear rings with balance holes, or pump out vanes. Even then, some thrust remains for the bearings.

scene.label: Imagine one side only: unequal areas create thrust

chapters.title: How double suction balances thrust
chapters.narration: Now look at the double suction impeller. It is symmetrical about its centre plane. The pressure acting on one shroud is mirrored on the other, and the liquid enters the two eyes in opposite directions. So the axial forces from the two halves act against each other. In an ideal, perfectly symmetrical arrangement, they substantially balance. This is a major advantage of the design. But it does not eliminate axial thrust. Real pumps are never perfectly symmetrical, so some residual thrust always remains.

chapters.title: Where residual thrust comes from
chapters.narration: Several factors upset the balance. Uneven flow to the two eyes, often caused by poor suction piping, is one of the most important. Small differences between the castings and passages on each side also matter. If the impeller is not centred in the volute, the pressures on the two shrouds differ. Uneven wear of the wear rings changes the leakage and the pressure on each side. Operation far from the best efficiency point, and transient events such as starting and stopping, can also change the thrust.

chapters.title: Who carries the residual thrust?
chapters.narration: The residual thrust has to go somewhere. It passes along the shaft to the locating bearing, which in this pump is the pair of angular contact bearings at the non-drive end. That bearing is selected to carry the expected residual thrust in either direction, together with its radial load. The drive-end bearing floats axially, so ideally it carries radial load only. This is why the two bearings are different. It is also why the locating bearing must always be of the type and arrangement that the manufacturer specifies.

scene.label: Residual thrust goes to the locating bearing

chapters.title: When thrust becomes excessive
chapters.narration: If the residual thrust becomes larger than expected, the locating bearing pays the price. Typical signs are a rising temperature at the locating bearing, more noise or vibration, and shorter bearing life. The rotor may also shift axially, which can change the loading on the mechanical seal faces and cause rubbing at the wear rings. When this happens, look for the root cause, rather than simply replacing the bearing. Check the suction piping, the operating point, the impeller position and the wear ring clearances.

scene.label: Investigate the cause, not just the bearing

lessons.title: Pump Installation and Alignment
lessons.objective: Describe, in sequence, the main steps for installing a split case pump set, from foundation and grouting to piping connection and final shaft alignment.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Foundation and baseplate
chapters.narration: A good installation starts with the foundation. It must be rigid and massive enough to support the pump set and resist vibration, as specified by the manufacturer and the civil designer. The baseplate is set on the foundation, with the anchor bolts in place. It is then levelled, using levelling screws or shims, to the tolerance the manufacturer requires. Finally, grout is placed under the baseplate. The grout must fill the space completely, so that the baseplate is supported evenly and acts together with the foundation.

chapters.title: Setting the pump and motor
chapters.narration: The pump and motor sit on machined mounting pads on the baseplate. Before final bolting, check every foot for soft foot. Soft foot means a foot that does not sit flat, so that tightening its bolt distorts the machine frame. Correct it with shims, never by forcing the foot down. Use clean, flat shims, in as few layers as practical. The pump is normally fixed first, and the motor is then aligned to the pump. Leave the motor bolts free enough to allow alignment moves.

chapters.title: Suction piping
chapters.narration: Suction piping has a strong influence on a double suction pump. It should deliver a steady, evenly distributed flow to the suction nozzle. Where a reducer is needed, an eccentric reducer is fitted with its flat side on top, so that air cannot collect. Avoid high points where air can gather. An elbow close to the nozzle, turning in a plane parallel to the shaft, can send more flow to one eye than to the other. Hydraulic Institute piping guidance and the manufacturer give recommendations on straight lengths and elbow orientation.

chapters.title: Supports and pipe strain
chapters.narration: Both suction and discharge pipework must be supported independently of the pump. The pump nozzles are not designed to carry the weight of the pipe, or to pull misaligned flanges together. Flanges should meet squarely, with the bolt holes lined up, before any bolt is tightened. A useful check is to watch dial indicators on the coupling while the flange bolts are tightened. If the readings move noticeably, the piping is straining the pump and must be corrected. Pipe strain is a common cause of misalignment, vibration and casing joint leakage.

chapters.title: Shaft alignment
chapters.narration: Shaft alignment brings the pump and motor shafts onto one common centreline. With the coupling spacer removed, misalignment is measured in two forms. Offset is where the shafts are parallel but displaced. Angularity is where they meet at an angle. Both are checked in the vertical and horizontal planes, using dial indicators or a laser alignment system. Corrections are made by moving the motor, with shims for height and jacking screws for sideways movement. The acceptable tolerances come from the manufacturer or the coupling supplier.

chapters.title: Final checks
chapters.narration: Alignment is not a one time task. Check it again after grouting, after the piping is connected, and before the first start. Some machines also need an allowance for thermal growth, so that they line up correctly at operating temperature. Where required, a hot alignment check is made after a run. Once the alignment is accepted, turn the rotor by hand to confirm that it is free. Then refit the coupling spacer and flexible elements, and fit the coupling guard before the motor is energised.

lessons.title: Commissioning and Operation
lessons.objective: State, in the correct order, the key pre-start, starting, running and stopping checks for a split case pump, with reference to the manufacturer's manual.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual
Site permit-to-work, isolation and lifting procedures

chapters.title: Pre-start checks
chapters.narration: Before the first start, confirm that the installation is complete and recorded, including the final alignment. Check that the bearings have the correct lubricant at the correct level. Check that seal flush or seal water lines are connected and open. Then check the direction of rotation. This is done with the coupling spacer removed, by briefly running the motor on its own. Running a pump in reverse can damage it, and on some designs it can loosen threaded parts. Refit the spacer and guard afterwards.

scene.label: Check rotation with the spacer removed

chapters.title: Priming and venting
chapters.narration: A centrifugal pump must be full of liquid before it starts. Running dry can damage the mechanical seals and wear rings very quickly. With a flooded suction, open the suction valve fully and let the liquid fill the casing. Open the vent connection at the top of the casing until all the air has escaped and a steady stream of liquid appears. Then close the vent. If the liquid level is below the pump, a priming system or foot valve is needed. Never start the pump just to find out whether it is primed.

chapters.title: Starting the pump
chapters.narration: Many split case pumps are started with the suction valve fully open and the discharge valve closed or only slightly open. For many designs, this reduces the starting power. The manufacturer's manual and the system design confirm the correct method for your pump. Once the motor reaches speed, open the discharge valve gradually until the required flow is reached. Do not run against a closed discharge valve for longer than necessary. With no flow, the input energy goes into the trapped liquid, which can heat up quickly.

chapters.title: Running checks
chapters.narration: With the pump running, record a set of baseline readings. These include suction and discharge pressure from the pressure tappings, flow, motor current, bearing temperatures and vibration. Check the shaft seals. A mechanical seal should show little or no visible leakage, while packing should show a steady, controlled drip. Listen for unusual noise. A crackling sound, like gravel passing through the pump, may indicate cavitation. These baseline readings become the reference for all future condition monitoring.

chapters.title: Staying in the operating window
chapters.narration: Every pump has a preferred operating region around its best efficiency point, and the manufacturer defines the allowable range. Running at very low flow can cause recirculation in the impeller, higher radial loads, vibration and heating. Running at very high flow increases the net positive suction head required, which raises the risk of cavitation, and it may overload the motor. Always make sure that the net positive suction head available exceeds the requirement with a suitable margin. If the operating point drifts, investigate the system as well as the pump.

scene.label: Operate near the best efficiency point

chapters.title: Stopping and standby
chapters.narration: To stop the pump, follow the site procedure. In many systems, the discharge valve is closed gradually before the motor is stopped, which helps to limit pressure surges. Then stop the motor and, if the pump is to be isolated, close the suction valve. Shut off the seal water or flush supply when the procedure says so. For standby pumps, follow the site routine for periodic running. Where there is a risk of freezing, a pump left out of service must be drained.

lessons.title: Common Failures
lessons.objective: Recognise the warning signs of seven common split case pump problems and name the first checks to make for each.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual

chapters.title: Cavitation
chapters.narration: Cavitation happens when the pressure near the impeller eye falls below the vapour pressure of the liquid. Vapour bubbles form, then collapse violently as they reach higher pressure further into the impeller. The signs are a crackling noise, vibration, falling head and, over time, pitting near the inlet edges of the vanes. Common causes are a low suction level, a blocked strainer, a high liquid temperature, or operation far beyond the best efficiency point. The cure is to restore an adequate margin between the net positive suction head available and the head required.

chapters.title: Air ingress and uneven suction flow
chapters.narration: Air in the liquid reduces flow and head, and makes the pump noisy and unstable. It can enter through leaking joints in the suction pipe, through packing when the suction pressure is below atmospheric, or through a vortex at a shallow intake. Air can also collect at high points, or in a reducer fitted the wrong way up. Uneven suction flow is a related problem. If one eye receives more liquid than the other, noise, vibration and residual thrust can increase. Check the suction pipework, joints and intake conditions first.

chapters.title: Wear ring wear
chapters.narration: Wear rings wear gradually in normal service, and faster with abrasive liquid, misalignment, shaft deflection or dry running. As the clearance grows, more liquid leaks from the impeller outlet back to the eyes. Head, flow and efficiency fall, so more power is used for less useful work. Rubbing can also cause local heating, noise and, in severe cases, seizure. During inspection, the measured clearances are compared with the manufacturer's limits. Rings that are outside the limits are replaced, often as a pair.

chapters.title: Bearing failures
chapters.narration: Bearing failures are among the most frequent causes of pump downtime. Lubrication problems lead the list. These include too little lubricant, too much, the wrong type, or lubricant contaminated by water or dirt. Other causes include misalignment, excessive residual thrust, poor fitting practice and vibration from other faults. Warning signs are rising temperature, new noises and increasing vibration, which often appear in the trends before failure. Always investigate why a bearing failed, because a new bearing will fail again if the cause remains.

scene.label: Find the cause of a bearing failure

chapters.title: Seal and packing leakage
chapters.narration: Mechanical seals usually fail at the faces or at the secondary seals. Common causes are dry running, loss of flush, abrasive particles, chemical attack on the elastomers, and excessive shaft movement from misalignment, worn bearings or vibration. Packing problems are often caused by overtightening, incorrect fitting of the rings, or a worn shaft sleeve. In both cases, a sudden increase in leakage is a warning sign. Examine the failed parts carefully, because the pattern of wear usually points to the cause.

chapters.title: Vibration and misalignment
chapters.narration: High vibration is a symptom, not a cause. Common mechanical sources are shaft misalignment, rotor unbalance, soft foot, pipe strain, a weak or cracked foundation, and loose bolting. Hydraulic causes include operation far from the best efficiency point, cavitation and uneven suction flow. Misalignment often shows up as wear of the coupling elements and a high drive-end bearing temperature. Trend vibration readings over time and compare them with the baseline taken at commissioning. Where available, frequency analysis helps to narrow down the cause.

chapters.title: Casing joint leakage and low performance
chapters.narration: Leakage at the horizontal casing joint is usually caused by a damaged or incorrect gasket, damaged joint faces, uneven tightening of the joint nuts, or casing distortion from pipe strain. It must be corrected with the pump isolated, never by tightening nuts while the casing is under pressure. Low discharge pressure or low flow has many possible causes. These include wrong rotation, air in the liquid, a partly blocked impeller, worn wear rings, a closed or throttled valve, or a change in the system. Work through the possibilities methodically.

lessons.title: Inspection and Maintenance
lessons.objective: Outline a safe inspection and maintenance routine for a split case pump that covers routine checks, lubrication, isolation, internal and rotor inspection, records and return to service.
references: OEM installation, operation and maintenance manual
Site permit-to-work, isolation and lifting procedures

chapters.title: A maintenance strategy
chapters.narration: Good maintenance combines three levels. Routine checks are made by operators during normal rounds. Condition monitoring trends vibration, temperature and performance, to show how the pump is changing over time. Planned inspections and overhauls open the pump when the evidence, or the manufacturer's recommendations, call for it. Intervals depend on the duty, the operating hours, the site's experience and the manufacturer's guidance. There is no single correct interval for every pump. Good records make every one of these levels more effective.

chapters.title: Routine checks
chapters.narration: During routine rounds, look, listen and record. Check the bearing oil levels in the sight glasses, or the condition of the grease points. Check seal or packing leakage against what is normal for that pump. Note the suction and discharge pressures and compare them with the baseline. Listen for any change in noise. Measure vibration and bearing temperature with suitable instruments, rather than by touch. Make sure that the coupling guard and all other guards are in place. Never reach near a rotating shaft or coupling.

chapters.title: Lubrication tasks
chapters.narration: Lubrication is one of the most frequent maintenance tasks. For oil lubricated bearings, change the oil at the interval the manufacturer recommends, or sooner if it shows water, discolouration or particles. Refill to the correct level with the specified grade. For grease lubricated bearings, add the specified quantity of the specified grease at the stated interval, through clean fittings. Where a relief plug is fitted, follow the manual's instructions for it while greasing. Record what was done, when it was done, and by whom.

chapters.title: Before opening the pump
chapters.narration: Any work that opens the pump begins with safe isolation. Follow the permit to work system. Isolate and lock off the motor, and prove that it cannot start. Close and lock the suction and discharge valves, and isolate the auxiliary supplies. Depressurise, drain and vent the casing, and allow it to cool. Use only approved, inspected lifting gear for the casing halves and the rotor. Work from the manufacturer's manual for the specific pump, because dismantling methods differ between manufacturers and models.

chapters.title: Internal inspection
chapters.narration: With the upper casing removed, inspect the hydraulic parts before cleaning them, because deposits are evidence. Examine the impeller for erosion, cavitation pitting, corrosion, cracks and blocked passages. Measure the wear ring clearances and compare them with the manufacturer's limits. Inspect the volute, including the tongue, for wear and damage. Check the casing joint faces for erosion or damage that could cause leakage. Photograph and record everything you find.

chapters.title: Rotor, bearing and seal inspection
chapters.narration: If the rotor is removed, inspect it on stands. Check the shaft runout and the condition of the bearing journals, keyways and threads. Inspect the shaft sleeves for grooving or wear under the seals or packing. Examine the bearings, or replace them as the manufacturer and site practice recommend. Inspect the seal faces, springs and elastomers, or the packing and lantern rings. Check the coupling hubs and flexible elements. Compare every measurement with the manufacturer's limits, and record it.

chapters.title: Reassembly and return to service
chapters.narration: On reassembly, fit new gaskets and O rings of the specified material. The casing joint gasket needs particular care. Its thickness can affect the fit of the wear rings and seal housings, so use only the gasket that the manufacturer specifies. Tighten the joint nuts in the specified sequence and to the specified torque. Recheck rotor freedom and shaft alignment, refit the guards, and remove the isolations under the permit system. Then recommission the pump, and record new baseline readings for future comparison.

questions.prompt: In a horizontal split case pump, along which plane is the casing divided into its two halves?
options: A vertical plane at right angles to the shaft, through the impeller centre
A horizontal plane containing the shaft centreline
An inclined plane at 45 degrees to the shaft axis
The casing is a single piece and is not split
questions.explanation: The casing of this pump type is axially split: the joint lies on the horizontal plane through the shaft axis, so the upper half can be lifted off the lower half. A joint at right angles to the shaft describes a radially split casing, as used on most end-suction pumps. A one-piece casing would not give the top access that defines this pump type.

questions.prompt: In the pump arrangement shown in this module, where are the suction and discharge nozzles located?
options: Both on the upper casing half, pointing upwards
Both on the lower casing half, horizontal and on opposite sides of the pump
Suction on the shaft axis at the non-drive end, discharge on top
Suction on the upper casing half and discharge on the lower casing half
questions.explanation: Both nozzles are cast into the lower casing half, horizontal and facing opposite sides; this is a common split case arrangement and the one modelled here. Because the main pipework connects only to the lower half, the upper half can be removed without disconnecting the suction or discharge piping. Some designs use other nozzle orientations, so always check the actual pump.

questions.prompt: What does 'double suction' mean when describing the impeller of this pump?
options: Two separate impellers mounted in series on the same shaft
One impeller that receives liquid through two eyes, one on each side
An impeller that has two discharge nozzles
An impeller that can pump in either direction of rotation
questions.explanation: A double-suction (double-entry) impeller is a single impeller shaped like two single-suction halves placed back to back, with an eye on each side and a common outlet at the periphery. Two impellers in series would make a two-stage pump, which is a different design. The nozzles and the direction of rotation are not what the term describes.

questions.prompt: What is the basic principle by which a centrifugal pump adds energy to the liquid?
options: It traps fixed volumes of liquid and pushes them out, like a piston pump
The rotating impeller increases the liquid's velocity and pressure, and the casing converts part of the velocity into further pressure
It heats the liquid so that it expands and flows out
It uses compressed air to lift the liquid
questions.explanation: A centrifugal pump is a rotodynamic machine: the vanes of the rotating impeller increase the angular momentum of the liquid, raising both its velocity and its pressure, and the volute then recovers part of the velocity as pressure. Trapping fixed volumes describes positive displacement pumps. Heating and compressed air are not how a centrifugal pump works.

questions.prompt: Which part of the pump collects the liquid leaving the impeller and converts part of its velocity into pressure?
options: The impeller eye
The volute casing
The bearing housing
The coupling
questions.explanation: The volute is a spiral passage whose cross-section grows around the impeller and then widens into the discharge nozzle, so the fast-moving liquid slows down and part of its kinetic energy becomes pressure energy. The eye is the impeller inlet, where pressure is lowest. Bearing housings and the coupling are mechanical parts with no hydraulic function.

questions.prompt: Why is this pump described as having a 'between-bearings' rotor?
options: The impeller sits between two bearing assemblies, one at each end of the shaft
The bearings are located between the pump and the motor only
The impeller overhangs beyond a single bearing housing
The bearings are fitted inside the impeller hub
questions.explanation: In a between-bearings pump the shaft is supported on both sides of the impeller, by a drive-end bearing and a non-drive-end bearing. This gives a stiff rotor that suits wide, heavy double-suction impellers. An impeller that overhangs beyond one bearing housing describes an overhung design such as a typical end-suction pump.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the pump bearings?
options: To seal the liquid inside the casing
To support the rotating shaft, carrying radial loads and locating the rotor axially
To increase the head produced by the pump
To connect the pump shaft to the motor shaft
questions.explanation: The bearings carry the weight of the rotor and the hydraulic radial loads, and the locating bearing also fixes the rotor's axial position and carries the residual axial thrust. Sealing is done by the mechanical seals or gland packing, and the coupling connects pump to motor. Bearings do not add head; they only allow the rotor to turn accurately.

questions.prompt: What is the main maintenance advantage of a horizontal split case pump?
options: The upper casing half can be lifted off to reach the rotor without disturbing the suction and discharge piping or the motor
It never needs maintenance
The impeller can be replaced while the pump is running
It has no bearings that need maintenance
questions.explanation: With the pump isolated and drained, removing the joint nuts and lifting the upper half exposes the impeller, wear rings, sleeves and seals while the lower half stays connected to the pipework and the motor stays in place. All pumps need maintenance, and no pump should be dismantled while running. The bearings still need lubrication and inspection.

questions.prompt: In this module, how is the pump shaft connected to the electric motor shaft?
options: By a V-belt drive
By a flexible spacer coupling
By a reduction gearbox
By welding the shafts together
questions.explanation: A flexible spacer coupling transmits torque while tolerating small residual misalignment, and its removable spacer leaves a gap for maintenance work. Flexibility is not a substitute for accurate alignment, which must still be set to the OEM tolerances. Belts and gearboxes are used on some installations but are not part of this model.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the shaft seal (mechanical seal or gland packing) fitted at each end of the casing?
options: To control leakage where the rotating shaft passes out through the stationary casing
To carry the axial thrust of the impeller
To increase the flow rate
To cool the motor windings
questions.explanation: The shaft leaves the casing at both ends, so a split case pump has two shaft seals. Depending on the service, these may be mechanical seals or gland packing; not every pump uses mechanical seals. Thrust is carried by the locating bearing, not by the seals.

questions.prompt: What happens to the liquid after it enters the suction nozzle of this pump?
options: All of it is sent to the drive-end eye of the impeller
The casing divides it into two side chambers that feed the two impeller eyes
It passes straight into the volute without going through the impeller
It mixes with the discharge flow before reaching the impeller
questions.explanation: The suction passage in the lower half splits the incoming flow into two side chambers, one on each side of the impeller, which turn the liquid into the two eyes. The two streams then leave the impeller together into a single volute and discharge nozzle. Liquid must pass through the impeller to gain energy, and suction and discharge passages are kept separate.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of the common baseplate?
options: To give the pump and motor a rigid common mounting, so alignment can be set and maintained, and to transfer loads to the foundation
To store lubricating oil for the bearings
To increase the head of the pump
To seal the horizontal casing joint
questions.explanation: The baseplate holds the pump and motor in a fixed relationship and, once levelled and grouted, transfers static and dynamic loads into the foundation. A poorly supported or distorted baseplate makes good alignment impossible to maintain. It has no role in lubrication, head or casing sealing.

questions.prompt: What is the 'eye' of an impeller?
options: The inlet region near the shaft where liquid enters the impeller
The outer tip of a vane at the impeller periphery
The keyway that locks the impeller to the shaft
The sight glass on the bearing housing
questions.explanation: The eye is the circular inlet opening around the hub through which liquid enters the vane passages; a double-suction impeller has one eye on each side. It is the lowest-pressure region in the pump, which is why cavitation damage often starts near the vane inlets. The vane tips are at the outlet, not the eye.

questions.prompt: In which direction does the liquid move through the impeller vane passages of this pump?
options: Inwards, from the periphery towards the eye
Outwards, from the eye towards the periphery
Only along the shaft axis, without moving outwards
It stays still while the impeller rotates around it
questions.explanation: Liquid enters each eye roughly axially, turns, and then flows radially outwards through the vane passages to the periphery, gaining energy on the way. Flow from the periphery to the eye would be the reverse of pumping action. Purely axial flow describes an axial-flow (propeller) pump, not this radial-flow impeller.

questions.scenario: A trainee has been asked to inspect the impeller of a horizontal split case pump. The pump has already been electrically isolated, locked out, valved off and drained according to the site procedure.
questions.prompt: Which part must be removed to gain access to the impeller without disturbing the main piping?
options: The suction pipe spool
The upper casing half, after removing the casing joint nuts
The electric motor
The baseplate
questions.explanation: Removing the joint nuts and lifting the upper half with suitable lifting gear exposes the impeller in the lower half, while the nozzles and pipework stay connected. Removing piping, the motor or the baseplate is unnecessary and creates extra alignment and leakage risks. The detailed sequence, lifting points and checks must follow the OEM manual.

questions.scenario: An operator notices a steady, small drip of water from the gland at each end of a split case pump fitted with gland packing. The drip rate is within the range that the site procedure describes as normal, and the glands are not hot.
questions.prompt: What is the best interpretation?
options: Gland packing is designed to allow a small controlled leakage that lubricates and cools the packing, so this is normal
The pump must be cavitating
The bearings have failed
The casing joint gasket has failed
questions.explanation: Packing relies on a small leakage to lubricate and cool the rings against the shaft sleeve; tightening the gland to stop all leakage makes the packing overheat and wears the sleeve. Cavitation, bearing failure and casing joint leakage have different symptoms and locations. A mechanical seal, by contrast, normally shows no visible leakage.

questions.prompt: Click the upper casing half.
questions.explanation: The upper half is the removable top casting, carrying the lifting lugs, vent connections and the upper halves of the seal housings. It is bolted to the lower half along the horizontal split flange. Because it carries no pipe connections, it can be lifted off for maintenance.

questions.prompt: Click the suction nozzle. Compare the two horizontal nozzles on the lower casing half and remember which one is normally larger.
questions.explanation: The suction nozzle is normally the larger of the two, because a lower inlet velocity reduces suction losses and helps keep enough NPSH available at the impeller. It sits on the opposite side of the lower half from the discharge nozzle. A pressure tapping near its flange is used to measure suction pressure for head and NPSH calculations.

questions.prompt: Click the discharge nozzle.
questions.explanation: The discharge nozzle is the outlet of the volute, cast into the lower half on the opposite side from the suction nozzle. It is usually smaller than the suction nozzle because the liquid leaves at a higher pressure and can tolerate a higher velocity. The discharge pressure tapping is located close to this nozzle.

questions.prompt: The upper casing has been removed. Click the double-suction impeller.
questions.explanation: The impeller is the wide, symmetrical rotating part in the middle of the lower casing, with an eye on each side and two sets of vanes between its shrouds. It is keyed to the shaft and located axially by the sleeves and sleeve nuts. The rings at each shroud neck are the wear rings, which are separate parts.

questions.prompt: The casing is hidden to show the internal assembly. Click the pump shaft.
questions.explanation: The shaft runs the full length of the pump, from the non-drive-end bearing, through both seals and the impeller, to the coupling hub at the drive end. It transmits the motor torque to the impeller and carries the rotor loads to the bearings. Much of it is covered by sleeves, the impeller hub and the bearings, so only parts of it are visible.

questions.prompt: Click the drive-end bearing housing (the bearing housing nearest the motor).
questions.explanation: The drive-end bearing housing sits between the casing and the coupling and contains the floating radial bearing. The non-drive-end housing, at the opposite end, contains the locating bearing. The two bearing arrangements are different, so the housings are not interchangeable in general.

questions.prompt: Match each numbered callout on the axial section diagram to its name.
questions.explanation: The upper and lower casing halves (1 and 2) meet at the horizontal split plane through the shaft centreline. The double-suction impeller (3) is mounted on the pump shaft (4), and the volute (9) is the spiral collecting passage formed between the two casing halves around the impeller.

questions.prompt: Match each numbered callout on the axial section diagram to its name.
questions.explanation: The pump shaft (4) is supported by the drive-end bearing housing (5), nearest the coupling, and the non-drive-end bearing housing (6) at the outboard end. The coupling (11) transmits torque from the motor to the drive end of the shaft.

questions.prompt: What is the main reason for using a double-suction impeller in a large-flow pump?
options: It doubles the head compared with a single-suction impeller of the same diameter and speed
The flow is shared between two eyes, so each eye handles less flow, which tends to lower NPSHr, and the opposed inlets largely balance axial thrust
It allows the pump to run in reverse without loss of performance
It eliminates the need for a thrust (locating) bearing
questions.explanation: Sharing the flow between two eyes reduces the flow and inlet velocity per eye, which tends to give a lower NPSHr for a given total flow and speed, and the mirror-image halves largely cancel each other's axial forces. Head depends mainly on impeller tip speed, so double suction does not double it. A residual axial thrust always remains, so a locating bearing is still required.

questions.prompt: Which statement about axial thrust on a double-suction impeller is correct?
options: Axial thrust is completely eliminated, so no locating bearing is needed
The hydraulic forces on the two sides are nominally opposed and largely cancel, but a residual axial thrust remains and is carried by the locating bearing
Axial thrust is always larger than on a comparable single-suction impeller
Axial thrust acts only when the pump is stopped
questions.explanation: Symmetry makes the pressure forces on the two shrouds nominally equal and opposite, so the net axial force is small compared with a single-suction impeller. Manufacturing tolerances, uneven wear-ring clearances, unequal flow to the two eyes and off-design operation all leave a residual thrust, whose size and even direction can change. That is why the rotor always needs a locating bearing.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the casing and impeller wear rings?
options: To provide a renewable close running clearance that limits leakage from the high-pressure impeller outlet back to the low-pressure eye
To carry the radial load of the rotor
To seal the shaft where it leaves the casing
To fix the impeller axially on the shaft
questions.explanation: Each impeller neck runs inside a stationary casing wear ring with a small radial clearance, which restricts the recirculating leakage from the impeller outlet back to the eye. When the clearance wears open, the rings can be renewed instead of replacing the impeller or casing. They are not designed to carry rotor load, seal the shaft exit or locate the impeller.

questions.prompt: What is the usual effect of wear-ring clearances increasing through wear?
options: Internal recirculation increases, so delivered flow, head at a given flow and efficiency fall, and the pressure distribution on the shrouds changes
Head increases because there is less friction
Bearing temperatures always fall
There is no measurable effect on the pump
questions.explanation: More leakage means more liquid circulates uselessly between the outlet and the eye, so efficiency and useful output fall and the leakage disturbs the flow entering the eye. The leakage also changes the pressure in the side spaces between the shrouds and the casing, so uneven wear on the two sides can unbalance the axial forces. Clearances are therefore checked against the OEM limits at each overhaul.

questions.prompt: In the baseline arrangement modelled, the NDE bearing is the locating bearing and the DE bearing is floating. Why is this arrangement used?
options: The locating bearing fixes the rotor axially and carries the residual thrust, while the floating bearing lets the shaft expand or contract axially with temperature without inducing extra axial load
Both bearings must locate the shaft so that it cannot move axially at all
The floating bearing carries all of the axial thrust
The positions of the bearings make no difference to the rotor
questions.explanation: Only one bearing should fix the rotor axially; the other must allow small axial movement, otherwise thermal growth of the shaft would force the bearings against each other. The locating bearing also keeps the impeller centred in the volute. Some designs locate at the drive end instead, so the OEM arrangement must always be followed.

questions.prompt: Why is a pair of angular-contact ball bearings mounted back to back often used as the locating bearing?
options: The pair carries radial load and axial load in both directions, and the back-to-back arrangement gives good resistance to tilting
Angular-contact bearings cannot carry axial load, so they let the shaft float freely
They allow unlimited axial movement of the shaft
They need no lubrication
questions.explanation: Each angular-contact bearing carries axial load in one direction, so a matched pair is used to take residual thrust whichever way it acts, which matters because the direction can reverse with operating conditions. The back-to-back arrangement also gives a stiff support against moments. A deep-groove ball bearing is an alternative where thrust is lower; selection and preload follow the OEM design.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct general sequence before lifting the upper casing half?
options: Isolate, lock out and drain the pump; disconnect auxiliary piping; release the seal or packing glands as the OEM manual requires; remove the joint nuts; break the joint; lift the upper half straight up using its lifting points
Lift the upper half first, then drain the pump
Disconnect the suction pipe, then lift the casing by its nozzles
Remove the motor, then lift the upper half together with the impeller
questions.explanation: The pump must be made safe and drained first, and anything bridging the joint, such as auxiliary piping and glands, must be released before the joint nuts are removed and the half is lifted vertically to avoid damaging the wear rings and seals. Lifting before draining is unsafe, the nozzles are on the lower half and are not lifting points, and the impeller stays in the lower half. Always follow the OEM manual and site lifting procedures.

questions.prompt: What locates the upper casing half accurately on the lower half during reassembly?
options: Dowel pins in the split flange
The coupling spacer
The bearing grease
The motor shims
questions.explanation: Dowel pins fix the relative position of the two halves so that the bores for the wear rings, seal housings and bearing fits line up as machined. Without them the upper half could be offset slightly, distorting fits and clearances. The coupling, grease and shims have nothing to do with casing registration.

questions.prompt: Why must the casing joint gasket be of the material and thickness specified by the OEM?
options: Its compressed thickness affects how the bores of the two halves line up, which influences wear-ring and seal housing fits as well as joint sealing
Any gasket will do because the bolts provide the sealing
A thicker gasket always gives a better seal and longer life
The gasket carries the axial thrust of the rotor
questions.explanation: The split joint is machined so that the bores formed by the two halves are round when the specified gasket is compressed. A wrong thickness can pinch or loosen the casing wear rings and seal housings and can cause internal or external leakage. The gasket seals the joint; it does not carry rotor loads.

questions.prompt: Why is a spacer coupling commonly used between a split case pump and its motor?
options: Removing the spacer gives working room to dismantle the drive-end bearing and seal, and to lift the rotor, without moving the motor or pump
The spacer increases the transmitted torque
The spacer removes the need for shaft alignment
The spacer acts as the pump's thrust bearing
questions.explanation: The gap left by the spacer lets the coupling hubs part so that drive-end components can be withdrawn and the rotor lifted without disturbing the motor, which preserves its position for re-alignment. The spacer does not increase torque capacity or remove the need for alignment. Thrust is carried by the pump's locating bearing.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the shaft sleeves in this pump?
options: To protect the shaft from wear and corrosion where it passes through the seal or packing area and, with the sleeve nuts, to help locate the impeller axially
To increase the head developed by the impeller
To carry the radial load of the rotor in place of bearings
To seal the horizontal casing joint
questions.explanation: The sleeves are renewable wearing surfaces for the packing or seal area, so the shaft itself does not have to be replaced when that area wears. In many designs the sleeves and sleeve nuts also clamp the impeller in its axial position. Details vary between manufacturers, so the OEM drawing defines the actual arrangement.

questions.scenario: Over several years, periodic tests on a split case pump show that the flow and head at a given valve position have slowly fallen and efficiency has dropped. Vibration levels and bearing temperatures are normal, and suction conditions are unchanged.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: Wear-ring clearances have opened up, increasing internal recirculation
The motor is now running too fast
The coupling element has become too stiff
The bearings have been over-greased
questions.explanation: A slow, steady loss of flow, head and efficiency with normal mechanical condition is the classic sign of increasing internal leakage through worn wear rings; impeller erosion can produce a similar trend. Over-speed would increase output, and coupling or grease problems show up as vibration or temperature changes. Measure the clearances against the OEM limits at the next opportunity.

questions.scenario: During reassembly, a fitter notices that the outer ring of the drive-end bearing is being clamped axially by its end cover in the same way as the locating bearing at the non-drive end. The drawing shows the DE bearing as floating.
questions.prompt: What is the main concern?
options: Both bearings would locate the shaft, so thermal expansion could not be accommodated and extra axial load would be forced into both bearings
There is no concern; clamping both bearings makes the rotor stiffer
The pump head would increase
Seal leakage would reduce
questions.explanation: The floating bearing must be free to move axially in its housing so that shaft growth with temperature does not load the bearings against each other. Clamping it creates a hidden axial load that raises temperature and shortens bearing life. The two bearing positions are deliberately different, so fit them exactly as the OEM drawing shows.

questions.scenario: After lifting the upper casing, an engineer finds heavy rub marks on the lower part of the NDE casing wear ring, while the DE ring looks normal. The NDE bearing is found to have excessive radial play.
questions.prompt: What is the most probable explanation?
options: Bearing wear allowed the rotor to run eccentrically, so the impeller wear ring contacted the casing wear ring
Wear rings are designed to touch continuously during normal running
The rub was caused by high suction pressure alone
Rub marks show correct running-in and need no further action
questions.explanation: Wear rings run with a small designed clearance, so contact means the rotor moved off centre, for example through bearing wear, shaft deflection or misassembly. The rub being on the NDE side, next to the worn bearing, supports this. Replace or recondition the rings as required and correct the bearing problem, otherwise the damage will recur.

questions.scenario: On a double-suction pump, the NDE locating bearing runs somewhat warmer than the DE floating bearing, although both carry similar radial loads. The temperature has been stable for many months.
questions.prompt: Which is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: The locating bearing also carries the residual axial thrust and has a different design and preload, so a stable, somewhat higher temperature can be normal; a rising trend would need investigation
Double-suction pumps have no axial thrust, so the NDE bearing must be faulty
The DE bearing must be faulty because it runs cooler
The two bearings are identical, so any temperature difference proves misassembly
questions.explanation: The two bearings are not identical: the locating bearing is a different type, carries the residual thrust and may be preloaded, so a modest, stable difference is not in itself a fault. What matters is the trend compared with the baseline and the OEM limits. A rise would prompt checks of lubrication, alignment, wear-ring condition and suction flow distribution.

questions.scenario: A technician has removed all 16 casing joint nuts of an isolated and drained split case pump, but the upper half will not separate from the lower half.
questions.prompt: What is the correct action?
options: Check that no fasteners, glands or auxiliary connections still restrain it, then use the jacking screws provided (if fitted) evenly to break the joint
Drive a chisel or wedge into the joint to force it open
Lift with the crane at increasing force until the joint releases
Heat the joint with a torch to release the gasket
questions.explanation: A sticking gasket is normal, and jacking screws are provided on many designs to part the joint evenly without damage. Wedges damage the machined joint faces, overloading lifting gear is dangerous, and heating can distort the casing. The OEM manual gives the approved method for the specific pump.

questions.prompt: The upper casing has been removed. Click a casing wear ring.
questions.explanation: The casing wear rings are the stationary rings seated in the casing around each impeller neck, one at each eye. Each one forms a close running clearance with the rotating impeller wear ring or impeller neck. They are held in the bore formed by the two casing halves and are usually prevented from turning by a locking feature.

questions.prompt: In this axial section, click the locating (thrust) bearing.
questions.explanation: In the baseline arrangement the locating bearing is at the non-drive end: a back-to-back pair of angular-contact ball bearings clamped axially in its housing. It fixes the rotor's axial position and carries the residual axial thrust as well as radial load. A deep-groove ball bearing variant is also available in this module.

questions.prompt: In this axial section, click the floating radial bearing.
questions.explanation: The floating bearing is the single radial ball bearing in the drive-end housing. Its outer ring is free to move axially in the housing, so the shaft can grow with temperature without loading the bearings against each other. It carries radial load only, while the NDE bearing locates the rotor.

questions.prompt: The upper casing has been removed. Click a dowel pin used to register the two casing halves.
questions.explanation: The dowel pins are the short pins in the split flange of the lower half that engage matching holes in the upper half. They make sure the halves go back together in exactly the position in which the bores were machined. Damaged or missing dowels can lead to misaligned bores and distorted fits.

questions.prompt: In this axial section, click a shaft sleeve.
questions.explanation: A shaft sleeve sits on the shaft on each side of the impeller, running through the seal or packing area. It provides a renewable wearing surface and, together with its sleeve nut, helps locate the impeller axially. The sleeve rotates with the shaft.

questions.prompt: A double-suction pump delivers a total flow of 0.36 m^3/s. Assuming an ideal, perfectly symmetrical split between the two impeller eyes, what flow enters each eye? Give the answer in m^3/s.
questions.hint: Under the ideal symmetrical assumption, Q_eye = Q / 2.
questions.explanation: Q_eye = 0.36 / 2 = 0.18 m^3/s. This is an idealisation used for design and for specific speed calculations; in a real installation the split can differ because of suction piping layout, casing tolerances and operating point. Uneven flow to the two eyes is one cause of residual axial thrust.

questions.prompt: A pump delivers 0.15 m^3/s of water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) against a total head of 40 m. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate the hydraulic (water) power, in kW.
questions.hint: P_h = rho * g * Q * H gives watts; divide by 1000 for kW.
questions.explanation: P_h = 1000 x 9.81 x 0.15 x 40 = 58860 W = 58.86 kW. This is the power actually transferred to the liquid; the shaft power is larger because of the pump's internal losses. Forgetting to convert from watts to kilowatts is a common slip.

questions.prompt: A pump shaft transmits 75 kW at 1480 rpm. Using T = 9550 * P(kW) / N(rpm), calculate the shaft torque, in N.m.
questions.hint: Substitute P in kW and N in rpm directly; the constant 9550 already contains the unit conversion.
questions.explanation: T = 9550 x 75 / 1480 = 483.95 N.m. The constant 9550 comes from 60000 / (2 x pi), which converts kW to W and rpm to rad/s. Torque matters for sizing the shaft, coupling and keys.

questions.prompt: A pump delivers 500 m^3/h at 1480 rpm. Its speed is reduced to 1184 rpm with the impeller diameter unchanged. Using the affinity laws, estimate the flow at the corresponding (geometrically similar) operating point, in m^3/h.
questions.hint: Flow scales directly with speed: Q2 = Q1 * (N2 / N1).
questions.explanation: Q2 = 500 x (1184 / 1480) = 500 x 0.8 = 400 m^3/h. The affinity laws describe how a point on the pump curve moves with speed; the actual operating point also depends on the system curve. Head would scale with the square and power with the cube of the speed ratio.

questions.prompt: Match each numbered callout on the axial section diagram to its name.
questions.explanation: Liquid reaches the double-suction impeller (3) through two side chambers; callout 8 marks the non-drive-end suction chamber. The casing wear ring (10) sets the leakage clearance at each impeller neck. The shaft sleeve (12) protects the shaft where it passes through the drive-end shaft seal (7).

questions.prompt: Why should a large double-suction pump not run for long periods far to the left of its best efficiency point (low flow)?
options: Suction and discharge recirculation, higher radial and fluctuating hydraulic loads, vibration, temperature rise and possible uneven loading of the two impeller sides
Efficiency is highest at low flow, so this is actually recommended
NPSH problems cannot occur at low flow
Motor power is always at its maximum at low flow for every pump type
questions.explanation: At low flow the incidence at the vane inlets and outlets is poor, recirculation develops in the eyes and at the outlet, and radial and pulsating loads rise, which increases vibration, bearing and seal loads and liquid temperature. Efficiency falls away from BEP. For typical radial-flow pumps power rises with flow, so the motor overload risk is usually at high flow, although high specific speed pumps can behave differently.

questions.prompt: Operating near runout (far to the right of BEP) on a typical radial-flow split case pump most commonly risks:
options: Rising NPSHr with cavitation risk, high power draw that may overload the motor, and increased radial loads
Zero power consumption
A head higher than the shut-off head
No change in behaviour compared with BEP
questions.explanation: Towards runout NPSHr rises steeply while NPSHa falls because suction losses grow with flow, so the cavitation margin shrinks from both sides. For a typical radial-flow pump the power curve rises with flow, so the motor may be overloaded if it was sized only for the duty point. Radial load also rises away from BEP in a single volute casing.

questions.prompt: Where should a split case pump normally be selected to operate continuously?
options: Within a preferred operating region around BEP, with limits taken from the manufacturer's data and guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.3
At shut-off, because the head is highest there
At runout, because the flow is highest there
Anywhere on the curve, since reliability is the same at every point
questions.explanation: Hydraulic loads, vibration and recirculation are lowest near BEP, so reliability and efficiency are best in a band around it. The width of the preferred and allowable operating regions depends on the pump and is defined by the manufacturer. Continuous running at shut-off or runout brings the problems covered in the previous questions.

questions.prompt: How is NPSHr commonly defined in standard pump performance testing?
options: The NPSH at which the pump's total head has fallen by 3% at a given flow because of cavitation (NPSH3)
The NPSH at which the first vapour bubbles appear (cavitation inception)
The reading of the suction pressure gauge
The NPSH at which the pump stops delivering any flow
questions.explanation: Following the conventions of ISO 9906 and ANSI/HI 14.6, NPSHr is commonly taken as NPSH3, the value at which head drops by 3%. Cavitation is already present at NPSH3, and inception occurs at a considerably higher NPSH, so NPSHa needs a margin above NPSHr chosen from guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.1 and the OEM. A gauge reading is only one input to NPSHa.

questions.prompt: A vibration spectrum on a split case pump shows a dominant peak at vane passing frequency (number of vanes x running speed). Which is a likely contributing factor?
options: A small gap between the impeller vane tips and the volute tongue, or operation well away from BEP, increasing pressure pulsations
Coupling unbalance only
A loose motor terminal box cover
Supply frequency variation only
questions.explanation: Vane passing frequency is a hydraulic excitation produced each time a vane passes the volute tongue, so it is sensitive to the tip-to-tongue gap and to off-design flow. Unbalance shows mainly at 1x running speed, and electrical problems appear at frequencies related to the supply. Many double-suction impellers stagger the vanes of the two halves to reduce these pulsations.

questions.prompt: A pump fitted with the deep-groove ball bearing locating option is dismantled. The locating bearing shows a running track displaced well to one side of both raceways, with flaking in that area. What does this pattern most likely indicate?
options: Heavy axial load on the bearing; investigate sources of residual thrust such as uneven wear rings, unequal flow to the eyes, impeller centring and off-BEP operation
Pure electrical erosion from stray currents
Too little radial load, causing skidding only
Normal end-of-life wear that needs no investigation
questions.explanation: Under pure radial load a deep-groove ball bearing runs with a track near the centre of the raceways; a track pushed towards one shoulder shows that a significant axial load was acting. Electrical erosion typically produces a washboard (fluting) or frosted pattern, and skidding gives smearing rather than an offset track. Replacing the bearing without finding the thrust source is likely to lead to repeat failure.

questions.prompt: Which of the following would most likely increase the residual axial thrust on a double-suction impeller?
options: Unequal wear-ring clearances on the two sides of the impeller
Equal wear-ring clearances on both sides
Correct axial centring of the impeller in the volute
A straight, uniform suction approach with even flow to both eyes
questions.explanation: Leakage through each wear ring influences the pressure in the side space behind that shroud, so unequal clearances give unequal pressure forces on the two shrouds. The other options all preserve symmetry and therefore keep the residual thrust low. Even with perfect symmetry some residual thrust remains, so it is never zero in practice.

questions.prompt: Why is an elbow close to the suction nozzle, lying in the plane of the shaft (a horizontal elbow on a horizontal pump), a known problem for double-suction pumps?
options: It skews the velocity profile so that one side chamber receives more flow than the other, giving unequal flow to the two eyes, residual axial thrust, noise, vibration and cavitation on one side
It has no effect, because the casing always splits the flow exactly in half
It increases NPSHa
It only affects the discharge side of the pump
questions.explanation: An elbow throws the flow towards its outer wall; if the elbow lies in the plane of the shaft, that bias is directed towards one eye. Piping guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.6 and OEM instructions therefore call for a straight run ahead of the suction nozzle and, where an elbow is unavoidable, an orientation in the plane perpendicular to the shaft. The extra losses of a poor layout reduce NPSHa rather than increase it.

questions.prompt: Why is the shut-off head important when specifying a pump installation with a curve that rises continuously to shut-off?
options: It is normally the highest head the pump can develop, so maximum suction pressure plus the shut-off pressure rise sets the pressure rating needed for the casing, discharge piping and valves
It is the head at which the pump should run continuously
It equals the system static head in every installation
It is the head at maximum flow
questions.explanation: With a closed or nearly closed discharge, the pump develops its shut-off head, and the resulting discharge pressure must be within the rating of the casing, piping and valves. Continuous operation at shut-off is not acceptable because the liquid heats up and loads are high. Shut-off head is at zero flow, not at runout, and it is a property of the pump rather than of the system.

questions.scenario: A double-suction pump on a cooling water system makes a crackling noise, like gravel passing through it, and its discharge pressure fluctuates when the sump level is low. At overhaul, pitting is found on the vane inlets near both eyes.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause and the most appropriate response?
options: Cavitation, because NPSHa has fallen close to or below NPSHr; raise the minimum sump level, reduce suction losses or move operation towards BEP, and verify the NPSH margin
Bearing failure; replace both bearings
Coupling misalignment; realign the motor
Worn wear rings only; replace them and restart
questions.explanation: Gravel-like noise, pressure fluctuation linked to low sump level and pitting at the vane inlets all point to cavitation. The fix is to restore the margin of NPSHa over NPSHr, by raising the liquid level, reducing suction losses or avoiding high-flow operation. Bearing and alignment faults do not depend on sump level, and wear rings alone do not explain inlet pitting.

questions.scenario: After a plant modification, a horizontal elbow was installed immediately upstream of the suction nozzle of a double-suction pump, turning in the plane of the shaft. Since then, the NDE locating bearing temperature has risen, vibration has increased, and cavitation pitting is found mainly at one eye.
questions.prompt: What is the probable root cause?
options: Non-uniform suction flow giving unequal flow to the two eyes, which creates residual axial thrust and localised cavitation on the overloaded side
Motor over-speed
Too much straight pipe upstream of the pump
The discharge valve being opened too far, with no link to the modification
questions.explanation: The elbow in the plane of the shaft biases the flow towards one side chamber, so one eye runs at higher flow and lower local pressure than the other. That eye cavitates first, and the unequal side forces raise the thrust carried by the locating bearing. The remedy is to correct the suction layout, for example with a straight run or an elbow in the perpendicular plane, following ANSI/HI 9.6.6 and OEM guidance.

questions.scenario: Vibration measurements on a split case pump show a dominant component at 1x running speed, mainly in the radial directions, with a steady phase. The level is much the same at all flow rates. Alignment has been checked and is within tolerance. The impeller was repaired by weld build-up at the last overhaul.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
options: Rotor unbalance, for example because the impeller was not re-balanced after the repair
Cavitation
Vane-pass pressure pulsation
Electrical supply imbalance
questions.explanation: A steady, mainly radial 1x vibration that does not change with flow points to unbalance, and a weld repair without re-balancing is a likely source. Cavitation produces broadband, random vibration that varies with suction conditions and flow, and vane-pass pulsation appears at vanes x speed. Electrical problems show at frequencies related to the supply and usually change when power is removed.

questions.scenario: A new motor has been fitted to a split case pump. Since then, vibration at both the pump DE bearing and the motor DE bearing is high in the axial direction, with strong 1x and 2x components, and the coupling elements show signs of wear and heat.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause and action?
options: Shaft misalignment between pump and motor; re-check and correct alignment, including soft foot and pipe strain, to the OEM tolerances
Cavitation; increase the sump level
Excessive wear-ring clearance; replace the wear rings
Low oil level in the NDE bearing housing only
questions.explanation: High axial vibration on both sides of the coupling, with 1x and 2x components and distressed coupling elements, is typical of misalignment, and the recent motor change makes it the prime suspect. Soft foot and pipe strain can distort the alignment even after a careful set-up. Cavitation, wear rings and a single bearing's lubrication would not produce this pattern on both machines.

questions.scenario: A standby split case pump has been idle for several months on a skid next to a duty pump that runs continuously. Shortly after it is put into service, its DE bearing becomes noisy. Inspection shows evenly spaced, line-shaped marks across the raceways at ball spacing.
questions.prompt: What is the most likely damage mechanism?
options: False brinelling from vibration transmitted while the shaft was stationary; rotate standby pumps periodically and limit transmitted vibration as the site procedure requires
True brinelling from very high running loads
Electrical fluting from stray currents during running
Normal fatigue at the end of the bearing's life
questions.explanation: Marks at ball spacing on a bearing that sat still while exposed to vibration are characteristic of false brinelling, a wear mechanism caused by small oscillating movements without a lubricant film. Electrical fluting produces a washboard pattern from current passing during rotation, and fatigue gives flaking rather than regular marks. Periodic rotation of standby units is a common preventive measure.

questions.scenario: After an overhaul, measurements show the impeller is axially offset from the volute centreline because the sleeve nuts were set incorrectly. The pump starts and runs, but the NDE bearing temperature is higher than before.
questions.prompt: What is the most appropriate assessment?
options: The off-centre impeller gives unequal side clearances and side-space pressures, adding residual thrust and hydraulic losses; reset the impeller centring as the OEM specifies
There is no consequence, because double-suction pumps are always perfectly balanced
The head will double because the impeller is closer to one wall
NPSHr will be eliminated
questions.explanation: Centring the impeller in the volute is part of keeping the two halves symmetrical; an offset makes the side spaces and their pressure forces unequal, so residual thrust and bearing load increase. It can also misalign the impeller outlet with the volute and reduce efficiency. Double-suction pumps are only nominally balanced, so assembly accuracy matters.

questions.scenario: A pump serves a system dominated by static head. To save energy, operators reduce the speed by 25% with a variable frequency drive. Flow falls far more than the 25% that the affinity laws seem to predict, almost to zero.
questions.prompt: Why did this happen?
options: The affinity laws scale the pump curve, but the operating point lies where the new pump curve meets the system curve; with high static head, the reduced head can barely exceed the static lift, so flow collapses
The affinity laws say flow does not depend on speed
A variable frequency drive does not change pump speed
Static head falls in proportion to pump speed
questions.explanation: At 75% speed the head at any similar point is about 0.75^2 = 0.56 of its original value; if the static head is close to or above that, the new pump curve crosses the system curve near shut-off. The affinity laws apply directly to the operating point only for a system curve that passes through the origin, such as a pure friction system. Operating near shut-off brings the low-flow risks discussed earlier.

questions.scenario: A split case pump with gland packing draws clean water under suction lift. The packing runs hot and dry, and air is being drawn into the pump at the stuffing boxes, causing loss of prime.
questions.prompt: What should be checked first?
options: The seal water supply to the lantern rings and the correct position of the lantern rings, so a positive liquid seal is maintained even when the stuffing box is below atmospheric pressure
Increase the motor speed so the pump primes faster
Remove the lantern rings to make room for more packing
Tighten the packing until there is no leakage at all
questions.explanation: Under suction lift the stuffing boxes can be below atmospheric pressure, so air leaks in unless a liquid seal is supplied through the lantern ring, which also lubricates and cools the packing. The lantern ring must line up with the flush connection. Over-tightening or removing the lantern ring makes overheating worse, and speed does not cure air ingress.

questions.prompt: A pump has suffered prolonged cavitation. Click the rotating part where cavitation pitting is most commonly found.
questions.explanation: Classic cavitation damage appears on the impeller vanes just downstream of their inlet edges, usually on the low-pressure side, and can extend onto the adjacent shroud near the eye. Vapour bubbles form where local pressure falls below vapour pressure and collapse as pressure rises along the vane. In a double-suction pump, damage concentrated on one eye suggests unequal flow to the two sides.
