questions.prompt: Conceptual thrust arrows are shown on the impeller. Click the component that carries the residual axial thrust to the bearing housing.
questions.explanation: Residual axial thrust is carried by the locating bearing, which in this arrangement is the paired angular-contact bearing at the non-drive end. The DE bearing is floating and deliberately carries no axial load. The arrows are conceptual; actual thrust magnitude and direction depend on design and operating conditions.

questions.prompt: This pump is fitted with gland packing. Click a lantern ring.
questions.explanation: The lantern ring is the perforated spacer ring placed between packing rings, aligned with the flush connection. It distributes seal water around the shaft sleeve to lubricate and cool the packing and, under suction lift, to stop air being drawn in. Its axial position in the stack must match the flush port.

questions.prompt: This pump is fitted with mechanical seals. Click the seal face that rotates with the shaft and forms one half of the primary sealing interface.
questions.explanation: The rotating face is driven by the shaft (through the sleeve and drive collar) and is held against the stationary seat by spring force and hydraulic pressure. The thin fluid film between the two lapped faces controls leakage. The stationary seat is mounted in the gland plate and does not turn.

questions.prompt: A double-suction pump delivers 0.20 m^3/s of water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) against a total head of 55 m. The pump efficiency at this duty is 84%. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate the shaft power required, in kW.
questions.hint: First find P_h = rho * g * Q * H, then divide by the pump efficiency expressed as a decimal.
questions.explanation: P_h = 1000 x 9.81 x 0.20 x 55 = 107910 W = 107.91 kW, and P_shaft = 107.91 / 0.84 = 128.46 kW. Shaft power is always larger than hydraulic power because of the pump's losses. Multiplying by the efficiency instead (giving about 90.6 kW) is a common error.

questions.prompt: A pump delivers 0.12 m^3/s of water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) against a total head of 60 m. Pump efficiency is 82% and motor efficiency is 95%; the motor drives the pump directly. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate the electrical input power to the motor, in kW.
questions.hint: Find P_h, divide by eta_p to get shaft power, then divide by eta_motor.
questions.explanation: P_h = 1000 x 9.81 x 0.12 x 60 = 70.632 kW; P_shaft = 70.632 / 0.82 = 86.14 kW; P_electrical = 86.14 / 0.95 = 90.67 kW. The overall efficiency is 0.82 x 0.95 = 0.779. A variable frequency drive, if fitted, would add its own losses.

questions.prompt: A pump develops 80 m of head at its BEP when running at 1480 rpm. The speed is reduced to 1184 rpm with a variable frequency drive, and the impeller diameter is unchanged. Using the affinity laws, estimate the head at the corresponding (similar) operating point, in m.
questions.explanation: N2 / N1 = 1184 / 1480 = 0.8, so H2 = 80 x 0.8^2 = 80 x 0.64 = 51.2 m. Head falls with the square of speed, which is why a large speed reduction can drop the head below the static head of a system. Using the ratio directly (64 m) or cubed (41 m) are common mistakes.

questions.prompt: A pump absorbs 150 kW of shaft power at 1480 rpm. Its speed is reduced to 1332 rpm with the impeller unchanged. Assuming the pump efficiency at the corresponding point is unchanged, use the affinity laws to estimate the new shaft power, in kW.
questions.explanation: N2 / N1 = 1332 / 1480 = 0.9, so P2 = 150 x 0.9^3 = 150 x 0.729 = 109.35 kW. A 10% speed reduction saves about 27% of the power at a similar point, which is why speed control is attractive in friction-dominated systems. In real systems efficiency changes and static head alter the result.

questions.prompt: Water at 30 °C (rho = 995.7 kg/m^3, vapour pressure 4.25 kPa absolute) is drawn from an open tank at an atmospheric pressure of 101.325 kPa. The free surface is 2.5 m above the impeller centreline, and the suction line friction and fitting losses at the duty flow total 1.2 m. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate NPSHa referred to the impeller centreline, in m.
questions.hint: NPSHa = (p_atm - p_v) / (rho * g) + z_s - h_fs, with z_s positive when the liquid level is above the pump datum.
questions.explanation: (101325 - 4250) / (995.7 x 9.81) = 97075 / 9767.8 = 9.938 m; NPSHa = 9.938 + 2.5 - 1.2 = 11.24 m. The flooded suction adds to NPSHa while the friction losses subtract from it. Forgetting the vapour pressure term overstates NPSHa by about 0.4 m.

questions.prompt: A pump lifts water at 20 °C (rho = 998 kg/m^3, vapour pressure 2.34 kPa absolute) from an open sump. The atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa, the water level is 3.0 m below the impeller centreline, and suction losses at the duty flow are 0.9 m. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate NPSHa, in m.
questions.hint: For a suction lift, z_s is negative: NPSHa = (p_atm - p_v) / (rho * g) - 3.0 - 0.9.
questions.explanation: (101300 - 2340) / (998 x 9.81) = 98960 / 9790.4 = 10.108 m; NPSHa = 10.108 - 3.0 - 0.9 = 6.21 m. Suction lift and friction both reduce NPSHa, and NPSHa also falls if the water warms up or the flow increases. Compare this value with the NPSHr at the same flow, with a suitable margin.

questions.prompt: During a site test, the suction pressure gauge (corrected to the impeller centreline) reads 35 kPa gauge. The local atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa, the water vapour pressure is 2.34 kPa absolute, the density is 998 kg/m^3 and the mean velocity at the suction tapping section is 3.0 m/s. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate NPSHa, in m.
questions.hint: Convert the gauge reading to absolute pressure first, then NPSHa = (p_abs - p_v) / (rho * g) + v^2 / (2 * g).
questions.explanation: p_abs = 35 + 101.3 = 136.3 kPa; (136300 - 2340) / (998 x 9.81) = 13.683 m; velocity head = 3.0^2 / (2 x 9.81) = 0.459 m; NPSHa = 14.14 m. When NPSHa is found from a suction gauge, the velocity head must be added because NPSH is defined on total head. Using gauge pressure without adding atmospheric pressure is the most common error.

questions.prompt: A double-suction pump has its BEP at a total flow of 0.36 m^3/s and a head of 45 m at 1480 rpm. Using the metric convention N_s = N * sqrt(Q) / H^0.75 with N in rpm, Q in m^3/s and H in m, and taking Q as the flow per eye (half the total, a convention commonly used for double-suction impellers), calculate N_s.
questions.hint: Q per eye = 0.18 m^3/s; 45^0.75 is about 17.37.
questions.explanation: sqrt(0.18) = 0.4243 and 45^0.75 = 17.374, so N_s = 1480 x 0.4243 / 17.374 = 36.1. Using the total flow instead gives about 51.1, which is why the convention (per eye or total flow) must always be stated. A value in this range indicates a radial-flow impeller.

questions.prompt: A pump delivers 0.25 m^3/s of water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) against a total head of 50 m with a pump efficiency of 85%, running at 1480 rpm. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate the torque at the pump shaft, in N.m.
questions.hint: Find the shaft power in kW (P_h / eta_p), then T = 9550 * P / N.
questions.explanation: P_h = 1000 x 9.81 x 0.25 x 50 = 122.625 kW; P_shaft = 122.625 / 0.85 = 144.26 kW; T = 9550 x 144.26 / 1480 = 930.9 N.m. Torque must be based on shaft power, not hydraulic power, since the shaft carries the full input including losses. This torque is used when checking shaft, key and coupling ratings against the OEM data.

questions.prompt: In a test, a pump delivers 0.10 m^3/s of water (rho = 1000 kg/m^3) against a total head of 35 m, and the measured shaft power is 42 kW. Use g = 9.81 m/s^2. Calculate the pump efficiency, in percent.
questions.hint: eta_p = P_h / P_shaft, with both powers in the same units; multiply by 100 for percent.
questions.explanation: P_h = 1000 x 9.81 x 0.10 x 35 = 34.335 kW, so eta_p = 34.335 / 42 = 0.8175 = 81.75%. Efficiency is output (hydraulic power) divided by input (shaft power), so it is always below 100%. If electrical input were used instead, the result would be the overall (wire-to-water) efficiency.

questions.prompt: Pressure gauges at the suction and discharge tappings, both at the same elevation, read 50 kPa and 450 kPa (gauge). The mean velocities at the tapping sections are 2.5 m/s at suction and 4.0 m/s at discharge. For water with rho = 1000 kg/m^3 and g = 9.81 m/s^2, calculate the pump total head, in m.
questions.hint: H = (p_d - p_s) / (rho * g) + (v_d^2 - v_s^2) / (2 * g) + (z_d - z_s), and here z_d - z_s = 0.
questions.explanation: Pressure term = 400000 / 9810 = 40.775 m; velocity term = (16 - 6.25) / 19.62 = 0.497 m; H = 41.27 m. The suction nozzle of a split case pump is usually larger than the discharge nozzle, so the velocity heads differ and should be included. If the gauges were at different heights, the elevation difference would also be added.

questions.prompt: Match each numbered callout on the axial section diagram to its name.
questions.explanation: The drive-end (5) and non-drive-end (6) bearing housings hold different bearing arrangements, floating and locating respectively. The drive-end shaft seal (7) runs on the shaft sleeve (12), the casing wear ring (10) controls internal leakage at the impeller neck, and the coupling (11) connects the pump shaft to the motor.

overview.title: Horizontal split case centrifugal pump
overview.summary: A horizontal split case pump is a single-stage centrifugal pump whose volute casing is split on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline, with a double-suction impeller supported between two bearings. It is widely used where large flows must be moved reliably over long running periods. Its main practical attraction is that the upper casing half can be lifted off to reach the rotor without disturbing the suction and discharge piping or the driver.

sections.title: What it is
sections.body:
The pump takes its name from its casing, which is divided into an upper and a lower half along a horizontal joint containing the shaft axis. This is called an axially split casing, in contrast to the radially split casing of a typical end-suction pump.

Inside, a single double-suction impeller receives liquid through two eyes, one on each side, and delivers it into one volute. The shaft passes right through the casing and is carried by a bearing at each end, so the rotor is of the between-bearings type rather than overhung.

sections.title: Construction
sections.body:
The lower casing half carries the suction and discharge nozzles, the casing feet and the bearing housing supports, so it stays bolted to the baseplate and the pipework. The upper half is a cover that completes the volute, the suction chambers and the seal housings, and is located on the lower half by dowel pins and clamped by studs and nuts through the split flange, with a gasket in the joint.

The rotor consists of the shaft, the impeller, shaft sleeves and sleeve nuts, wear rings, the rotating parts of the shaft seals and the coupling hub. It runs in a floating radial bearing at the drive end and a locating bearing at the non-drive end. A flexible spacer coupling connects the pump to an electric motor on a common baseplate.
points: Casing: upper and lower halves, split flange, gasket, studs, nuts and dowel pins.
Impeller: single-stage, double-suction, closed, keyed to the shaft and located by sleeves and sleeve nuts.
Wear rings: renewable close-clearance rings at each impeller neck.
Shaft seals: mechanical seal or gland packing at each of the two shaft exits.
Bearings: drive-end floating radial ball bearing; non-drive-end locating bearing (paired angular-contact in the baseline).
Drive: flexible spacer coupling, electric motor and common baseplate on a grouted foundation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body:
Liquid enters the suction nozzle and is divided by the casing into two side chambers that feed the two impeller eyes. The rotating impeller increases the angular momentum of the liquid, raising its pressure and velocity as it flows outwards through the vane passages.

The two streams leave the impeller together around its periphery and are collected by the volute, whose growing cross-section and diffusing discharge section convert part of the velocity energy into pressure. The liquid then leaves through the discharge nozzle on the opposite side of the lower half. Because the two halves of the impeller mirror each other, their axial forces largely, but not completely, cancel.

sections.title: Where it is used
sections.body: Split case pumps are typically chosen for medium to large flows at moderate heads, often in continuous or long-duty service where efficiency and easy maintenance justify a larger, heavier machine. Typical users include water utilities, power stations, building services, fire protection systems, process industries and irrigation schemes. Materials of construction are selected to suit the liquid, from cast iron for clean water to stainless steels or bronzes for corrosive services.

sections.title: Advantages and limitations
sections.body: The design trades size and initial cost for maintainability, hydraulic balance and good suction performance at high flows. Whether it is the right choice depends on the duty, the space available and the life-cycle cost.
points: Advantage: the rotor can be inspected and removed by lifting the upper half, without disconnecting the main piping or moving the motor.
Advantage: the double-suction impeller largely balances axial thrust, reducing the load on the locating bearing.
Advantage: sharing the flow between two eyes tends to give a lower NPSHr than a comparable single-suction pump at the same flow and speed.
Advantage: the between-bearings rotor is stiff, which helps control shaft deflection at the seals and wear rings.
Limitation: larger footprint, weight and, in small sizes, higher cost than an end-suction pump of similar duty.
Limitation: two shaft seals and two bearing housings to maintain.
Limitation: sensitive to uneven suction flow; suction piping layout must give an even flow to both eyes.
Limitation: residual axial thrust still exists and must be carried by a correctly selected locating bearing.

sections.title: Configurations and variations
sections.body: Split case pumps are built in many variants. This module lets you switch some of them on the 3D model; others are described for awareness only. Always check the actual pump and its OEM documentation, because arrangements differ between manufacturers.
points: Shaft sealing: mechanical seals or gland packing at both ends (switchable in this module).
Volute: single volute or double volute with a splitter rib to reduce radial load (switchable).
Bearing lubrication: oil bath with constant-level oiler or grease (switchable).
Locating bearing: paired angular-contact ball bearings or a deep-groove ball bearing (switchable).
Rotation and drive side: clockwise or anticlockwise, with the motor at either end, depending on the installation.
Mounting: horizontal is most common; vertical mounting versions of split case pumps also exist.
Related designs: two-stage and multistage axially split pumps, and designs to industry specifications such as API 610 (type BB1) for petroleum service.

sections.title: How to use this module
sections.body:
Start with the 3D model: rotate, zoom and click any part to see its name, function and position in the assembly. Use the section, transparency and explode tools to see inside, and the configuration switches to compare variants.

Then work through the working-principle stages and the axial thrust lesson, which drive the model to show each idea, and use the hydraulic parameters and formulas as a reference when solving the numerical questions. Finish with the assessment, which includes clicking parts on the model, labelling a section diagram, troubleshooting cases and calculations.
points: Explore: click parts, use sections, x-ray and explode views.
Learn: follow the working-principle stages and the thrust lesson.
Apply: use the parameters and formulas for calculations.
Check: take the beginner, intermediate and advanced assessments.

keyFeatures: Axially split volute casing, divided on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline.
Suction and discharge nozzles on the lower casing half, horizontal and on opposite sides.
Single-stage, double-suction closed impeller with two eyes.
Suction flow divided into two side chambers, recombined in a single volute and discharge nozzle.
Between-bearings rotor: floating radial ball bearing at the drive end, locating bearing at the non-drive end.
Renewable casing and impeller wear rings, shaft sleeves and sleeve nuts.
Mechanical seal or gland packing at each of the two shaft exits.
Flexible spacer coupling to an electric motor on a common baseplate.
Top access to the rotor by lifting the upper casing half, without disturbing the main piping.
applications: Municipal water supply, treatment and distribution
Cooling water circulation in power plants and industrial plants
Chilled water and condenser water circulation in large building services systems
Fire protection systems, where the pump is listed or approved for that purpose
Industrial process water and general transfer duties
Seawater intake and desalination plants, with suitable corrosion-resistant materials
Pipeline and refinery transfer duties, with designs to industry specifications such as API 610

comparison.splitCase: Between bearings: bearings on both sides of the impeller.
comparison.endSuction: Overhung: impeller cantilevered beyond the bearing housing.

comparison.splitCase: Typically a double-suction closed impeller with two eyes.
comparison.endSuction: Single-suction impeller, closed, semi-open or open.

comparison.splitCase: Axially split on the horizontal plane through the shaft centreline.
comparison.endSuction: Radially split, with the cover joint at right angles to the shaft.

comparison.splitCase: Lift the upper half; the rotor is accessible without disturbing the main piping or motor.
comparison.endSuction: Back pull-out: the rotating assembly is withdrawn rearwards, usually with a spacer coupling, leaving the casing in the pipework.

comparison.splitCase: Largely balanced by the opposed inlets; a residual thrust remains and is carried by the locating bearing.
comparison.endSuction: Larger net thrust; often reduced with balance holes, back vanes or a back wear ring, with the remainder taken by the thrust bearing.

comparison.splitCase: Flow shared between two eyes tends to give a lower NPSHr for a given flow and speed.
comparison.endSuction: All flow through one eye; NPSHr tends to be higher for the same flow and speed.

comparison.splitCase: Larger and heavier for a given duty; wide casing across the shaft.
comparison.endSuction: More compact and lighter in small and medium sizes.

comparison.splitCase: Medium to large flows at moderate heads, often continuous duty.
comparison.endSuction: Small to medium flows across a wide range of general services.

comparison.splitCase: Side-side nozzles on the lower half; suction layout must give an even flow to both eyes.
comparison.endSuction: Axial end suction and top discharge; a uniform approach is still needed but there is no flow split between eyes.

comparison.splitCase: Two shaft seals, one at each shaft exit.
Pump-to-motor alignment plus axial centring of the impeller in the volute; two bearing housings to set up.
comparison.endSuction: Pump-to-motor alignment; overhung shaft deflection at the seal is a design consideration.

comparison.splitCase: Carried by bearings on both sides of the impeller; double-volute casings are common on larger sizes.
comparison.endSuction: Carried through an overhung shaft, so radial load produces larger deflection at the seal for a given shaft.

comparison.splitCase: Tends to be higher in small sizes; often competitive at large flows.
comparison.endSuction: Tends to be lower in small and medium sizes.

overview.modelNotice: The 3D model in this module is an educational geometry model built to show the arrangement and function of a typical horizontal split case pump. Its proportions are illustrative: it is not OEM CAD, it does not represent any particular manufacturer's pump, and no dimensions, clearances, ratings or performance values should be taken from it. Always use the manufacturer's documentation and site procedures for real equipment.

workingStages.title: Suction entry
workingStages.narration: Liquid from the suction pipe enters the suction nozzle on the lower casing half. Inside the casing, the suction passage divides the incoming stream into two side chambers, one on each side of the impeller. Each chamber guides the liquid around the shaft and turns it into one impeller eye, so the impeller is fed from both sides at once. This is the lowest-pressure region of the pump, so the suction pressure must stay sufficiently above the vapour pressure of the liquid to avoid cavitation. The passages are shaped to keep the suction velocity moderate and the approach flow as even as possible. Ideally each eye receives half the flow, but in a real installation the split depends on the upstream piping, the casing and the operating point. The moving particles are a qualitative illustration, not a CFD result.
keyPoints: The suction nozzle is on the lower casing half, so the upper half can be removed without disturbing the suction pipe.
The casing divides the flow into two side chambers that feed the two impeller eyes.
Pressure is lowest at the impeller eyes; the margin above vapour pressure is expressed as NPSH.
An equal split between the eyes is an ideal; the real split depends on the suction approach and operating point.

explains.text: The inlet connection on the lower casing half. It is normally larger than the discharge nozzle so that the inlet velocity, and therefore the suction loss, stays low.
How the incoming flow is shared between the two side chambers. A uniform velocity profile at the nozzle, helped by a straight suction run, gives the most even split.
The impeller receives liquid from both sides, in opposite axial directions, through two eyes. Each half handles roughly half the total flow.
The pressure at the pump inlet, measured at a tapping near the suction flange. It can be below atmospheric pressure on a suction lift, so it must be stated as gauge or absolute.
The mean velocity in the suction passage, Q divided by the flow area. Lower velocities reduce friction losses and help keep NPSH available high.
The particle paths show the general route of the flow only. They are not computed from fluid dynamics and do not show real velocities or pressures.

workingStages.title: Double-suction impeller
workingStages.narration: The motor drives the shaft through the coupling, and the shaft turns the impeller: this is where mechanical energy enters the liquid. Liquid arriving at each eye is picked up by the vanes and forced to rotate with the impeller. As it moves outwards through the vane passages, both its pressure and its tangential velocity rise. Centrifugal action raises the pressure with radius, and the vanes do work by increasing the angular momentum of the liquid. The Euler turbomachine equation expresses this idea: the ideal head depends on the blade speed and the swirl velocity at the outlet, minus any swirl at the inlet. The vanes are usually curved backwards relative to the direction of rotation. The two halves of the impeller work in parallel, each handling roughly half of the flow, and their axial forces largely oppose each other.
keyPoints: Shaft torque from the motor is the energy input; the vanes transfer it to the liquid.
Pressure and velocity both increase as liquid flows outwards through the vane passages.
The two halves of the impeller work in parallel and discharge into a common outlet.
Actual head is lower than the ideal Euler head because of slip and hydraulic losses.

explains.text: Shaft power P_shaft = T * omega, where T is shaft torque and omega the angular speed. Part of it becomes hydraulic power; the rest is lost to hydraulic, leakage and mechanical losses.
Liquid forced to rotate with the impeller experiences a pressure rise with increasing radius, much like liquid in a spinning container.

Backward-curved vanes, with an outlet angle chosen by the designer, give a stable head-flow curve. On many double-suction impellers the vanes of the two halves are staggered to reduce pressure pulsations.

The ideal head is H_th = (u2 * c_u2 - u1 * c_u1) / g, where u is the blade speed and c_u the tangential component of absolute velocity at outlet (2) and inlet (1). With no pre-swirl at the inlet, H_th = u2 * c_u2 / g.
Inside the impeller the static pressure and the absolute velocity both rise. The high velocity leaving the impeller is the energy the volute later partly converts into pressure.

The liquid does not follow the vanes exactly at the outlet, so the actual swirl is less than the vane angle suggests. Together with friction and turbulence, this makes the real head lower than the ideal Euler head.

scene.label: Stage 2: energy transfer in the double-suction impeller

workingStages.title: Discharge from the impeller
workingStages.narration: Liquid from both halves of the impeller leaves together around the whole periphery, at high velocity and at a pressure well above suction pressure. Its absolute velocity has a large tangential component, so it leaves on a spiral path rather than straight outwards. Just outside the impeller it enters the casing passage that surrounds it. Near the volute tongue, also called the cutwater, the passage is at its narrowest. From there the volute runs around the impeller, collecting liquid from every part of the periphery. The tongue separates the start of the volute from the discharge throat, and the gap between the tongue and the vane tips affects pressure pulsations and noise. A small part of the flow leaks back from the outlet towards the eyes through the wear-ring clearances.
keyPoints: Liquid leaves the impeller around its full circumference with high velocity and strong swirl.
The flows from the two impeller halves recombine at the common outlet and enter a single volute.
The volute tongue (cutwater) divides the start of the volute from the discharge throat.
A small fraction of the flow leaks back to the eyes through the wear-ring clearances.

explains.text: The outer diameter of the impeller, where the vane passages of both halves open into the casing. Tip speed here largely sets the head the pump can develop.
The space formed between the two casing halves around the impeller, made up of the volute and the side spaces beside the shrouds.
The sharp edge where the volute wall meets the discharge throat. Its clearance from the vane tips is a design choice that balances efficiency against pressure pulsation and noise.
Each section of the volute receives the flow leaving the part of the impeller upstream of it, so the flow in the volute increases steadily towards the throat.
Liquid at outlet pressure in the side spaces leaks back to the eyes through the wear-ring clearances. This flow is pumped again, so it reduces efficiency, and it increases as the rings wear.

scene.label: Stage 3: discharge from the impeller periphery

workingStages.title: Volute action
workingStages.narration: The volute is a spiral passage whose cross-sectional area grows steadily from the tongue towards the discharge throat. Because each section collects the flow leaving the impeller upstream of it, the growing area keeps the velocity in the volute reasonably uniform at the design flow. Beyond the throat, the passage widens further into the diffusing discharge section, so the liquid slows down and part of its velocity energy is converted into pressure energy. This conversion is never complete, and some energy is lost to friction and turbulence. Away from the design flow, the pressure around the impeller becomes uneven and produces a radial hydraulic load on the rotor. A double-volute casing, available as a variant in this model, uses a splitter rib to reduce that load, although it does not remove it entirely.
keyPoints: The volute area increases around the impeller to collect the flow at a controlled velocity.
The widening discharge section converts part of the velocity energy into pressure energy.
Pressure around the impeller is most uniform near the design flow; off-design operation creates radial load.
A double volute reduces the net radial load but does not eliminate it.

explains.text: Kinetic energy per unit weight of liquid, the velocity head v^2 / (2 * g). Liquid leaving the impeller carries a large share of its energy in this form.
Slowing the flow in a gradually widening passage converts velocity head into pressure head. Too rapid an expansion causes flow separation and losses.
The volute area grows roughly in proportion to the flow it has collected, so the velocity in the volute stays nearly constant around the impeller at the design flow.
Off the design flow, the pressure around a single volute is not uniform, giving a net radial force on the impeller that the shaft and bearings must carry. It is commonly smallest near BEP.
A splitter rib divides the volute into two passages about 180 degrees apart, so that the radial forces from the two halves largely oppose each other.

scene.label: Stage 4: volute action and pressure recovery

workingStages.title: Discharge
workingStages.narration: The liquid leaves through the discharge nozzle on the lower casing half, on the opposite side from the suction nozzle. It now carries the energy added by the pump, expressed as total head: the difference in total energy between the discharge and suction measuring points, including pressure, velocity and elevation terms. The discharge pressure is read at a tapping close to the discharge nozzle and the suction pressure at a tapping near the suction flange. From here the discharge pipe, usually fitted with a check valve and an isolating valve, carries the flow into the system. The operating point is where the pump curve meets the system curve, so the same pump can deliver different flows in different systems, or in the same system as valves open and close.
keyPoints: The discharge nozzle is on the lower casing half, opposite the suction nozzle.
Pump total head is the difference in total energy between the discharge and suction measuring points.
The flow delivered is set by the intersection of the pump curve and the system curve.
A check valve and an isolating valve are normally installed in the discharge line.

explains.text: The pressure at the pump outlet, measured at a tapping near the discharge nozzle and corrected to the reference datum.
H = (p_d - p_s) / (rho * g) + (v_d^2 - v_s^2) / (2 * g) + (z_d - z_s). It is the energy added per unit weight of liquid, expressed as a height of liquid.
Connections near the suction and discharge flanges used for gauges or transmitters. Test standards specify how they are located and how readings are corrected.
The head the system needs at each flow: static head plus friction and other losses, which rise roughly with the square of flow.
The flow and head at which the pump curve and the system curve intersect. It moves if the speed, impeller diameter or system resistance changes.

thrustLesson.intro: Axial thrust is the net force acting along the shaft axis on the rotating assembly. On a single-suction impeller it can be large, because the pressures on the two sides of the impeller act on unequal areas. A double-suction impeller is built as two mirror-image halves, so most of these forces oppose each other and largely cancel. This lesson explains how that balance works, why it is never perfect, and how the bearings deal with what remains.

points.title: Why double-suction impellers are used
points.body: Double-suction impellers are chosen mainly for large flows. Sharing the flow between two eyes means each eye handles about half of it, which tends to reduce the NPSH required for a given flow and speed and avoids an excessively large single eye. The symmetrical construction also gives nominal axial balance, and the between-bearings rotor supports the wide impeller stiffly. Double suction does not double the head; head depends mainly on impeller diameter and speed.

points.title: How fluid enters from both sides
points.body: The suction passage in the lower casing divides the incoming flow into two side chambers. Each chamber turns the liquid around the shaft and into one eye, so liquid enters the impeller from the drive-end side and the non-drive-end side at the same time, in opposite axial directions. The two streams pass through the two halves of the impeller in parallel and leave together at the common periphery into a single volute.

points.title: How hydraulic forces are distributed
points.body: The impeller is surrounded by liquid at different pressures. The eyes are at roughly suction pressure, while the side spaces between the outer faces of the shrouds and the casing walls contain liquid close to impeller outlet pressure, falling towards the wear rings because the liquid in these spaces rotates. Each shroud therefore carries an axial pressure force acting over the area between the periphery and the wear ring, while the eye area sees low pressure. The turning of the incoming flow from axial to radial adds a smaller momentum force. On a single-suction impeller these forces act on unequal areas and do not cancel.

points.title: How symmetrical pressure distribution helps balance axial thrust
points.body: In a double-suction impeller, the shroud, wear ring and eye on one side mirror those on the other. The pressure force on the NDE shroud is opposed by a nominally equal force on the DE shroud, and the inlet momentum forces at the two eyes also oppose each other. The shaft passes out through both ends of the casing, typically with similar seal chamber pressures at each end, so there is no large unbalanced shaft-area force of the kind found on overhung designs. The nominal net thrust is therefore small, without the balance holes or back vanes a single-suction impeller often needs.

points.title: Why actual operating conditions may create residual axial thrust
points.body: Perfect balance exists only on paper. Casting and machining tolerances make the two halves slightly different, the impeller may not be exactly centred in the volute, the approach flow may favour one eye, for example because of an elbow in the plane of the shaft, and away from BEP recirculation may develop differently on each side. Wear changes the balance over time. The resulting residual thrust is usually small compared with a single-suction impeller, but its magnitude and even its direction can change with flow, speed and condition, including transients at start-up and shut-down.

points.title: How wear-ring clearances influence pressure distribution
points.body: Liquid leaks from each side space, through the wear-ring clearance, back to the eye. This leakage, and the swirl it carries inwards, affects how the pressure in the side space falls with radius. When the two clearances are equal, the side-space pressure distributions stay similar and the shroud forces still oppose each other. If one ring wears more than the other, the leakage and pressure distribution on that side change, the shroud forces no longer match, and residual thrust increases. Measuring both clearances at each overhaul, and renewing rings as the OEM manual requires, helps keep the rotor balanced.

points.title: How bearing arrangements support the rotor
points.body: The rotor is supported at both ends. In the arrangement modelled, the drive-end bearing is a floating radial ball bearing: it carries radial load, but its outer ring can slide axially in the housing so that thermal expansion of the shaft does not load the bearings. The non-drive-end bearing is the locating bearing, a back-to-back pair of angular-contact ball bearings clamped in its housing; it carries radial load plus the residual axial thrust in either direction and fixes the axial position of the impeller in the volute. The two bearings therefore differ in type, fit and function. Some designs locate at the drive end instead, and large pumps may use sleeve bearings with a separate thrust bearing.

points.title: Why thrust-bearing selection is important
points.body: Because residual thrust is never zero and can reverse, the locating bearing must be selected for the worst credible combination of loads, not only for the nominal balanced condition. Selection considers thrust magnitude and direction across the operating range, wear-ring wear, transients, speed, lubrication, temperature and required life. Paired angular-contact bearings suit higher or reversing thrust, while a deep-groove ball bearing may be adequate where thrust is low. Some purchasing specifications, such as API 610 for petroleum and natural gas service, add their own thrust-bearing requirements. Bearing type, arrangement and preload must always follow the OEM design.

singleSuction: Liquid enters through one eye, on one side of the impeller.
Pressure forces on the front and back shrouds act on unequal areas, so a significant net axial thrust develops, typically towards the suction side for a closed impeller without balancing features.
Thrust is commonly reduced with balance holes, back vanes or a back wear ring, and the remainder is carried by a thrust bearing.
Balancing features reduce thrust at the cost of extra leakage or power loss.
Common in overhung designs, where the impeller is cantilevered from one bearing housing.
doubleSuction: Liquid enters through two eyes, one on each side, in opposite axial directions.
Mirror-image shrouds, wear rings and eyes make the axial pressure forces nominally equal and opposite.
Axial balance comes from the symmetry itself, so balance holes or back vanes are not needed in the basic design.
A residual axial thrust always remains and is carried by the locating bearing.
Normally used with a between-bearings rotor that supports the impeller on both sides.

residualFactors: Casting and machining tolerances that make the two impeller halves or casing passages slightly different.
Impeller not centred axially in the volute, for example through incorrect setting of the sleeve nuts.
Unequal wear-ring clearances, from manufacture or uneven wear in service.
Unequal flow to the two eyes caused by the suction piping, such as an elbow in the plane of the shaft close to the suction nozzle.
Operation away from BEP, where recirculation at the eyes and impeller outlet may develop differently on each side.
Cavitation affecting one eye more than the other.
Deposits, erosion, corrosion or damage on one side of the impeller.
Transient conditions at start-up, shut-down and during rapid changes in flow.
Differences between the two seal chamber pressures, where the design allows them.
thrustLesson.caution: This is a conceptual comparison. Actual axial forces depend on the specific impeller and casing design, clearances, the operating point and the installation, and a double-suction impeller does not eliminate axial thrust. Thrust values and bearing selection must come from the manufacturer's design data, not from this illustration.

hydraulicParameters.name: Flow rate
hydraulicParameters.units: m^3/s (also m^3/h or L/s in practice)
hydraulicParameters.definition: The volume of liquid delivered by the pump per unit time, at the pumping temperature.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Usually measured with a flowmeter in the discharge line, installed with the straight upstream and downstream lengths its type requires. Leakage through wear rings is recirculated inside the pump and is not part of the delivered flow. In a double-suction pump, Q is the total flow; each eye handles a share of it, ideally half.

hydraulicParameters.name: Total dynamic head (pump total head)
hydraulicParameters.definition: The energy added by the pump per unit weight of liquid: the difference in total head between the discharge and suction measuring points.
hydraulicParameters.notes: 'Total dynamic head' is common North American usage; test standards such as ISO 9906 and ANSI/HI 14.6 use pump total head. Pressures are read at tappings near the flanges and referred to a datum, with gauge elevations and the velocity heads included. Because head is expressed in metres of the pumped liquid, a pump develops about the same head on any low-viscosity liquid, although the pressure rise varies with density.

hydraulicParameters.name: Suction pressure
hydraulicParameters.units: Pa (commonly kPa or bar), gauge or absolute
hydraulicParameters.definition: The static pressure at the pump inlet, measured at the suction tapping near the suction flange.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Always state whether the value is gauge or absolute; NPSH calculations need absolute pressure. On a suction lift it is below atmospheric pressure. Readings should be corrected to the reference datum, and the tapping should be in a region of steady, uniform flow.

hydraulicParameters.name: Discharge pressure
hydraulicParameters.units: Pa (commonly kPa or bar), usually gauge
hydraulicParameters.definition: The static pressure at the pump outlet, measured at the discharge tapping near the discharge nozzle.
hydraulicParameters.notes: The maximum discharge pressure, which occurs near shut-off on a curve rising to shut-off, together with the maximum suction pressure, sets the pressure rating needed for the casing, discharge piping and valves. Correct the reading for gauge elevation when calculating head.

hydraulicParameters.name: Differential head
hydraulicParameters.definition: The head corresponding to the static pressure difference between the discharge and suction tappings.
hydraulicParameters.notes: On many datasheets 'differential head' is used to mean the pump total head. Strictly, the pressure-difference term alone omits the velocity head and elevation differences; these are often small, but they matter where the suction nozzle is larger than the discharge nozzle, as is usual on split case pumps.

hydraulicParameters.name: Pump speed
hydraulicParameters.definition: The rotational speed of the pump shaft.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Induction motors run slightly below synchronous speed because of slip, so the actual speed should be measured, for example with a tachometer, when testing. Flow, head and power all change with speed according to the affinity laws.

hydraulicParameters.name: Hydraulic power
hydraulicParameters.definition: The power transferred to the liquid by the pump, also called water power or pump power output.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Uses the delivered flow and the pump total head at the same operating point. It is always less than the shaft power; the difference is the pump's internal losses.

hydraulicParameters.name: Shaft power
hydraulicParameters.definition: The mechanical power delivered to the pump shaft by the driver, also called brake power or power input to the pump.
hydraulicParameters.formula: P_shaft = P_h / eta_p = rho * g * Q * H / eta_p = T * omega
hydraulicParameters.notes: Measured directly with a torque meter, or estimated from motor input power and motor efficiency. Used for sizing the motor, with an allowance across the operating range; for a typical radial-flow pump it rises with flow towards runout.

hydraulicParameters.name: Motor input power
hydraulicParameters.definition: The electrical power drawn by the motor from the supply.
hydraulicParameters.formula: P_electrical = P_shaft / eta_motor; for a balanced three-phase supply P_electrical = sqrt(3) * V_L * I_L * cos(phi)
hydraulicParameters.notes: Measured with a power analyser at the motor terminals. If a variable frequency drive is fitted, its losses come on top, and the drive input differs from the motor input. Overall (wire-to-water) efficiency is P_h / P_electrical.

hydraulicParameters.name: Pump efficiency
hydraulicParameters.definition: The ratio of hydraulic power output to shaft power input.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Losses include hydraulic losses (friction, turbulence, incidence), volumetric losses (leakage through wear rings) and mechanical losses (bearings, seals, disc friction on the shrouds). Efficiency is highest at the best efficiency point and falls on either side; it also falls as wear-ring clearances open.

hydraulicParameters.name: Net positive suction head available
hydraulicParameters.definition: The absolute total head at the pump suction, above the vapour pressure head of the liquid, referred to the pump datum. It is a property of the system.
hydraulicParameters.formula: NPSHa = (p_s,abs - p_v) / (rho * g) + v_s^2 / (2 * g), or from the supply: NPSHa = (p_a - p_v) / (rho * g) + z_s - h_fs
hydraulicParameters.notes: For a horizontal pump the datum is commonly the impeller (shaft) centreline. NPSHa falls as flow rises (more suction loss), as the liquid temperature rises (higher vapour pressure), as the supply level falls and at higher altitude. It must exceed NPSHr at every operating flow with a suitable margin.

hydraulicParameters.name: Net positive suction head required
hydraulicParameters.definition: The NPSH the pump needs at a given flow and speed, determined by test. It is a property of the pump.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Commonly defined as NPSH3: the NPSH at which the total head at a given flow has fallen by 3% because of cavitation, following the conventions of ISO 9906 and ANSI/HI 14.6. Cavitation is already present at NPSH3 and begins at a higher NPSH, so a margin of NPSHa over NPSHr is needed, chosen from guidance such as ANSI/HI 9.6.1 and the manufacturer. NPSHr usually rises steeply towards runout and may also rise at low flow.

hydraulicParameters.name: Axial thrust
hydraulicParameters.definition: The net force acting along the shaft axis on the rotating assembly, from pressure forces on the impeller and rotor surfaces and from the change of momentum of the flow.
hydraulicParameters.formula: F_a = (sum of axial pressure forces on all rotor surfaces) + (inlet momentum forces), taken with sign (conceptual)
hydraulicParameters.notes: On a double-suction impeller the forces on the two halves are nominally equal and opposite, so the nominal net thrust is small, but a residual thrust always remains. It can change in magnitude and direction with flow, wear-ring wear, impeller centring, suction flow distribution and transients, and is carried by the locating bearing. Values come from the manufacturer's design calculations.

hydraulicParameters.name: Radial hydraulic load
hydraulicParameters.definition: The net radial force on the impeller caused by non-uniform pressure around its periphery.
hydraulicParameters.formula: F_r = K_r * rho * g * H * D2 * b2 (empirical form; K_r is a coefficient from design data)
hydraulicParameters.notes: In a single volute casing it is commonly smallest near BEP and increases towards shut-off and runout. K_r depends on the casing type, specific speed and the ratio Q / Q_BEP, and D2 and b2 are the impeller outlet diameter and width (including shrouds in some conventions). A double volute reduces the net radial load. It is carried by both bearings and causes shaft deflection at the wear rings and seals.

hydraulicParameters.name: Specific speed
hydraulicParameters.units: Dimensional index; value depends on the units used (here rpm, m^3/s, m)
hydraulicParameters.definition: An index of impeller type, calculated at the best efficiency point at maximum impeller diameter, that relates speed, flow and head.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Low values indicate radial-flow impellers, higher values mixed-flow and then axial-flow designs. For double-suction impellers Q is commonly taken as the flow per eye (Q / 2), but some sources use the total flow, so always state the convention. In US units (rpm, US gpm, ft) values are about 51.6 times the metric values with Q in m^3/s. A related index, suction specific speed, uses NPSHr in place of H and the flow per eye.

hydraulicParameters.name: Best efficiency point
hydraulicParameters.units: Flow in m^3/s or m^3/h; head in m
hydraulicParameters.definition: The point on the head-flow curve, for a given speed and impeller diameter, at which the pump efficiency is at its maximum.
hydraulicParameters.notes: Hydraulic loads, vibration and recirculation are generally lowest near BEP, so pumps are selected to run within a preferred operating region around it. ANSI/HI 9.6.3 describes preferred and allowable operating regions; the actual limits for a given pump come from the manufacturer. BEP moves with speed according to the affinity laws.

hydraulicParameters.name: Shut-off head
hydraulicParameters.definition: The head developed by the pump at zero flow, with the discharge valve closed.
hydraulicParameters.notes: For a curve rising continuously to shut-off it is the highest head the pump develops and is used, with the maximum suction pressure, to check pressure ratings of the casing, piping and valves. Running at or near shut-off is acceptable only briefly, because the absorbed power heats the trapped liquid and hydraulic loads are high; minimum flow limits come from the manufacturer. Some designs have a curve that droops towards shut-off, with peak head at a small flow instead.

formulas.title: Hydraulic power

variables.meaning: Density of the liquid at pumping temperature

formulas.explanation: Head is energy per unit weight of liquid, and rho * g * Q is the weight of liquid delivered per second, so their product is the power transferred to the liquid. Divide the result in watts by 1000 to obtain kW. Flow must be in m^3/s; a flow in m^3/h must first be divided by 3600.
assumptions: Steady flow at a single operating point.
Q and H are measured at the same operating point.
The liquid is effectively incompressible.
limitations: Gives the useful power output only; it says nothing about the losses inside the pump.
For viscous liquids, density and head must be those actually achieved with that liquid, not water-test values.

formulas.title: Shaft power
formulas.formula: P_shaft = rho * g * Q * H / eta_p

variables.meaning: Power input to the pump shaft
Pump efficiency at that operating point (decimal)

formulas.explanation: The shaft must supply the hydraulic power plus all the pump's losses, so the hydraulic power is divided by the pump efficiency. Because eta_p is less than 1, shaft power is always greater than hydraulic power. The result is used to size the driver and check the shaft and coupling.
assumptions: The efficiency used is the pump efficiency at the same flow, head and speed.
Steady operation with the liquid properties stated.
limitations: Efficiency varies across the curve, so the shaft power at one point cannot be scaled to others without the efficiency at those points.
The driver should be sized for the highest power over the intended operating range, not only at the duty point.

formulas.title: Electrical (motor input) power

variables.meaning: Electrical power drawn by the motor
Shaft power delivered to the pump

formulas.explanation: The motor converts electrical power to mechanical power with its own losses, so its input is the shaft power divided by the motor efficiency. With direct coupling, the overall (wire-to-water) efficiency is eta_p * eta_motor, and P_electrical = P_h / (eta_p * eta_motor).
assumptions: The motor drives the pump directly through a coupling whose losses are negligible.
The motor efficiency used is the value at the actual load.
limitations: Motor efficiency changes with load, so a single nameplate value is approximate at part load.
Variable frequency drives, gearboxes or belts add losses that must be included separately.

formulas.title: Shaft torque
formulas.explanation: Power equals torque times angular speed, P = T * omega, with omega = 2 * pi * N / 60. Rearranging with P in kW gives T = 1000 * P * 60 / (2 * pi * N) = (60000 / (2 * pi)) * P / N, and 60000 / (2 * pi) = 9549.3, which is rounded to 9550. The formula is therefore a unit-converting form of T = P / omega.
assumptions: P is in kW and N in rpm; other units need a different constant.
Steady running torque at constant speed.
limitations: Gives the steady torque only; starting and transient torques can be higher.
Use shaft power, not hydraulic power, when checking shafts, keys and couplings.

formulas.title: Pump efficiency
formulas.explanation: Efficiency compares the useful power given to the liquid with the power put into the shaft. The shortfall is made up of hydraulic losses, volumetric (leakage) losses and mechanical losses. Overall efficiency, P_h / P_electrical, also includes the motor losses.
assumptions: Both powers are measured at the same operating point and in the same units.
Flow, head and power are measured to a recognised test method.
limitations: A single value applies only to one operating point; efficiency varies along the curve.
Site measurements have larger uncertainty than test-bed results to ISO 9906 or ANSI/HI 14.6.

formulas.title: Affinity laws (speed change)

variables.meaning: Flow at the original and new speed (corresponding points)
Head at the original and new speed
Shaft power at the original and new speed

formulas.explanation: For the same pump with an unchanged impeller diameter, operating at geometrically similar (corresponding) points, flow scales with speed, head with speed squared and power with speed cubed. The laws move a point on the pump curve to a new point on the curve at the new speed; the actual operating point is then where that new curve meets the system curve.
assumptions: Geometrically and kinematically similar operation (corresponding points).
Unchanged impeller diameter.
Pump efficiency is assumed constant between the two corresponding points.
limitations: Efficiency is not exactly constant, especially for large speed changes, so results are estimates.
In systems with significant static head the operating point does not follow the affinity parabola, and flow can fall much more than the speed ratio suggests.
Viscosity effects and Reynolds number changes reduce accuracy, particularly at low speed or with viscous liquids.
NPSHr does not follow a simple law reliably; scaling it with speed squared is only a rough guide.

formulas.title: Net positive suction head available

variables.meaning: NPSH available at the pump datum
Absolute pressure on the liquid surface of the supply (atmospheric for an open tank)
Vapour pressure of the liquid at pumping temperature (absolute)
Height of the liquid surface above the pump datum (negative for a suction lift)
Friction and fitting losses in the suction line at the flow considered

formulas.explanation: NPSHa is the margin of absolute total head at the pump inlet above the vapour pressure head. From the supply side it is the surface pressure head, plus the static height of the liquid above the datum, minus the suction losses and the vapour pressure head. From a suction gauge reading it is NPSHa = (p_s,abs - p_v) / (rho * g) + v_s^2 / (2 * g), where the gauge reading is converted to absolute pressure and corrected to the datum.
assumptions: All pressures are absolute.
The datum is the pump reference level, commonly the impeller centreline for a horizontal pump.
The velocity of the supply surface is negligible.
limitations: Valid only at the flow for which h_fs was calculated; NPSHa falls as flow rises.
Sensitive to temperature through vapour pressure, and to altitude and supply level.
Does not account for dissolved or entrained gas, which can cause problems even when NPSHa exceeds NPSHr.

formulas.title: Specific speed

variables.meaning: Flow at BEP; for double suction commonly the flow per eye (Q / 2)
Head at BEP, per stage, at maximum impeller diameter

formulas.explanation: Specific speed characterises the shape of an impeller and its typical performance: low values for narrow radial-flow impellers, higher values for mixed-flow and axial-flow designs. In this module the metric convention with N in rpm, Q in m^3/s and H in m is used, with Q taken per eye for double-suction impellers. The same pump gives a value about sqrt(2) times larger if the total flow is used, and about 51.6 times larger in US units (rpm, US gpm, ft).
assumptions: Evaluated at the best efficiency point.
Maximum impeller diameter, single stage (head per stage for multistage pumps).
Units and flow convention (per eye or total) are stated.
limitations: The numerical value is meaningless without its units and flow convention.
It is an index for classification and comparison, not a performance prediction for a particular pump.

formulas.title: Flow per eye in a double-suction impeller
formulas.explanation: With perfectly symmetrical casing passages, a uniform approach flow and identical impeller halves, each eye receives half of the total flow. This ideal value is used for design, for specific speed and suction specific speed calculations, and for estimating eye velocities. In practice the split can differ: an elbow in the plane of the shaft near the suction nozzle, swirl or a disturbed velocity profile, casting differences, uneven wear-ring leakage and off-design recirculation can all send more flow to one eye than the other.
assumptions: Symmetrical casing passages and impeller halves.
Uniform velocity profile at the suction nozzle.
Equal wear-ring clearances and leakage on both sides.
limitations: Real installations do not guarantee an equal split; suction piping layout has a strong influence.
An unequal split causes residual axial thrust and can make one eye cavitate before the other.
Wear-ring leakage adds to the flow passing through each eye, so the eye flow is slightly more than Q / 2 even when the split is equal.
